Go-kit (Oregon OEM checklist) Medications and medical devices · glasses · food and plenty of water · important documents · phone chargers · battery AM/FM radio · first-aid kit · flashlight · N95 masks · long sleeves, long pants, sturdy shoes, hat. Plan two routes out. Move livestock early.

Around the house (defensible space) - First 5 ft around the house (🖼️ the three zones): nothing that burns. Firewood and lumber 30 ft away (OSFM, p. 13; the ODF Josephine County handout says at least 20 ft). - Within 100 ft: grass mowed to 4 in or less, 10 ft between tree crowns, limbs 10 ft from the chimney, no "ladder fuels" (brush under trees — 🖼️ drawing). - Clean roofs and gutters; cover vents with 1/8-inch metal mesh (🖼️ how embers get in); clear around propane tanks; keep the driveway clear enough for a fire engine.

Smoke Make one cleaner-air room (windows shut, AC on recirculate). A DIY air cleaner = a box fan (made 2012 or later, UL/ETL label) + a MERV-13 furnace filter. Unplug it when you leave the house. Use N95 masks outdoors. Details: the Wildfire\ folder (Ready-Set-Go guide, OSFM defensible-space guide, OSU fire-resistant plants, EPA/OHA smoke sheets). Fire news: swofire.com (ODF Southwest Oregon). 📚 Go deeper: Evacuation levels flyer and checklist — print for the fridge; ODF Josephine County handout — defensible space on one page; EPA Wildfire Smoke Guide, p. 61 — setting up a cleaner-air room; Wildfire prep for pets and livestock.

🌎 Earthquake (Cascadia) and tsunami - A Cascadia magnitude-9 quake would shake for 4–6 minutes, with aftershocks for months (CREW scenario, p. 10). Drop, Cover, Hold On. - Expect landslides on mountain roads and damage to bridges. Coast-to-inland routes like US-199 are exactly the kind expected to be cut, so the valley may be isolated for a long time. - State estimates for inland western Oregon: power out 1–3 months, water/sewer 1 month to 1 year, main highways 6–12 months to partly reopen, fuel shortages (Oregon's fuel hub is near Portland) (Oregon Resilience Plan, p. 6). - Plan to be on your own for at least 2 weeks — longer in rural areas. - At the coast (Brookings, Gold Beach, Crescent City): if you feel a long quake, walk to high ground immediately. The first waves can arrive in 15–30 minutes; surges continue 12+ hours and the first is not the largest. Details: Earthquake-Tsunami\ (Living on Shaky Ground, 2 Weeks Ready toolkit, Cascadia scenario, tsunami evacuation maps for Brookings-Harbor, Gold Beach, Crescent City, Smith River). Bolting the house to its foundation, bracing cripple walls, chimneys, roof and window repair, and building with logs or earth: Shelter, Building & Repair. ☢️ Nuclear fallout - Get inside, stay inside, stay tuned. Fallout is dust; put mass between you and the roof and outside walls (🖼️ drawing). It loses 90% of its strength in 7 hours and 99% in 2 days (FEMA H-20, p. 8). - A one-story wood house with no basement is poor shelter. Know now where you'd go: a basement or masonry building nearby, a shielded crawl space, or a trench shelter. - Potassium iodide (KI) protects only the thyroid, from radioactive iodine — adults 130 mg, children less (FDA, p. 9). - Everything else — shielding, how long to stay in, decontamination, food, water, livestock, homemade fallout meter: Nuclear Fallout Guide and Nuclear-Radiation\. 📚 Go deeper: CDC: Get Inside, Stay Inside, Stay Tuned — where to shelter, on one page; Nuclear War Survival Skills — expedient shelters and fallout meters.

🦌 Hunting and 🎣 Fishing While seasons and tags are still enforced, the 2026 rule booklets are in Hunting\ and Fishing\ (big game, fishing) (the 2027 big game and fishing booklets come out around December 2026 — see Keeping this current). With or without rules, the units, waters and seasons below tell you where game and fish are, and when — and leaving breeding animals and spawning runs alone is what keeps them there next year. Hunting units: US-199 is the line. West of the highway (Illinois River canyon, Kalmiopsis) is Chetco Unit 27 (82% public land). East of it (Lake Selmac, Takilma, Oregon Caves, Williams) is Applegate Unit 28 (57% public land). In Cave Junction, Kerby, Selma and O'Brien, which side of the highway you're on decides the unit. North of the Rogue at Grants Pass is Evans Creek Unit 29. 2026 general seasons, for orientation (check the current booklet): western Oregon buck rifle Oct 3–Nov 6 · archery deer & elk Aug 29–Sep 27 · Unit 28 coast elk rifle Nov 14–17 and Nov 21–27 (Unit 27 is controlled hunts only) · black bear Aug 1–Dec 31 · cougar all year (quotas) — bear and cougar must be checked in at ODFW within 10 days · grouse and quail Sep 1–Jan 31 · fall turkey Sep 1–Jan 31 · spring turkey Apr 15–May 31. and Fishing\How-To (knots, rigs, casting, cleaning and filleting). Game meat safety: - Cook bear and other wild game to 165 °F inside. Freezing, curing, smoking or drying does not reliably kill the trichinella worms in wild game. - Wear gloves when cleaning rabbits and rodents (tularemia). - Shot with lead? Trim generously around the bullet path: fast-expanding lead bullets scatter fragments 5–14 in from the wound, sometimes 18 in (Minnesota DNR X-ray study, p. 6; the older 4-in rule in OSU PNW 517, p. 1 is too small). Give lead-shot meat to adults, not children or pregnant women (rule of thumb). - Don't bring deer or elk brain or spine parts back into Oregon from another state (chronic wasting disease rule). 🪤 Trapping How-to: start with the national Trapper Education Manual and the NY trapper manual (trap types, baits, water and land sets, snares, running a trapline, fur handling), then the species guides (beaver, coyote, raccoon, bobcat, gray fox). For improvised traps with no store-bought gear, see the 1907 Deadfalls and Snares (illustrated) and the snare and deadfall chapters of the Army survival manuals (Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals; FM 21-76, p. 95). Hides and furs: USDA Home Tanning of Leather and Small Fur Skins. - Check traps at least daily — animals spoil, suffer, or get taken by other predators. - Beaver, raccoon, muskrat and rabbits are the most dependable meat from traps here; wear gloves for rabbits and rodents (tularemia), and cook all wild meat thoroughly. - Don't catch your own dogs: the AFWA dog-friendly guides show sets that avoid pets. While Oregon's rules are still enforced (details in the 2026–2028 furbearer booklet in Trapping\): - License: trapping needs an Oregon Furtaker's License — that includes "unprotected" animals like coyote, skunk, opossum and porcupine. A landowner can get a free license for land they own and live on (register the land with ODFW first). - Trapper education (free, online at hunter-ed.com/oregon/trapper) is required if you were born after June 30, 1968 or are trapping in Oregon for the first time — except on your own or family land, or when controlling damage to

if you were born after June 30, 1968 or are trapping in Oregon for the first time — except on your own or family land, or when controlling damage to livestock or crops. - Every trap and snare must carry your ODFW brand number. Check traps at least every 48 hours. - Banned: toothed jaws; oversized footholds and land killing traps (size limits are in the booklet); game meat as bait; visible bait within 15 ft of a foothold set for carnivores. In the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest west of I-5 (that includes the Illinois Valley), no traps or snares hung in trees. On public land, stay 50 ft from trails and 300 ft from trailheads, campgrounds and picnic areas. - 2026–27 seasons: bobcat Dec 1–Feb 28 (needs a record card) · gray fox Oct 15–Feb 28 · raccoon, river otter and beaver Nov 15–Mar 15 · mink and muskrat Nov 15–Mar 31 · marten closed west of I-5 · fisher and ringtail closed all year. - Wolves are federally endangered here. Use coyote traps no bigger than #3 and snares with breakaways. A wolf track is about 5 in long; a coyote's is about 2.5 in (furbearer booklet, p. 16; 🖼️ side by side). Report any wolf caught by accident right away: ODFW, US Fish & Wildlife (503) 231-6179, or OSP (541) 664-4600. 📚 Go deeper: Furbearer booklet, p.

Record low: −6 °F (1972). - About 61 in of precipitation a year, but only 5–7 in falls April–September, so summer gardens need irrigation (see the drip and water-wise guides). - Serpentine soils (common here — greenish rock, sparse "barrens"; photos): very high magnesium, low calcium, plus nickel and chromium, and they can contain natural asbestos. - Grow vegetables in raised beds with imported soil and lots of compost. - Wet the soil before digging, don't work it when it's dusty or windy, keep it mulched 3–6 in, and take shoes off indoors. - Get a soil test before adding amendments (don't add gypsum by default). - Some local clay

⚡ Off-grid power and creek hydro Start with the US Navy NEETS modules (electricity basics, AC, circuit protection, wiring, generators) in Off-Grid-Power\Electrical-Basics, then the solar guides, then the micro-hydro handbooks in Off-Grid-Power\Micro-Hydro. Generators - Never run one indoors, in a garage, crawlspace or shed, even with doors open. Carbon monoxide kills in minutes. Keep it outdoors, away from windows and vents, and use battery-powered CO alarms. - Never plug a generator into a wall outlet ("backfeeding"). It sends power back through the lines and can kill anyone working on them. Wire into the house only through a transfer switch. - Store fuel outside living areas, in proper cans. Let the engine cool before refueling. - Engine won't start, carburetor gummed up, generator makes no power? See the Engines, Motors and Generators guide — it also covers chainsaws, rewinding motors, and turning motors and car alternators into generators. - Fuel: how long gas and diesel keep, rescuing stale or watery fuel, and getting fuel out of station tanks, drums and vehicles with no power: Fuel Guide. - EMP or solar storm: protecting solar gear, inverters and spares, and Faraday containers: EMP Guide. Sizing a solar system (Sandia and IEA guides) - Panel size (kW) ≈ (kWh you use per day ÷ peak sun hours) × 1.2. - Lead-acid batteries: count on only 40% of the rated capacity. At our latitude, plan

Panel size (kW) ≈ (kWh you use per day ÷ peak sun hours) × 1.2. - Lead-acid batteries: count on only 40% of the rated capacity. At our latitude, plan 7–9 days of storage for a solar-only system, and vent battery rooms at the top (hydrogen rises). - System voltage: 12 V under 1 kWh/day, 24 V for 1–4 kWh/day, 48 V above that. Low voltage over long wires needs very heavy wire. Sizing creek hydro (NRCan, NCAT) - Real output (watts) ≈ flow (liters/second) × drop (meters) × 9.8 × 0.5. In US units: kW ≈ flow (cubic ft/min) × drop (ft) ÷ 709 × 0.5. Example: 50 gallons/minute falling 100 ft ≈ 470 W around the clock ≈ 11 kWh a day, more than solar gives most of the year here. - Design for late-summer low flow (the flow you have 95% of the time). Size the pipe so friction eats less than 10% of the drop. Screen the intake and leave water in the creek. - A hydraulic ram pump (Clemson plans) lifts creek water uphill with no fuel or power. Firewood (OSU, heat per cord when dry): Oregon white oak and madrone ≈ 30 million BTU, Douglas-fir ≈ 21, alder ≈ 18, ponderosa pine ≈ 17. Each 1% of extra moisture costs about 1% of the heat: split and stack wood through one dry summer (two is better) and keep it covered through the rains. A good stove is 60–80% efficient; an open fireplace 10–15%. Carbon monoxide kills. Never run a generator, grill, charcoal, camp stove or a wood-gas unit indoors, in a garage or near windows. CO feels like flu without a fever. A battery CO alarm near the bedrooms is cheap insurance. A wood-gas generator keeps making CO-rich gas for ~20 minutes after the engine stops. Lye (for soap and biodiesel): wear gloves and goggles, keep children away, add lye to cold water a little at a time (never water to lye), never use aluminum pots. 📱💻 Start the Library on Any Device This library works on almost anything: a Windows laptop, a Mac, a Linux computer or Raspberry Pi, an Android tablet or phone, even an old computer. Nothing needs the internet, and nothing you search for ever leaves your device. There are two ways to use it: 1. Just open the files. Open START-HERE.html in any web browser. Every guide and book on the drive opens like a web page or PDF. Works on every device, no setup at all. 2. The Library Assistant (recommended). One search box for everything on the drive (every book, guide and encyclopedia) plus an offline AI that writes a short answer from what it finds, with numbered links to the exact pages. It runs on the device itself. ### ⚠️ Please remember - The AI can be wrong. Always check the sources it links to, especially for medicine, electricity, chemicals or food safety. - Keep the window (or the Termux app) open while you use the assistant. Closing it stops it. - Nothing is sent anywhere. You can turn off Wi-Fi and it works the same.

This is the easiest way to serve a whole household, or a whole street, from one laptop or tablet. On the device with the library (laptop, Android tablet or Raspberry Pi): 1. Turn it on, connect the sharing device and the

You don't need the internet, just a local Wi-Fi network: - An Android phone's hotspot works with mobile data turned off. Turn it on, connect the sharing device and the other phones to it. - A small travel Wi-Fi router (powered from USB) is the most reliable: plug it in and everyone joins its network. Good to keep in the emergency kit. - A Raspberry Pi or Linux laptop can make its own Wi-Fi network. - iPhone hotspots usually need a working phone plan, so don't count on them. Good to know: - Anyone on that Wi-Fi can read the library, but only the sharing device can change settings or turn sharing off. Use a password on the hotspot or router. - Search is instant for everyone. If several people ask the AI at once, it answers them one at a time. - A laptop sharing all evening uses about as much power as a bright light bulb; keep it plugged in or on solar. - To stop, tap Stop sharing in Settings, or close the library.

💾 Get the Whole Library on a USB Drive This website holds the guides and tools. The full library also has every book, all of Wikipedia with pictures, maps you can use with no signal, and an AI that runs with no internet. It is too big for a website, so you put it on a USB drive, external hard drive or SD card while you still have internet. After that it works with the power and phones out. You don't need to type any commands. You download a small kit (about 85 MB), double-click one file, and a page opens in your web browser where you pick the drive and press Start. ### ⚠️ Before you start - Do it now, while the internet works. The full download is large and takes hours. A library you meant to download does nothing for you in an outage. - Use a drive with nothing important on it, or plenty of free space. The installer only adds files; it never erases a drive. - Leave the computer plugged in and awake until the bar reaches 100%. If it stops (the internet drops, the laptop sleeps), just run it again and press Continue. It picks up where it left off.

📥 Step 1: Download the kit ⬇️ Download the installer kit (so-survival-kit.zip) It is one zip file, about 85 MB. It works on Windows, Mac and Linux computers. (Phones and tablets can't make the drive, but they can use one afterwards. See Start on any device.)

✅ Step 3: Pick the drive and press Start The installer page has three simple steps: 1. Pick the drive. Plug in the USB drive first. Each drive shows its name and how much free space it has. 🩹 Injuries & Illness When No Help Is Coming What to do when someone is hurt or sick and no ambulance, hospital or doctor is coming — from the first minutes through weeks of nursing. It follows the newest books on the drive: the US Army's 2026 first-aid manual (ATP 4-02.11), the Joint Trauma System (JTS) guidelines for care when evacuation is delayed, and WHO-ICRC Basic Emergency Care. Older books are used only where nothing has changed. The books are in Medical\Field-Care\ (Trauma-Bleeding, Wounds-Burns-Fractures, Nursing-Care, Dental, Childbirth-Newborn), Medical\Manuals-PDF, Medical\Where There Is No Doctor and Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals. Medicines and doses are in the companion guide, Medical — READ ME FIRST. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Make sure whatever hurt them can't hurt you — fire, a falling tree, a downed power line, traffic. Then check the person in order, bleeding first (ATP 4-02.11, p. 52). - Life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg: tourniquet FIRST. Heavy bleeding can kill in about 3 minutes (ATP, p. 62). Older books call a tourniquet a "last resort" — that is outdated. - Never cut, suck, ice or tie off a snakebite (JTS snakebite guideline, p. 27). - Never close a dirty or old wound. When in doubt, leave it open (JTS wound guideline, p. 10). - Heat stroke: cool them first, right now (Emergency War Surgery, p. 428). - Keep every

or old wound. When in doubt, leave it open (JTS wound guideline, p. 10). - Heat stroke: cool them first, right now (Emergency War Surgery, p. 428). - Keep every injured person warm and off the ground, even in summer — cold blood doesn't clot well (ATP, p. 103).

🚨 The first look: check in this order Fix each problem before moving on. The Army calls it MARCH; WHO uses the same idea as ABCDE (ATP, p. 53; WHO-ICRC, p. 49). | Letter | Check | Do | | M — Massive bleeding | Spurting or pooling blood | Tourniquet or packing (next section) | | A — Airway | Noisy, gurgling, unconscious | Clear the mouth; recovery position or jaw thrust (🖼️ ATP, p. 78) | | R — Respiration | Breathing? Hole in the chest? | Tape plastic over a chest wound; lift it if breathing gets worse (ATP, p. 94; 🖼️ chest seals, p. 88; Occlusive dressing) | | C — Circulation | Pale, confused, weak wrist pulse (🖼️ feeling it, WTND ch. 3, p. 4) | Treat for shock (🖼️ shock position, ATP p. 99) | | H — Hypothermia, Head | Cold, wet, knocked out | Insulate; watch the head | Then pain, antibiotics, wounds and splints ("MARCH-PAWS"). Recovery position (unconscious but breathing, no injury suspected): roll them onto the left side, bend the top leg forward, and rest the head on the straight lower arm with the mouth pointing down so vomit drains out (WHO-ICRC, p. 190). If the neck might be hurt, push the jaw forward ("jaw thrust") instead of tilting the head back (p. 49; 🖼️ ATP drawing, p. 78; Jaw

out (WHO-ICRC, p. 190). If the neck might be hurt, push the jaw forward ("jaw thrust") instead of tilting the head back (p. 49; 🖼️ ATP drawing, p. 78; Jaw thrust), and turn the body as one unit — a "log-roll" (ICRC First Aid, p. 163; 🖼️ WHO-ICRC, p. 188). Recovery position; 🖼️ ATP drawing, p. 79. CPR: push hard and fast in the center of the chest, at least 2 inches deep, 100–120 a minute, letting it come all the way back up — 30 pushes, then 2 breaths (ATP, p. 95; CPR). Know its limits: - When an injured person's heart stops, assume blood loss — CPR can't pump blood that isn't there (ICRC First Aid, p. 119). - The ICRC advises 5 minutes of CPR when the cause is not an injury, and none for an injured person with obvious signs of death (p. 167). - With no defibrillator, the best chances are drowning, lightning and very cold people (general practice). Feel a cold person's pulse for a full 60 seconds first (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 221). 📚 Go deeper: ATP 4-02.11 — the whole MARCH-PAWS sequence with drawings; WHO-ICRC Basic Emergency Care — the ABCDE check for any sick or hurt person.

🩸 Stopping life-threatening bleeding, then shock Tourniquet — arm or leg, blood spurting or pooling (ATP, p. 62): 1. Put it 2–3 inches above the wound, directly on the skin. 2. Tighten until the bleeding stops and there's no pulse below it. It will hurt badly — that means it's tight enough. 3. Still bleeding? Add a second tourniquet just above the first (often needed on the thigh). 4. Write down the time it went on (p. 63). No tourniquet? A band at least 2 inches wide twisted tight with a stick — never wire or a shoelace (FM 4-25.11, p. 48; this tip still holds; 🖼️ stick-and-knot steps, pp. 49–50). Tourniquet; Combat Application Tourniquet. Where a tourniquet can't go (groin, armpit, neck — 🖼️ ATP, p. 69): pack the wound. Stuff gauze or clean cloth tightly in, right down to where the blood comes from, press hard at least 3 minutes — sometimes up to 10 — then wrap a pressure bandage over it (ATP, p. 64; JTS wound guideline, p. 5; 🖼️ direct pressure, WHO-ICRC p. 169; 🖼️ pressure dressing, FM 4-25.11 p. 45; Hemostatic agent). The hand or foot beyond should stay warm and pink (ATP, p. 65). - Never pack a chest or belly wound (p. 64). - Leave stuck objects in. Pad bulky cloth around the stick or shard and bandage it so it can't

65). - Never pack a chest or belly wound (p. 64). - Leave stuck objects in. Pad bulky cloth around the stick or shard and bandage it so it can't move (p. 65). Tourniquet timing when no surgeon is coming (JTS Prolonged Casualty Care, p. 18): - Under 2 hours is the safe window; after about 6 hours the limb is probably lost. - If packing plus a pressure bandage can hold the bleeding, loosen ("convert") the tourniquet before 2 hours and watch for bleeding. Leave it in place, loose, ready to re-tighten (rule of thumb). - Never remove a tourniquet that has been on more than 6 hours. - (ATP says only medics remove them — but it assumes a hospital is coming.) Shock. An injured person who is confused (no head injury) with a weak or missing wrist pulse has lost a lot of blood and will die without fast action (ATP, p. 98). Stop the bleeding, lay them flat with feet raised (after any broken leg is splinted), loosen tight clothing, and insulate them above and below (p. 100; 🖼️ shock position, p. 99; Shock)). Drinks: standard first aid says nothing by mouth (same page), because surgery may come soon. With no help coming, that changes: if they're awake and can swallow, give sips of electrolyte (rehydration) drink, not plain water, which can drop the body's salt

may come soon. With no help coming, that changes: if they're awake and can swallow, give sips of electrolyte (rehydration) drink, not plain water, which can drop the body's salt dangerously (JTS, p. 18). 📚 Go deeper: ATP 4-02.11, ch. 4 — tourniquets, packing and pressure bandages step by step; JTS Prolonged Casualty Care — hour-by-hour care when evacuation is delayed.

🔥 Burns First aid (ATP, pp. 131–132): - Stop the burning. Put out flames. Cut clothing away around the burn, leaving cloth that is stuck to the skin. - Small burn: clean cool water right away, not ice, for no more than 20 minutes. Never put ice, grease, fat, herbs or dung on a burn (WTND, p. 22). - Chemical: brush off powder, then flush with lots of running water. Not in a tub — it chills them and spreads the chemical. - Electrical: shut off the power, or drag them clear with dry rope, cloth or wood. - Big burns: don't soak them. Keep them warm and off the ground — they chill fast in any weather. How big? Their own palm is about 1%. Rule of nines: head 9%, each arm 9%, each leg 18%, front of trunk 18%, back 18%. Don't count red skin without blisters (ATP, p. 130; adult chart in WHO-ICRC, p. 197, child chart on p. 198). Rule of nines; 🖼️ adult and child charts, JTS p. 53; 🖼️ photos of 1st-, 2nd- and 3rd-degree burns, JTS burn guideline p. 5; Burn. Fluids without an IV (JTS burn guideline, pp. 6–8): - Burns over 20% cause shock in the first 1–2 days. With "coached" drinking on a schedule, burns up to about 30% can be treated by mouth. - Rehydration drink, not plain water:

20% cause shock in the first 1–2 days. With "coached" drinking on a schedule, burns up to about 30% can be treated by mouth. - Rehydration drink, not plain water: 1 liter clean water + 6 level teaspoons sugar + ½ level teaspoon salt. - Adult rate: burn % × 10 = ml an hour (30% burn ≈ 300 ml an hour). - Enough? An adult passes more than 180 ml of urine every 6 hours (30–50 ml an hour). - Can't keep it down? Last resort: the same drink as an enema, up to 500 ml an hour (p. 7). Dressings (p. 9): leave unbroken blisters alone; cover with clean, dry gauze (wet dressings chill). For longer care, once a day wash gently with mild soap and clean water, remove loose dead skin, apply silver sulfadiazine cream (or a thin layer of honey — WTND, p. 22), re-cover (🖼️ washing and covering a burn, ICRC First Aid p. 217). Give pain medicine first. 📚 Go deeper: JTS Burn Wound Management — sizing, drinking schedules, urine targets, daily care; WHO Surgical Care at the District Hospital — burns in a small hospital.

🧼 Wounds and infection when there's no hospital Wash it out with lots of water (JTS wound guideline, pp. 4–5): - Cleanest water you have. Not safe to drink? Boil 3 minutes, cool to body temperature. - 1–3 liters for a small cut, 4–8 for a medium or dirty wound, 9 or more for a large dirty one. A syringe, or a bottle with holes poked in the cap, gives the right pressure (🖼️ washing a dirty wound, ICRC War Surgery p. 218). - Washing the whole person lowers infection too. Iodine, alcohol or antibiotic in the water does not help. Close it or leave it open? (p. 10) - Only close a cut that is clean, under 12 hours old (24 on the face or scalp) and closes without pulling. - Leave everything else open under a clean dressing. If it stays clean, close it 3–7 days later, or let it heal from the bottom up. Red Cross surgeons do the same (ICRC War Surgery, p. 219). - A closed wound that turns red, hot and full of pus: reopen it and let the pus out (p. 11). Bites (dog, cat, human): scrub at once with soap and water, let them heal open, think about rabies; most need antibiotics (p. 12). Tetanus: check vaccination with every wound (p. 10) — and get boosters now (general practice). When infection spreads:

let them heal open, think about rabies; most need antibiotics (p. 12). Tetanus: check vaccination with every wound (p. 10) — and get boosters now (general practice). When infection spreads: - In the wound: worsening pain, spreading redness, pus (p. 11; Cellulitis; Abscess). Draw a pen line around the red edge; if it spreads past the line on antibiotics, the treatment is failing (drug choices: MSF, p. 145). - Whole body (sepsis): fever or unusually low temperature, pulse over 90, breathing over 20 a minute, confusion, less urine. Low blood pressure comes late — don't wait for it (JTS sepsis guideline, p. 5). Sterilizing instruments — scrub off blood and dirt first (JTS, pp. 17–18): | Method | How | Result | | Pressure cooker | Tools on a rack above the water, 60 minutes once it vents | Sterile | | Oven | 338 °F (170 °C) 1 hour, or 320 °F (160 °C) 2 hours | Sterile | | Plain bleach | Soak undiluted 5 minutes, rinse | Disinfected | | Boiling | Last resort | Clean, NOT sterile (WHO, p. 115) | Autoclave; Pressure cooker. 📚 Go deeper: JTS Acute Traumatic Wound Management — washing, closing, bites, sterilizing; ICRC War Surgery Vol 1 — dirty wounds and delayed closure; WTND — skin infections — plain-language pictures.

🦴 Broken bones, sprains, spine and head Splinting (WHO-ICRC, p. 191; arm slings: 🖼️ ATP pp. 141–143, Sling)): 1. Take off rings and jewelry. 2. Before and after, check beyond the injury: pulse, color, feeling, movement. 3. Pad the splint and bony points; reach past the joint above and the joint below (🖼️ board and improvised splints, ATP pp. 146–148; 🖼️ the good leg as a splint, p. 149). 4. Deformed, no pulse (cold, pale): gently straighten it. Deformed with a good pulse: don't force it. Cast too tight from swelling: split it and rewrap with an elastic bandage (Hospital Corpsman, p. 96; 🖼️ cutting a cast, WHO Surgical Care p. 393). Splint). Sprains — treat like a break (WTND, p. 28): keep it still, wrap firmly from the toes up (loosen briefly every hour or two), keep it raised. Cold wet cloths 20–30 minutes every hour for a day or two, then warm soaks. Never rub or massage it. A bad sprain takes 3–4 weeks. Dislocated shoulder — the longer you wait, the harder it gets (WTND, p. 27): lay them face down on a table, arm hanging over the edge. Pull steadily down 15–20 minutes, or hang 5–10 kg from the arm (start with 5). Then bind the arm to the body for a week to a month; no lifting with it for a month. Other methods: WHO

kg from the arm (start with 5). Then bind the arm to the body for a week to a month; no lifting with it for a month. Other methods: WHO Surgical Care, p. 403 (🖼️ drawings, p. 404). Dislocated shoulder. Spine: suspect it with numbness, weakness, or a head injury. Keep them flat; log-roll to check the back or let them vomit. A hard board is only for moving them — hours on one cause pressure sores (WHO-ICRC, pp. 55, 189; 🖼️ lifting without bending the spine, WTND p. 26; Spinal board). Head injury danger signs: unequal pupils (🖼️ WTND ch. 3, p. 5; Anisocoria), weakness on one side, seizures, vomiting, worsening confusion, clear fluid or blood from the nose or ears (ATP, p. 121). With no neck injury and no shock, raise the head of the bed about 30°. During a seizure, put nothing in the mouth (WHO-ICRC, p. 33). 📚 Go deeper: ATP 4-02.11, ch. 13 — splints from improvised materials; WHO Surgical Care — setting fractures, traction, plaster.

🐍 Rattlesnakes, spiders and stings Rattlesnakes (the Northern Pacific rattlesnake; 🖼️ how to tell a pit viper, ATP p. 176), yellow jackets, ticks (western black-legged tick) and poison oak are normal hazards along the Rogue (BLM, p. 4). Rattlesnake bite — DO (JTS snakebite guideline, p. 16; ATP, p. 179): - Keep them calm and still. Take off rings, watches and tight clothing. - Loosely splint the limb, a little below heart level. Wash the bite gently. - Get them to antivenom as fast as possible, even if they have to walk — it's the only real treatment. DON'T cut, suck, shock, burn, use chemicals, ice, or tie on a band or tourniquet, or use "venom extractor" kits — "outdated interventions that should not be performed" (p. 27). If a band is already on, don't rip it off: people can collapse when it comes off. Remove it with them lying down, ready to treat shock (p. 16). Without antivenom, expect permanent damage or death, and weeks of nursing (p. 27). Black widow (Western black widow; 🖼️ venomous spiders and other biters, ATP p. 180): shiny black or brown, usually a red or yellow mark. Lives in woodpiles and sheds; bites often happen in bed in fall and early winter. Painful cramps spread from the bite within 15–60 minutes; the belly can go board-hard. Death or lasting harm is extremely unlikely

often happen in bed in fall and early winter. Painful cramps spread from the bite within 15–60 minutes; the belly can go board-hard. Death or lasting harm is extremely unlikely — pain medicine, wound care, tetanus check, no routine antibiotics (JTS spider guideline, pp. 4–5). Brown recluses don't live in western Oregon (general practice); "spider bite" sores are often abscesses (p. 5). 📚 Go deeper: JTS Snakebite Envenomation (2026) — first steps and what not to do (Appendix F: North America); JTS Spider and Scorpion Envenomation — widow and recluse bites.

🌡️ Heat and cold in the Valley Heat. Grants Pass has hit 108 °F (Josephine soil survey, p. 5), — and summer is when wood gets cut and fires get fought. | | Heat exhaustion | Heat stroke — emergency | | Looks like | Heavy sweat, pale, faint, cramps | Confused, odd behavior, collapse — may still sweat | | Do | Shade, lie down, legs up, sip electrolyte drink (ATP, p. 189) | Cool first: into cold water (creek, tub), or wet sheets and hard fanning (ATP, p. 190) | Fast cooling cuts heat-stroke deaths from about 50% to 5%; stop at about 101 °F (38.3 °C) so they don't get too cold (Emergency War Surgery, p. 428). ATP lists "hot, dry skin," but people who collapse from hard work often still sweat — don't wait for dry skin (general practice). Too much plain water lowers blood salt and also causes confusion (ATP, p. 190). Heat stroke. Cold. Cave Junction winters average 40 °F, nights near freezing, with about 85% of the rain October to March (soil survey, p. 5). Wet makes hypothermia possible even in mild weather (ATP, p. 103). - Mild (shivering, alert): wet clothes off, wrap them including the head, warm sweet drinks (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 221). - Severe (not shivering, drowsy): lying flat, handled gently. No walking, no hot bath, nothing by mouth.

wrap them including the head, warm sweet drinks (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 221). - Severe (not shivering, drowsy): lying flat, handled gently. No walking, no hot bath, nothing by mouth. Wrapped heat on the chest and armpits, never on bare skin (same page; JTS hypothermia guideline, p. 5). - No dry clothes? Wrap them in plastic sheeting (a vapor barrier) under the blankets, with insulation underneath (JTS, p. 5; 🖼️ improvised wrap, p. 7). Hypothermia. 📚 Go deeper: Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 221 — mild to severe hypothermia; JTS Hypothermia Prevention — keeping hurt people warm; ATP, ch. 17 — heat illness.

🦷 Teeth: pain and emergencies WHO's protocols for non-dentists (WHO Oral Health, p. 56): - Knocked-out adult tooth: rinse it and push it back in within 1 hour, without touching the root. Where There Is No Dentist allows up to 12 hours, but sooner is far better. Wash with saline, milk or clean water; don't scrape the root; don't replace a baby tooth (p. 107; 🖼️ pushing it back and waxing it in place, p. 108; Dental avulsion). - Loosened tooth: gently push it back into place. - Broken tooth: temporary filling — zinc oxide mixed with oil of cloves (p. 156; 🖼️ the instruments, p. 155; Zinc oxide eugenol). - Infection: antibiotics, pain relief, and drain any abscess. - Don't put medicines directly on the tooth or gum. Abscess signs: constant pain (even at night), the tooth feels "long" or loose, a gum boil, a swollen gum or face. Swelling pressing on the throat, or fever, is an emergency (p. 103; penicillin doses p. 104). Bring swelling down before pulling a tooth — the numbing shot won't work in a swollen jaw. Dental abscess. 📚 Go deeper: Where There Is No Dentist — abscesses, pulling teeth, fillings; WHO AFRO protocols — urgent-care flowcharts (images only).

🛏️ Nursing a bedridden person for days and weeks From the JTS nursing guideline (CPG 70): - Turn them at least every 2 hours (hourly on a hard surface). Pad heels, elbows, tailbone and the back of the head; pillows between knees and ankles (p. 10). Pressure sores. - Head up about 30° if unconscious — it lowers pneumonia risk (same page). - A red patch that doesn't fade when pressed is a sore starting: circle it, keep weight off it (p. 11; 🖼️ where sores form, WTND ch. 15, p. 22). - Mouth care: brush every 12 hours; unconscious, wipe with moist gauze every 4 hours (same page). - Washing and toileting: bed bath daily; check every 2 hours for soiling; dry skin folds (p. 12). - Food and fluids: 5–6 small high-protein meals a day. Judge fluids by urine — little or dark means more to drink (p. 9). - Moving: sit up, then the bed edge, a chair, short walks with help; move every joint at least every 8 hours — this also helps prevent leg clots (pp. 13–14). Diarrhea (WHO Treatment of Diarrhoea; signs of dehydration: 🖼️ the skin-pinch test, WTND ch. 13, p. 1): - After each loose stool: under 2 years 50–100 ml; ages 2–10, 100–200 ml; older, as much as they want (p. 14). Dehydrated: about 75 ml per kg over 4 hours

After each loose stool: under 2 years 50–100 ml; ages 2–10, 100–200 ml; older, as much as they want (p. 14). Dehydrated: about 75 ml per kg over 4 hours (p. 15). - Small children: a teaspoon every 1–2 minutes, not a bottle (p. 16). - Children get zinc 10–20 mg a day for 10–14 days; no anti-diarrhea drugs under age 5 (p. 9). - Recipes differ: WTND uses 8 level teaspoons sugar + ½ salt per liter (WTND ch. 13, p. 2); WHO, 6 + ½. Both work. Oral rehydration. Childbirth has its own books in Medical\Field-Care\Childbirth-Newborn. Heavy bleeding after birth: rub the womb until it's hard, baby to the breast, help her urinate, check the placenta came out whole (A Book for Midwives, ch. 13). 📚 Go deeper: JTS Nursing Interventions — turning, mouth care, bed baths, exercises; WHO Treatment of Diarrhoea — plans A, B and C; WHO Newborn Care — birth step by step.

⚖️ Knowing when someone can't be saved Some people will die whatever you do. Seeing it early lets you save those who can, and comfort the dying instead of putting them through useless treatment. - Many hurt at once: the Red Cross sorts people into urgent (simple care now saves them), serious (can wait a little), minor, and not to be treated or moved — injuries care can't help, and the dying (ICRC First Aid, p. 125; Triage). - No CPR on an injured person with obvious signs of death (p. 167). - A newborn with no heartbeat after 10 minutes of good breaths has died (WHO, p. 152). - Snakebite without antivenom, very large burns, sepsis that keeps worsening, a limb under a tourniquet past 6 hours — expect to lose some lives and limbs; do what you can, but not at the cost of those who can live (rule of thumb). Caring for the dying (Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 17, p. 28): keep them comfortable and free of pain, have family sit with them, let them make their own decisions and talk about death if they want — pretending they aren't dying doesn't help. Then look after the carers (Community guide). 📚 Go deeper: ICRC First Aid in Armed Conflicts — triage; ICRC War Surgery — sorting casualties with few resources.

🧰 The kit to build now The Army's first-aid kit (ATP, p. 231) — one per adult (rule of thumb): 2 tourniquets, 2 clotting (hemostatic) gauzes, 2 compressed gauzes, 2 gauze rolls, a triangular bandage, a vented chest seal (🖼️ ATP, p. 88), 2 eye shields, 2 pairs of gloves, a safety cutter, tape and a marker. First aid kit. For the household (rule of thumb unless a page is given): - An irrigation syringe; a pressure cooker with a rack kept for instruments (JTS, p. 18) - Tweezers, scissors, a thermometer, elastic bandages, splints, clean cloth - Salt, sugar and level measuring spoons for rehydration drink - Silver sulfadiazine cream (JTS, p. 9); zinc oxide and oil of cloves (WTNDentist, p. 156) - Medicines from the WTND kit list — doses and storage in the Medical guide - A notebook for times, pulses, urine and doses Now, while you can: practice a one-handed tourniquet on yourself (🖼️ ATP, p. 62), update everyone's tetanus shots, and take a first-aid or CERT class (general practice). 📚 Go deeper: ATP 4-02.11, Appendix A — kit lists; WTND — the medicine kit — home and village kits.

🚑 The first few minutes When someone is hurt, check in this order and act on the first problem you find (FM 4-25.11, p. 18–19; the newer Army order is MARCH — ATP 4-02.11, p. 53): 1. Protect yourself — gloves or a clean plastic bag on your hands if there's blood. 2. Responsive? Tap and ask "Are you OK?" 3. Breathing? If not, open the airway and give rescue breaths (🖼️ head-tilt, ATP p. 77; 🖼️ mouth-to-mouth, WTND p. 80). 4. Bleeding? For heavy, life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg, put a tourniquet on first — 2–3 inches above the wound, on bare skin, tight until the bleeding stops (it will hurt; that means it's tight enough), and write the time on the person (ATP 4-02.11 (2026), p. 62). For other bleeding, press hard on the wound with a thick, clean cloth (🖼️ WHO-ICRC, p. 169), or pack the wound tightly where a tourniquet can't go (groin, armpit, neck — 🖼️ ATP, p. 69). The library's older FM 4-25.11 calls the tourniquet a "last resort" — that advice is out of date. Full steps: Injuries & Illness guide. 5. Shock)? Weak, fast pulse, pale cold sweat, confusion. Lay them down with feet a little raised (🖼️ ATP, p. 99), keep warm; unconscious = on the side (🖼️ ATP, p. 79; Recovery position), nothing by mouth (WTND — shock).

Don't move them unless their life is in immediate danger (🖼️ how to lift without bending, WTND p. 100). 💊 Using found or expired medicines 1. Identify it. US pills must carry an imprint code. Open Pill-Identifier\PILL-IDENTIFIER.html, type the code, then check that the color, shape and size also match — the same code can be two different drugs (e.g. "I2" is ibuprofen 200 mg or amitriptyline 25 mg depending on size; "N 4" is nitroglycerin or a diet pill). No code at all = a supplement, a foreign or compounded product, or an illegal pill. 2. Never trust street pills. Pills that didn't come from a pharmacy can be counterfeits pressed with fentanyl — fake blue "M30" oxycodone, Xanax and Adderall are common, and many contain a deadly dose. 3. Look it up before giving it. In the WHO Model Formulary or MSF Essential Drugs (Medicines\), read what it treats, the dose, who must not take it, and interactions. For children, use the WHO Formulary for Children — children's doses go by weight. Give the right dose, no more and no less; finish every antibiotic course; antibiotics do nothing for colds (WTND, p. 56). 4. Expired medicines. Most tablets and capsules kept sealed, cool and dry lose potency slowly — military testing extended most stockpiled lots by years (88% of 3,005 lots, on average by 66 months), and some drugs kept 90% strength decades past their date (Zilker 2019, p. 54–55). That was warehouse storage, and inhalers and

(88% of 3,005 lots, on average by 66 months), and some drugs kept 90% strength decades past their date (Zilker 2019, p. 54–55). That was warehouse storage, and inhalers and epinephrine often failed. But: - Don't rely on expired or badly stored: insulin (lasts only ~28 days unrefrigerated; never use if it froze), nitroglycerin) tablets (lose strength once opened — keep in the original glass bottle; WHO: discard 8 weeks after opening, p. 276), epinephrine pens (photo; weaker when expired — but an expired pen with clear liquid is better than none in anaphylaxis), and mixed liquid antibiotics (amoxicillin suspension: 14 days in the fridge). - Throw out anything discolored, crumbling, sticky or smelling odd — especially tetracycline-family antibiotics, which can damage the kidneys when degraded. Also caked, brownish rehydration salts, and melted creams or suppositories (MSF, p. 648). - Don't raise the dose to make up for age — MSF warns of overdose. Heart and seizure medicines need exact doses, so respect their dates (p. 649). - Store medicines cool and dry (not the bathroom, kitchen or a car — a vehicle can reach 50–60 °C, MSF, p. 647), in their original containers, out of children's reach. 5. The biggest dangers - Allergy — face or throat swelling, trouble breathing or widespread hives after a medicine is anaphylaxis: give epinephrine if you have it. After any reaction, never use

biggest dangers - Allergy — face or throat swelling, trouble breathing or widespread hives after a medicine is anaphylaxis: give epinephrine if you have it. After any reaction, never use that medicine again (WTND, p. 70). - Acetaminophen (Tylenol) — no more than 4,000 mg a day for adults, counting every product; it's hidden in Norco, Vicodin, Percocet and many cold medicines. Too much causes liver failure (MSF, p. 244) — and an overdose needs urgent care even if the person feels fine (WHO, p. 68). - Opioids — a dose that's normal for someone used to them can stop the breathing of someone who isn't, or of a child. Never combine with benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium, Klonopin), alcohol or other sedatives. Naloxone (Narcan) reverses opioid overdose — keep some. - Children — no cough/cold medicines under age 2, no aspirin for children or teens (Reye syndrome — WHO, p. 226). - Interactions — check the formulary when someone already takes blood thinners, heart medicines or antidepressants. - Poisoning: Oregon Poison Center 1-800-222-1222 (24/7, while phones work). 6. Measure it right (WTND ch. 8): 1 g = 1,000 mg · 1 mg = 1,000 mcg · 1 grain = 65 mg · 1 teaspoon = 5 ml · 1 tablespoon = 15 ml. Kitchen spoons vary — mark one at 5 ml measured with a syringe (🖼️ WTND p. 61; cutting

· 1 teaspoon = 5 ml · 1 tablespoon = 15 ml. Kitchen spoons vary — mark one at 5 ml measured with a syringe (🖼️ WTND p. 61; cutting tablets: 🖼️ p. 60). Check the mg on the label: strengths differ. Never give medicine by mouth to someone asleep, unconscious or having a seizure (p. 62). 7. Getting rid of medicines — mix with coffee grounds or cat litter and seal; flush only what the FDA lists, like fentanyl patches — deadly to children even after use (FDA; 🖼️ FDA decision flowchart). Stock up now: ask your doctor about extra supplies of the medicines your household depends on, and keep an emergency kit (wound care, pain/fever medicine, antihistamines, oral rehydration salts, naloxone). 📚 Go deeper: WTND Green Pages — uses, doses and warnings for each medicine; MSF Essential Drugs, p. 646 — storage, spoilage and expiry; Zilker 2019 — what testing shows about old medicines.

💧 Diarrhea and dehydration: the homemade drink Most children who die of diarrhea die of dehydration. Signs: thirst, little or dark urine, dry mouth, sunken tearless eyes, skin that stays up when pinched (🖼️ the pinch test, WTND p. 151). Start the drink at the first watery stools (WTND, p. 151–152). Rehydration Drink (🖼️ drawn step by step, Hesperian Ch 5, p. 53; Oral rehydration): in 1 liter of clean water, stir ½ level teaspoon of salt and 8 level teaspoons of sugar. Taste before adding the sugar: it must be less salty than tears. - Give sips every 5 minutes until they urinate normally — 3 liters or more a day for a large person, at least 1 liter for a small child. - Keep giving it even if they vomit. Keep feeding, and keep breastfeeding babies. - No repeat doses of medicines that can build up until they urinate normally (WTND, p. 54). - Getting worse, or other danger signs? Get medical help. 📚 Go deeper: WTND, p. 152 — the sugar and cereal recipes, with pictures; MSF Clinical Guidelines — severe diarrhea and cholera.

🌿 Medicinal plants — go carefully Signs a home remedy probably doesn't work: many different "cures" for one illness, disgusting remedies, and anything using animal or human waste — that causes infections (WTND, p. 10–11). Deadly look-alike: foxglove leaves have been mistaken for comfrey (🖼️ foxglove photos, WSU p. 28), with fatal "comfrey tea" poisonings — and comfrey itself can harm the liver (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 243). If in doubt, don't — and call the Poison Center. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Monographs Vol 1 — evidence plant by plant (Vols 1–4); WSU Poisonous Plants of the PNW, p. 28 — foxglove and other local poisons.

👶 Childbirth, Newborns & Young Children When No Help Is Coming Getting a mother and baby through pregnancy, birth and the first weeks, and keeping young children alive and learning, with no hospital, pharmacy or phone. Current WHO guidance comes first. Hesperian's A Book for Midwives (2026) and Where There Is No Doctor (2025) add detail; where they differ from WHO, this guide gives the WHO answer. The books are in Medical\Childbirth-Children (Birth, Newborn, Mothers, Child-Health), Medical\A Book for Midwives, Medical\Field-Care\Childbirth-Newborn, Medical\Where There Is No Doctor and Southern-Oregon\Children-Learning. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Bleeding after birth kills fastest. Every mother gets a bleeding medicine within 1 minute of the last baby (WHO 2025, p. 19), and someone feels her womb every 15 minutes for the first hour (p. 29). - Never push on the belly, pull the cord, put anything in the vagina, or give drugs to speed labor (PCPNC, p. 170). - A baby not breathing by 1 minute needs breaths now, 40 a minute. Stop only after 10 minutes with no heartbeat (PCPNC, p. 152). - Put nothing on the cord stump. Keep it clean and dry. - Count a sick child's breaths for a full minute. Fast breathing means pneumonia. - Never make a child vomit, and never give salt water.

📋 Plan now, while doctors and pharmacies still exist Cheap medicines bought ahead save mothers and children. Clean birth kit (PCPNC, p. 169; BfM, p. 152; 🖼️ the kit drawn, WTND p. 254): soap and a nail brush, gloves (or very clean plastic bags), a new razor blade, 3 strings 8 in (20 cm) long, a suction bulb (🖼️ using one, BfM p. 214), many clean cloths, a warm blanket, 3 bowls, plastic for the placenta, clean water and a way to heat it, light, and the bleeding medicine. Add a blood-pressure cuff and stethoscope (🖼️ how to use them, BfM p. 123), a newborn bag-and-mask (Bag valve mask), a digital thermometer and a hanging scale (general practice). Transport: there is no 24-hour ER in the Illinois Valley (Start Here). The nearest delivery hospital is in Grants Pass, about 30 miles, an hour or more once roads or fuel fail (general knowledge). Decide now who drives or carries her, and save fuel for it. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Bleeding After Birth — medicines; WHO catch-up table — missed vaccines; A Book for Midwives, ch. 9 — supplies.

🤰 Pregnancy: checkups and danger signs - Due date: add 9 months and 7 days to the first day of the last monthly bleeding (BfM, p. 88). - Checkups: monthly, then weekly in the last month (general practice): blood pressure, urine and the womb's height. The top of the womb rises about 2 finger-widths a month: just above the pubic bone at 3 months, the navel at about 5, nearly the ribs by 8½–9. Much faster or slower is a warning sign (BfM, p. 130; Fundal height). - Pre-eclampsia causes fits and death before, during or after birth. Surest signs: blood pressure 140/90 or higher plus protein in the urine. Also: strong headache, spots or blurred vision, steady pain high in the belly, puffy face or hands on waking (BfM, p. 125). - Urine protein test: boil the top of a tube of urine. If cloudy, add a few drops of vinegar. Still cloudy means protein. Low-dose aspirin (81 mg a day) may prevent pre-eclampsia; ask a doctor now (BfM, p. 127). - Breech? If the hard, round head is at the top of the belly late in pregnancy (MCPC, p. 234; 🖼️ listening for the heartbeat above the navel, WTND p. 252), WHO wants the birth in a hospital (p. 239). Go before labor. Go for help at once, day or night, for bleeding from the vagina, fits, severe

WTND p. 252), WHO wants the birth in a hospital (p. 239). Go before labor. Go for help at once, day or night, for bleeding from the vagina, fits, severe headache with blurred vision, fever with weakness, severe belly pain, or fast or difficult breathing (PCPNC, p. 162). She eats more, rests and drinks no alcohol (same page). Smoke harms pregnant women more: in fire season keep her in a "cleaner air room" with a box-fan filter (EPA). 📚 Go deeper: A Book for Midwives, ch. 8 — every prenatal check; PCPNC counselling sheets — birth plans.

🛏️ Labor and birth: what helpers do Labor has started with painful contractions every 20 minutes or less, waters breaking, or a bloody sticky discharge (PCPNC, p. 162). During labor (WTND, p. 259): - The first stage can last over 20 hours with a first baby. Don't hurry it. - She doesn't push until she feels she must. - She urinates and drinks often, eats lightly, walks, and doesn't lie flat on her back for long (🖼️ positions for labor, MCPC p. 111; 🖼️ for the birth, p. 123; 🖼️ WTND p. 260). - Helpers scrub hands, keep nails short and wear gloves. Never: drugs to speed labor (they can kill mother and child — WTND, p. 266), anything in the vagina, pushing on the belly (it can tear the womb — BfM, p. 205), pulling on the cord. Leave for Grants Pass now if waters broke with no labor after 6 hours, contractions last over 12 hours, she soaks over 2–3 pads in 15 minutes, or the placenta isn't out 1 hour after the baby (PCPNC, p. 170). Right after the baby is born (🖼️ a head-first birth, WTND p. 261; Childbirth): 1. Dry the baby, lay it skin-to-skin on the mother's belly, and cover it, head too (BfM, p. 240). 2. Feel her belly for a second baby, then give the bleeding medicine within 1 minute. Never before

on the mother's belly, and cover it, head too (BfM, p. 240). 2. Feel her belly for a second baby, then give the bleeding medicine within 1 minute. Never before the last baby is out (WHO, p. 19). 3. Cut the cord after 1–3 minutes (same page), once it is white and stops pulsing; waiting gives the baby iron. Tie it tightly 2 finger-widths from the belly, tie a second string farther out, and cut between with a new or sterilized blade (BfM, pp. 214–215; 🖼️ tying and cutting, WTND p. 262; Umbilical cord). A baby needing breathing help gets it cut at once. 4. Let the placenta come by itself, and check it is whole (PCPNC, p. 169; Placenta). 5. First breastfeed within the hour. No bath the first day. Don't leave the mother alone for 24 hours (same page). Cord care: clean and dry, nothing on it. Dirt and dung cause tetanus (WTND, p. 263; Neonatal tetanus). WHO's one exception is 7.1% chlorhexidine daily for a week, where a health authority recommends it (PCPNC, p. 169). Fold the diaper below the stump; it falls off in 5–7 days. 📚 Go deeper: A Book for Midwives, ch. 12 — the birth in drawings; PCPNC home delivery.

🩸 Heavy bleeding after birth: the #1 killer Bleeding after birth kills more mothers than anything else (general knowledge), and delay is a common reason they die (WHO, p. 59). A soft womb causes about 70% of it (p. 9). Feel the womb every 15 minutes for the first hour. Hard like your forehead is good. Soft like the tip of your nose needs rubbing (🖼️ how to rub it, BfM p. 224). The top should be at or below the navel (WHO, p. 29). Teach the family to check and rub (BfM, p. 236). Dangerous bleeding: measure, don't guess (WHO, p. 43; p. 15): - 500 mL or more (about 2 cups), or - 300 mL or more plus a warning sign: pulse over 100, top blood-pressure number under 100, bottom under 60, or pulse higher than the top number. - No cuff? Soaking 2–3 pads in 15 minutes, or faint, pale, sweaty or confused (BfM, p. 239). A slow steady trickle is as dangerous as a gush (p. 226). - Mark 250 and 500 mL lines on the basin that will catch blood (rule of thumb). Then do ALL of these within 15 minutes, in any order (WHO "MOTIVE", p. 47): | Step | What to do | | Massage | Cupped hand on top of the womb; rub in circles until hard. Alone? Massage first | |

"MOTIVE", p. 47): | Step | What to do | | Massage | Cupped hand on top of the womb; rub in circles until hard. Alone? Massage first | | Oxytocic | Misoprostol 800 µg under the tongue, or oxytocin 10 units in the thigh. Nauseous? Pills go in the rectum (BfM, p. 231) | | TXA | 1 g into a vein over 10 minutes, if someone trained and under 3 hours | | IV fluids | If you can; if not, sips of rehydration drink while awake (BfM, p. 239) | | Examine | Baby to the breast; help her urinate; placenta whole? torn and bleeding? (BfM, p. 236) | | Escalate | Head for Grants Pass if bleeding stays heavy or passes 1,000 mL (WHO, p. 57) | Still bleeding? 1. Squeeze the womb between two hands: a gloved fist in the vagina above the cervix, the other hand pressing the womb down onto it (BfM, p. 237; 🖼️ WHO drawing, MCPC p. 178). Hold at least 5 minutes; it hurts, so tell her. Don't wait for shock, and don't pack the vagina (WHO, p. 73). 2. Or press a fist hard on the belly just above the navel until the pulse in her thigh disappears, and keep pressing (BfM, p. 238; 🖼️ WHO drawing, MCPC p. 179). 3. Shock: feet up, keep her warm, sips if

the navel until the pulse in her thigh disappears, and keep pressing (BfM, p. 238; 🖼️ WHO drawing, MCPC p. 179). 3. Shock: feet up, keep her warm, sips if awake, nothing by mouth if unconscious (BfM, p. 239). 4. Help more than 1 hour away? Amoxicillin 1 g plus metronidazole 1 g by mouth, once (BfM, p. 231). 📚 Go deeper: WHO action plans — the bundle and shock; A Book for Midwives, ch. 13 — the family's part.

🔄 Stuck shoulders and breech Stuck shoulders: the head is born, pulls back like a turtle, and the shoulders won't come. The baby has about 5 minutes before brain damage (BfM, p. 210). Call every helper. WHO's order (MCPC, pp. 243–244): 1. Knees to chest: two helpers push her bent knees firmly up to her chest (🖼️ MCPC p. 244). 2. Press hard just above the pubic bone, not on the belly, while you draw the head steadily downward. Cup the head; don't grip the neck; never jerk. 3. Hand inside along the baby's back: push a shoulder toward the baby's chest to turn it. 4. Bring the back arm out, swept across the chest. Hesperian tries hands-and-knees first (BfM, p. 211); use it if WHO's steps fail. Never push on top of the womb: it can burst. Be ready to help the baby breathe. Breech (bottom first) with no hospital (BfM, pp. 215–217): feet first is the most dangerous kind. No pushing until the cervix is fully open. Hands off: the bottom, belly and legs come on their own, and you never pull on the baby. Wrap the body so it doesn't chill and gasp inside her. A helper presses above the pubic bone to keep the head tucked. Hold the baby by the hips, never the belly (p. 217; 🖼️ "hold the baby at the hips, but do

presses above the pubic bone to keep the head tucked. Hold the baby by the hips, never the belly (p. 217; 🖼️ "hold the baby at the hips, but do not pull," MCPC p. 378). 📚 Go deeper: A Book for Midwives, ch. 12 — each move drawn; WHO Managing Complications — hard births.

🫁 A baby who isn't breathing Most babies breathe within 1–2 minutes, and drying is often enough. Never hold a baby upside down or slap it (BfM, p. 241). WHO's steps (PCPNC, p. 152; Neonatal resuscitation): 1. Dry and rub the back. Not breathing, or only gasping? Start within 1 minute of birth. Cut the cord; move the baby to a warm, dry, flat place. 2. Open the airway: head slightly tipped back, a folded towel no thicker than ¾ in (2 cm) under the shoulders (🖼️ MCPC p. 311). Suction only if the mouth or nose is full. 3. Breathe for the baby: mask over chin, mouth and nose (🖼️ fitting the mask, MCPC p. 313). Give 5 squeezes and watch the chest rise; if it doesn't, fix the head and seal. Then 40 breaths a minute (one every 1½ seconds). 4. No bag? Your mouth over the baby's mouth and nose: small puffs from your cheeks only (BfM, p. 242). 5. After 1 minute, check the heart with a stethoscope or 2 fingers on the chest. Count 6 seconds, times 10 (BfM, p. 243). 6. Stop when the baby breathes over 30 times a minute without deep chest sucking-in. Skin-to-skin, check every 15 minutes. 7. No heartbeat (or under 60) after 10 minutes of good breaths: the baby has died. Stop and care for the family. Alone with

sucking-in. Skin-to-skin, check every 15 minutes. 7. No heartbeat (or under 60) after 10 minutes of good breaths: the baby has died. Stop and care for the family. Alone with a bleeding mother? Baby first, then her medicine and womb check as soon as you can (WHO, p. 17). 📚 Go deeper: PCPNC resuscitation chart; A Book for Midwives, p. 242 — rescue breathing drawn.

🌡️ Warmth, small babies and newborn danger signs Warmth: skin-to-skin, head covered, out of drafts. A baby needs only one more layer than an adult (BfM, p. 240). Watch for overheating in valley summers over 100 °F, and chilling November–March (general knowledge). Kangaroo care for babies under 2,500 g (5½ lb) or born 3+ weeks early (WHO KMC, p. 10): - Skin-to-skin as close to 24 hours a day as possible, at least 8, an hour or more at a time, breastfeeding every 2–3 hours (p. 20). - Baby upright between the breasts, head to one side, hips spread; a cloth wrap tied high across the chest, its top just below the baby's ear (p. 32; 🖼️ IYCF p. 84). - Room at 77–82 °F (25–28 °C) (PCPNC, p. 140). Continue to about 2,500 g, or until the baby wriggles out (KMC, p. 40). Newborn danger signs: treat as an emergency (Caring for the Newborn at Home, p. 71): - not feeding, or stopped feeding well; fits - 60 or more breaths a minute (count twice, baby calm); chest sucking in - 99.5 °F (37.5 °C) or more, or 95.7 °F (35.4 °C) or less (digital thermometer in the armpit — p. 78) - yellow soles; moves only when touched, or not at all - red or pus-draining navel (Omphalitis), boils, or pus from the eyes (Neonatal conjunctivitis) Newborn antibiotic

— p. 78) - yellow soles; moves only when touched, or not at all - red or pus-draining navel (Omphalitis), boils, or pus from the eyes (Neonatal conjunctivitis) Newborn antibiotic doses: BfM, p. 279. Jaundice (IMCI, p. 46): - Yellow on the first day, or yellow palms and soles at any age, is severe. It needs hospital light treatment; there is no home cure. Press the soles with your thumbs and look in daylight (Caring for the Newborn, p. 81). - Yellow after day 1 with palms and soles clear: breastfeed often, check daily. Yellow past 14 days needs a check. - No direct sun. WTND's bright window light is harmless if the baby doesn't chill or overheat, but don't count on it (WTND, p. 274). 📚 Go deeper: WHO Caring for the Newborn at Home — checking each sign; WHO KMC guide — pictures.

🤱 Breastfeeding and the mother's recovery Breast milk only for 6 months. Unmodified animal milk is not suitable under 6 months; it can damage the kidneys (WHO IYCF, p. 18). A baby who can't suckle is fed by cup, not bottle (p. 81; 🖼️ cup feeding, p. 86). No breast milk? See the Food Security guide for wet-nurses, relactation and formula. Enough milk? After day 5: 8–12 feeds a day with visible swallowing, pale urine at least 6 times a day, yellow stools 3+ times a day until 6 weeks, birth weight back by 2 weeks, then 5–7 oz (150–200 g) a week. Few wet diapers or dark urine is a reliable warning (IYCF, pp. 135–136). Breast problems (🖼️ good and poor attachment, IYCF p. 42): - Overfull, hard breasts (Breast engorgement): get the milk out by feeding or hand-expressing (🖼️ IYCF p. 155; 🖼️ WTND p. 277); warmth before, cool cloths after (IYCF, p. 140). - Mastitis (fever, red painful breast): keep breastfeeding, good side first. She rests; the family does her work. Antibiotics only if not better after 24 hours of good draining (p. 142; doses BfM, p. 289). Womb infection (fever 100.4 °F / 38 °C or more, bad-smelling discharge, chills, belly pain, fast pulse) can kill quickly. Antibiotic plan: BfM, p. 271. Check mother and baby within 24 hours, on day 3, on days 7–14 and

more, bad-smelling discharge, chills, belly pain, fast pulse) can kill quickly. Antibiotic plan: BfM, p. 271. Check mother and baby within 24 hours, on day 3, on days 7–14 and at 6 weeks (PCPNC, p. 170). Depression after birth hits 1 in 10 to 1 in 5 mothers, and her baby grows worse too (Thinking Healthy, p. 11): - Sadness or worry that is very strong, or lasts over 2 weeks, is depression. The family takes over chores, lets her sleep, sees she eats and moves a little each day (BfM, p. 274). - Thinking Healthy lets a trusted neighbor run home sessions in 3 steps: spot unhelpful thoughts, swap in healthier ones, practice healthy actions (p. 15). - Ask her directly about suicide and whether she has a plan. Asking doesn't make it more likely. A woman with a plan needs help now and must not be left alone (Where Women Have No Doctor, p. 431). 📚 Go deeper: WHO Infant Feeding (2025) — breastfeeding problems; Thinking Healthy — the sessions.

🤒 Sick children under 5: fever, breathing, diarrhea, measles, worms Danger signs: act now — can't drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, has had fits, very sleepy or can't be woken (IMCI, p. 5), or fever with a stiff neck (p. 8). Fever is a sign: look for the cause. Give plenty to drink, boiled water for babies (WTND, p. 76). Paracetamol (acetaminophen) every 6 hours for high fever: one 100 mg tablet at 2 months–3 years, 1½ at 3–5 years (IMCI, p. 17). No aspirin for children. Pneumonia: count breaths for a full minute, child calm (IMCI, pp. 6, 45): | Age | Fast breathing | | Under 2 months | 60 or more | | 2–12 months | 50 or more | | 1–5 years | 40 or more | Fast breathing or chest sucking in means pneumonia: amoxicillin 250 mg twice a day for 5 days — 1 tablet at 2–12 months, 2 at 1–3 years, 3 at 3–5 years (p. 16). Diarrhea. Severe dehydration is two or more of: very sleepy or unconscious, sunken eyes, drinks poorly or not at all, a pinch of belly skin taking over 2 seconds to flatten (IMCI, p. 7; 🖼️ the pinch, WTND p. 151; Dehydration). - Keep breastfeeding and feeding, plus zinc 10–20 mg a day for 10–14 days (WHO, p. 14). - After each loose stool, by spoon: under

pinch, WTND p. 151; Dehydration). - Keep breastfeeding and feeding, plus zinc 10–20 mg a day for 10–14 days (WHO, p. 14). - After each loose stool, by spoon: under 2 years, 50–100 mL (¼–½ cup); ages 2–10, 100–200 mL (same page). - ORS packets are best. Home mix: 1 liter clean water, ½ level teaspoon salt, 6 level teaspoons sugar (JTS, p. 7), no saltier than tears (Oral rehydration). - Blood in the stool needs an antibiotic (IMCI, p. 7). Measles starts like a cold with red eyes; days later a rash spreads from behind the ears downward (WTND, p. 311). Give vitamin A: 100,000 IU at 6–12 months, 200,000 IU from 1 year (IMCI, p. 20). Clouded eyes or deep mouth sores mean severe measles (p. 8). Worms: pinworm itches at night. Cut nails short, wash hands and bottoms every morning, treat the whole family (WTND, p. 141). Hookworm enters bare feet (🖼️ how it spreads, WTND p. 142): latrines and shoes (p. 142). Mebendazole 500 mg once, from age 1, at most every 6 months (IMCI, p. 20). Untreated creek water brings giardia and weeks of diarrhea (general knowledge). 📚 Go deeper: WHO IMCI charts — every decision and dose; WHO Treatment of Diarrhoea — plans A, B, C.

📏 Growth, malnutrition and toddler food Weigh monthly and plot it on the WHO-standard charts in pounds and inches (boys; girls; Growth chart). A homemade beam scale works (WTND, p. 297; Steelyard balance). A baby whose weight drops across 2 lines is not growing well (IYCF, p. 136). Arm measurement (MUAC), 6 months–5 years, around the middle of the upper arm (IMCI, p. 10; MUAC): under 11.5 cm, or swelling of both feet (Kwashiorkor), is severe malnutrition; 11.5–12.5 cm is moderate; 12.5 cm or more is OK. Mark a paper strip at 11.5 and 12.5 cm (rule of thumb). Refeeding a severely malnourished child needs care: WHO 1999 and the Food Security guide. Toddler food and water (WHO, p. 38; p. 46; 🖼️ "five keys to safer food," IYCF p. 56): - Boil water, and boil milk that isn't pasteurized (goat milk too). - Eat cooked food within 2 hours, or reheat it until it is all boiling hot. - Feed by cup or spoon, never a bottle. Wash hands with soap. Keep animals out of the house. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Complementary Feeding — first foods; WTND, ch. 21 — growth charts.

🛡️ Accidents: drowning, burns, poisoning Drowning: a small child can drown in a few centimeters of water in a bucket (WHO, p. 78). Empty buckets and tubs; cover wells, cisterns and barrels (p. 86). Here that means rain barrels (Rain barrel), stock tanks, ditches, and the cold, deep pools of the Illinois and Rogue rivers (general knowledge). Burns: keep babies away from fires and wood stoves; turn pan handles inward. Cool a burn in clean cool water (not ice) up to 20 minutes. Never grease, fat, herbs or dung (WTND, p. 96). Canning kettles and soap-making lye are local hazards; see the Field Care guide. Poisons: lock up lye, kerosene and lamp oil, rat poison and medicines (iron pills especially), and never store them in drink bottles (WTND, p. 103). Teach children to leave alone western water hemlock by creeks and ditches, "the most poisonous plant in North America" (PNW 109; Cicuta douglasii), and the death cap mushroom (BCCDC; Death cap). If a child swallows poison (WHO, p. 155): 1. Get them away from it; strip soaked clothes; flush skin and eyes with lots of water. 2. Airway and breathing first. Unconscious: on their side (🖼️ ATP p. 79). 3. Activated charcoal within 1 hour helps for many poisons, not fuels, lye, alcohol or iron. 4. Do not make the child vomit. WHO no longer uses it, and it harms

Activated charcoal within 1 hour helps for many poisons, not fuels, lye, alcohol or iron. 4. Do not make the child vomit. WHO no longer uses it, and it harms with fuels and caustics. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Child Injury Prevention — what works; WTND first aid.

📚 Keeping children learning at home Babies and toddlers learn through play and talk (WHO/UNICEF cards): | Age | Play and talk | | Newborn | Skin-to-skin; look into the baby's eyes and talk | | 6–9 months | Clean household things to bang and drop (pot and spoon) | | 9–12 months | Peek-a-boo; hide a toy under a cloth; name things | | 1–2 years | Stack, fill and empty containers; simple questions | | 2 years + | Count, name and compare; stories, songs, picture books | Reading: the McGuffey Primer adds about 6 new words a lesson, by phonics or whole words (Primer), then the First, Second and Third Readers. Arithmetic: count real beans, corn or pebbles before pictures, then write out the sums to 20 (Ray's Primary). Mental math needs no paper (Intellectual); written math goes on in the Practical, with answers for parents in the Key. Older children teach younger ones: a 6th-grader working at 4th-grade level can help a 2nd-grader. Train tutors, or they fall back on threats and put-downs (Peer Tutoring, p. 21). 📚 Go deeper: Care for Child Development — if a child seems slow; Key to Ray's — worked answers.

🧼 Sanitation, Hygiene & Stopping Disease When sewers, pumps and power fail, cholera, dysentery, typhoid and hepatitis follow, and they all travel from human waste to someone's mouth. This guide covers toilets for every season in our clay soils, septic systems with no power, greywater, handwashing, keeping clean with little water, lice and scabies, stopping an outbreak, flies and mice, garbage, sickroom waste, and caring for the dead. The books are in Sanitation-Hygiene\ (Latrines-Toilets, Septic-Greywater, Hygiene-Washing, Disease-Outbreaks, Pests-Vectors, Waste-Burial) and Homestead-Skills\Sanitation-Water. The twin-bucket toilet, soap and cleaners are in the Make-Do Household guide; nursing the sick is in the Field Care guide. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Keep every latrine, garbage pit and grave at least 100 ft (30 m) from wells, springs and creeks, and downhill of them, with the pit bottom 5 ft (1.5 m) above groundwater (Sphere, p. 140). Some books say 65 ft (20 m). Use 100. - Wash hands with soap or ash after the toilet and before food. It cuts diarrhea by 42–47% (Tippy-Tap, p. 1). - Diarrhea kills by drying people out. Start the rehydration drink at the first watery stool (WTND ch. 13, p. 2). - Never climb down into a septic tank, pit or vault. The gases can kill in minutes (rule of thumb). - Never mix bleach with urine, ammonia or vinegar. It makes poison gas

down into a septic tank, pit or vault. The gases can kill in minutes (rule of thumb). - Never mix bleach with urine, ammonia or vinegar. It makes poison gas (Make-Do guide). - Never sweep or vacuum mouse droppings (hantavirus), and never burn plastic.

🗺️ Choosing and siting a toilet in our soils Siting: 100 ft (30 m) from any well, spring or creek, downhill of it, with the pit bottom 5 ft (1.5 m) above the water table; more in cracked rock (Sphere, p. 140). Keep latrines downwind and well away from the kitchen (FM 21-10, p. 77). On gravelly Illinois River terraces sewage travels fast toward shallow wells, so add distance (rule of thumb). Our clay is waterlogged in winter. Valley-floor soils such as Brockman clay loam have a perched winter water table only 24–36 in down and very slow drainage; septic drainfields "function poorly" on them (Soil Survey, p. 33). A pit dug there in winter fills with water. So: - Dig pits in the dry season, on higher, well-drained ground. - November to April, on the valley floor, use a bucket toilet or a compost toilet built on top of the ground. The Army switches to a pail latrine whenever the water table is too high (FM 21-10, p. 134; 🖼️ pail latrine, p. 135). | Situation | Use | | One use, away from home | Cat hole (🖼️ FM 21-10, p. 131) | | First 1–3 days, a few people | Straddle trench (🖼️ FM 21-10, p. 133) | | Indoors, any season; winter on clay | Twin-bucket toilet (🖼️ photo, OSU p. 2) or a container toilet

⛏️ Latrines step by step - Cat hole: 6–12 in deep, used once and covered at once (🖼️ FM 21-10, p. 131). - Straddle trench: 1 ft wide, 2½ ft deep, 4 ft long, parallel trenches at least 2 ft apart. Cover each use with the dug earth (Special Forces Handbook, p. 162; 🖼️ FM 21-10, p. 133), and cover well: a thin layer of soil can increase fly breeding (Rozendaal, p. 321). - Simple pit: a bit under 3 ft (1 m) across and 3–6½ ft (1–2 m) deep, under a slab whose hole has a lid that stays on (WTND ch. 12, p. 9). Hesperian says at least 6½ ft deep, with the top lined so the edge can't collapse (Ch 7, p. 19). - VIP latrine (pit latrine): add a vent pipe that rises at least 20 in (50 cm) above the roof, with fly screen on top (Hesperian Ch 7, p. 22), and keep the shelter dark, door shut. Smells go up the pipe; flies head for the light at its top and die there (Practical Action VIP Latrine, p. 1; 🖼️ how the air flows, Rozendaal p. 163; 🖼️ Hesperian Ch 7, p. 22). - Neighborhood trench latrine: about 3 ft wide, 5–10 ft deep, no more than 20 ft long, one stall per 3 ft (🖼️ WHO/WEDC, p. 57). Line the top 20 in

Neighborhood trench latrine: about 3 ft wide, 5–10 ft deep, no more than 20 ft long, one stall per 3 ft (🖼️ WHO/WEDC, p. 57). Line the top 20 in so the edges don't cave in. Solids build up at 3–5 litres (about a gallon) per person per month (Compendium, p. 44): a family of 5 fills about a cubic yard every 3 years (arithmetic). - Closing a full pit: when the waste is 1 ft below the surface, fill the rest in packed 3-in layers and mound at least 1 ft of earth on top so fly pupae can't dig out (Special Forces Handbook, p. 162). Or let it settle, top up, and plant a tree on it (Hesperian Ch 7, p. 19; 🖼️ a toilet for tree planting, p. 26; Arborloo). Indoor vented bucket: a lidded 5-gallon can lined with a heavy bag, with a hose taped into a hole near the top and run outdoors to 6 in above the ground. A full bag lifts out tied (Kearny, p. 108). Bury or compost the bags; piled outside, they breed flies. 📚 Go deeper: WHO/WEDC Technical Notes, p. 55 — trench and family latrines; Practical Action VIP Latrine — vent and slab.

♻️ Composting toilets, humanure and urine After every use, cover the deposit with 1–2 cups (200–500 mL) of wood ash or lime. It dries it, raises the pH to kill germs over time, and cuts flies and smell (SEI EcoSanRes, p. 39; Humanure). Lime burns skin and eyes: wear gloves and goggles. How long to store it before it touches a garden (SEI, pp. 39–40), with nothing fresh added: | Treatment | Store at least | | Average temperature 36–68 °F (2–20 °C) — our climate | 1½–2 years | | Average temperature 68–95 °F (20–35 °C) | More than 1 year | | Kept alkaline, pH above 9 (plenty of ash or lime) | More than 6 months | | Hot compost: all of it above 122 °F (50 °C) for a week | Hard to do at home | Then wait 1 month between spreading and harvest (p. 40). Our mean annual air temperature is 48–54 °F (Soil Survey, p. 32), so use the 2-year rule: in home composting toilets, temperatures "typically never become high enough to rapidly destroy pathogens" (EPA, p. 4). Build two chambers on top of the ground, not in it, so they work in waterlogged soil, and use them in turn (Practical Action, p. 2; 🖼️ a 2-chamber dry toilet, Hesperian Ch 7, p. 28; 🖼️ double-vault toilet, Compendium p. 60). Make each big

waterlogged soil, and use them in turn (Practical Action, p. 2; 🖼️ a 2-chamber dry toilet, Hesperian Ch 7, p. 28; 🖼️ double-vault toilet, Compendium p. 60). Make each big enough to take a year or more to fill (rule of thumb). Urine carries few germs (Kearny, p. 108), and keeping it apart (urine-diverting toilet; 🖼️ urine-separating seats, SEI p. 35) stops the smell (OSU, p. 3). On your own garden, dilute it with water and pour it on, but stop on food crops a month before harvest. For crops others will eat, store it sealed 1 month, or 6 months to be safe (SEI, pp. 21, 39). Using the finished product: worm eggs survive in soil for years (SEI, p. 23). Use aged humanure around fruit trees, berries, and crops whose edible parts don't touch soil, never on greens or root crops (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: SEI Safe Use of Urine and Faeces — the storage tables; Practical Action Compost Toilets — building a two-chamber toilet.

🏠 Septic systems with no power, and greywater Find out now which kind of septic system you have (🖼️ tank cross-section, Compendium p. 68; Drain field). - Gravity (pipes slope down to the tank and drainfield) keeps working with no power (Texas AgriLife, p. 2). Flush with a bucket of used wash water (rule of thumb). - Pump tanks, sand filters, aerobic units, pressure or drip lines stop. The reserve may be only 80 gallons for a 3-bedroom house. Use water only to flush and wash hands, stop if drains slow, and stop all use in a long outage (Texas AgriLife, p. 3); switch to a bucket toilet. Many Josephine County homes on clay or serpentine have these (rule of thumb). With no pump trucks: a tank needs pumping when scum is within 6 in of the outlet or sludge within 12 in, normally every 3–5 years. Additives do nothing. Never pour grease, oil, solvents or paint down a drain (EPA SepticSmart, pp. 3, 4, 7); keep food scraps and wipes out too (rule of thumb). After a flood: don't use it until water has left every part, and don't pump a tank empty while the ground is soaked: it can float out of the ground (Texas, p. 4). Greywater, following Oregon's rules (DEQ, pp. 3–4): - Store it no more than 24 hours. - Release it at least 2

can float out of the ground (Texas, p. 4). Greywater, following Oregon's rules (DEQ, pp. 3–4): - Store it no more than 24 hours. - Release it at least 2 in under soil or mulch, 4 ft above groundwater, 100 ft from wells, and never onto edible parts of crops or root vegetables (🖼️ a simple system, DEQ p. 15). - A soak pit (🖼️ FM 21-10, p. 130) is 5–13 ft deep, filled with rocks, 6½ ft above the highest groundwater. Clay won't take it (Compendium, p. 150). On valley clay in winter, carry greywater to higher ground or use it to flush (rule of thumb). - Kitchen water: a barrel grease trap (gravel, then ashes or sand, burlap on top), cleaned every 2 days (Special Forces Handbook, p. 164; 🖼️ FM 21-10, p. 131; Grease trap). 📚 Go deeper: Texas AgriLife Septic Systems in Outages and Floods — which systems stop; EPA Homeowner's Guide to Septic Systems; Oregon DEQ Reusing Graywater.

🧼 Handwashing and water for hygiene Build a tippy tap (USAID, pp. 1–2): 1. Take a 1½-gallon (5 L) plastic jug with a handle. Warm the base of the handle over a candle, pinch it shut with pliers, and let it cool watertight. 2. With a candle-heated nail, make a small hole in the handle just above the seal, and two bigger holes in the back, halfway up, for the hanging string. 3. Hang it from a stick so the full jug tilts at 45°. Hang soap on a string under an upside-down tin can. Pull a string tied to the cap to tip water onto your hands. 4. Scrub the outside daily; clean the inside weekly. Put one within 16 ft (5 m) of every toilet and wherever food is made. No water? Rub hands with ash or alcohol hand rub (Compendium, p. 40). Sanitizer needs 60%+ alcohol and fails on visibly dirty hands (OSU, p. 4). See hand washing (🖼️ the steps, WHO/WEDC p. 40; 🖼️ WHO handwashing steps, MCPC pp. 51–53; 🖼️ field handwashing devices, FM 21-10 p. 139) and hand sanitizer. Wash hands before cooking, eating or feeding anyone, and after the toilet, caring for someone with diarrhea, cleaning a child's bottom, cleaning up feces or vomit, or touching a body (MSF Cholera, p. 46).
