🍞 Leavening without store yeast or baking powder - Wild sourdough starter: mix equal weights of flour (whole-grain or rye starts fastest) and unchlorinated water in a jar. Every day, discard all but a little and feed it equal weights of flour and water (twice a day from day 4). Keep it at 70–82 °F. Usable around day 7, strong in 2–4 weeks — it's ready when it doubles within 4–6 hours of feeding and smells yeasty and pleasant. Throw it out if mold appears. (Illinois Sourdough 101, pp. 1–3) - Keep it going: save ½ cup each time you bake; the night before, feed it equal parts flour and water and leave it warm 6–8 hours. Store in glass, not metal, with the lid loose. (Alaska's guide warns against all metal; Illinois allows stainless steel but never copper, iron or galvanized.) (UAF Sourdough, p. 2) - Back-up: spread some starter thin, dry it until brittle, and store it airtight. Revive by crumbling into warm water overnight, then feeding. - Sourdough pancakes and muffins get ½ tsp baking soda dissolved in 1 Tbsp water, stirred in last. Never put soda in the starter itself — it can kill the yeast (UAF, pp. 2–3). - Potato yeast and "saving a piece of dough" for next time: USDA Bread and Bread Making (FB 807, p. 10) — liquid yeast keeps about two

(UAF, pp. 2–3). - Potato yeast and "saving a piece of dough" for next time: USDA Bread and Bread Making (FB 807, p. 10) — liquid yeast keeps about two weeks in a cool, dark place. - Quick breads: sour milk or buttermilk + ½ tsp baking soda per cup replaces sweet milk and baking powder (FB 1136, p. 22). Homemade baking powder = 1 part baking soda : 2 parts cream of tartar (Fannie Farmer, p. 92). | Starter trouble | Fix | | Not rising after a week | Somewhere warmer; switch to rye or whole-grain flour; avoid very hard or chlorinated water (Illinois, pp. 1–2) | | Dark liquid on top ("hooch") | It's hungry — pour it off or stir it in, then feed (Illinois, p. 3) | | Any mold | Throw it out; restart from your dried back-up (Illinois, p. 3) | 📚 Go deeper: Illinois Sourdough Bread 101, p. 4 — step-by-step loaf and schedules; UAF Sourdough, p. 3 — hotcakes, muffins and bread; USDA FB 807, p. 10 — potato yeast and saved dough.

🧂 Salt, 🍯 sweeteners and 🥓 fat - Salt from seawater (sea salt): seawater is about 3.5% salt — roughly 4–5 gallons per pound of salt in practice. Collect it away from harbors and outfalls, filter through cloth, boil down to a slush, then finish drying slowly; pour off the last bitter liquid for better taste. - Bigleaf maple syrup (OSU 2025 guide): tap after leaf drop and a hard freeze, through winter freeze–thaw days, until buds break. 5/16-inch spile in a 2-inch hole (🖼️ tapping, step by step); collect sap daily and boil it within 24 hours. Bigleaf sap is thin — about 80 gallons of sap per gallon of syrup (20 gallons ≈ 1 quart after ~8 hours of boiling). Syrup is done at 7 °F above the boiling point of water where you are — about 216 °F around Cave Junction's elevation (219 °F at sea level). (OSU EM 9163, pp. 2–8) Keep buckets lidded — "ropey" (stringy) sap is spoiled (🖼️ photos). Let syrup settle and pour it off the gritty "sugar sand"; to keep it on a shelf, bottle it at 180–190 °F into just-boiled jars (pp. 6, 8–9). - Honey: strain through progressively finer cloth, keep it sealed (wet honey ferments); render the wax for candles and salves (Practical Action brief, p. 1). Never heat honey to dry it — blow air over a

cloth, keep it sealed (wet honey ferments); render the wax for candles and salves (Practical Action brief, p. 1). Never heat honey to dry it — blow air over a pan instead. Solid ("granulated") honey is fine. (pp. 3–4) Honey replaces sugar cup for cup in baking (FB 1136, p. 23). - Lard and tallow: chill fat and render it within about a week. Melt slowly with a little water, stirring, at 235–245 °F (no copper pots), until bubbling stops and the cracklings float and turn chestnut-brown (cracklings); strain into clean jars, fill full, store cool and dark. (Minnesota, pp. 2–3) Leaf (kidney) fat makes the best lard; strong-tasting gut fat is for soap. Slightly rancid lard can be rescued by heating it with sliced potatoes until they're dark brown, then straining (pp. 2, 4). - Nut oil (hazelnuts, acorns): grind, boil with water, and skim the oil as it rises; clarify and store cool (Practical Action brief, p. 2). Discard moldy nuts first; store oil dark and airtight, never in copper (pp. 1, 6; 🖼️ hand oil presses, p. 3). - Butter: sour the cream mildly at 65–75 °F, churn at 52–66 °F until grains the size of wheat form, drain, wash twice in cold water, and work in ¾ oz salt per pound (USDA FB 876, pp. 23–24; 🖼️ the churn, p. 10; 🖼️ working the butter, p.

form, drain, wash twice in cold water, and work in ¾ oz salt per pound (USDA FB 876, pp. 23–24; 🖼️ the churn, p. 10; 🖼️ working the butter, p. 16; 🖼️ a small churn; butter churn). - ⚠️ Homemade vinegar (FB 1424) is fine for cooking, but never for canned pickles — its acid strength is unknown, and canning recipes need tested 5% vinegar (USDA Canning Guide 1, p. 28). 📚 Go deeper: OSU Making Bigleaf Maple Syrup, p. 3 — tapping, sanitation and bottling, with photos; Minnesota Making Lard at Home — rendering and what spoils lard; Practical Action Honey Processing — straining, moisture and wax; USDA FB 876 Making Butter — cream, churning and storage.

🥩 Jerky - Heat the meat to 160 °F (poultry 165 °F) before or right after drying — drying alone doesn't kill E. coli, Salmonella or trichinosis. Ten people caught trichinosis from cougar jerky in 1995 (PNW 632, p. 8); cougar and bear are hunted in our units (ODFW, pp. 67–68). Either dip strips 1½–2 minutes in simmering brine before drying, or heat the dried strips 10 minutes in a 275 °F oven (pp. 9, 17; 🖼️ oven-heated jerky, p. 14). - Dry at 145–155 °F (check with a thermometer; an oven with the door propped open works). Sun drying isn't recommended. Done when a cooled strip cracks but doesn't snap (pp. 9, 18; photos). It keeps 1–2 months. 📚 Go deeper: PNW 632 Making Jerky at Home Safely — tested methods and the hot-brine recipe; NDSU Preservation of Game Meats and Fish, p. 5 — game jerky, smoking and curing.

🥖 Staples - No oven thermometer? Put a scrap of white paper or ½ tsp flour on a tin plate in the oven; if it turns light golden brown in 5 minutes, it's right to start bread (FB 807, p. 15). Over a fire, cook on coals, not flames (OSU EM 9331, p. 4). - Danger zone: cooked food left between 40 °F and 140 °F for over 2 hours can make you sick (OSU EM 9331, p. 5). Basic yeast bread — per loaf (USDA FB 807, pp. 13–17): 1 cup lukewarm liquid, about 3 cups flour, 1 tsp salt, 1 Tbsp sugar or honey, up to 1 Tbsp fat, and yeast (or ½ cup active sourdough starter in place of yeast and part of the liquid). Knead until smooth and springy, let it double, shape, let it rise again, and bake at about 400 °F for 40–50 minutes, until it sounds hollow when tapped. Stop adding flour once the dough doesn't stick to unfloured hands — too much flour makes heavy bread. Rise it covered, at about 80 °F; it's ready for the oven when a light touch leaves a slight dent. Simple sourdough loaf: 1 cup active starter + 1 cup water + about 3 cups flour + 1½ tsp salt. Knead, let rise 4–8 hours (longer when cool), shape, rise 2–4 hours more, bake at about

starter + 1 cup water + about 3 cups flour + 1½ tsp salt. Knead, let rise 4–8 hours (longer when cool), shape, rise 2–4 hours more, bake at about 425 °F for 35–45 minutes. Poke test: a floured finger-dent that springs back halfway means bake now; one that stays means over-risen — bake at once. A preheated Dutch oven (lid on 30 minutes, then off) gives a good crust without a real oven (Illinois, pp. 5–6). Flour tortillas / flatbread: 2 cups flour, ¼ cup lard, 1 tsp salt, about ¾ cup warm water. Knead, rest 20 minutes, roll thin, cook on a hot dry pan 30–60 seconds a side. Works with part acorn or barley flour. Barley flatbread with no yeast: FAO Barley, p. 63. Biscuits (USDA FB 1136, p. 23): 2 cups flour, 1 tsp salt, 2 tsp baking powder (or the soda and sour milk swap above), 2 Tbsp fat, ⅔–¾ cup liquid. Bake hot (about 450 °F) 12–15 minutes. Keep it all cold and handle it lightly. Too much soda makes them yellow and bad-tasting (p. 22). Crackling bread: for each cup of cornmeal, ¾ tsp salt and ½ cup cracklings left from rendering lard; pour on boiling water until you can mash it by hand, shape into cakes and bake (FB 1236, p. 12). Pasta / egg noodles: 2 cups flour, 1 egg +

pour on boiling water until you can mash it by hand, shape into cakes and bake (FB 1236, p. 12). Pasta / egg noodles: 2 cups flour, 1 egg + 2 yolks, ½ tsp salt, about ⅓ cup water (or the old way: one egg, a pinch of salt and enough flour for a very stiff dough). Knead 8–10 minutes, rest 10–20, roll paper-thin, cut ⅛–¼ inch strips. Cook fresh 2–4 minutes, dried 10–12. To store, dry until the noodles snap; keep airtight about a month (longer frozen). (Illinois Extension, p. 2; Fannie Farmer 1896, p. 167) Because of the raw egg, Illinois says don't air-dry over 2 hours — finish them at about 135 °F. Hardtack (keeps for years): 3 parts flour to 1 part water (no salt — salt draws moisture and mold), stiff dough, ½ inch thick, prick with holes, bake 1 hour at 375 °F, then dry 3 more days. Soak or crumble into soup to eat. (City of Alexandria) Beans: soak overnight (6 cups water + 2 tsp salt per pound) or quick-soak (boil 2 minutes, stand 1 hour), then simmer 2–4 hours. Old beans take longer; lentils and split peas need no soak. Beans + corn (or wheat) together make complete protein. Add tomatoes or vinegar only after they're tender — acid stops beans softening (USU, pp. 2–4). Canning beans needs a pressure canner:

+ corn (or wheat) together make complete protein. Add tomatoes or vinegar only after they're tender — acid stops beans softening (USU, pp. 2–4). Canning beans needs a pressure canner: at Cave Junction's elevation a weighted-gauge canner runs at 15 lb (OSU EM 9435, p. 3). Porridge and mush: cracked wheat, oats, barley, cornmeal or leached acorn meal simmered in about 3–4 times their volume of water with a pinch of salt. Hominy grits can finish overnight in a hay box (🖼️ how to build one; 🖼️ its parts) after a 10-minute boil; coarse hominy needs longer on the fire first (FB 1236, p. 19). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 807 Bread and Bread Making, p. 12 — kneading, rising and baking; USDA FB 1136 Quick Breads and Biscuits, p. 22 — biscuits, muffins and griddle cakes; Fannie Farmer 1896, p. 92 — hundreds of everyday recipes; Practical Action Fireless Cookers, p. 5 — hay-box cooking times.Old recipes in these books are fine for methods; for food safety (canning, curing, storing) follow the modern USDA guides in Gardening-Food\.

🫙 Preserving Food Without a Freezer How to keep a garden, a deer or a run of salmon through the year with no power: canning, jars and lids when the stores are gone, jam, pickles and sauerkraut, drying, jerky and pemmican, smoking and salting fish, curing meat, and keeping lard, eggs and vinegar. Cellar storage is in the Root Cellar guide; how much to put up is in the Food Security guide. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent botulism and poisoning - You can't see, smell or taste botulism. Meat, fish, poultry, milk, beans and every vegetable except most tomatoes are low-acid. They go in jars only in a pressure canner. There is no tested way to can them without one, so dry, ferment, salt or cellar them instead. - Use a tested recipe, set for our elevation (about 1,300 ft): the 15-lb weight or 11 lb on a dial for pressure canning; water-bath times plus 5 minutes. - Boil home-canned meat and vegetables 11 minutes before anyone tastes them. - Never taste a suspect jar. Bulging lid, leaks, spurting, bad smell or mold: detoxify it and throw it out. Low-acid jars can be deadly with no signs at all. -

Never taste a suspect jar. Bulging lid, leaks, spurting, bad smell or mold: detoxify it and throw it out. Low-acid jars can be deadly with no signs at all. - Weigh curing nitrite exactly. Too much is poison. - Smoke and drying don't cook food. Cold-smoked fish is raw. Jerky must reach 160 °F.

☠️ Botulism: why low-acid food needs a pressure canner Clostridium botulinum spores are on most fresh food. Sealed in a jar of moist, low-acid food at 40–120 °F with no air, they can make a deadly toxin in 3–4 days (USDA Guide 1, p. 6). The food can look, smell and taste normal (PNW 361, p. 2). | Acid foods (pH 4.6 or lower) | Low-acid foods | | Fruit, jam, pickles, sauerkraut, tomatoes with acid added | Meat, fish, poultry, milk, beans, every fresh vegetable, most soups and stews | | Boiling-water or steam canner | Pressure canner only | The spores die only at 240–250 °F, which takes a pressure canner (🖼️ what one looks like). A boiling-water canner would need 7–11 hours, and no such times have been tested (USDA Guide 1, p. 8). Signs of botulism, usually 18–36 hours after eating: double or blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, dry mouth and weakness, then paralysis spreading down to the breathing muscles (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 110). Bad cases need weeks on a breathing machine, so prevention is everything. No honey for babies under 12 months (p. 111). Boil before eating: 10 minutes plus 1 minute per 1,000 ft above 1,000 ft, so 11 minutes here, timed from a full boil. This destroys the toxin, not the spores (PNW 361, p. 2). No pressure

1 minute per 1,000 ft above 1,000 ft, so 11 minutes here, timed from a full boil. This destroys the toxin, not the spores (PNW 361, p. 2). No pressure canner? Don't can low-acid food at all. Keep beans, corn and grain dry and roots in the cellar; ferment or salt vegetables; jerk, cure or salt meat; salt, dry, or smoke-and-can fish; and keep animals alive until you need them (general practice). Canned fruit, tomatoes, vegetables and meat need no sugar or salt for safety, only flavor (USDA Guide 1, p. 31). Jam, pickles and ferments do. 📚 Go deeper: USDA Guide 1, p. 8 — acid, heat and why the pressure canner; FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 110 — botulism symptoms; Wikipedia: Home canning.

♨️ Running a pressure canner off-grid Choose a weighted-gauge canner. It never needs testing. A dial gauge must be tested yearly; one reading high gives unsafe food (PNW 421, p. 5). The canner must hold at least 4 quart jars. Every batch (USDA Guide 1, pp. 20–22; PNW 421, p. 9; 🖼️ step-by-step drawing): 1. 2–3 inches of hot water, or 4–5 inches for fish and other long processes. Jars on the rack (🖼️ photo). 2. Lock the lid, weight off. Heat until steam pours out, then vent a full 10 minutes. Put the weight on. 3. Start timing when the weight jiggles. If pressure ever drops below the target, bring it back up and start the whole time over. 4. Turn off the heat and let it cool by itself. Never cool it with water. At zero pressure, take off the weight, wait 10 minutes, and open the lid away from your face. On a wood stove, campfire or outdoor burner there is no tested method. Canner makers forbid outdoor LP burners and any burner over 12,000 BTU. In Utah State tests, canners boiled dry within minutes and warped, and cold outdoor air breaks jars and spoils seals (WSU flyer, p. 1). Never "can" in any oven (PNW 361, p. 2). If a wood range is your only heat (general practice: untested, so the risk is yours): - Water-bath

flyer, p. 1). Never "can" in any oven (PNW 361, p. 2). If a wood range is your only heat (general practice: untested, so the risk is yours): - Water-bath canning works if you hold a full rolling boil and restart the timer whenever it stops (USDA Guide 1, p. 18). - For pressure canning, practice first with jars of plain water. Use 4–5 inches of water. Control heat by sliding the canner between hotter and cooler parts of the stovetop, not by adding wood. Restart the timer every time pressure dips. Never walk away. - If you can't hold steady pressure, don't can low-acid food. Care (PNW 421, pp. 6–8, 12): stock spare gaskets and safety (overpressure) plugs now (🖼️ where they sit). Replace a gasket that's worn, stretched or hardened. Small steam leaks are fine if pressure holds; add extra water. Clean the vent with a string. Store it dry, lid upside down, not locked. | If this goes wrong | Do this | | Steam pouring out at the lid | Replace the gasket | | Jars under-processed (boiled dry, lost the time) | Reprocess within 24 hours with new lids for the full time, or throw them out (PNW 450, p. 4) | | A jar didn't seal | New lid and reprocess within 24 hours, or keep it cold and eat it within days (USDA

🥫 Jars, lids, storage and spoilage - Mason jars last for years; only the flat lid must be new (🖼️ jar, lid, sealing compound and band). Throw out chipped jars (PNW 361, p. 3). Mayonnaise-type jars are for acid foods in a water bath only, never a pressure canner (USDA Guide 1, p. 13). - One-time metal lids shouldn't be reused. Opening warps them and the sealing compound is spent. Unused lids keep about 5 years, so stockpile them. Buy from the maker; many other sellers' lids were poor in 2021 (FN2028, p. 1). - Reusable plastic lids with rubber rings (the Tattler type) sealed safely in University of Georgia research. Follow the maker's directions exactly, which may include tightening the band as soon as the jar comes out (FN2028, p. 1). - If you must reuse a one-time lid (general practice, not tested): only on high-acid jars (jam, fruit, pickles, kraut), where failure shows as mold or fizzing, not hidden toxin. Never on low-acid food. Test seals after 12–24 hours, bands off. Press the middle: if it springs back, it's not sealed. Tap with a teaspoon: a ringing note means sealed; a dull one means not (USDA Guide 1, p. 25; 🖼️ photo). Store cool, dark and dry, 50–70 °F, never above 95 °F; use within 2 years (p. 26). Attics, sheds and garages here pass 95 °F in

p. 25; 🖼️ photo). Store cool, dark and dry, 50–70 °F, never above 95 °F; use within 2 years (p. 26). Attics, sheds and garages here pass 95 °F in summer, so use the cellar or under the house (general practice). Throw it out if the lid is loose or bulging, food has streaked down the jar, bubbles rise, the liquid is cloudy or spurts, it smells bad, or there's mold (USDA Guide 1, pp. 26–27). Also badly dented, bulging, rusty or leaking store cans (USU, p. 40). Getting rid of a suspect jar (USDA Guide 1, p. 27): 1. Gloves on. Lay jars and lids on their sides in a big pot, cover with water, and boil 30 minutes. Then discard. 2. Wipe every surface with 1 part bleach to 5 parts water, leave 30 minutes, and do it again. 📚 Go deeper: FN2028 Put a Lid On It — one-time and reusable lids; USDA Guide 1, p. 26 — storage and spoilage.

🍑 Water-bath and steam canning; jam without pectin Water bath (USDA Guide 1, p. 18; 🖼️ illustrated steps): keep 1–2 inches of water over the jars. Start timing at a hard boil; if the boil stops, start over. At the end, take the lid off, wait 5 minutes, lift the jars out, and leave them alone 12–24 hours. Steam canner (saves fuel and water): approved for acid foods only, using a tested boiling-water recipe. The total time must be 45 minutes or less. Vent until a full column of steam shows, and never open it to add water (K-State MF3241, p. 2). Jam and jelly without bought pectin: - Apples, crab apples, gooseberries, some plums and grapes have their own pectin; strawberries, cherries and blueberries don't. For jelly, use ¾ ripe and ¼ under-ripe fruit (USDA Guide 1, p. 29). - Berry jam: 4 cups crushed berries and 4 cups sugar makes 3–4 half-pints. Boil hard to 217–218 °F, or until two drops run together off a cool spoon. Process 10 minutes here (USDA Guide 7, p. 6; PNW 652, p. 26). Feral blackberries ripen by the bucketful in July and August (general practice). - Don't cut the sugar. Too little gives a weak gel, mold and yeast (USDA Guide 1, p. 30). 📚 Go deeper: PNW 652 Boiling Water Canning Project Manual — fruit, tomatoes, jam and jelly step

little gives a weak gel, mold and yeast (USDA Guide 1, p. 30). 📚 Go deeper: PNW 652 Boiling Water Canning Project Manual — fruit, tomatoes, jam and jelly step by step; USDA Guide 7 — tested jams and jellies; Wikipedia: Fruit preserves.

A 1-gallon crock) per 5 lb (🖼️ crocks and jars). - Weight it with a sealed bag of brine (3 quarts water + 4½ Tbsp salt), so a leak won't weaken the brine. October–November rooms here sit near 60–65 °F (general practice). - To can it: hot pack, 15 minutes for pints, 20 for quarts here. per gallon: 4 lb of 4-inch cucumbers, ½ cup salt, ¼ cup 5% vinegar, 8 cups water, dill. 3–4 weeks at 70–75 °F; skim scum often. Soft, slimy or bad-smelling: throw them out (USDA Guide 6, p. 7). Keep them weighted under brine at 60–70 °F. Heavy salting, no fermenting (1918): 15–25% brine keeps beans, beets, corn, chard and cabbage until spring. ☀️ Drying in our dry summers Trays and solar dryers are in the Root Cellar guide. - Sun drying needs about 90 °F, low humidity and clean air. A solar dryer (🖼️ USDA solar drier; 🖼️ brick-and-plastic dryer plan) is dependable with 3–5 days in a row near 95 °F, which is an ordinary July to September here (PNW 651, p. 16). - Not in wildfire smoke. Bring trays in when smoke settles in the valley (general practice). - Dries well (photos): apples, pears, plums, cherries, peaches, grapes, huckleberries. Not blackberries. - No sulfite dips for anyone with asthma (p. 18). - Fruit leather from windfalls: heat the purée to 160 °F first (p. 20). - Done? Pack it loosely in covered jars 2–4 days, shaking daily. Moisture on the lid means dry it more (p. 18). - Kill insect eggs before storing: 160 °F for 30 minutes (general practice). 📚 Go deeper: PNW 651 Drying Project Manual — fruit by fruit; Wikipedia: Food drying.

🥩 Jerky and pemmican Safe jerky (PNW 632): 1. Slice lean meat into strips. 2. Bring it to 160 °F (poultry 165 °F): dip strips 1½–2 minutes in simmering brine before drying (p. 9), or heat dried strips 10 minutes at 275 °F (p. 17; 🖼️ photo). 3. Dry at 145–155 °F, checked with a thermometer (🖼️ which kind), until a cooled strip cracks but doesn't snap (p. 18; 🖼️ photo). 4. Keep it sealed; it's best within 1–2 months (p. 21). Don't sun-dry meat (USU, p. 59). Bear and cougar carry trichinosis; ten people caught it from cougar jerky (PNW 632, p. 8). Pemmican: lean meat dried by sun, wind or smoke (not salt-cured), pounded, and mixed with hot rendered fat. About 6 lb of meat makes 1 lb, and it keeps for years, depending on the fat (Special Forces handbook, p. 174). There's no modern tested recipe, so (general practice): do the 160 °F step, then dry the meat brittle; render the fat until it stops bubbling; use about equal weights of meat and fat; firm tallow (deer, elk, beef) keeps better than lard; fully dry any berries. Store it cool, dark and airtight; throw it out if rancid or sour. 📚 Go deeper: PNW 632 Making Jerky at Home Safely — tested methods and the hot-brine dip; Food From Scratch — jerky basics.

Here, use red alder, bigleaf maple, oak or fruitwood (general practice). Smoke) alone doesn't preserve. With no refrigerator, can it (PNW 450, pp. 1–3): 1. Smoke lightly, up to 2 hours, to about 10% weight loss (weigh a piece before and after). Don't eat it yet. 2. Can it the same day: pints, no liquid. This recipe uses 4 quarts of cool water in the canner; don't heat it or use less (p. 3). Vent 10 minutes, then 110 minutes at the 15-lb weight or 11-lb dial. The old way, no canner (🖼️ a small fish smokehouse; 🖼️ its plan): 24 hours of cold smoke keeps fish about 2 weeks; longer keeping takes 5+ days of smoke at or below 90 °F (Fishery Leaflet 18, p. 15). Our summers are too hot, so cold-smoke October to April, when fall Chinook and winter steelhead run. In fire season, smoke only on bare ground with water at hand (general practice). Salting fish (Fishery Leaflet 18, pp. 2–7): - Bleed, gut and clean the fish well. To hold it a day with no ice, rub in about 1 Tbsp salt per ¾ lb and keep it under wet burlap in the shade. Rolled in salt, it keeps about 10 days; soak it 10 hours before cooking. - Dry salting keeps longer than brine and suits warm weather. Brined fish keeps up to 9 months if you change the brine at 3 months. Dried salt fish (what it looks like) is done when a thumb leaves no dent in the thick part. - No modern guide tests long-term salting of fatty salmon. Treat it as an old-time method and cook it well. 📚 Go deeper: PNW 238 Smoking Fish at Home Safely — brines and temperatures; PNW 450 Canning Smoked Fish — shelf-stable smoked fish.

🥓 Curing pork and venison Cold is the key: 36–40 °F for the whole cure. Warmer risks spoilage; colder slows the salt (USDA Leaflet 273, p. 5), and curing stops below 34 °F (NDSU, p. 4). Cure December to early February, when nights here fall to the low 30s (general practice). Pink premixes (curing salt): Cure #1 (6.25% nitrite) for short cures, Cure #2 (with nitrate) for long dry cures. Follow the label, commonly 1 level tsp Cure #1 per 5 lb of meat, and store it away from table salt and children (general practice). - A sweet-pickle brine should just float an egg. If it turns ropy, take the meat out and boil or replace the brine (NDSU, p. 4). - Barrel-salted meat (12–18% salt) keeps 3–4 months at room temperature (Practical Action, p. 4). 🥚 Lard, confit, eggs and vinegar - Lard: render slowly, never above 240–255 °F. The fuller the rendering, the less water and the better it keeps (Minnesota, p. 3). Steps are in Food From Scratch. - ⚠️ Confit and potted meat (meat sealed under lard) are airless and low-acid, exactly what botulism needs. No method is tested. Use them only short-term in a cold winter cellar, and boil before eating (general practice). - Eggs: fresh, clean, uncracked spring eggs, wiped not washed, in 1 quart water glass (sodium silicate) to 9 quarts boiled, cooled water, 2 inches over them, or in clear limewater (2 lb lime in 5 gallons boiled water). Prick the shell before boiling (USDA 1935, pp. 3–4). USDA says 6–9 months, FAO only 1–6 (FAO, p. 83); plan on the shorter. - Vinegar: yeast turns fruit juice to alcohol in 4–6 days. Then add 1 part unpasteurized vinegar to 4 parts juice, leave it open under cheesecloth at 70 °F or warmer, and don't disturb the "mother." It takes 3–6 months (USDA FB 1424, pp. 9–12; 🖼️ barrel "converter"). Only a titration test proves its strength (p. 30), so use it for cooking, never for canned pickles. 📚 Go deeper: USDA Home Methods of Preserving Eggs — water glass and lime; USDA FB 1424 Making Vinegar.

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - Open-kettle canning: jars "filled to overflowing," turned upside down, never processed, even vegetables (Henley, p. 605; Household Discoveries, p. 542, p. 544), and cotton batting or mutton suet "as if hermetically sealed" (p. 549). Instead: process every jar (USDA Guide 1, p. 10). - Oven canning: jars can seal and explode, and the food never gets hot enough (FB 1186, p. 37). Instead: a pressure canner. - Paraffin seals on jam (mold toxins; USDA Guide 1, p. 30), on kraut fermented at 86 °F (FB 1438, p. 14) and on smoked fish (Fishery Leaflet 18, p. 2). Instead: process jam; ferment at 60–75 °F under brine. - Borax, boric acid, salicylic acid (the folk "aspirin in the jar" trick) and salts up to 40% saltpeter (Henley, p. 363). Poisons. Instead: heat, acid and salt by a tested recipe. - "10:1 table salt and saltpeter," about ten times modern levels (Special Forces handbook, p. 174). Instead: the MSU amounts or a premix label. - Hot-smoking fish in 130–150 °F air for 2–3 hours (Fishery Leaflet 18, p. 14). Instead: 150–160 °F inside the fish for 30 minutes (PNW 238, p. 2). - Jerky dried at 120 °F with no heat step, "almost indefinitely" keeping (NDSU, p. 5), and sun-dried jerky (Special Forces handbook, p. 174). Instead: the 160 °F step. - Half-fried

Jerky dried at 120 °F with no heat step, "almost indefinitely" keeping (NDSU, p. 5), and sun-dried jerky (Special Forces handbook, p. 174). Instead: the 160 °F step. - Half-fried chops sealed under lard "until required" (Household Discoveries, p. 589). Instead: cold-cellar winter use only, boiled, or pressure-can the meat. - "Steam canners are not currently recommended" (USDA Guide 1, p. 10) is out of date. They're approved for acid foods (K-State MF3241, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: USDA Guide 1, p. 10 — the methods USDA rejects, and why; K-State MF3241, p. 2 — the current rules for steam canners.

🥔 Root Cellars & Food Storage Without Power How to keep a year's harvest with no refrigerator: root cellars, storage rooms, pits and buried barrels, cooling with water and evaporation, sun and solar drying, curing and smoking meat, fermenting, and keeping eggs. The manuals are in Food-Storage\ (Root-Cellars-Pits, Cooling-Without-Power, Drying, Curing-Smoking, Fermenting-Eggs-Vinegar); canning and freezing are in Gardening-Food\. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent food poisoning and losses - Low-acid food in sealed jars needs pressure canning — never "water bath" or "oven can" vegetables, meat or beans, and never can wild mushrooms. Follow the USDA canning guide exactly. - Cured meat needs exact amounts. Weigh salt and any curing salt (nitrite/saltpeter) — too little lets meat spoil, too much nitrite is poisonous. Follow one tested recipe; don't mix them. - Cold-smoked fish is not cooked. Hot-smoke fish to 150–160 °F inside for 30 minutes (PNW 238) unless it's heavily salted and dried. - Green potatoes are toxic (why) — store potatoes in the dark and cut away green parts. - Check stored food weekly. One rotting apple or potato spreads; remove it at once.

🌡️ The Illinois Valley problem: warm ground Old root-cellar books assume cold ground. Deep soil stays near the average yearly air temperature, and across most of the U.S. that's 49–58 °F; at 6 ft down clay still swings about ±11 °F through the year (MSU Earth Tempering, p. 2; 🖼️ ground-temperature map and chart). Here the yearly average is roughly 54 °F (rule of thumb, from Cave Junction's average highs and lows). So: - A cellar here idles around 50–58 °F. That's perfect for winter squash, pumpkins, sweet potatoes, and fine for a few weeks of most other crops. - To get it down to the 32–40 °F that potatoes, carrots, cabbage and apples want, you must cool it with cold night air in winter: open the vents on cold nights, close them on warm days (USDA FB 1939 (1960), p. 5; Agriculture Canada Pub. 1478, p. 12; 🖼️ where the cold air comes in). November–February nights here regularly fall into the 20s and 30s. - In a 50–60 °F space, root crops keep only 3–4 weeks loose — about twice as long packed in damp (not wet) sand or soil (USDA FB 1939 (1943), pp. 29–30). - Mild winters are also an advantage: many crops can simply stay in the garden all winter (see below), so you need less cellar than people in cold country. 📚 Go deeper: USDA

are also an advantage: many crops can simply stay in the garden all winter (see below), so you need less cellar than people in cold country. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1939 (1943) — storage in a 50–60 °F space, p. 29; MSU Earth Tempering — ground temperature map, p. 2; PNW 548 — winter vegetables west of the Cascades.

Below about 38 °F they turn sweet; above 40 °F they sprout sooner; they freeze near 30 °F. Keep them dark. (USDA Ag Handbook 66, p. 517) - Winter squash and pumpkins: cure about 2 weeks at 80–85 °F (a sunny porch in October), then store at 50–55 °F — colder than 50 °F damages them. 🏗️ Building a root cellar The essentials (Canada A Practical Farm Root Cellar, pp. 2–6; Novia Handbook for Building a Root Cellar; 🖼️ plan of a 10×14 ft farm cellar): 1. Drainage first. Pick a slope or high ground. On the wet valley floor, build at or above ground level and heap earth over it rather than digging into a winter water table; lay a drain pipe along the footings (Novia, pp. 8–9; 🖼️ plan and section drawings). 2. Earth cover: at least 3½ ft of soil and straw over the roof (layers of ~6 in straw and 8–12 in soil), carried well past the sides. Add soil as the straw rots. 3. Two vents at opposite ends, about 12 in square for a 10×14 ft cellar (🖼️ how the air flows through; 🖼️ vents in a cellar cross-section): - Intake: brings outside air down to about 1½ ft above the floor. - Outlet: starts at the ceiling and rises well above the roof (warm air leaves high). - Both adjustable, and screened against rodents and insects. 4. Double doors about 4 ft apart act as an air lock. Face the door north and keep it shaded so summer sun doesn't heat it (Novia, pp. 13–14). 5. Floor of earth or gravel — it holds moisture. Shelves of slats 4 in off the floor and walls so air moves around

doesn't heat it (Novia, pp. 13–14). 5. Floor of earth or gravel — it holds moisture. Shelves of slats 4 in off the floor and walls so air moves around everything. 6. A thermometer and a humidity gauge inside (or a wet rag test: if things shrivel, it's too dry — sprinkle the floor). Simpler options: - Basement-corner storage room: about 10×10 ft with an outside window. Insulate the two inside walls and the ceiling (vapor barrier on the warm side), and run an intake duct from the window down to about 18 in above the floor (Pub. 1478, pp. 8–12; 🖼️ perspective view; 🖼️ cross-section). - Above-ground and part-underground cellars: plans in USDA FB 1939 (1960) (🖼️ partly underground cellar; 🖼️ outdoor cellar, side view). - Unheated outbuilding, porch or garage: works for squash, onions and dry goods — not for the cold & moist group. 📚 Go deeper: Canada A Practical Farm Root Cellar — full plan, p. 2; Novia Handbook for Building a Root Cellar — photo step by step; USDA FB 1939 (1943) — cellars, pits and banks; Wikipedia: root cellar.

🕳️ Pits, clamps, buried barrels — and the garden itself - Cone pit (USDA FB 1939 (1943), p. 16; 🖼️ cross-section): on well-drained ground, dig 6–8 in deep, line with straw or leaves, pile the vegetables in a cone, cover with straw, then 2–3 in of earth, thickened as winter comes. Leave a tuft of straw sticking out the top as a vent and cap it with a board. Open a pit all at once and use a new spot each year (FB 1939 (1960), p. 9). - Clamp (long mound) for potatoes: a straw bed, a vent duct along the bottom, about 8 in of packed straw and up to 12 in of soil; in mild climates use more straw and less soil (FAO Prevention of Post-Harvest Losses; 🖼️ clamp drawing). - Buried barrel or trash can: a clean food-safe barrel laid in the ground on a slant so water runs out, mouth facing the path, covered with straw and earth (USDA FB 1939 (1943), p. 18; 🖼️ barrel pit; 🖼️ buried trash can). Line or wrap it with ¼-inch hardware cloth against gophers and voles (rule of thumb). - Leave it in the ground (🖼️ in-garden and mound storage): parsnips, carrots, beets, leeks, kale, collards and rutabagas can stay in the garden through most Illinois Valley winters — in raised or ridged beds so roots don't rot in

storage): parsnips, carrots, beets, leeks, kale, collards and rutabagas can stay in the garden through most Illinois Valley winters — in raised or ridged beds so roots don't rot in waterlogged soil, with straw over the roots in hard cold (FB 1939 (1960), pp. 14–17; PNW 548; 🖼️ raised beds). Gophers and voles are the main risk. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1939 (1943) — pits, banks and barrels, pp. 16–18; FAO — potato clamps.

❄️ Cooling without power - Springhouse: water from a spring or deep well sits near ground temperature — about 52–55 °F here (rule of thumb). Run it through an insulated tank or a shaded stone trough and stand crocks, milk cans and butter in it (USDA FB 976; 🖼️ insulated cooling tank). See springhouse. - Evaporative cooler — made for our dry summers: a screened cabinet covered in flannel or burlap, kept wet by wicks from a pan of water on top, in shade and breeze. In hot, dry weather it can hold about 50 °F inside; it works poorly in humid weather (USDA The Iceless Refrigerator). Bigger versions use a wall of wet charcoal, or a double brick wall with wet sand between (about 400 bricks keeps 220 lb of produce), wetted twice a day (Practical Action Evaporative Cooling, p. 2; 🖼️ charcoal cooler; 🖼️ brick cool chamber). The clay-pot zeer is the small version (Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools; 🖼️ how it works; 🖼️ pot sizes). - Ice house): ice packed in at least 15 in of sawdust on all sides, on a drained floor, keeps through summer (USDA FB 475, pp. 6, 12–13; 🖼️ insulation diagram). Valley ponds rarely freeze thick, but the bulletin shows freezing ice in metal cans on cold nights. Realistically a small ice store is a winter-only luxury here. 📚 Go deeper: USDA The Iceless Refrigerator; Practical

☀️ Drying food Our hot, dry late summer is ideal drying weather. Sun drying needs about 90 °F, low humidity and clean air; dependable drying needs several days in a row near 95 °F (PNW 651, p. 16). - Trays: wooden frames with food-safe screen (not galvanized); cover with cheesecloth or netting against insects; bring trays in at night so dew doesn't re-wet the food (USDA FB 984, pp. 13–14; 🖼️ screened solar drier). - Solar dryer: a dark box with a clear top, vents low and high, and screened trays — a 3×6 ft dryer serves a household of 4–6 (Practical Action A Simple Solar Dryer; 🖼️ layout); more designs in the Peace Corps solar food technologies manual and Practical Action Solar Drying (🖼️ cabinet and tent dryers). - Is it dry? Fruit is leathery with no moist center (photos); vegetables are brittle. Squeeze a handful of fruit: it should spring apart "like rubber bands." Then condition it 1–2 weeks in a covered jar, shaking daily — if moisture beads up, dry it more (USDA FB 984, p. 47; PNW 651, pp. 17–19). - Don't dry outdoors in wildfire smoke — ash settles on the food (rule of thumb). - Jerky: PNW 632 (🖼️ dry enough: cracks, doesn't snap). Store everything dry in sealed jars. 📚 Go deeper: PNW 651 Drying Project Manual — fruit-by-fruit and vegetable-by-vegetable; USDA FB

- Jerky: PNW 632 (🖼️ dry enough: cracks, doesn't snap). Store everything dry in sealed jars. 📚 Go deeper: PNW 651 Drying Project Manual — fruit-by-fruit and vegetable-by-vegetable; USDA FB 984 Farm and Home Drying — sun driers and evaporators.

🥓 Curing and smoking meat Dry-cured country ham and bacon keep without refrigeration once cured, smoked and aged. - Cure in the cold season: meat must stay 36–40 °F for the whole cure — warmer risks spoilage, colder stops the salt from soaking in (USDA Curing Pork Country Style, p. 5). Here that means December–February, in a cellar or shed vented on cold nights. Carver's bulletin covers curing where winters are too warm (Carver 1912). - The cure: about 8 lb salt + 2 lb sugar per 100 lb of meat, rubbed in, repeated after about a week; 1½–2 days per pound of ham (🖼️ parts of a ham; 🖼️ rubbing in the cure; Virginia Tech 458-223, p. 3; Kentucky ASC-213). Curing salt (nitrite) must be weighed exactly — use a commercial premix by its label. - Smoke with hardwood (never pine) at 100–120 °F for cured pork (Leaflet 273, p. 8). A barrel smoker at the top of a sloping covered trench, fire at the bottom, is the simplest smokehouse (USDA AWI-68; 🖼️ firebox plan). - Store: wrap cooled hams, bag in muslin or paper (🖼️ wrapped and bagged), and hang in a dark, dry, airy, rat-proof place; skipper flies don't breed below 45 °F (Leaflet 273, p. 8; 🖼️ ham pests). - Fish: dry-salting keeps longer than brining in warm weather (Fishery Leaflet 18, p. 5); hot-smoke fish

flies don't breed below 45 °F (Leaflet 273, p. 8; 🖼️ ham pests). - Fish: dry-salting keeps longer than brining in warm weather (Fishery Leaflet 18, p. 5); hot-smoke fish to safe temperatures (PNW 238; 🖼️ smoker layout). 📚 Go deeper: Kentucky How to Make a Country Ham — modern step by step; USDA Curing Pork Country Style; Fishery Leaflet 18; Wikipedia: country ham.

🥬 Fermenting, salting, eggs and vinegar - Sauerkraut: 2½% salt — 1 lb salt to 40 lb cabbage (about 3 Tbsp per 5 lb); pack in a crock) (🖼️ crocks and jars), weight it so brine covers the cabbage, skim scum. Ferment 3–4 weeks at 70–75 °F or 5–6 weeks at 60–65 °F; below 60 °F it may not ferment, above 75 °F it goes soft (USDA FB 1438, p. 14; USDA canning Guide 6). Old bulletins say 86 °F and paraffin seals — don't. - Salted vegetables (beans, greens, corn) in crocks: recipes in the 1918 Food Administration bulletin. - Eggs for 6–9 months: fresh, clean, uncracked spring eggs in a crock of 1 quart water glass (sodium silicate) to 9 quarts boiled, cooled water, with 2 in of liquid over them; or clear lime water. Prick the shell before boiling (USDA Home Methods of Preserving Eggs). - Vinegar: fruit juice → alcohol (yeast) → vinegar (air-loving bacteria). Leave the container open to air under cheesecloth and keep it at least 70 °F (USDA FB 1424; 🖼️ barrel "converter"). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1438 Fermented Pickles and Sauerkraut; USDA canning Guide 6 — fermented foods; Wikipedia: sauerkraut.

🐀 Keeping rats, mice and bugs out - Mice get through ¼-inch gaps. Use ¼-inch hardware cloth on vents and storage bins (rule of thumb); line corncribs and grain bins with galvanized hardware cloth (USDA Rat Proofing Buildings, p. 10; 🖼️ rat-proof grain bin and walls). - Foundations: concrete curtain walls 2 ft below ground, and metal or stucco on lath 2 ft up the walls, stop burrowing rats (Rat Proofing, p. 8; 🖼️ concrete curtain wall). - Grain, beans and dried food in metal or glass with tight lids. Freeze dry beans and grain 3 days (or heat them) to kill weevils — not the old chemical fumigants. - Cats, traps and tidiness — no open feed, no clutter for nesting. 📚 Go deeper: USDA Rat Proofing Buildings and Premises; Food From Scratch — storing grain.

🌱 Your Seed Bank: Grow, Harvest and Save Seed How to keep a heirloom seed bank alive for good in the Illinois Valley: store it so it lasts, test it, plant each variety at the right time here, keep varieties from crossing, and save your own seed every year — including seed from the fruits (tomatoes, cucumbers, melons, squash, peppers). It ends with the calorie crops the kit is missing and how to propagate fruit trees and berries, whose seeds don't grow true. The manuals are in Gardening-Food\Seed-Saving, Gardening-Food\Fruit-Propagation and the rest of Gardening-Food\. Written for the Heaven's Harvest "10 Year" seed bank. The company's list has 39 varieties (they note some may be swapped when seed is short), so check your own packets — the rules below are by crop, so they still apply. ### The five rules of a seed bank 1. Don't plant it all. Plant part of each packet; keep the rest sealed as a backup. 2. Start saving seed in year one — the short-lived ones first: onions, leeks, sweet corn, peppers and okra keep only 1–2 years. 3. Test germination every winter so you know what still sprouts before you need it. 4. Know which varieties cross. Several in this kit cross with each other; save seed from only one of each group per year (or hand-pollinate). 5. Vegetables aren't enough calories. Add potatoes,

which varieties cross. Several in this kit cross with each other; save seed from only one of each group per year (or hand-pollinate). 5. Vegetables aren't enough calories. Add potatoes, dry beans, a flour corn and grains. Every variety in this kit is open-pollinated (heirloom): seed you save grows the same plant as long as it didn't cross with a relative. Hybrids ("F1" on a packet) don't come true — don't save from those. (OSA Seed Saving Guide, p. 5)

🗄️ Keeping the seed bank alive Seed dies from heat and damp. Two rules from seed-storage research (Seed Processing and Storage, p. 9): - Every 10 °F cooler roughly doubles seed life. - Every 1% less moisture in the seed roughly doubles it too (🖼️ chart: moisture, humidity and storage life). - Quick test for a storage spot: temperature (°F) + relative humidity (%) should add up to less than 100. (OSA, p. 17) Where to keep it here: - Not in a shed, garage, attic or vehicle — Illinois Valley summers top 100 °F. - Best: the coolest, driest room of the house, a closet on a north wall, or a dry root cellar. - Fridge or freezer only for very dry seed in an airtight jar. Let the jar warm to room temperature before opening, or moisture condenses on the cold seed. Very dry seed (about 5% moisture) held below 20 °F still sprouted well after 20 years. (Seed Processing and Storage, p. 9) - Once you open a Mylar packet, reseal it, or move the seed into a glass jar with a desiccant packet (silica gel; 🖼️ chart: how the container affects sprouting). Label every jar with the variety and year. How long seed stays good in ordinary cool, dry storage (Univ. of Illinois seed life table, p. 2; McCormack, p. 17): | Years of good sprouting

🧪 Germination test ("rag doll") Do this every winter, and before planting any packet more than a year old (what germination looks like). (OSA, p. 18; Univ. of Illinois, p. 1) 1. Dampen a paper towel — damp, not dripping. 2. Lay out 10 seeds (more is more accurate) spaced apart, roll the towel up, and put it in a plastic bag with a little air. Label it. 3. Keep it warm: about 70 °F for most crops; 75–80 °F for peppers, eggplant, melons. Lettuce and celery sprout better with some light. 4. Check from day 3; remove sprouted and moldy seeds and count them. Slow crops (peppers, parsley-type seeds) can take up to 3 weeks. 5. Read the result: 10 of 10 — plant normally. 7–9 — sow thicker. 6 or fewer — this packet is failing: plant it now and save fresh seed this year. Fresh spinach, lettuce and pepper seed can be dormant for a few months — retest before giving up on it. 📚 Go deeper: OSA germination test, p. 18; McCormack — germination testing, p. 20.

🏡 Growing it here - Raised beds with good soil (🖼️ how they drain wet ground). Many valley soils are serpentine (high magnesium, low calcium) or slow-draining clay. Build raised beds, get a soil test before adding amendments, and add lots of compost. (OSU Soil Test Guide; Improving Garden Soils) - Water is the summer limit. Only 5–7 in of rain falls April–September. Rogue Valley gardens can lose ½ inch of water a day in hot wind (Growing Your Own, p. 21). Apply 1–1.5 in per watering (EC 871, p. 9), use drip lines, and mulch thickly. - Frost pockets: cold air drains to low ground. Plant warm crops on the warmest, sunniest ground you have, and keep row cover or old sheets ready for late-May frosts (🖼️ row cover on hoops). - Heat: lettuce, spinach and cabbage-family crops bolt or go bitter in July heat. Grow them in spring and fall, or under shade cloth on the north side of taller crops. - Deer and gophers: a 7–8 ft fence for deer; hardware-cloth bottoms on raised beds or wire baskets around roots for gophers (rule of thumb). - Bugs: encourage beneficial insects rather than spraying (PNW 550). 📚 Go deeper: Growing Your Own — Rogue Valley section, p. 21; Drip Irrigation in the Food Garden; Food Gardening with Less Water; Josephine County soil survey.

✋ Hand-pollinating and caging Squash, pumpkin and cucumber — save pure seed even when relatives grow nearby (Cucurbit Seed Production, p. 12; 🖼️ male and female squash flowers; hand pollination): 1. In the evening, find male and female flowers that will open tomorrow (yellow showing at the tips; the female has a tiny fruit behind the flower). Tape or tie them shut (🖼️ taped flowers). 2. Next morning, once the dew is off, pick a male flower, peel back its petals, and rub its pollen onto the center of the opened female — use 2–3 males. 3. Tape the female shut again and tie a tag or yarn on its stem. Save seed only from tagged fruit. Corn: cover young ear shoots with paper bags before silks appear; when silks show, bag a tassel that's shedding pollen, shake the pollen into the bag the next morning, pour it onto the silks and re-bag (OSA sweet corn guide, p. 6; 🖼️ bags and tools). Cabbage family, carrots, peppers: cover them with a cage of row cover on hoops (🖼️ row cover on hoops). Cabbage-family plants need insects to set seed (they can't pollinate themselves), so put flies or bees in the cage — or alternate-day caging: uncover only one variety each day and cover them all at night (Isolation Distances, p. 17). 📚 Go deeper: Cucurbit Seed Production, pp. 12–17; OSA

cage — or alternate-day caging: uncover only one variety each day and cover them all at night (Isolation Distances, p. 17). 📚 Go deeper: Cucurbit Seed Production, pp. 12–17; OSA sweet corn hand pollination, pp. 5–8; Isolation Distances — caging, p. 17.

🍅 Saving seed from the fruits Fruit crops have wet seed (seed saving): let the fruit get riper than you'd eat it, scoop out the seeds, clean them, and dry them. (OSA, pp. 15–16, 21–24) Tomatoes — ferment them: 1. Pick fully ripe fruit from several healthy plants of the variety. 2. Squeeze the seeds and juice into a jar; add a little water if thick. Label it. 3. Leave it at about 70–80 °F for 2–3 days, stirring 2–3 times a day. A white mold on top is normal — it eats the gel coat that keeps seed from sprouting. Stop before any seed sprouts, and keep it out of high heat (liquid in the high 80s °F can kill half the seed). (Tomato Seed Production, p. 11) 4. Add water and stir: good seed sinks; pour off the mold, pulp and floaters. Rinse in a strainer. 5. Spread thin on a plate or screen to dry (paper towels stick). Cucumbers: leave the fruit on the vine 4–5 weeks past eating stage, until it's big, yellow to orange-brown and slightly soft. Scrape the seeds and pulp into a jar and ferment about 3 days at 70–75 °F like tomatoes; good seed sinks. (Cucurbit Seed Production, p. 18) Melons and watermelon: seed is ripe when the fruit is ripe to eat. Scoop the seeds, rinse them in a strainer (watermelon

good seed sinks. (Cucurbit Seed Production, p. 18) Melons and watermelon: seed is ripe when the fruit is ripe to eat. Scoop the seeds, rinse them in a strainer (watermelon can ferment 2–3 days), and dry. (OSA, pp. 22, 24) Squash and pumpkins: leave on the vine until hard — a thumbnail won't dent it — and the stem dries. Summer squash for seed gets "about the size of your leg." Then store winter squash and pumpkins about 2 months (summer squash a few weeks) before cutting them open: the seed keeps filling out. Scoop, rinse, dry. Ferment no more than a day, if at all. (OSA, p. 24; Cucurbit Seed Production, p. 15) Peppers: pick at full color (red for both kit peppers), hold them 7–10 days at room temperature, then cut them open and scrape out the seeds. Good seed is ivory, not brown. Seed from green peppers often won't sprout. Wear gloves for jalapeños. (OSA, p. 23; Pepper Seed Production, p. 9; 🖼️ ways to get the seed out) Eggplant: leave the fruit until it turns dull brown and hard, 2–3 weeks past eating. Grate or blend the seedy end with water; good seed sinks. (OSA, p. 21) Drying all of them: a thin layer out of direct sun, below 95 °F (dark seeds in sun can overheat at 80 °F), stirred daily. (OSA, p. 16) 📚 Go deeper: OSA — wet seed processing and fermentation, p. 15; Cucurbit Seed Production — fruit maturity and washing, p. 17; Seed Processing and Storage — wet processing, p. 5.

🫘 Saving seed from dry crops These dry on the plant; harvest, thresh (beat or stomp the seed out), and winnow (pour in a breeze to blow off chaff). (OSA, pp. 19–24; 🖼️ threshing box; 🖼️ winnowing in front of a fan) - Beans and peas: let pods dry on the plant; pull plants when 70–80% of pods have turned color and finish drying under cover. Freeze shelled seed 3 days to kill bean weevils. (zine, p. 6) - Lettuce: let a few of the best plants bolt) (don't save from the first to bolt). When heads look fluffy ("feathered"), shake them into a paper bag; repeat a week or two later. In our hot summers, lettuce must flower by May or early June or seed set suffers. (OSA, p. 21; Climatic Considerations — Rogue Valley, p. 19) - Radish: dig the best roots, replant them, and let them flower; harvest when 60–70% of pods are brown and papery. (OSA, p. 23) - Spinach: sow early (it bolts as days lengthen); harvest when most seed is brown. (OSA, p. 23) - Onions and leeks: cut the seed head (umbel) when about a quarter-sized patch of black seeds shows; dry 10–14 days on paper. (OSA, p. 22) - Sweet corn: let ears dry on the stalk, rub the kernels off, finish drying below 95 °F. Save from at least 100 plants

days on paper. (OSA, p. 22) - Sweet corn: let ears dry on the stalk, rub the kernels off, finish drying below 95 °F. Save from at least 100 plants if you can — corn weakens fast when inbred. (zine, p. 9) - Okra: let a few pods dry on the plant until they rattle. - Asparagus: female plants make red berries in fall; mash, rinse and dry the black seeds. 📚 Go deeper: OSA crop-by-crop tips, pp. 19–24; OSA Bean Seed Production; OSA Lettuce Seed Production; OSA Spinach Seed Production.

🥕 Biennials: seed in the second year Carrots, beets, onions, leeks, celery, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, collards, kale, turnips and rutabagas flower only after a winter (biennials; vernalization) — they need 8–12 weeks below 50 °F. (OSA, p. 4) - Leave them in the ground where winters rarely drop below about 14 °F — true for most of the valley, but use well-drained raised beds so roots don't rot, and watch for voles. - Or dig and store the best roots ("stecklings") at 35–38 °F and high humidity — in moist sand in a root cellar — and replant them in early spring. This lets you choose the best-looking roots. (OSA, p. 4; OSA Carrot Seed Production, p. 7; 🖼️ carrot stecklings trimmed for storage) - Carrots for seed: sow in June, not April, so roots are small going into winter (small roots survive cold better). (zine, p. 15) - Cabbage: overwinter a loose, full-size head; in spring cut an X in the top so the flower stalk can get out. Kale and collards: sow June 20–July 15 and overwinter them in place. (OSA, pp. 20–21) - Beets: small roots (1–1.5 in) overwinter best. (OSA Beet Seed Production; 🖼️ trimming beet tops) 📚 Go deeper: OSA Carrot Seed Production; OSA Beet Seed Production; Climatic Considerations — Rogue Valley, pp. 19–20.

🌾 Filling the calorie gap This kit is mostly vegetables — vitamins and variety, but not many calories. To live from a garden you also need: - Potatoes — the most food per square foot in this climate. Save your own "seed potatoes": keep healthy, egg-sized tubers cool and dark over winter (rule of thumb). - Dry beans — protein that stores for years. Your Provider and Blue Lake beans can be left to dry and eaten as dry beans. (OSU Preserving Dry Beans) - Winter squash — your butternut and pumpkin store for months. - Flour or flint corn — Golden Bantam is a sweet corn; it dries for parched corn but makes poor meal. - Grains (wheat, oats, barley) and garlic — see the Food From Scratch guide for growing, threshing and milling. 📚 Go deeper: OSU Survival Basics — Food; Growing Your Own — amounts for a family of four, p. 9.

🍎 Fruit trees and berries: seeds don't come true An apple seed grows a new, different apple tree — usually a poor one. Fruit trees are kept true by grafting a twig ("scion") of the variety you want onto a rootstock (🖼️ whip-and-tongue graft, step by step). (Univ. of Minnesota Grafting and Budding; Univ. of Kentucky, p. 1) - Grow rootstocks from seed: apple and pear seeds need 70–90 days cold and moist) (in damp sand or a damp paper towel in a sealed bag in the fridge); peach 90–120 days. Then plant them; graft when the seedling is about pencil-thick. (Mississippi State Basic Grafting, p. 3) - Collect scionwood while trees are dormant (here, January–February, before buds swell): last year's growth, pencil-thick, a foot or more long. Wrap in damp (not wet) paper towel or sawdust in a sealed bag, label it, and keep it at 34–38 °F. Never store scions with apples or pears — the gas they give off ruins them. (Mississippi State, p. 3; Kentucky, p. 4; 🖼️ scion wood ready for storage) - When to graft: whip-and-tongue Feb–early March while dormant; cleft graft late Feb–March (🖼️ cleft graft); bark graft in spring once the bark slips (🖼️ bark graft). Budding (a single bud under the bark) in July–September. (Mississippi State, pp. 3–4; USDA FB 1567, p. 43; 🖼️ T-budding) - Peaches and apricots from seed

slips (🖼️ bark graft). Budding (a single bud under the bark) in July–September. (Mississippi State, pp. 3–4; USDA FB 1567, p. 43; 🖼️ T-budding) - Peaches and apricots from seed often give usable fruit, but not the same as the parent (rule of thumb). - Berries and grapes are easier: - Raspberries and blackberries: bury a cane tip in late summer — it roots ("tip layering") — or dig suckers. (Virginia Tech, p. 4; 🖼️ tip layering; Layering) - Strawberries: root the runners. (Virginia Tech, p. 5) - Grapes: dormant hardwood cuttings. 🍄 Mushroom Guide How to identify, use, preserve and grow mushrooms in the Illinois Valley — and how not to die doing it. The field guides, poisoning reports and growing manuals are in Mushrooms\ (Identification, Poisoning-Safety, Uses-Growing-Preserving). Wild-Plants\ also has the Forest Service Wild Edible Mushrooms of the Pacific Northwest and death cap ID sheets. ### ⚠️ The rules that keep foragers alive 1. Only eat a mushroom you have identified with complete certainty — every feature, including the spore print and the base of the stem. "Pretty sure" is how people die. 2. No folk test works. Silver turning dark, a peeling cap, animals or insects eating it, soaking in salt water, cooking — none of these tell you anything. Cooking, drying, freezing and canning do not destroy the deadly toxins. (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 218) 3. The deadliest ones taste fine and make you sick late — 6 to 24 hours or more after eating. By then the toxin is already in your liver or kidneys. 4. Dig up the whole mushroom — the cup or bulb at the base is what tells you it's a deadly Amanita. Never eat unopened "buttons" of gilled mushrooms; nobody can tell a deadly button from a safe one. (USDA FB 796, pp. 3, 6) 5. Cook every wild mushroom thoroughly. Try a small amount of any new kind, eat in

tell a deadly button from a safe one. (USDA FB 796, pp. 3, 6) 5. Cook every wild mushroom thoroughly. Try a small amount of any new kind, eat in moderation, and keep one uncooked specimen in the fridge in case someone gets sick. (PNW/BC White Paper, p. 10)

🔎 How to identify a mushroom Check all of these, every time: - Underside: gills (thin blades), pores (a sponge of tubes — boletes), teeth or spines (hedgehogs), or blunt ridges (chanterelles). (See gills); 🖼️ labeled drawing of the parts; 🖼️ gills, pores, ring and cup.) - Stem base: dig it up. A cup (volva) or bulb at the base, plus a ring on the stem and white gills, means Amanita — leave all of them alone. (FB 796) (See volva) and ring); 🖼️ a death cap dug up, showing both; 🖼️ the "egg" the cup comes from.) - Spore print: cut off the stem of a mature cap, lay the cap gills-down on half white, half dark paper, cover with a glass, and wait a few hours. The color (white, pink, brown, rusty, purple-black) places the mushroom in its family. (Thomas Field Book; Atkinson, p. 373; pictures: Spore print; 🖼️ a spore print) - Where it grows: on wood or soil, under which trees (oak, tanoak, Douglas-fir, pine), alone or in clumps, and the season. - Flesh, smell and bruising: does it stain when cut? Is the flesh brittle or stringy? Spore print colors and what they point to: | Print color | Examples here | Note | | White | Deadly Amanitas, oyster, shiitake, matsutake, false chanterelle | White alone proves nothing — the death cap is white-spored

| Print color | Examples here | Note | | White | Deadly Amanitas, oyster, shiitake, matsutake, false chanterelle | White alone proves nothing — the death cap is white-spored (Hard, p. 40; GTR-576, p. 35) | | Yellowish white | Pacific golden chanterelle | (GTR-576, p. 38) | | Pink to salmon | Pluteus, Entoloma | (Hard, p. 255) | | Rusty to brown | Deadly Galerina, Cortinarius webcaps, poison pax | A brown print on a "shiitake" means Galerina (Cornell-UVM, p. 41) | | Purple-brown | Agaricus (meadow mushroom family) | (Hard, p. 327) | | Black | Inky caps | (Hard, p. 351) | Collecting, step by step: 1. Carry a basket, a knife, a trowel and paper bags or wax paper. Plastic makes mushrooms sweat and rot. (Thomas, p. 29) 2. Dig out the whole mushroom — don't snap the stem — so the base stays attached. 3. Keep each kind in its own bag. Some poisons sicken people even from a sauce the mushroom was cooked in (Bad Bug Book, p. 218), so one stray deadly cap in a basket of edibles is a real danger. 4. Note the tree, the ground, the date. Take a photo of the spot. 5. At home, sort on a clean table, make spore prints, and throw out anything you can't name with certainty — and wash your hands.

a photo of the spot. 5. At home, sort on a clean table, make spore prints, and throw out anything you can't name with certainty — and wash your hands. 6. Learn from someone who knows. CDC's advice after the 2016 California outbreak: have wild mushrooms checked by an experienced mycologist before eating (CDC MMWR 2017, p. 4). In Switzerland, where trained checkers inspect foragers' baskets, none of the checked mushrooms caused a hospitalization in 15 years (White Paper, p. 11). 📚 Go deeper: Wild Edible Mushrooms of the PNW (USFS PNW-GTR-309) — labeled drawing of mushroom parts and the life cycle; Thomas Field Book — how to collect, and a key by spore color; Atkinson — making spore prints, many photos. Poisoned 5 Oregonians in 1988; 4 needed liver transplants. | | Western destroying angel (Amanita ocreata) | All-white, cup at the base, under oaks. Brittle flesh. | Kidney failure, 2–5 days later (White Paper, p. 6). | | Deadly webcaps (Cortinarius, orellanine; e.g. C. rubellus) | Orange to red-brown, dry, fibrous cap, rusty gills, under conifers (🖼️ photos). | Kidney failure, 3–14 days later. | | False morels (Gyromitra) | Brain-like or saddle-shaped cap, not pitted, chambered stem (🖼️ photo). | Vomiting, seizures, liver damage; fumes from cooking

| Kidney failure, 3–14 days later. | | False morels (Gyromitra) | Brain-like or saddle-shaped cap, not pitted, chambered stem (🖼️ photo). | Vomiting, seizures, liver damage; fumes from cooking can poison the cook. | (CDC 2017 death-cap report; NAMA poisoning registry; PNW/BC White Paper; USFS reports) Death cap checklist (BC Forests profile, pp. 5–7; 🖼️ color photos; 🖼️ young and open caps; 🖼️ old photo: cup, ring, scaly stem): cap 4–16 cm (1½–6 in), usually olive or greenish but can be pale brown, yellow or white, with a satiny sheen when dry · white gills · a skirt-like ring · a loose, sac-like cup at the base, often below ground · near hardwoods, especially planted ones. Fruits in fall, but in summer where lawns or orchards are watered (BCCDC briefing, p. 8). - How little it takes: a lethal dose can be as low as 0.1 mg per kg of body weight, and one mushroom can hold up to 15 mg (CDC MMWR 2017, p. 3). Half a cap can kill a small child (White Paper, p. 8). - Boiling and pouring off the water doesn't help (BCCDC, p. 5). - Young death caps look like puffballs — see the puffball slice test below (🖼️ sliced side by side; 🖼️ more look-alikes). - Dogs die from it too — puppies especially (BC Forests, p. 8). Poisoning timeline — deadly

the puffball slice test below (🖼️ sliced side by side; 🖼️ more look-alikes). - Dogs die from it too — puppies especially (BC Forests, p. 8). Poisoning timeline — deadly Amanita, Galerina, Lepiota: nothing for 6–24 hours, then violent vomiting and diarrhea, then a false recovery around day 1–2, then liver (and kidney) failure at day 3–5. 10–20% die even with hospital care. (CDC MMWR 2017, p. 3) Sources differ on the death rate: BC public health says 10–30% even with treatment (BCCDC, p. 5); NAMA's records show about 11% of people who got sick (NAMA 2018–20, p. 3); FDA says 50–90% for people who reach care late, about 10% for those treated almost at once (Bad Bug Book, p. 219). Without a hospital, expect the worst. When did the symptoms start? A quick guide (Bad Bug Book, pp. 219–221; White Paper, p. 6): | Symptoms begin | Likely cause | Usual outcome | | 15 min – 2 hours: nausea, cramps, diarrhea | Many "stomach upset" mushrooms | Recover in hours to 2–3 days; replace fluids | | 15–30 min: heavy sweating, tears, drooling | Muscarine (Clitocybe, Inocybe) | Recover in about 2 hours | | 1–2 hours: drowsy, confused, excited | Fly agaric (🖼️ old photo), panther cap | Recover after several hours | | About 6 hours: bloated, bad headache, vomiting | False morel (gyromitrin), Verpa |

confused, excited | Fly agaric (🖼️ old photo), panther cap | Recover after several hours | | About 6 hours: bloated, bad headache, vomiting | False morel (gyromitrin), Verpa | Recover in 2–6 days; some deaths from liver failure | | 6–24+ hours: violent vomiting and watery diarrhea | Amatoxin — death cap, Galerina, small Lepiota | False recovery, then liver failure; often fatal | | 2–5 days: kidney trouble | Amanita smithiana | Kidney failure | | 2 days – 3 weeks: burning thirst, peeing a lot, then kidney failure | Orellanine — deadly webcaps | Months to recover, or death | | ½–2 hours after drinking alcohol, within 3 days of eating: flushing, racing heart | Inky cap (coprine) | Passes in a few hours | The rule this table teaches: if symptoms start 6 hours or more after the meal, treat it as deadly until proven otherwise (rule of thumb from the table above). 📚 Go deeper: FDA Bad Bug Book, mushroom chapter — each poison type, onset and outcome; PNW/BC White Paper — color photos of our six deadliest; BC Forests death cap profile — death cap photos, look-alikes and host trees; NAMA Cortinarius rubellus report — the kidney-destroying webcap.

🚑 If someone may have eaten a bad mushroom - Get medical help immediately, even if they feel fine — the dangerous ones are delayed. Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222. - Bring the mushroom — leftovers, the uncooked ones, even scraps from the trash — in a paper bag (they rot in plastic). A photo is far less useful than a sample. (White Paper, p. 6; Michigan sheet, p. 2) - The main hospital treatment for amatoxin is aggressive IV fluids — NAMA calls it "by far the best single intervention" (NAMA 2018–20, p. 4; CDC MMWR 2017, p. 3). Liver drugs such as silibinin (from milk thistle) are tried, but proof is thin. Sources disagree on activated charcoal: FDA lists it as part of prompt treatment (Bad Bug Book, p. 229), CDC says it has no proven benefit for amatoxin, and NAMA says it's useless more than about 1 hour after eating. With no hospital: replace fluids constantly (oral rehydration solution — see the Medical guides), give activated charcoal only if they ate the mushroom within the last hour or so, and rest. Survival odds are much worse without a hospital — which is why rule 1 matters so much. - Don't be fooled by the false recovery. In the 2016 California outbreak, people sent home with "stomach flu" came back in liver failure (CDC MMWR 2017, p. 3). One Québec

Don't be fooled by the false recovery. In the 2016 California outbreak, people sent home with "stomach flu" came back in liver failure (CDC MMWR 2017, p. 3). One Québec man with orellanine poisoning put up with mild symptoms for 18 days before his kidneys failed (NAMA 2021, p. 2). - Write down (rule of thumb): what was eaten and how much, raw or cooked, the time of the meal, the time symptoms started, who else ate it, and any alcohol. Check everyone who shared the dish — and any pets. 📚 Go deeper: CDC MMWR 2017 death cap outbreak — 14 real cases, hour by hour; NAMA 2018–2020 summary — what treatments work and which don't; BCCDC Wild Mushrooms May Be Poisonous — one-page symptoms and what to do.

🫙 Cooking, drying and storing - Cook all wild mushrooms — never raw, and morels especially well done. Don't mix alcohol with morels the first time (some people react). - Eat a few mouthfuls, not a plateful, of any wild mushroom, and not several days running — big servings cause reactions even with "safe" kinds like morels (White Paper, pp. 10–11). In 1991, 77 of 483 guests at a Vancouver banquet got sick from morels served raw (p. 10). - Fresh storage: in the refrigerator (40 °F or colder) in a paper bag — CDC's advice for morels (CDC 2024, p. 5). Don't freeze them raw — bacteria keep growing (NAMA 2018–20, p. 2). - Dry slices about ½ inch thick at about 120 °F with good airflow (dehydrator) until crisp; morels lose about 90% of their weight. Store airtight. Rehydrate in hot water. Ventilate while drying — spores can trigger asthma. (OSU SP 50-919, p. 2; USFS PNW-GTR-710, pp. 66–67) - No dehydrator? In warm, dry weather, dry on screens, threaded on fishing line, or in a single layer on a tarp, turning them; or use the warm air near a wood stove with a fan. Moving dry air matters more than heat — don't go over 120 °F (GTR-710, pp. 66–67). Shiitake dried in sunlight gain vitamin D; 7 lb fresh makes about 1 lb dried (Agroforestry Note

matters more than heat — don't go over 120 °F (GTR-710, pp. 66–67). Shiitake dried in sunlight gain vitamin D; 7 lb fresh makes about 1 lb dried (Agroforestry Note 13, p. 4). - Freeze after sautéing (best) or steam-blanching. To steam: soak 5 minutes in 1 teaspoon lemon juice per pint of water, then steam whole 5 minutes, quarters 3½, slices 3, cool in ice water, pack and freeze (OSU SP 50-919, p. 2). - Never can wild mushrooms — only store-type button mushrooms have tested canning times (OSU SP 50-919, p. 1). Improperly canned chanterelles gave diners botulism in Vancouver in 1987 (White Paper, p. 10). - Recipes from the old books — fine for cooking ideas once the mushroom is safely identified: McIlvaine's 15-page recipe chapter (p. 813), Mrs. Rorer's recipes in Atkinson (p. 379), Gibson (p. 321) and Thomas (p. 381). Skip their raw-mushroom salads and anything about canning. 📚 Go deeper: OSU Preserving Mushrooms SP 50-919 — freezing, drying and why only button mushrooms can be canned; Morels of Western North America — drying with and without power; McIlvaine recipe chapter — old-time cooking and drying methods.

🪵 Growing your own - Shiitake on logs: fresh hardwood logs (oak is among the best) 4–6 inches across, cut in the dormant season while the bark is tight. Drill holes 7/16 inch wide, 1¼ inches deep, 3 inches apart in a diamond pattern, plug with spawn, seal with wax (🖼️ drill, plug, wax). Keep shaded and moist. Mushrooms start in 6–18 months; after that, soak a log 24 hours and it fruits about a week later. Rest logs 8–12 weeks between soaks. (UVM/Cornell, p. 20; USDA Agroforestry Note 13, p. 3) - Oysters on straw: chop straw 4–5 inches, soak overnight, pasteurize at 165 °F for 1–2 hours, mix in 5–10% spawn, pack into bags with holes, keep warm and humid. Fruits in weeks. (UF IFAS SS662, p. 2; 🖼️ step-by-step photos) - Keep your strain going: a piece of a fruiting log or colonized straw can start the next batch, so you don't need to buy spawn again. Shiitake details: - Logs: 3–8 inches across and 2–4 feet long. A 4-foot, 8-inch log can weigh 80 lb. Cut from live trees roughly Thanksgiving to St. Patrick's Day, and inoculate within two weeks (Agroforestry Note 13, pp. 2–3). - Hole spacing: the sources differ — Cornell says 3 inches apart with as many rows as the log has inches of diameter (p. 20); the USDA note says 6 inches

Hole spacing: the sources differ — Cornell says 3 inches apart with as many rows as the log has inches of diameter (p. 20); the USDA note says 6 inches apart with one row fewer (p. 3). Either way, stagger the rows in a diamond pattern. - Spawn: one 5-lb bag of sawdust spawn does about 20–25 logs 4–6 inches by 3 feet (Cornell-UVM, p. 21). - Laying yard (🖼️ ways to stack logs): 75–100% shade all year — under conifers is best; the north side of a house or shed works for a few logs. Keep logs above 30% moisture; in a dry spell soak them a few hours or sprinkle them (Cornell-UVM, p. 23). - Harvest when caps are 60–75% open, edge still slightly curled under (Agroforestry Note 13, p. 4; Cornell-UVM, p. 39). Logs keep producing for up to 6 years; about 10 logs feed a family. - Check every brown mushroom on your logs. Deadly Galerina can pop up on shiitake logs. Make a spore print: shiitake is white, Galerina brown; shiitake never has a ring (Cornell-UVM, p. 41; 🖼️ Galerina photo; Galerina vs. shiitake photos). Oyster details (UF SS662, pp. 2–4; 🖼️ bags as they colonize and fruit): incubate filled bags in the dark at 75–77 °F and 80–90% humidity until white all through (mycelium, 2–3 weeks); then give them light, about 68 °F, 90%

colonize and fruit): incubate filled bags in the dark at 75–77 °F and 80–90% humidity until white all through (mycelium, 2–3 weeks); then give them light, about 68 °F, 90% humidity and fresh air. Pick clusters by twisting. Expect 2–4 more flushes. If this goes wrong: | Problem | What to do | | Logs haven't fruited after 18 months | Check the log ends for white mycelium. Force with a 24-hour cold soak once nights average above 50 °F (Cornell-UVM, p. 32). | | First flush was tiny | Normal. Try again about two months later (p. 32). | | Slugs eating the crop | Pick slugs by flashlight at night, let chickens into the yard by day, put gravel under fruiting logs (p. 38). | | Green or black mold on logs | Competing fungi. 🌿 Medicinal mushrooms Turkey tail, reishi, lion's mane and shiitake have real research behind them as add-ons to treatment — turkey-tail extract (PSK) is a prescribed cancer add-on in Japan — but most evidence is from lab and animal studies. They are not cures. Turkey tail and reishi are traditionally simmered for hours as tea. (VA Mycomedicinals, pp. 1–3) - Making the tea: simmering or boiling in water for 20 minutes to 2 hours breaks down the tough cell walls and releases the active compounds (VA, p. 1). - Who should be careful: people with leukemia or lymphoma, after a bone-marrow transplant, or on drugs that suppress the immune system — these mushrooms act on the immune system (VA, p. 3). - No panacea: in one mouse study a reishi extract made tumors grow faster (GTR-309, p. 31). 📚 Go deeper: VA Mycomedicinals — what the research shows for turkey tail, reishi, lion's mane and shiitake; Agroforestry Note 13 — growing lion's mane on logs.The old mushroom books here (1895–1928) are great for pictures, descriptions and recipes, but some of their safety advice is wrong and has killed people: Marshall's Mushroom Book lists false morels as edible, Thomas says the parasol has no poisonous look-alike, and USDA FB 796 recommends raw mushrooms and old first aid. Bullets pass through game and keep killing. Never shoot at a sound, a color or movement. - Cook all wild meat through. Bear, cougar, raccoon and beaver can carry trichinella worms that survive freezing, smoking and drying. - Wear gloves to skin rabbits, rodents, beaver and anything with fleas (tularemia, plague). Never shoot a deer or elk that looks sick, and never eat its brain, spine, eyes or lymph nodes. - Check every trap every day at first light. Never set man-killing traps where people or pets walk. - Take the surplus, never the breeding stock. Never poison a

🌱 Take the surplus, never the seed Every year a wild population has two parts. The breeding stock is what the land can carry through the hard season. The surplus is the animals that will die anyway before next year's young are born. Take the surplus and the land feeds you again next year. Take the breeding stock and it doesn't (NY trapper manual, p. 13). Game laws were written to do exactly this, after the last time it went wrong. While ODFW and the state police still work, follow the rules. If enforcement stops, the reasons don't: - Elk nearly vanished from our forest. In 1910 the Forest Service called elk "very scarce" on the Siskiyou National Forest, and in 1932 it counted about 40. Elk mate in October, calve in June, and have one calf, so a shot-out herd takes decades to recover (Bailey 1936, p. 114; p. 115). - Deer: "unrestricted hunting soon cleans out the deer." Keep no more than about 5 does per buck. If does aren't each raising their usual two fawns, there are too few bucks or too many predators (Bailey, p. 120; written for mule deer, but it holds for blacktails). - Spare the hens. "Adult hens are the backbone of Oregon's forest grouse flocks." They are most exposed early in the season while tending chicks. Spring turkey is one bearded bird

Spare the hens. "Adult hens are the backbone of Oregon's forest grouse flocks." They are most exposed early in the season while tending chicks. Spring turkey is one bearded bird only, because hens are nesting (ODFW bird regs, p. 32; p. 24). - Let small fish go. Fit traps with escape gaps (🖼️ drawing). A gill net's mesh should be about 0.4 × the girth of the fish you want; smaller mesh kills young fish before they spawn (FAO, p. 24; Twinework, p. 64). - Lost gear keeps killing for days or months, and nylon nets never rot. Mark and anchor gear, and tie one panel with cotton or plant twine that rots away (FAO, p. 59; Twinework, p. 41). - The Hupa weir. On the Trinity River, about 70 miles south, Hupa families built a salmon weir in late summer, fished it at night, and kept family fishing spots that were "always respected." The first high water swept it away (Goddard 1903, p. 34; p. 36). A weir left across a whole river all season would take the whole run. Leave gaps, and fish only part of each night and part of the run (general practice). Illinois River coho are federally threatened. 📚 Go deeper: NY trapper manual, p. 13 — surplus and carrying capacity; Bailey, p. 120 — how deer herds were shot out; Goddard, p. 34 —
