🎯 Safe shooting, shot placement and tracking The four rules (Hunter ed, p. 40): 1. Point the muzzle in a safe direction. 2. Treat every gun as loaded. 3. Be sure of your target and what is in front of it and beyond it. 4. Finger off the trigger until you are ready to shoot. Shot placement (Hunter ed, p. 61; CT DEEP, p. 3; 🖼️ where the organs lie in deer, elk, bear and small game): - Big game: heart and lungs, just behind the front shoulder, broadside. With a bow, a third of the way up the chest when the near leg is forward. - Never take head-on, rear-end, running or straight-away shots. A wounded, stressed animal suffers, and its meat tastes stronger. - Turkey (🖼️ gobbler and hen): head and neck. Rabbits and squirrels: head or chest (Ohio DNR, p. 2). Oregon's legal minimums are also humane-kill minimums: no .22 rimfire on deer, elk or bear; broadheads unbarbed and at least 7/8 in wide; bows at least 40 lb draw; bow shots 40 yards or less (ODFW big game regs, p. 22; Hunter ed, p. 70). After the shot (Hunter ed, pp. 62–63): 1. Watch every move the animal makes after the shot. Wait 30–60 minutes unless it is down in sight. 2. Follow blood, hair, kicked leaves and broken twigs. Wounded animals often head downhill toward

the animal makes after the shot. Wait 30–60 minutes unless it is down in sight. 2. Follow blood, hair, kicked leaves and broken twigs. Wounded animals often head downhill toward water. Flag the trail; if you lose it, search in a circle or grid. 3. Approach from above and behind the head. If the open eye doesn't blink when touched with a stick, it is dead. 📚 Go deeper: Hunter ed manual, p. 61 — shot angles with drawings; Big Game Recovery — reading blood sign; CT DEEP — vital zones.

🔪 Field dressing and the gutless method Field dressing (PNW 517, pp. 7–8; Hunter ed, p. 64; 🖼️ step drawings; 🖼️ step photos): 1. Prop the animal on its back with its head slightly downhill. 2. Cut the hide from the inside out, so hair stays off the meat. Open the belly without cutting the stomach (rumen). 3. Cut the diaphragm and the windpipe. Tie off the colon before you pull it through. 4. Don't touch the dark-haired glands inside the hind legs, just below the hock. They taint the meat. 5. Drain the blood. If you must drag it, sew the cavity shut. Gutless method) — best on steep ground, alone, or in hot weather (Kentucky, p. 1; PNW 517, pp. 9–10; 🖼️ illustrated steps): 1. Skin the top side. Take off the front shoulder (no joint holds it on) and the hindquarter. 2. Take the backstrap and neck meat. Ease the tenderloins out last, without nicking the gut. 3. Flip the animal and repeat. You never open the body or saw the spine, which also avoids the spinal cord (chronic wasting disease). Drag the gut pile at least 25 ft from where you hang the meat (PNW 517, p. 12). 📚 Go deeper: OSU PNW 517 Big Game from Hunt to Home — dressing and quartering with photos; Kentucky gutless method; Kentucky elk quartering.

🌡️ Cooling meat in our heat Heat is the enemy. Cave Junction's summer average is 67 °F and Grants Pass has hit 108 °F (Josephine soil survey, p. 5), and archery deer season falls in late August and September. - Get the meat below 40 °F within 24 hours (PNW 517, p. 6). - Hang it in a shady thicket at night. By day, wrap it in cold canvas and lay sleeping bags over it to hold the night's chill. Skin the carcass unless the night will freeze (Montana State, p. 2). - Don't wrap warm meat. Game bags, canvas and paper hold heat in. Keep it in moving air until it is below 40 °F (PNW 517, p. 11). - Meat from a warm day, or from an animal that ran hard or was wounded, should not be aged. Cut it up and preserve it as soon as it is chilled. - Scrape off blowfly egg clusters. Black pepper on moist spots and flapping cloth strips keep flies and ravens off (p. 12). - Birds: keep them at 40 °F or below (NDSU game birds, p. 2). - With no refrigerator, cut and preserve meat the same day: can it, cure it in winter, or make safe jerky (see the Preserving Food guide). 📚 Go deeper: PNW 517, p. 11 — cooling, game bags and flies; Montana State Field
it, cure it in winter, or make safe jerky (see the Preserving Food guide). 📚 Go deeper: PNW 517, p. 11 — cooling, game bags and flies; Montana State Field Care — keeping meat cold in warm weather.

🥩 Butchering, using the whole animal, and hides Bone it out (Wyoming B-884R, p. 2; p. 4): - Take the shoulder off along its natural seam, then the loin. Follow the hind leg's muscle seams into the sirloin tip, top, bottom and eye of round (🖼️ photos of each cut). - Grind the tough heel and trimmings, and preserve trimmings the day you cut them. - A 349-lb field-dressed cow elk gave 148 lb of boneless meat, about 42%. Use the whole animal: - Heart, liver, tongue and kidneys are good. Wash the heart and liver in cold water at once. A healthy liver is smooth, wet and deep red-purple. Throw out a spotted or odd-colored liver; the muscle meat may still be fine (PNW 517, p. 12). - Beaver, muskrat and raccoon are good eating: the quarters and back. The rib cage is usually discarded (Trapper Education Manual, p. 106; FM 3-05.70, p. 153). - Save the fat. People living on lean meat alone get sick ("rabbit starvation," (rule of thumb); see the Rabbits & Chickens guide). Brain-tanned buckskin), no chemicals (Farnham 1916, pp. 73–74; brain tanning)): 1. Soak the hide in water, or water and wood ashes, until the hair slips. Flesh it, then scrape off the hair and grain (🖼️ unhairing). 2. Boil the brains about an hour in a gallon of water. Cool until you can

the hair slips. Flesh it, then scrape off the hair and grain (🖼️ unhairing). 2. Boil the brains about an hour in a gallon of water. Cool until you can hold your hand in it. 3. Work the hide in it, and stretch it while it dries. Repeat until soft (🖼️ softening over a stake). 4. Smoke it over smoldering punky wood, never flame (p. 145). Use brains only from healthy animals, and wear gloves (chronic wasting disease). Bark tanning uses 30–40 lb of ground oak or hemlock bark per hide (USDA FB 1334, p. 14); our tanoak was the old "tanbark" (general practice). Full tanning steps are in the Clothing & Leather guide. 📚 Go deeper: Wyoming Skinning and Boning Big Game — cuts with photos; Farnham, p. 73 — buckskin the old way; USDA FB 1334 — bark and alum tanning.

🪤 Trapping, snaring and deadfalls Where you set matters more than the trap (FM 3-05.70, pp. 127–128): - Set on a run (small, used by one species) or at feeding, watering and bedding spots. A trail is used by many species. - Funnel the run with sticks down to just wider than the animal (🖼️ drawing). Don't use freshly cut green wood, which smells of sap. Hide your scent with mud or smoke. - A squirrel pole carries several wire nooses 2–2¼ in across, set 1 in off the pole (p. 132; 🖼️ drawing). Traps with no store-bought gear: the figure-4 and Paiute deadfalls need only sticks and cord (FM 3-05.70, p. 137; 🖼️ Paiute deadfall). Harding's 1907 Deadfalls and Snares shows many more (🖼️ spring-pole snare, 🖼️ trail snares). A box trap keeps rabbits unhurt ("the best for eating") and lets you release a cat, dog or hen unharmed (p. 146; 🖼️ drawing). Check every trap every day, at first light. Most furbearers move at night. Early checks mean less suffering, fewer escapes and less theft by other animals. Don't set more traps than you can check, and stay away from places where pets roam (Trapper Education Manual, p. 99; NY manual, p. 3). Keeping pets out (AFWA body-grip guide, pp. 9, 15–16): - For raccoon, use sweet baits (marshmallow, molasses, corn syrup, corn) that dogs and cats ignore,

99; NY manual, p. 3). Keeping pets out (AFWA body-grip guide, pp. 9, 15–16): - For raccoon, use sweet baits (marshmallow, molasses, corn syrup, corn) that dogs and cats ignore, not meat or fish. - Raise body-grip cubbies 4–6 ft up a tree (🖼️ cubby on a tree). - Set trail traps 5–6 ft in front of a fence crossing, not under it, so big dogs pass by (🖼️ trail-set drawings). Beaver: #330 body-grip traps or cable devices at slides, scent mounds and channels. Bait with fresh poplar, willow or cottonwood sticks. Use sliding-lock sets in water so the beaver drowns quickly (Trapper Education Manual, p. 138). 📚 Go deeper: Trapper Education Manual — sets, baits and running a trapline; Harding Deadfalls and Snares — illustrated improvised traps; AFWA dog-friendly sets — keeping pets safe.

🎣 Fishing, nets, fish traps and fish care While the rules are enforced (ODFW fishing regs, p. 19): one rod per person, lines closely attended (so no unattended set lines), and no snagging. Local waters and seasons are on Start Here. Nets and stream traps (AFH 10-644, pp. 311, 314): - Set a gill net at a slight angle to the current so debris washes off (🖼️ drawing). Check it at least twice a day. - In small streams, a brush or stake fence that funnels fish into a pen works. Leave a way through for most of the run (general practice) (🖼️ fish-trap layouts; 🖼️ maze traps). - Nets are knotted with the sheet bend, using a netting needle (🖼️ drawing) and mesh gauge (🖼️ drawing) (Twinework, p. 46). A fyke net (a netting hoop trap with wings) is the river version of a fish trap (p. 137). Fish care (NDSU, p. 2; NYSDEC, p. 4): 1. Bleed the fish by cutting the throat. Pull the gills and guts (🖼️ filleting drawing). 2. Scrape out the dark kidney along the backbone. Wipe it and keep it cold. 3. Don't let cleaned fish sit warm more than 2 hours. 4. Contaminants collect in fat: skin the fish and trim the fat (🖼️ where to trim). Smoke alone does not preserve fish. Hot-smoked fish must reach 150 °F inside (160 °F

Contaminants collect in fat: skin the fish and trim the fat (🖼️ where to trim). Smoke alone does not preserve fish. Hot-smoked fish must reach 150 °F inside (160 °F better) for 30 minutes, and still keeps only in a refrigerator (PNW 238, pp. 1–2). Without one, can it or salt it (see the Preserving Food guide). Mercury: Oregon has a statewide mercury advisory on bass, and Applegate Lake has one for resident fish. Sea-run salmon and steelhead carry fewer local contaminants. Children under 6 and pregnant or nursing women should eat the fewest resident fish (ODFW fishing regs, p. 24). 📚 Go deeper: Practical Twinework — making and mending nets by hand; FAO Fishing with Traps and Pots — funnels, doors and escape gaps; NYSDEC Care of Your Catch — cleaning and filleting.

🦞 Crawfish, mussels and lamprey - Crawfish (signal crayfish) come out at night. By day, look under stream stones. They grab offal tied on a string; pull them in before they let go. Cook all freshwater shellfish and fish (FM 3-05.70, p. 118). While the rules stand: open all year, no license, by hand, line with no hook, net, ring or trap, 100 a day (ODFW fishing regs, p. 22). - Freshwater mussels are famine food only. Some, like the western pearlshell (🖼️ shells), live over 100 years. About 1 in 100,000,000 larvae becomes a young mussel, and the larvae must ride on salmon or trout to survive (🖼️ life-cycle drawing). A bed stripped bare does not come back in a lifetime (Xerces, p. 12; p. 18). Taking them is illegal while the rules stand. - Pacific lamprey: leave it to the tribes (🖼️ photo on the ODFW Rogue fishes poster). The Hupa netted lamprey on warm spring nights and dried them over the fire (Goddard, p. 35). Tribes still prize it as food and medicine, but it is in steep decline (PLCI fact sheet, p. 1), and Oregon allows it only by tribal or Willamette Falls permit (ODFW, p. 22). 📚 Go deeper: Xerces Freshwater Mussels of the PNW — ID and why beds don't recover; PLCI fact sheet — lamprey and the tribes.

☣️ Disease and safety Trichinella in bear, cougar, raccoon and beaver: wild strains survive freezing (larvae lived 5 years in frozen bear meat), and curing, smoking and drying don't reliably kill them. Cook it through (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 142; NY manual, p. 26). Jerky is safe only if the meat reaches 160 °F (PNW 632, p. 8). Tularemia (rabbit fever) comes from rabbits, hares, beaver and muskrat, and from ticks and deer flies. An infected liver and spleen have white spots. As few as 10 bacteria breathed in can infect you, so don't make dust or spray while skinning. Wear gloves and cook thoroughly (Trapper Education Manual, p. 92; Bad Bug Book, p. 64). It needs antibiotics for 14–21 days (CDC, p. 34). Chronic wasting disease isn't in Oregon yet but is in California, Idaho and Washington. Never shoot or eat a deer or elk that looks sick. Never eat the brain, eyes, spinal cord, spleen or lymph nodes. Bone out the meat, and soak tools in half bleach, half water for an hour (ODFW big game regs, p. 48; Hunter ed, p. 65; Kentucky elk guide, p. 2). Ticks: the western blacklegged tick (Lyme disease) lives here (🖼️ tick photos and sizes). Soft ticks in rodent nests in rustic cabins spread relapsing fever, in the hills above about 1,500 ft. Pull a tick with fine tweezers close

(🖼️ tick photos and sizes). Soft ticks in rodent nests in rustic cabins spread relapsing fever, in the hills above about 1,500 ft. Pull a tick with fine tweezers close to the skin, straight up, no twisting, no heat or petroleum jelly (🖼️ removal photos). Treat clothing with permethrin (CDC, p. 50; ODFW fishing regs, p. 15). Plague): southern Oregon is one of the two US plague regions. Its main flea lives on the California ground squirrel, and a trapper caught plague from a cut while skinning a bobcat. Bag any flea-covered catch at once, spray insecticide in the bag and tie it shut (Plague in Washington, p. 4; Trapper Education Manual, p. 102). Hantavirus comes from deer mice. Never sweep or vacuum droppings. Soak them in 1 part bleach to 9 parts water for 5 minutes, then wipe up with gloves (🖼️ cleanup steps). Use snap traps, not live or glue traps (CDC 2021, pp. 11–12). Lead: fast-expanding lead bullets threw fragments 5–14 in from the exit hole, and lead turned up 18 in away. Rinsing didn't help. A solid copper bullet left few fragments, mostly within about 4 in. Trim wide, throw out bloodshot or bone-flecked meat, and grind one animal at a time (Minnesota DNR, p. 6; PNW 517, p. 1). Give lead-shot meat to adults, not children or pregnant women (general practice). Coastal clams and mussels:

grind one animal at a time (Minnesota DNR, p. 6; PNW 517, p. 1). Give lead-shot meat to adults, not children or pregnant women (general practice). Coastal clams and mussels: paralytic shellfish toxin and domoic acid aren't destroyed by cooking or freezing, and there's no antidote. Numb lips or tingling hands within hours means get help. With no state testing, leave coastal shellfish alone (ODA, p. 1; OHA, p. 1). Cold rivers: the Illinois and Rogue stay dangerously cold even in summer. Sudden cold water causes gasping (cold shock) and drowning, and water drains body heat 25 times faster than air. Strainers (logjams, overhanging branches) pin people under (OSMB handbook, p. 17; p. 14). 📚 Go deeper: CDC Tickborne Diseases — tick ID, symptoms and treatment; Minnesota Bullet Fragmentation — the X-rays; OHA PSP sheet — symptoms that mean get help now; Field Care guide — treating illness with no doctor.

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - "You can eat these raw" for sea fish caught far offshore, and "there are no poisonous freshwater fish" (FM 3-05.70, p. 121). Ocean fish commonly carry worms, and mercury advisories apply here. Instead: cook all fish. - Poisoning fish with rotenone plants, lime or walnut husks (FM 3-05.70, pp. 148–150; AFH 10-644, p. 315). It kills every fish, the young salmon and the insects they eat, and ruins a stream for years. Never do it. - Bow traps and pig-spear traps (FM 3-05.70, pp. 138–140), which the manual itself calls deadly to people. Instead: snares, deadfalls and box traps, never near homes, trails or where children walk. - Smoked meat eaten "without further cooking," eating the brain (FM 3-05.70, p. 154), and sun-dried raw strips (p. 156). Smoked or dried bear still carries trichinella, and deer and elk brain carries chronic wasting disease risk. Instead: cook it through; jerky reaches 160 °F. - Ixodes dammini as the Lyme tick (Trapper Education Manual, p. 92), an old eastern name. Ours is the western blacklegged tick, Ixodes pacificus (CDC, p. 4). - A "minimum" 4-inch trim around the bullet path (PNW 517, p. 1; also repeated on the Start Here page). Instead: trim much wider; fragments went 5–14 in (Minnesota DNR, p. 6). - Aging birds at 40–45 °F (Wyoming waterfowl sheet, p.

1; also repeated on the Start Here page). Instead: trim much wider; fragments went 5–14 in (Minnesota DNR, p. 6). - Aging birds at 40–45 °F (Wyoming waterfowl sheet, p. 1). That is above the danger line. Instead: 40 °F or below (NDSU, p. 2). - Arsenic sprayed on hides (Farnham, p. 64), plus the book's chrome (bichromate) and sulfuric acid tanning. These are poisons. Instead: brain, bark, or salt and alum. 📚 Go deeper: CDC Tickborne Diseases, p. 4 — tick ID pictures; USDA FB 1334 — safe tanning methods.

🐇🐔 Rabbits & Chickens for Meat and Eggs How to keep meat rabbits and a self-renewing chicken flock with no feed store, vet or hatchery: breeds, hutches and coops, local predators, feeding on hay, greens, grain and scraps, breeding and kindling, hatching chicks under hens, eggs, summer heat, common diseases, slaughter and butchering, manure, and keeping the breeding lines going for years. The books are in Small-Livestock\ (Rabbits, Chickens, Slaughter-Processing) and Animals\ (Poultry, Rabbits-Other, Veterinary, Planning-Predators-Toxic-Plants). ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst losses - Lock birds in every night behind hardware cloth, not chicken wire, buried at least 12 inches. A weasel kills several birds at once and fits through a ¼-inch gap (Kentucky ID-245, pp. 3, 6). - Heat kills rabbits. Plan litters for spring and fall, not July–August, and have shade, airflow and water ready before 100 °F days (USDA FB 1730, p. 31). - Never feed heated, moldy or sprayed greens, or plants from where dogs and cats go. Scotch broom and foxglove — everywhere here — are toxic (WSNWCB, p. 55). - Keep breeds that can renew themselves. Hybrid layers and Cornish-cross broilers rarely go broody and won't rebuild a flock (FAO, p. 10). - Rabbit meat alone is not a diet — it is very lean. Eat it with fat and starch. - The old bulletins' medicines are poisons (sodium fluoride, carbon tetrachloride, nicotine,

Rabbit meat alone is not a diet — it is very lean. Eat it with fat and starch. - The old bulletins' medicines are poisons (sodium fluoride, carbon tetrachloride, nicotine, DDT, lindane). See the last section.

🐇 Choosing breeds and starting stock Rabbits: - New Zealand or Californian — by far the leading meat breeds, for steady color and growth (🖼️ meat breeds). Most meat rabbits are butchered by 10 weeks (OSU EC 1651, p. 1). - Start with 2–3 does per buck (6 does and 2 bucks is typical). Buy from several different breeders to avoid inbreeding. Pick thick-boned rabbits, as deep as they are wide (EC 1651, p. 2; 🖼️ body shape to look for). Chickens (USDA FB 1508, p. 6; FB 1363, p. 8): | Breed | Good for | Notes | | Plymouth Rock, Rhode Island Red, Wyandotte, Orpington, Australorp | Eggs and meat | Most make good mothers — the best choice for a self-renewing flock (🖼️ Buff Orpington) | | Leghorn, Ancona, Minorca | Eggs | Fly over fences; "fickle mothers" (🖼️ Leghorn flock) | | Brahma, Jersey Giant, Cochin | Meat | Sit well but are clumsy on eggs | | Commercial hybrids, Cornish-cross | Short-term only | "Very low mothering ability and broodiness" (FAO, p. 10) | 📚 Go deeper: OSU EC 1651 — meat breeds and picking breeding stock; USDA FB 1508, p. 6 — back-yard chicken breeds; Practical Poultry Raising — low-input flocks.

🏠 Hutches and coops Rabbit hutches (USDA AIB 358, pp. 8–10; OSU EC 1654, p. 2; 🖼️ two-compartment hutch; 🖼️ building plans): - About 2 ft high, no more than 2½ ft deep; 3 ft long for small breeds, 4 ft for medium, 6 ft for large. At least ¾ sq ft per pound of rabbit. - Scrap lumber and hardware cloth work. Give each hutch) shade, a rain-proof roof and no drafts. - Water bottles or nipples, not crocks (crocks get fouled). No cedar shavings. - A resting board on part of a wire floor prevents sore hocks (R-41, p. 26). Colony or ground pens (rule of thumb): they save wire and work, but rabbits dig out (bury mesh or a 2-ft wire apron; cover the top), catch coccidiosis and tapeworm from soil, and you lose track of matings. Does in heat ride each other and conceive less (R-41, p. 41); extra bucks fight — castrate or remove them (p. 67). Keep breeding does in their own hutches; put only growing fryers on grass in movable pens. Chicken coops (OSU EC 1644, pp. 1–2; 🖼️ coop photo): - 3 sq ft per bird in the coop with a run, 8–10 sq ft without one. - Raise the coop 1 ft off the ground. Roosts 2 ft high, 5–10 inches of pole per bird (🖼️ roost layouts). - Run of

8–10 sq ft without one. - Raise the coop 1 ft off the ground. Roosts 2 ft high, 5–10 inches of pole per bird (🖼️ roost layouts). - Run of 1×2-inch mesh, top covered, fence buried 6–12 inches (Kentucky says 12+). - A movable pen (a chicken tractor) puts birds on fresh grass and breaks the parasite cycle. 📚 Go deeper: USDA AIB 358, p. 10 — scrap-lumber hutch plans; OSU EC 1654, p. 1 — cages, drafts and bedding; OSU EC 1644 — coop design for Oregon.

🦝 Predators of the Illinois Valley Who did it? (Kentucky ID-245, pp. 2–3) — all of these live here: | Predator | What you find | | Bobcat | Whole bird eaten or gone; leftovers covered with leaves and grass (nothing else does this) | | Raccoon | Head, crop and breast eaten; heads pulled through the wire; eggs carried 50+ yards | | Fox | Bird gone; a few drops of blood and feathers | | Opossum | Feeding started at the vent | | Weasel or mink | Several birds killed, bloody, little eaten. A least weasel fits a ¼-inch hole | | Hawk or owl | Daytime (hawk) or night (owl) losses from open runs | Keeping them out (ID-245, pp. 5–6; 🖼️ photos): 1. Hardware cloth, buried at least 12 inches. Chicken wire keeps chickens in, not raccoons out. 2. Lock birds in every night. Feed them inside at dusk and they learn to go in on their own. 3. Cover the run against hawks and owls, and remove perches within 100 yards. Hawks and owls are federally protected — don't shoot them. 4. A guardian dog (such as a Great Pyrenees) that stays with the flock works day and night (raising one). 5. Rabbits too: hawks swoop into open pens; dogs and raccoons bend wire and open simple latches (OSU EC 1654, p. 1) —

flock works day and night (raising one). 5. Rabbits too: hawks swoop into open pens; dogs and raccoons bend wire and open simple latches (OSU EC 1654, p. 1) — use clips a paw can't work (rule of thumb). Big predators: for cougars, fence and shelter stock and shut them in sheds at night; Oregon law lets a landowner kill a cougar that is damaging livestock (ODFW, p. 2). For black bears, a properly installed electric fence is the most reliable protection for a coop (ODFW, p. 2; 🖼️ building a bear fence, step by step (beehive version)). 📚 Go deeper: Kentucky ID-245, p. 2 — predator signs and fixes in detail; ODFW Raising Chickens in Bear Country — electric fence setup; USDA Livestock Guarding Dogs, p. 13 — raising a guardian pup.

🌾 Feeding on little bought feed Rabbits without pellets (USDA AIB 358, p. 12): - Leafy legume hay (alfalfa, clover, vetch) + whole grain (oats, wheat, barley, rye, sorghum, buckwheat, soft corn) + salt. - Roots all year, especially winter: carrots, turnips, beets, mangels, sweet potatoes, Jerusalem artichokes (FB 1730, p. 11). - Expect 3–9 oz of feed per rabbit a day, and slower growth than on pellets — home mixes are hard to balance (OSU EC 1655, p. 1). Feeding greens safely (FB 1730, p. 12; R-41, pp. 37–38): 1. Fresh, once a day, only what they eat in 4–5 minutes, in a manger, never on the floor. 2. Dew-wet greens are fine. Greens that sat in a pile and heated are dangerous. 3. Never forage from where dogs or cats defecate (tapeworm, coccidiosis), or that was sprayed. 4. Change the diet slowly. A big feed of lush greens can kill rabbits used to pellets. Chickens on scraps, greens and range: - Mix each day's table scraps into a grain mash. Give greens all the time (clippings, cabbage, lettuce). No onion tops, geranium leaves or strong-flavored scraps — they taint eggs (FB 1508, pp. 26–27). Scraps are a supplement: too many lower laying (PNW 477, p. 4). - Winter greens: sprouted oats. Soak oats 24 hours in a pail with small holes in the bottom, keep moist and rinse

too many lower laying (PNW 477, p. 4). - Winter greens: sprouted oats. Soak oats 24 hours in a pail with small holes in the bottom, keep moist and rinse daily until they sprout (FB 1508, p. 27). - Foragers eat insects, worms, snails, seeds, grass and leaves; village hens' crops held 72% household waste (FAO, pp. 17–18). You can grow fly maggots on wet seed husks or dung (p. 24) — black soldier fly larvae are a common choice (rule of thumb). - With a dairy goat or cow: layers can live on skim milk or buttermilk to drink, all the grain they want, and oyster shell — about 4–5 gallons of milk a day per 100 hens (FB 1841, pp. 23–24). - Calcium always: oyster shell, limestone or crushed baked eggshell. The flock's own shells aren't enough, and short hens start eating their eggs (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 117). Grit or gravel for confined birds (FB 1508, p. 28). Our dry season: scavenged feed dries up (FAO, p. 36) — here, roughly July–October when the grass browns. Store hay, grain, squash and roots for summer as well as winter (rule of thumb). Toxic plants: rhododendron, nightshades, foxglove, Scotch broom, poison oak, tansy, black locust, false hellebore, snowberry, clematis (WSNWCB, p. 55). Penned birds are at more risk — they eat what they're given (p. 54). Also never feed

broom, poison oak, tansy, black locust, false hellebore, snowberry, clematis (WSNWCB, p. 55). Penned birds are at more risk — they eat what they're given (p. 54). Also never feed moldy feed, avocado, raw dried beans, green or sprouted potatoes, or rhubarb leaves (rule of thumb). Water: a doe and her 8-week litter of seven drink about a gallon a day in summer (FB 1730, p. 12). Fresh water for chickens every day (FB 1508, p. 28; 🖼️ homemade waterers). A hen drinks about a pint a day, double in heat, and a day without water can stop laying for weeks (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: USDA AIB 358, p. 12 — rabbit feeds without pellets; FAO, p. 17 — scavenging flocks and home-grown feed; USDA FB 1841, p. 23 — home-grown grain and milk rations.

in spring and fall, not July–August. If this goes wrong (rule of thumb): doe won't take the buck → try again in a few days or another buck. Kits cold on the wire → warm them in your hands and return them to the nest. 🐤 Hatching and raising chicks With a broody hen — the dependable way without power (USDA FB 1363): 1. Broody hens cluck and ruffle up when approached. After she has stayed on the nest 2–3 days, move her at night to a quiet nest with dummy eggs (p. 9). 2. Set 10–13 eggs in cold weather, 13–15 in warm (p. 3). Use fresh eggs — quality drops after 5 days, and 3-week-old eggs rarely hatch (p. 5). 3. Candle on day 7 and day 14 (hold each egg to a bright light in the dark) and remove clear ones (p. 18; 🖼️ the air cell on days 7, 14 and 18; 🖼️ candling). 4. Chicks start pipping the evening of day 19 and are out by day 21 (FB 1538, p. 11). Don't help them out — those that can't hatch alone rarely thrive (p. 15). Incubators (only if you have steady power) (FB 1538, pp. 11, 16): fan type 99.5–100 °F, about 57% humidity, eggs turned 5–6 times a day; still-air about 102 °F at egg height. Turn at least twice a day from day 2 to day 18 (FB 1363, p. 3). Homemade: a foam cooler (🖼️ photos) with a 40-watt bulb and thermostat at 99–100 °F, or a double cardboard box with the bulb in a chimney touching nothing (fire risk) — plan on hatching no more

with a 40-watt bulb and thermostat at 99–100 °F, or a double cardboard box with the bulb in a chimney touching nothing (fire risk) — plan on hatching no more than half the eggs. Brooding: - With the hen: shut hen and chicks in a brood coop (🖼️ drawing) at night (rats, cats). Move the coop weekly to fresh short grass (FB 1538, p. 18). Raise chicks on ground old birds haven't used for a year (p. 17). - Without a hen: start at about 95 °F. Chicks crowding to the heat are cold; panting with open mouths are too hot (p. 22; 🖼️ what each looks like). Wire across corners stops piling and smothering. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1363 — setting hens and choosing eggs; USDA FB 1538, p. 11 — incubation and brooding; Wikipedia: egg incubation — pictures of embryo development.

🥚 Eggs: how many, which hens, storing On little bought feed, expect far fewer eggs (FAO, p. 9): | How the hens live | Eggs per hen per year | | Scavenging only | 20–30 | | Scavenging + shelter and disease control | 40–60 | | Some feed | about 100 | | Fully fed | 160–220 | So two eggs a day (730 a year) takes 7–8 part-fed hens, or 25+ scavengers (our arithmetic). Which hens to keep (USDA FB 1727): hens lay most in year one and about 20% less in year two. Eat early molters and non-layers in June–July; keep hens still laying in August–September for a second year and for breeding (p. 5). A non-layer has a shrunken, dull, dry comb) (p. 8), pubic bones close together, only two fingers from the keel (p. 9; 🖼️ layer vs. non-layer), and yellow returning to beak and shanks (p. 10). Storing eggs: - Collect at least once a day. Wash only dirty eggs, in water 20 °F warmer than the egg (OSU EM 9350, p. 5). - Clean, unwashed eggs keep 2–3 weeks at cool room temperature, longer in a cold cellar (rule of thumb). - Spring surplus: water glass or limewater crocks keep eggs 6–9 months (USDA 1935, p. 3; FB 1508, p. 32). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1727 — telling layers from loafers, with

surplus: water glass or limewater crocks keep eggs 6–9 months (USDA 1935, p. 3; FB 1508, p. 32). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1727 — telling layers from loafers, with pictures; USDA Home Methods of Preserving Eggs — water glass and lime; Root Cellar guide — storing eggs cool.

🌡️ Heat, smoke and fire season Rabbits (USDA FB 1730, p. 31): - Newborn litters and does late in pregnancy suffer most. - Signs: fast breathing, wet mouth, slight bleeding from the nostrils. - Do: shade and airflow (🖼️ a cooling basket for young rabbits). Wetting hutch tops and floors cools the hutch 6–10 °F. Lay a sick rabbit on a feed sack soaked in cold water. Chickens (FAO, p. 27): they have no sweat glands and cool by panting. Severe stress above 104 °F (40 °C); 115 °F (46 °C) kills most. They eat less, drink more and lay smaller eggs. Give shade, airflow and cool water; white paint reflects up to 70% of the sun's heat on a roof. Heat-stressed birds peck each other. Wildfire smoke (PNW 783, p. 10): watch for coughing, open-mouth breathing, watery eyes, weakness. Keep water clean and fresh, cool them, mist down dust, and put off stressful jobs (weaning, moving). Evacuation plan: Illinois Valley page. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1730, p. 31 — rabbits in hot weather; FAO, p. 27 — heat and housing; PNW 783, p. 8 — evacuating or sheltering stock.

🩺 Common diseases with no vet Rabbits: - Quarantine new rabbits a month, downwind, and do their chores last (OSU EC 1654, p. 1). - Watch for: runny nose and matted front paws (snuffles; 🖼️ photo), crusty ears (ear mites), diarrhea, sores. - The common killers — coccidiosis, pneumonia and enteritis — come mostly from poor sanitation (R-41, p. 52). Keep floors dry, clear droppings, keep droppings out of feed and water (p. 57). - Bloat or diarrhea with no fever: more hay and roughage; beware fermented or spoiled feed (p. 57). - Snuffles: cull (p. 56) — it spreads. - At butchering: white spots on an enlarged liver = liver coccidiosis (p. 56). Throw that liver away. Chickens: - Coccidiosis: bloody droppings, droopy young birds; at death the two blind guts (ceca) are swollen with blood (FB 1652, pp. 52–53; 🖼️ life cycle). If you stocked amprolium, it treats it; chicks kept off their droppings (wire or slat floors, fresh ground) get less (Where There Is No Animal Doctor, p. 317). - Marek's disease (paralysis; 🖼️ swollen nerves) strikes at 12–25 weeks (UF PS044, p. 7). No cure — cull, and hatch from survivors' lines (rule of thumb). - Lice and mites: ruffled feathers, scabs, fewer eggs (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 132; 🖼️ louse, 🖼️ mite). Give a dust bath of fine dry soil and wood ash, keep nests

Lice and mites: ruffled feathers, scabs, fewer eggs (Practical Poultry Raising, p. 132; 🖼️ louse, 🖼️ mite). Give a dust bath of fine dry soil and wood ash, keep nests clean with fresh straw (rule of thumb). - Burn or deeply bury birds that die of disease (FB 1652, p. 13). - Gloves and eye protection with lye or lime disinfectants (FB 1538, p. 17). 📚 Go deeper: Where There Is No Animal Doctor, p. 312 — poultry diseases with no vet; Raising Healthy Rabbits and Raising Healthy Poultry — illustrated care; USDA FB 1652 — disease signs (ignore its drugs).

🔪 Humane slaughter and butchering Killing — practice on a carcass first; the AVMA says neck dislocation is humane only when done by trained people on small animals (AVMA, p. 44): - Rabbit: hold the hind legs, thumb just behind the ears, fingers under the chin; stretch and raise the head sharply (🖼️ how to hold it). Or a heavy blow at the base of the skull (FB 1730, p. 52). - Chicken: hang it head-down in a killing cone and cut the side of the neck (Kansas State EP71, p. 1). Chickens (EP71, p. 1; UMN EB 385): 1. No feed for 8–10 hours before. 2. Scald at 140 °F for 30–40 seconds, dunking up and down; a little detergent helps. Pluck at once. 3. Gut (🖼️ step by step), then chill in ice water to 40 °F (UMN, p. 6); keep unfrozen under 4 days (EP71, p. 2). - Don't eat a bird with lumps or spots on the liver, fluid in the body, or orange fat on a thin carcass. - Pinfeathery birds: wait a week or two (UMN, p. 1). Allow 1–2 gallons of water per bird (OSU EM 9273, p. 2). Rabbits (FB 1730, pp. 52–55): 1. No feed the day before (R-41, p. 77). 2. Hang by a hook through the hock tendon of one hind leg; cut off the head at once to

52–55): 1. No feed the day before (R-41, p. 77). 2. Hang by a hook through the hock tendon of one hind leg; cut off the head at once to bleed. 3. Remove tail, free hind foot and front feet, then peel the skin off like a sock (🖼️ steps). 4. Gut. Heart, kidneys and liver are good food. Stretch the pelt on a wire frame to dry (🖼️ pelt on a stretcher); tan with salt-alum (FB 1334, p. 27). - Yield: a 4–4½ lb fryer at 8 weeks dresses to 50–59% of live weight, 78–80% of that edible (p. 47). Keeping the meat: pressure-can it (soak dressed rabbit 1 hour in salted water first) (USDA canning guide 5, p. 5), or dry thin strips (CVM, p. 90) — 16 oz raw makes about 4 oz jerky (PNW 632, p. 7). 📚 Go deeper: UMN Home Processing of Poultry — illustrated plucking and gutting; USDA FB 1730, p. 52 — slaughter and skinning with drawings; UF Humane Euthanasia — putting down a sick animal.

🌱 Manure for the garden - Rabbit manure has about 2% nitrogen — more than most farm manures — and won't burn plants: dig it straight in (USDA Rabbit Manure, pp. 4–5). A doe and her litters make about 6 cubic feet a year (9 with bedding); a buck about 3. Raise earthworms in the pile under the hutches (vermicomposting) — they cut odor and flies (p. 6). - Chicken manure: compost it at least 120 days (🖼️ compost bins) before use, and never put it raw on seedlings or growing plants. Spread raw litter in fall, after harvest, so winter rains leach out the salts (Idaho CIS 1194, pp. 2, 6) — our wet winters suit this. 📚 Go deeper: USDA Value and Use of Rabbit Manure, p. 6 — composting and worm beds; Idaho CIS 1194 — the 120-day rule and spreading rates.

🧬 Keeping the lines going for years How many feed a family (our arithmetic from the sources): - A doe at full production raises about 28 fryers a year — roughly 60 lb of carcass, 48 lb of meat (FB 1730, pp. 19, 47). Each pound of fryer takes 3½–4½ lb of feed. Rabbit twice a week for four people ≈ 100 fryers ≈ 4 does + 1 buck; keep 6 does and 2 bucks to cover losses and smaller litters on home feed. - FAO's village flock: 15 hens laying 30 eggs each = 450 eggs, some set under broodies (FAO, p. 36). About half of each hatch is cockerels — eat them at 12–20 weeks before they compete for feed (rule of thumb). Avoid inbreeding: - Inbreeding isn't harmful in itself, but it quickly brings out hidden defects; beginners usually inbreed just to avoid getting a new buck (FB 1730, p. 20). Keep at least two unrelated bucks and trade bucks with neighbors every few generations (rule of thumb). - Roosters: one per 12–15 Leghorn-type hens, 10–12 Rock or Wyandotte, 10 or fewer of the heaviest; with 20–30 hens keep two and alternate them (FB 1508, p. 10). FAO replaces the cock with a new cockerel every year (p. 36). Trade for an unrelated rooster every 2–3 years, or keep 2–3 hen families and rotate roosters (rule of

FAO replaces the cock with a new cockerel every year (p. 36). Trade for an unrelated rooster every 2–3 years, or keep 2–3 hen families and rotate roosters (rule of thumb). - Keep records of matings and litter sizes (🖼️ a hutch card); breed from the best mothers. Don't live on rabbit. It is high in protein but low in fat (EC 1651, p. 1). People who live mainly on lean meat get "rabbit starvation" within 1–2 weeks — nausea, diarrhea, weakness and a craving for fat that more lean meat won't fix. Keep protein under about a third of calories and pair rabbit with fat (egg yolks, chicken fat, lard, nuts) and starch (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1730, p. 20 — inbreeding and selection; FAO, p. 36 — a self-renewing village flock; Food Security guide — fitting meat and eggs into a ration.

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - Sodium fluoride dusted on setting hens for lice — FB 1363, p. 9. It is poisonous. Instead: a dust bath of dry soil and wood ash, clean straw in the nest. - Poisons as wormers and mite killers in FB 1652: carbon tetrachloride (p. 63, p. 77), nicotine sulfate (p. 78), DDT (p. 49), phenothiazine (p. 79), kerosene emulsion and carbolineum (p. 7). Instead: use the bulletin for signs and prevention only; rotate ground, keep litter dry, cull. Also nicotine sulfate painted on roosts in Practical Poultry Raising, p. 132 — don't. - Lindane for rabbit ear mites — Peace Corps Livestock Manual Vol 4, p. 341. Banned and nerve-toxic. - "Salt-acid" tanning with concentrated sulfuric acid — FB 1730, p. 60. Instead: salt-alum (p. 61; FB 1334, p. 27). - Formalin for tanning and preserving paws in R-41, pp. 81, 83 — toxic; use salt-alum. Ipil-ipil (leucaena) as feed (p. 37) — toxic in quantity (not grown here anyway). Many drugs R-41 names won't be available. - Cresol disinfectant — FB 1508, p. 31. Toxic. Instead: scrub, sun and dry; lime with gloves and goggles. - "Don't mix your own rabbit feed" (OSU EC 1655, p. 1) is right while pellets exist. After that, home-grown feed is the only choice — expect slower growth and smaller litters, not failure. 📚

🐐 Milk Goats, Home Dairy & Bees How to keep dairy goats healthy with no vet or feed store, get clean milk and keep it without a fridge, turn it into butter, ghee, yogurt, kefir and cheese, and keep honey bees for honey and wax. The books are in Animals\Goats-Sheep, Animals\Dairy-Cheese, Animals\Bees and Animals\Veterinary, with the old farm butter and cheese bulletins in Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools and milk cooling in Food-Storage\Cooling-Without-Power. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Raw milk can carry brucellosis, tuberculosis and Listeria (which causes miscarriage). Pasteurize milk for children, pregnant women, the old and the sick: 145 °F for 30 minutes, or 161 °F for 15 seconds, then cool it fast (UMN, p. 1). - Never give honey to a baby under 1 year — infant botulism (FDA Bad Bug Book, p. 108). - Never feed hedge or garden trimmings. Yew kills before any sign shows; rhododendron, azalea and oleander poison goats (WSU, p. 2). - Oregon is short of selenium. Keep a covered selenium goat mineral out all year, and never let sheep eat goat mineral — its copper poisons them. - Shut goats in every night (cougars) and put an electric fence around the hives (black bears). - Anyone who has had a whole-body reaction to a sting must not work bees without epinephrine at hand.

🐐 Choosing and feeding milk goats What to expect: a doe giving about 1,000 lb (about 500 quarts) in a 10-month lactation is a fair milker; 1,600 lb or more is excellent (USDA FB 920, p. 5). That is about 1½ quarts a day (our arithmetic). Two does bred a few months apart keep milk coming all year (rule of thumb). Breeds (FB 920, p. 10): Saanen, Toggenburg, Nubian and Alpine (🖼️ Saanen, 🖼️ Toggenburg, 🖼️ Nubian, 🖼️ Alpine). Nubians give the richest milk, best for butter and cheese. LaMancha and the small Nigerian Dwarf are newer (rule of thumb). Feeding (FB 920, pp. 25–26): - Goats browse: they prefer leaves, twigs and weeds to grass. - Grain: about 1 lb for every 3–4 lb of milk. - One doe for a year: about 500 lb of hay and 450 lb of grain with 6 months of pasture; about twice the hay with none. One acre of good pasture carries 2–3 goats for a 5–6-month season. - House the buck away from milking does — his smell gets into the milk. Here (rule of thumb): pasture browns from June to the October rains and winter is mud, so plan hay for both. Browse: blackberry, willow, maple and oak leaves. Goats eat poison oak; its oil rubs off their coats onto your hands. Change feed slowly, over 7–10 days. Plants that

for both. Browse: blackberry, willow, maple and oak leaves. Goats eat poison oak; its oil rubs off their coats onto your hands. Change feed slowly, over 7–10 days. Plants that kill goats — mostly hungry goats in unfamiliar brush (the "where" column is local knowledge, rule of thumb): | Plant | Where | What happens | | Western azalea, rhododendron, laurel | Along valley creeks and serpentine meadows; gardens | Drooling, vomiting (rare in goats — a red flag), bloat, tremors, collapse; activated charcoal may help (WSU, p. 15) | | Pacific yew, garden yew | Shady creek forest; hedges | Often fatal before any sign (AIB 415, p. 113) | | Oleander | SW Oregon yards | All parts very poisonous (OSU, p. 12) | | Chokecherry, cherry | Wilted or frosted leaves | Cyanide (AIB 415, p. 26) | 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 920 Milk Goats — breeds, rations, housing; USDA AIB 415 — western poisonous plants in color.

🏠 Fences, shelter and minerals - Fences: no barbed wire. Field fence traps horned heads. Electric works once goats are trained: two hot wires held mature does but not kids (OSU EC1646, pp. 1–2). - Shelter: a dry three-sided shed with fresh air but no drafts, and something to climb (🖼️ shelter, 🖼️ climbing structure). Keep goats dry and out of cold wind (FB 920, p. 35). - Cougars: shut goats in a shed or barn every night (ODFW, p. 2). Selenium (OSU EM 9094, pp. 1–6): - Most Oregon livestock are low in selenium (🖼️ map). White muscle disease was first described here, in 1958. It strikes kids 3–8 weeks old: stiffness, trembling, weak hind legs, can't stand or suckle, heart failure. Low selenium also causes abortion, stillbirth and more mastitis. - Free-choice selenium mineral salt is simplest. Keep the feeder covered — rain leaches selenium out. - Injections (such as Bo-Se) need a vet, last under a month, and an overdose kills. - Stock a year or more of selenium goat mineral now (rule of thumb). Copper: copper oxide wire particles help control barber pole worm in goats, but copper poisons sheep. Never feed goat mineral to sheep, and don't use low-copper sheep mineral for goats (UF VM271, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: OSU EM 9094 — selenium salt vs injections; OSU EC1646 — fences and sheds.

🍼 Breeding, kidding and kids | | What to know | | Heat | Fall and early winter; every 18–21 days; lasts 24–36 hours. Bleating, tail wagging, swollen vulva, less milk (Peace Corps Vol 4, p. 419) | | First breeding | Doelings at 7–8 months, not earlier (same page) | | Gestation | 146–152 days; twins usual, triplets common (FB 920, p. 24). Fall breeding = kids February–April (rule of thumb) | The first hour (KSU MF3689, pp. 11, 13): 1. "Clip, dip, strip, sip": cut the navel cord under 2 inches and dip it in iodine; strip the wax plugs from the doe's teats; make sure the kid nurses. 2. Colostrum within 30–60 minutes, at least 10% of body weight: a 10-lb kid needs about 7 oz in the first hour and 16 oz over 24 hours, in 2–4-oz feeds (🖼️ tube-feeding photos). 3. Kid under 99 °F? Warm it first — a chilled kid can't absorb colostrum. 4. Never pull on the afterbirth. For a stuck kid see the Langston guide (🖼️ normal and wrong positions; 🖼️ KSU drawings). Bottle kids (FB 920, pp. 28, 31): 1½–2 pints of warm (90–98 °F) milk a day, in 3 feeds, until 6 weeks; after 10 weeks hay and grain replace most of it; wean at 3–4 months. feeds, until 6 weeks; after 10 weeks hay and grain replace most of it; wean at 3–4 months. Use the doe's milk for people only from the 4th–5th day after kidding. Disbudding (FB 920, p. 34): 1. In the first days of life, always before 3 weeks. On a naturally hornless kid the skin slides over the spot. 2. Heat a disbudding iron (or a ¾-inch steel pipe on a handle) cherry-red (🖼️ where to burn). Hold it on each bud 5–10 seconds, rotating, until a copper-colored ring shows. 3. Give tetanus antitoxin. Every 2–4 weeks, score the inner eyelid against the FAMACHA card (1 = red, 5 = white), and check back (body condition), rear (scours), jaw (bottle jaw) and nose (🖼️ pale eyelid and bottle jaw, in sheep). 2. Deworm only the goats that need it. 20% of goats carry 80% of the worms; treating all of them breeds resistant worms. 3. 80% of larvae live in the bottom 2 inches of forage: don't graze short. Rest pastures at least 30 days. 4. Goats browsing brush at head height pick up far fewer worms (rule of thumb). Hooves: trim every 4–6 weeks, wall level with

short. Rest pastures at least 30 days. 4. Goats browsing brush at head height pick up far fewer worms (rule of thumb). Hooves: trim every 4–6 weeks, wall level with the sole (🖼️ hoof parts; 🖼️ trimming). Wet winters bring hoof rot (🖼️ photo; smelly, contagious): dry pens, a 15–18% zinc sulfate foot bath, clean trimmers (MSU M2487, p. 1). 📚 Go deeper: Where There Is No Animal Doctor — no-vet livestock care; Raising Healthy Goats — illustrated care (pictures only).

🥛 Clean milk: milking, cooling, pasteurizing Milking (Lincoln Univ, pp. 1–2; 🖼️ milking stand): 1. Clip the udder hair. Squirt the first milk into a strip cup and look for clots every milking. 2. Dip the teats; wipe each goat with her own towel. Milk without wringing the teats; dip again after. 3. Filter, and chill to 38 °F within an hour. Cold raw milk keeps 12–14 days. Cooling without power (USDA FB 976, pp. 6, 15; 🖼️ cooling tank): a can of 85 °F milk set in 3 times its volume of 37 °F water only gets to about 50 °F — use more water and stir. Spring water is often as warm as 65 °F; check it with a thermometer. In our 95 °F summers, milk you can't chill should become yogurt, cheese or ghee the same day (rule of thumb). Why pasteurize: raw milk and soft raw-milk cheeses spread brucellosis, TB and Listeria; hard, aged cheeses are safer (Zoonoses, p. 92). Young children should not get raw milk; yogurt resists contamination better (WHO, p. 16). Plant poisons pass into milk too — lupine can cause birth defects in people (WSU, p. 15). Pasteurizing at home (UMN, p. 1): 1. Use a double boiler, or a pot set in a pan of water, so the milk doesn't scorch. 2. Heat to 145 °F and hold 30 minutes, stirring,

1): 1. Use a double boiler, or a pot set in a pan of water, so the milk doesn't scorch. 2. Heat to 145 °F and hold 30 minutes, stirring, or to 161 °F for 15 seconds. If it drops below 145 °F, restart the 30 minutes (rule of thumb). 3. Cool it at once in cold running water or ice water. Kept cold, it lasts 7–10 days. 4. No thermometer? Bring it just to a boil (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Lincoln Milking the Sanitary Way — clean milking and the mastitis test; USDA FB 976 — spring-water cooling tanks.

🧈 Cream, butter and ghee Goat cream barely rises, and goat butter is pure white (FB 920, p. 7), so sour the whole milk and churn it. Cow milk can be skimmed from a shallow pan 4 inches deep after 36 hours (ILCA, p. 38; 🖼️ drawing). Butter from soured whole milk (ILCA, p. 60): 1. Let the milk sour until it tastes pleasantly sour. Fresh milk churns slowly and loses fat. 2. At 59–79 °F, rock or shake it in a closed vessel until butter grains form (🖼️ small churns). Colder can take 5 hours. Butter from cream (USDA FB 876, p. 23): ripen it at 65–75 °F until mildly sour, then churn at 52–66 °F for 30–40 minutes until the grains are wheat-sized. Drain the buttermilk (🖼️ photo) and wash the butter twice. Salted to 3% (about ½ oz per pound (our arithmetic)), butter keeps up to 4 months sealed, cool and dark (ILCA, p. 49). Ghee keeps a year without a fridge (Practical Action, p. 4): 1. Boil butter gently until the water is gone and the milk solids turn golden brown. 2. Let it settle; strain through boiled cheesecloth. 3. Store airtight, dark and cool — not in iron or copper, which speed rancidity. It keeps more than 12 months at room temperature. 📚 Go deeper: ILCA Rural Dairy Technology — village dairying with no power;

not in iron or copper, which speed rancidity. It keeps more than 12 months at room temperature. 📚 Go deeper: ILCA Rural Dairy Technology — village dairying with no power; Practical Action Butter and Ghee — step by step.

🧀 Yogurt, kefir and cheese Yogurt (Practical Action, pp. 1–3): 1. Heat milk to 176–185 °F and hold 15–20 minutes, stirring. Cool fast to 104–113 °F. 2. Stir in 20–50 g of live yogurt per liter (about 1½–3 tablespoons per quart (our conversion)). 3. Keep warm 4–6 hours — a haybox or a cooler with jars of hot water works — then chill. 4. Keep a "mother culture" going; replace it if flavors go off. Kefir needs no warm box (ILCA, p. 59): heat milk to 185 °F for 30 minutes and cool it, add kefir grains, and leave about 12 hours at room temperature (72 °F). Reuse the grains; they multiply (rule of thumb). Lemon or vinegar cheese (queso blanco, paneer) (ILCA, p. 50; 🖼️ step chart): 1. Heat milk to 180 °F, or a simmer. 2. Stir in lemon juice, about 3 mL per 100 mL of milk (about 2 tablespoons per quart (our conversion)), diluted with equal water — or vinegar. Curds form at once. Settle 15 minutes. 3. Drain in a cloth, salt, press overnight. Keeps about 3 days cold, 5 in brine (Practical Action, p. 1). Cottage cheese with no bought culture (USDA FB 1451, pp. 6–7): 1. Let skim milk clabber at about 75 °F (about 30 hours) until clean and pleasantly sour. 2. Cut it in 2-inch pieces; set the pan in hot

pp. 6–7): 1. Let skim milk clabber at about 75 °F (about 30 hours) until clean and pleasantly sour. 2. Cut it in 2-inch pieces; set the pan in hot water to bring it to 100 °F; hold about 30 minutes, stirring gently. Drain in a cloth, rinse cold, salt. A gallon makes about 1½ lb. 3. Homemade starter: set several boiled pint jars of fresh milk at 75 °F (🖼️ starter jars). Keep the one that curdles in about 30 hours with a smooth curd and a clean, sharp sour taste, and carry it on daily. A simple rennet cheese (FB 920, p. 8): stir a junket tablet dissolved in cold water into 1 gallon of milk at 88 °F. Cut the curd after 30 minutes, warm it to 98 °F, bag and press it (🖼️ homemade lever press), and rub with salt for several days. Ready at 10 days. Making your own rennet (Book of Cheese, pp. 55–56): 1. Take the stomach of a young kid, lamb or calf that has had nothing but milk. Clean it, blow it up, dry it. 2. Cut it open and soak it in 3–5% salt water (about 4–6 oz salt per gallon (our arithmetic)) for days to weeks. 3. Filter, add more salt, and keep it cool and dark (stone jugs, colored glass) — light destroys it. 4. Strength varies and

gallon (our arithmetic)) for days to weeks. 3. Filter, add more salt, and keep it cool and dark (stone jugs, colored glass) — light destroys it. 4. Strength varies and it can spoil: test it on a small batch. Aging (FB 1191, p. 15): a cellar at 50–60 °F is ideal. Turn cheeses daily and wipe off mold; coat them at 2 weeks (beeswax works); eat from 6 weeks. Cover cellar windows with cheesecloth — the cheese-skipper fly gets through screen. Whey (Book of Cheese, p. 319): heat it to about 200 °F and skim the curds that float — ricotta. Boil the rest down to sweet brown mysost. Whey also feeds hens and pigs (rule of thumb), but never feed raw milk to pigs — it spreads TB (Zoonoses, p. 27). 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Cheese Making — soft cheeses and plant coagulants; USDA FB 1451 — cottage cheese and starters; The Book of Cheese — rennet, hard cheeses, curing rooms (old book: raw-milk methods).

Here (rule of thumb): manzanita and willow bloom February–March, bigleaf maple in April, and blackberry in June–July is the main flow. A dearth follows from late July to the fall rains, when robbing and yellowjackets peak: reduce entrances (🖼️ entrance reducer), never spill syrup or leave comb out, and keep water within half a mile (OSU EM 9186, p. 4). Swarms) are free bees: - They come mostly March–June: the old queen and half the bees hang in a cluster for an hour or so (AH 335, p. 38; 🖼️ resting swarm). Swarming bees are full of honey and gentle (Langstroth, p. 41). - Shake the cluster into a box of old comb (🖼️ hiving a swarm); close it at dusk. A bait

bees are full of honey and gentle (Langstroth, p. 41). - Shake the cluster into a box of old comb (🖼️ hiving a swarm); close it at dusk. A bait hive of old dark comb catches swarms by itself (rule of thumb). - Your own colony swarms when it has more than 6 frames of bees and is crowded: split it when swarm cells appear (OSU EM 9186, p. 11; 🖼️ swarm cells). - Package bees from California will stop after a collapse, so swarms will be the only new bees (p. 14). Feeding (AH 335, pp. 49–51): 1:1 sugar syrup in spring; thick 2:1 for new colonies and fall stores; dry sugar on the inner cover in a late-winter emergency. Feed late in the day with narrowed entrances. Never feed honey from unknown hives — it spreads disease. A broodless colony eats about 4 lb of honey a month (p. 72); the book's 90-lb winter store is for cold climates, and our mild winters need roughly 40–60 lb (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: FAO Bees and Forest Livelihoods — building top-bar hives; USDA AH 335 — swarming, feeding, wintering.

🦠 Bee health: varroa and foulbrood Varroa mites are the main killer; unchecked they double every month (HBHC, p. 5; 🖼️ mites on bees and larvae). Here they peak in August–September, as the winter bees are raised (rule of thumb). Counting mites (HBHC, pp. 9–10): 1. Shake bees from 1–3 brood frames (not the one with the queen) into a tub. 2. Scoop ½ cup (about 300 bees) into a jar of rubbing alcohol or soapy water, shake, and count the mites. 3. Mites ÷ 300 × 100 = mites per 100 bees. Treat at 1+ in winter and spring, 2+ in summer and fall. Controls with nothing bought (pp. 39–40): cut out capped drone) brood 2–3 times in spring, or force a brood break by caging the queen 1–2 weeks or making a split. Oxalic acid dribble (p. 29): 35 g, weighed (roughly 2⅓ level tablespoons if you have no scale (rule of thumb)) in 1 liter of 1:1 syrup; 5 mL on the bees in each occupied gap between combs, 50 mL at most per colony, best with no capped brood (late fall, winter). Corrosive: gloves and goggles. Vaporizing it is extremely dangerous. Stockpile pure oxalic acid dihydrate now (rule of thumb). American foulbrood (AFB) — the disease that means burning: - Signs: spotty brood; sunken, darker, pierced cappings; foul smell (FAO 2006, p. 10; 🖼️ dead larvae

now (rule of thumb). American foulbrood (AFB) — the disease that means burning: - Signs: spotty brood; sunken, darker, pierced cappings; foul smell (FAO 2006, p. 10; 🖼️ dead larvae in cells). - Matchstick test: push a matchstick into a dead larva and draw it out slowly. About an inch of ropy brown goo means AFB (FAO Forest, p. 150; 🖼️ photo). - Then: burn combs, frames, honey and dead bees in a pit about 3 ft deep and fill it in; scorch the inside of the boxes until slightly brown. Shaking the bees onto clean new combs can save them (FAO 2006, p. 11). 📚 Go deeper: HBHC Tools for Varroa Management — mite counts and every treatment; FAO Honey Bee Diseases and Pests — photos of brood diseases, mites and wax moth.

🍯 Honey, wax, bears and stings Honey with no extractor (FAO Forest, p. 91; Practical Action, p. 3): take only sealed comb and leave winter stores. Cut it as comb honey, or crush it and strain through coarse, then fine, cloth. Keep everything bone-dry — honey over 19–20% water ferments. Don't heat it; crystallized honey is fine. Beeswax (FAO Forest, pp. 112–113): melt comb in water, strain through sacking, and let the wax cake float and set; repeat through finer cloth. A solar melter (a black box with a glass lid) also works. Wax is highly flammable — never heat it dry over a flame (🖼️ double boiler). Beeswax candles need a thicker wick than tallow (Practical Action, p. 2). Bear fence (UF ENY-2060, pp. 1–5): bears come for the brood, and come back. Run three electric wires at 8, 20 and 32 inches on heavy T-posts every 8 ft, at least 3 ft from the hives, with a 6-ft ground rod (🖼️ step photos; 🖼️ finished fence). Test for 6,000–8,000 volts and keep plants cut back 2–3 ft. Bait the wire with foil smeared with bacon grease so a bear's nose gets the first shock (rule of thumb). Stings: pain and swelling at the spot are normal; scrape the stinger out at once (rule of thumb). A whole-body reaction (anaphylaxis: throat swelling, trouble breathing, faintness) follows 0.3–7.5% of stings

pain and swelling at the spot are normal; scrape the stinger out at once (rule of thumb). A whole-body reaction (anaphylaxis: throat swelling, trouble breathing, faintness) follows 0.3–7.5% of stings (OSU EM 9186, p. 4). - Give epinephrine (adrenaline) into the thigh muscle: adults 50 kg+ 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000), repeated every 5 minutes as needed; children 0.15 mg (WHO, p. 235). See the Field Care guide. 📚 Go deeper: FAO Bees and Forest Livelihoods — straining honey, rendering wax, solar melter; ODFW Living with Black Bears — bears and attractants.

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - Phenothiazine mixed into salt as a constant dewormer — FB 920, p. 26. Breeds resistant worms. Instead: FAMACHA-targeted deworming. - Iodoform in mineral oil put into the uterus — FB 920, p. 30. Outdated. Instead: never pull the afterbirth (KSU, p. 13). - Caustic-stick disbudding — FB 920, p. 34. It runs into eyes and burns other kids or the doe. Instead: a hot iron. - Pasteurizing at 140 °F (60 °C) for 30 minutes — Zoonoses, p. 31. Too low. Instead: 145 °F for 30 minutes or 161 °F for 15 seconds. - Paraffin heated to 240 °F for dipping cheese — FB 1191, p. 15 (220 °F in Book of Cheese, p. 287). Fire and burn hazard. Instead: melt wax in a pot set in water, never unattended. - Soft cheese from raw milk — Book of Cheese, p. 167; FB 920, p. 8. It carries Listeria and brucellosis. Instead: pasteurize milk for soft cheese. - Bee drugs — AH 335, p. 132. The 1980 book predates varroa in the US (1987). Instead: the HBHC varroa guide. - Killing colonies over burning sulfur to take the honey — Langstroth, p. 264. Instead: take only surplus honey. Burn a colony only for AFB. - Butter coloring and old dairy "preservatives" — FB 876, p. 13. Instead: salt to 3%, or

🐴 Horses, Mules and Draft Animals How to keep, feed, handle, ride, shoe and pack horses, mules and donkeys, and how to put them to work in harness — written for a time when there may be no feed store, vet or farrier. The manuals are in Horses-Draft-Animals\ (Care-Feeding, Riding-Training, Hoof-Care-Shoeing, Packing-Travel, Draft-Harness). Horse health, vital signs, colic and first aid are in Animals\ and the Animals and vet care section of the Illinois Valley page. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst accidents - A horse can kill you without meaning to. Stay where it can see you, speak before you touch it, keep a hand on it as you move around the hindquarters, and never stand directly behind or in front of it. - Never wrap a lead rope or reins around your hand or body, and never tie a horse with a knot you can't pull loose. Never tie with a chain lead. (4-H Horse Project PNW 587, p. 51; Basic Horse Safety) - Wear a helmet and boots with a heel when riding. - The old books here (1867–1940s) teach good handling and shoeing but also harsh "breaking" methods and dangerous old medicines (purges, firing, chloroform). Use them for skills, not for doctoring.

🐎 Choosing an animal - For a first horse, pick an older, calm, well-trained one over a young or green horse — the 4-H manual says 6 to 18 years suits most purposes, and "a young horse and an inexperienced rider do not learn together" (PNW 587, p. 24). For hard work, not much under 5; with good care many stay useful past 20 (USDA FB 779, p. 8). Check it sound before you take it: walk and trot it on hard ground, look for limping, swellings, bad feet and bad habits. (USDA How to Select a Sound Horse; 🖼️ points of the horse; 🖼️ where unsoundness shows; conformation) - Age by the teeth: after about 12 years the front teeth turn triangular and slant forward. (USDA AIB 353, p. 18; PNW 587, p. 48; 🖼️ mouths from 4 to 8 years; 🖼️ 14- and 22-year-old mouths) - Mules are tough, sure-footed, eat less and handle heat and rough country better; they tend to stand and fight rather than bolt. A well-trained mule is very steady; a badly trained one is hard work. Donkeys need shelter always — their coats aren't waterproof, which matters in our wet winters. (Donkey Care Handbook, p. 44) - Who's who: a mule is a mare bred to a jack (male donkey); a hinny is a jenny bred to a stallion and is smaller and

Handbook, p. 44) - Who's who: a mule is a mare bred to a jack (male donkey); a hinny is a jenny bred to a stallion and is smaller and rarer. Mules are hardy but can still founder, and they fret if stabled long or kept alone. Donkeys live just over 30 years and should be kept with a companion. (Donkey Care Handbook, pp. 15–19; 🖼️ points of the donkey) 📚 Go deeper: 4-H Horse Project (PNW 587) — choosing a horse, breeds, behavior; USDA How to Select a Sound Horse — unsoundness, blemishes and vices to check; Donkey Care Handbook — how donkeys and mules differ from horses; USDA Mule Production — breeding and raising mules.

🌾 Feeding and water - Total feed: 1.5–2.5% of body weight a day, most of it hay or pasture. Never less than 8–10 lb of hay a day for a 1,000-lb horse; an idle horse holds weight on about 18 lb of good hay. (Nebraska G1781, pp. 1–2; FM 25-5, p. 101) - Weigh a horse with a string: weight (lb) = heart girth (in) × heart girth (in) × body length (in) ÷ 330. Body length is point of shoulder to point of buttock. (G1781, p. 1; 🖼️ where to measure) - Working horses: about 1.1 lb grain + 1.25 lb hay per 100 lb of body weight a day, grain split into 3 feeds. Keep each grain meal under about 5 lb for a 1,000-lb horse. Feed by weight: a quart of oats ≈ 1 lb, a quart of corn ≈ 1.7 lb. (USDA FB1419, p. 9; G1781, p. 3; UGA B1356) - Water: 5–15 gallons a day, double in heat or hard work (an idle horse drinks about 10–12 — G1781, p. 4). Give an exhausted horse small drinks every 5–10 minutes until it recovers. In cold weather, take the chill off the water or salt the feed (1–2 oz) so it keeps drinking (prevents impaction colic). (UGA B1356, p. 2; FM 25-5) - Salt: about 3 oz a day; loose salt-mineral beats a block. Western Oregon

feed (1–2 oz) so it keeps drinking (prevents impaction colic). (UGA B1356, p. 2; FM 25-5) - Salt: about 3 oz a day; loose salt-mineral beats a block. Western Oregon soils are low in selenium — use a mineral that contains it. (Rule of thumb) (AIB 353; UGA B1356, p. 3) - Army feeding rules that prevent colic: water before feeding (or wait an hour after); never grain a hot horse (hay is fine); a little hay before grain; change feeds gradually over 1–2 weeks; never feed moldy or dusty hay. (FM 25-5, p. 103) - Body condition: keep them at 5–7 on the 1–9 scale — feel ribs, back and tailhead with your hands; a winter coat hides thinness. (G1781, p. 2; 🖼️ where to feel) Body condition at a glance (G1781, p. 3): | Score | Ribs | Back | | 1–3 (thin) | Easy to see | Backbone sticks up | | 4 | Faint outline shows | Slight ridge | | 5 (ideal) | Can't see, easy to feel | Level | | 6–7 | Felt with pressure | Slight crease | | 8–9 (fat) | Hard or impossible to feel | Deep crease, bulging fat | More feeding rules from the modern bulletins: - Turning out onto lush spring grass: a few hours a day for 2–3 days, then half days for 2–3 days, then

| More feeding rules from the modern bulletins: - Turning out onto lush spring grass: a few hours a day for 2–3 days, then half days for 2–3 days, then full time — or fill them up on hay first (G1781, p. 4). - Never feed cattle feed containing Rumensin — it kills horses (G1781, p. 4). - A horse that bolts its grain: put a few fist-sized rocks in the feed box (USFS Horse Packing, p. 3). - Plan the winter hay: at 1.5–2% of body weight, a 1,000-lb horse eats 15–20 lb of hay a day — roughly 450–600 lb for every month off pasture (arithmetic from G1781's table). Add a margin for waste and a late spring. - Donkeys are different: they do best on good barley straw (high fiber, low sugar), not rich horse hay (Donkey Care Handbook, p. 16; 🖼️ a homemade straw feeder). Pasture in our wet climate (OSU EC1558): 1. Keep horses off pasture through the wet months. Wet soil compacts, the grass dies, and you buy more hay next year. Hold them in a sacrifice area (a dry lot) instead (pp. 4–5; 🖼️ photo). 2. Graze only when the grass is over 3 inches tall and the soil is firm. Move them when it's grazed to 3–4 inches; let it regrow to 6–8 inches before grazing again (p. 7; 🖼️ why: leaves

3 inches tall and the soil is firm. Move them when it's grazed to 3–4 inches; let it regrow to 6–8 inches before grazing again (p. 7; 🖼️ why: leaves feed the roots). 3. Keep clover and alfalfa under 30% of the mix to reduce colic risk (p. 10). 📚 Go deeper: Nebraska G1781 — feed by body weight, weight tape formula, condition scoring; UGA B1356 — 25 feeding rules that prevent colic; OSU EC1558 Small-Acreage Horse Farms — western Oregon pasture, mud and manure; USDA FB 1030 Feeding Horses — rations from home-grown hay and grain.

🦷 Teeth and worms - Teeth: check at least yearly (twice for older horses). Sharp edges form on the outside of the upper molars and inside of the lowers — float (rasp) them (🖼️ how to hold the float) or the horse drops feed and loses weight. (PNW 587, p. 46; Merillat Animal Dentistry) - Signs of tooth trouble: dropping grain while chewing, holding the head sideways, eating slowly, whole grain in the manure, losing condition (G1781, p. 4). - Worms: don't deworm blindly every 8 weeks. Adults need 1–2 treatments a year (one in fall for bots and tapeworms); youngsters 3–4. When dewormers run out: pick up manure, don't overgraze, rotate pastures and graze with cattle or sheep. (Penn State/SARE, pp. 1–2) - Know your high shedders: most horses carry few worms; a few shed most of the eggs. Penn State's line: deworm a horse whose fecal egg count is over about 300 eggs per gram; over 500 is a "high shedder" (Penn State, pp. 1–2). Foals need a special schedule — ask the books, not guesswork. - Kill eggs without drugs: a manure pile that heats to 130–150 °F kills most parasites, flies and weed seeds (OSU EC1558, p. 16; 🖼️ covered piles); dragging or harrowing pastures in dry weather spreads droppings so eggs dry out (p. 15). - Donkeys can carry lungworm with no signs and pass

p. 16; 🖼️ covered piles); dragging or harrowing pastures in dry weather spreads droppings so eggs dry out (p. 15). - Donkeys can carry lungworm with no signs and pass it to horses — worm them together (Donkey Care Handbook, p. 16). 📚 Go deeper: Penn State Managing Equine Parasites — the egg-count method and when to treat; 4-H PNW 587 — teeth and aging; Merillat Animal Dentistry — floating and dental work by hand (old book: skills only).

🦶 Hoof care and shoeing - Pick out the feet every day (🖼️ how). A healthy frog feels like firm rubber (🖼️ parts of the hoof). Thrush) (black, stinking rot in the frog) comes from wet, dirty footing — trim away dead tissue, apply an antiseptic, and get the horse onto dry ground. In our wet winters, give horses a dry gravel or wood-chip standing area. (TM 2-220, p. 97; PNW 587; OSU EC1558, p. 2) - Hooves grow about ⅜ inch a month. Trim barefoot horses every 6–12 weeks, donkeys and mules every 6–10; the Army reset shoes every 3–6 weeks (🖼️ untrimmed vs. trimmed). (NMSU B-707, p. 2; Donkey Care Handbook, p. 14; TM 2-220) - Going barefoot (when shoes and nails run out): leave the sole, balance the wall, round off the outer edge so it doesn't chip (🖼️ using the rasp), and check weekly. Most horses do fine barefoot on soft ground; hard rocky work wears feet faster than they grow. (TM 2-220, p. 98) - Making and fitting shoes: TM 2-220 The Horseshoer teaches forging shoes from bar stock, fitting and nailing (🖼️ nailing and clinching), and even shoeing in the field with a ground fire and a rail for an anvil. Lungwitz's Text-Book of Horseshoeing is the standard reference (🖼️ the foot from the side; farrier). Pair with the Blacksmithing guide. Taking shoes off

Taking shoes off for good (TM 2-220, p. 97): 1. Pull the shoes, then trim to balance and round the edge of the wall. Leave the dead sole. 2. Expect the hoof to break away and the horse to go a bit tender for the first few weeks. It isn't serious and passes as new horn grows. 3. On rough, rocky pasture, leave the front shoes on for the first few days while the horse settles, then pull them. 4. Even shod horses do better with 2–3 months a year barefoot. Mud is the enemy here. Wet ground softens hooves and soles, leading to cracks, stone bruises, abscesses and thrush; mud also causes "mud fever" (scratches) — crusty scabs on the lower legs (OSU EC1558, p. 2). For the dry lot, lay down twice as much footing as you have mud: landscape fabric, 3 inches of ¾–1½-inch crushed rock, then 6 inches of gravel or sand or up to 12 inches of wood chips (p. 5; 🖼️ photo). Field tips from the Army farrier: store horseshoe nails wrapped in an oiled cloth in a watertight can, and a worn rasp can be re-sharpened with a three-cornered file and re-hardened (TM 2-220, p. 99)

🤠 Handling, saddling and riding - Leading: from the left side, right hand near the halter, slack folded (never wrapped) in your left hand. If the horse rears, let go with the hand nearest the halter so you stay on the ground. (PNW 587, p. 51) - Tying: use a quick-release knot (🖼️ drawing; 🖼️ step by step), about 3 ft of rope, tied at or above withers height to something solid. Any rope around the neck gets a bowline (it can't tighten), never a slip knot. Untie before taking the halter off. (PNW 587, p. 51; Basic Horse Safety, p. 3) - Saddle fit: with pad and rider on, the gullet must clear the withers. After a sweaty ride, even sweat marks = good fit; dry spots = pressure. A sliding saddle needs a breast collar, not a tighter cinch. Dry spots with raised skin lead to saddle sores and white hair — fix the fit now (UF Saddle Fit, p. 3). - Cinching): snug it gradually until a flat hand just slips under, walk the horse a few steps, then recheck after a short ride — many horses puff up their bellies. On the trail, stop after 1–2 miles to retighten. (PNW 587; Animal Management) - Mounting and riding: mount from the left, reins short enough to stop the horse (🖼️ holding the reins), sit deep with heels

miles to retighten. (PNW 587; Animal Management) - Mounting and riding: mount from the left, reins short enough to stop the horse (🖼️ holding the reins), sit deep with heels down. The 4-H manual (PNW 587) and FM 25-5 walk through riding step by step. - Starting young horses: handle foals early and teach them to lead before weaning. Light harness or saddle work at 2–3 years; no heavy work until they're nearly mature. First tie with a neck rope through the halter ring, tied with a bowline. (USDA FB1368) - Holding a horse for treatment: have a helper hold up another foot while you work on a leg; a twitch on the upper lip works for short jobs — tighten it only enough to stay on and take it off as soon as you can (PNW 587, p. 30). - Tack repair: cutting leather, hand-stitching with waxed thread and riveting are in TM 10-430 The Saddler and Hasluck's Harness Making (🖼️ sewing awls; 🖼️ stitching clamp). 📚 Go deeper: 4-H PNW 587 — handling, safety knots, tack, saddling and riding; UF Saddle Fit — checking tree fit and sweat patterns; The Saddler TM 10-430 — hand-repairing saddles and tack; USDA Breaking and Training Colts — gentling and starting young horses.

🩺 Health checks and first aid Normal vital signs at rest — the sources differ a little, so learn your own horse's normal by taking it twice a day for a week (PNW 587, p. 28; 🖼️ vital-signs chart): | | Temperature | Pulse (beats/min) | Breaths/min | | 4-H PNW 587 | 99–101 °F (102+ = sick) | 32–48 (over 50 = distress) | 8–20 | | Raising Healthy Horses | 99–101.5 °F | 40–48 | 10–14 | | UGA B1356 | 99.5–101.5 °F | 32–36 | 8–12 | Take the pulse under the jawbone for 15 seconds × 4. A pinched fold of neck skin should flatten in 1–2 seconds; gums should be pink and moist; a healthy horse passes several piles of manure a day (PNW 587, p. 28). Act fast (no vet coming? treat these as emergencies) — temperature 102 °F or more, signs of colic, a deep puncture, a wound near an eye, joint or tendon, severe lameness, choking, off feed 12–24 hours, worsening cough, persistent diarrhea, or a mare in trouble foaling (PNW 587, p. 29). Colic (belly pain) — looking at or kicking at the belly, pawing, rolling, getting up and down, sweating, little or no manure, pulse over 60 (PNW 587, p. 31; UF VM275, pp. 3–4; 🖼️ a horse in colic): - Take away all feed. Let it stand or lie

little or no manure, pulse over 60 (PNW 587, p. 31; UF VM275, pp. 3–4; 🖼️ a horse in colic): - Take away all feed. Let it stand or lie quietly; walk it only briefly if it's throwing itself around — don't walk it to exhaustion. - Don't syringe in oil or water, and never put a hose down its nose or throat — the fluid goes into the lungs. Don't repeat painkillers without advice. - Water: sources disagree — UF lets the horse drink; the 4-H manual says no food or water until the vet sees it. - If it recovers on its own, no feed for 12–24 hours, then small meals over 3–5 days, and watch for manure (8–12 piles a day is normal) (UF VM275, p. 4). Choke) (feed stuck in the gullet) — saliva and feed running from the nose (🖼️ photo), retching, sometimes a lump you can see or feel in the neck. It can still breathe. Remove all feed and water, keep it on bare ground or muzzle it, gently massage a visible lump; many cases clear in a couple of hours. Watch for fever over 101.5 °F or coughing in the days after — food in the lungs causes pneumonia (UF VM275, pp. 4–5). Wounds: hose with cold water, pat dry, apply antiseptic. For heavy bleeding use a pressure bandage, not a tourniquet;

— food in the lungs causes pneumonia (UF VM275, pp. 4–5). Wounds: hose with cold water, pat dry, apply antiseptic. For heavy bleeding use a pressure bandage, not a tourniquet; a horse can lose up to 4 gallons of blood without severe stress. Watch for proud flesh (red, lumpy tissue) in wounds over joints (PNW 587, p. 30). Eyes: rinse gently with saline (1 teaspoon salt in a pint of boiled water — Raising Healthy Horses, p. 9) or weak-tea-colored dilute betadine. Never alcohol or chlorhexidine near the eye, and no steroid ointments. Put on a fly mask (UF VM275, pp. 5–6; 🖼️ a painful eye). Swollen face, noisy breathing (snakebite, bee sting): horses can't breathe through the mouth. Cut two pieces of soft hose as long as from the inner corner of the eye to the nostril, lubricate them, slide one into each nostril and tape them in place (UF VM275, p. 6; 🖼️ photo). Donkeys hide illness. A dull donkey off its feed is an emergency — it can fall into hyperlipaemia (fat flooding the blood) and die. Coax it to eat with fresh grass or favorite food and warm water. When a donkey loses its companion, let it stay with the body until it loses interest, and watch it closely for three weeks (Donkey Care Handbook, pp. 108–110). 🎒 Travel and packing | | | | Walk / trot | about 4 mph / 8–9 mph | | Steady day's travel | 20+ miles on easy ground, 10–15 in mountains | | Rider | no more than about 20% of the horse's weight (250 lb max) | | Pack load | 200–250 lb per 900–1,000-lb animal; 300 lb only short-distance | | Load balance | side packs within 2–3 lb of each other | (FM 25-5; FM 25-7; USFS Instructions on Horse Packing, pp. 2, 20; Montana outfitters manual) - On the road: rest 5–10 minutes every hour; every 2–3 hours unsaddle, let the horse roll and graze. Walk them up steep hills. Only hardened horses can do 40–50 miles a day for days on end. Condition animals 2–4 weeks before hard travel. (Animal Management) - Packing: sawbuck and Decker pack saddles (🖼️ Decker, 🖼️ sawbuck), hitches and loading are in the 1943 Forest Service manual (written for Oregon and Washington) and FM 25-7, which also shows improvised pack saddles and a travois (🖼️ pack saddle improvised from horseshoes). - Lighter loads when breaking in a pack string, on long or fast trips, or on steep rough trail.
