🚜 Harness and draft work - What an animal can pull all day: about one-tenth of its body weight in steady draft (a big horse pulling 150 lb at 2½ mph ≈ 1 horsepower). Donkeys pull about a fifth of their weight for 3–4 hours. A cart donkey should pull no more than twice its weight, cart included, on the flat. (Peace Corps Animal Traction, p. 20; Donkey Care Handbook) Sources differ: Starkey quotes 15% of body weight as normal pulling power for horses (Starkey, p. 118). - Collar fit: a flat hand should just pass between the collar and the windpipe (🖼️ drawing). A short collar chokes; a long one bruises the shoulders. Give each horse its own collar and wipe it after every use. Sore shoulders are the #1 harness problem. (USDA FB1419; FM 25-5; 🖼️ where collar sores form) - Harness, hitching, driving pairs and teams, carts, plows and sledges: FM 25-5, Mounted Instruction for Field Artillery, the Peace Corps Animal Traction manual and Starkey's Harnessing and Implements (🖼️ harnessing options). Big-team hitches and eveners: Sommerfeld's How to Hitch Horses (🖼️ five-horse evener; 🖼️ eveners for four horses). Preventing sore shoulders, step by step (USDA FB1419, pp. 17–20): 1. Fit: flat hand at the windpipe, fingertips at the sides of the neck just above the shoulder points. A narrow collar pinches; a wide one rubs. 2. Skip

17–20): 1. Fit: flat hand at the windpipe, fingertips at the sides of the neck just above the shoulder points. A narrow collar pinches; a wide one rubs. 2. Skip sweat pads — they cause more sore shoulders than a clean, smooth collar. 3. Set the hames snug so the pull comes about one-third of the way up from the point of the shoulder (🖼️ point of draft; 🖼️ hames). 4. Spring toughening: for the first 2–3 weeks of work, wash the shoulders after work with warm water and mild soap, then rinse with cold water with a little salt in it. 5. At midday, lift the collar forward, wipe off sweat and dirt, and let the shoulders cool. 6. Allow for winter hair and extra flesh when fitting a collar in spring — the fit changes as the horse works down. Harness care: hang it in a dry room; wipe the collar face after every use; once a year take it apart, soak 15 minutes in lukewarm water with mild soap, clean, oil and restitch. Keep a repair kit: punch, rivets, awls, needles, waxed thread, a clamp, spare leather, snaps and buckles (FB1419, p. 18). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB1419 Farm Work Horses — collar fitting, sore shoulders, harness care; Peace Corps Animal Traction — choosing and training draft animals, yokes, plows and carts; Starkey Harnessing and Implements —

🏠 Shelter, Building & Repair The best shelter you will ever have is the house you already live in — if you keep the water out. This guide covers keeping an existing house sound (roof leaks, flashing, gutters, rot and insects), heating one warm room, reglazing windows, durable local woods, hand-tool carpentry, splitting your own shakes, drying lumber, log and earth building, chimneys, earthquake and wildfire hardening, and emergency tarp shelters. The books are in Shelter-Building\ (House-Repair, Carpentry-Timber, Earth-Natural-Building, Wildfire-Quake-Hardening). Hand tools and saws are in Blacksmithing-Tools\Hand-Tools; quake and fire guides are in Earthquake-Tsunami\ and Wildfire\; cob, straw bale, light straw-clay, hempcrete, earth and lime plasters, making lime and thatch are in the Natural Building guide and Natural-Building\. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Roof work kills. Use scaffolds, ladders or a safety rope (USDA FB 1751, p. 24). Never work on a wet or mossy roof, or alone (rule of thumb). - Old houses hold lead paint (before 1978) and asbestos (old shingles, siding, pipe wrap). Don't sand, cut, heat or burn them. Scrape paint wet and keep children away (rule of thumb). - Carbon monoxide. Any fuel heater without a chimney needs an open window — 1 sq in per 1,000 Btu (MSU E-1669, p. 3). Keep a battery CO alarm by the beds. - Cascadia will shake hard. Brick chimneys were damaged in most

— 1 sq in per 1,000 Btu (MSU E-1669, p. 3). Keep a battery CO alarm by the beds. - Cascadia will shake hard. Brick chimneys were damaged in most big U.S. quakes (FEMA 232, p. 144), and heavy unreinforced earth walls can collapse. Build light, keep earth walls low and single-story, and bolt the house to its foundation (FEMA 232, p. 168). - Wildfire comes as embers. Screen vents with 1/8-in metal mesh, keep gutters clear, and keep firewood 30 ft from the house (OSFM, p. 8; FEMA P-737, p. 23). - Never use the old poisons the old bulletins recommend — DDT, arsenic, pentachlorophenol, coal-tar creosote. See the last section.

🏚️ Finding and patching roof leaks Inspect the roof regularly for breaks, missing shingles, choked gutters and damaged flashing (USDA FB 1751, p. 22) — every fall before the rains, and after big storms (rule of thumb). Finding the leak (p. 22): - A wet spot near a chimney or outside wall usually means bad flashing or loose mortar. - Under an open roof, the drip can land well downslope from the hole. Follow the stain uphill. - If you see daylight from the attic, push a straw through the hole so you can find it from outside. - South-facing slopes wear out faster. Check them most often. Emergency patches: - Missing wood shingle: cut a piece of tin-can metal, paint it on both sides, and slide it under the course above. Don't loosen the good shingles. Cut old nails with a long, thin cold chisel, and dab roofer's cement on any exposed nail heads (p. 22). - Metal roof or gutter, no solder: plug small holes with roofer's cement. For big holes, stick canvas or several layers of cloth over the hole with thick paint, then give it several more coats (p. 23). - Bigger damage: tarp it (see the tarp section) until you can repair it. Both shorten a wood roof's life (NPS Brief 19, p. 6). Cut back limbs over the roof — that helps in fire season too. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1751 Roof Coverings for Farm Buildings — finding leaks and repairing every kind of roof; FM 5-426 Carpentry — roofing and flashing details. 💧 Flashing, gutters and keeping water away Roofs leak most where two surfaces meet: valleys, chimneys, dormers and walls. Flash these with galvanized or copper sheet (FM 5-426, p. 119; valleys at p. 124; 🖼️ valley flashing drawings (ignore its red-lead paint); 🖼️ chimney flashing). Flashing over window and door heads should run at least 4 in up behind the siding above the drip cap (USDA AH 73, p. 163; 🖼️ where flashing goes). Move the water away from the house (AH 73, pp. 8–9, 169): - Downspouts should empty onto splash blocks at least 3 ft long that carry water away from the foundation (🖼️ drawing). - The top of the foundation should sit at least 8 in above the ground. - A crawl space needs at least 18 in between the soil and the floor joists, with vents on opposite sides (FB 1993, p. 3). - Grade the soil so it slopes away from the walls, and clean gutters every fall (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: USDA Wood-Frame House Construction (AH 73) — illustrated flashing, gutters, foundations and crawl spaces; FM 5-426 — valley flashing. 🔥 One warm room: drafts, plastic and heat With little fuel, heat one room, not the house. The relief-shelter order of priorities in winter (IFRC/Oxfam Plastic Sheeting, p. 30): 1. Clothing and bedding first. 2. Waterproofing (the roof). 3. Bedding up off the damp floor. 4. Windproofing. 5. Then heat one room. Make a plastic-curtained buffer (a lobby) between the warm room and the cold rest of the house. Insulate floors and walls with straw sandwiched between plastic. Treat any stove in a small room as a fire risk. Seal the drafts (HUD, In the Bank or Up the Chimney, pp. 36–37; 🖼️ caulking drawings): - Caulk wherever two different materials meet: drip caps over windows and doors, frame-to-siding joints, sills, siding corners, where wood meets the foundation, pipe and wire holes, and where a chimney meets siding. - Stuff wide cracks (like the sill) with oakum or fiber first, then caulk. Plastic storm windows (HUD, p. 42): tape clear plastic over the inside of the window frame (easier, and it lasts longer), or tack it outside with 1/4 × 1 1/4 in wood slats. Pull it tight and trim the extra. Heaters without a chimney make carbon monoxide. Leave 1 sq in of open window for every 1,000 Btu of heater output. A 9,100-Btu heater in a room with a 24-in window means opening it almost 1/2 in (MSU

1 sq in of open window for every 1,000 Btu of heater output. A 9,100-Btu heater in a room with a 24-in window means opening it almost 1/2 in (MSU E-1669, p. 3). No fuel at all? Insulate the people: towels, paper bags and layers of newspaper held under old raincoats and shirts (Kearny, p. 130). 📚 Go deeper: HUD In the Bank or Up the Chimney — caulking, weatherstripping and insulation, step by step; IFRC/Oxfam Plastic Sheeting — warm rooms in winter; CMHC wood-heating guide — stove and pipe safety. 🪟 Reglazing and saving windows ⚠️ Paint on windows made before 1978 almost certainly contains lead. Don't sand it dry or heat it until it scorches. Scrape it wet, collect the chips, and keep children away (rule of thumb). Replacing a pane (NPS Brief 9, p. 5; 🖼️ window parts named): 1. Dig out the old putty without gouging the wood. Soaking the glass in linseed oil loosens putty stuck to it. 2. Pull the glazing points (the small metal tabs) and lift out the glass. 3. Lay a thin bed of putty in the rabbet (the groove the glass sits in) and press the pane in. 4. Push in new glazing points. 5. Run a final bead of putty and bevel it with a putty knife so water runs off. 6. Paint when the putty skins over, usually in 2–3 days. Lap the paint slightly onto the glass to seal it. Where window rot starts: the sill, the sill-to-jamb joints, the bottom-rail corners and the muntin (glass-bar) joints — wherever water sits. The sill must slope outward. Cracked putty lets water soak the joints (NPS Brief 9, p. 2). Saving partly rotted wood: let it dry, brush on 2–3 coats of boiled linseed oil, 24 hours apart, fill cracks with putty, then paint (p. 5). Rags soaked in linseed oil can catch fire by themselves — dry them spread

coats of boiled linseed oil, 24 hours apart, fill cracks with putty, then paint (p. 5). Rags soaked in linseed oil can catch fire by themselves — dry them spread flat outdoors or keep them in a can of water (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: NPS Preservation Brief 9 — reglazing, sash cords, weatherstripping and sill repair. Pictures: Putty, Sash window, Putty knife.

🐜 Rot, termites, carpenter ants — and woods that last Dry wood does not rot. Decay needs wood wetter than about 30% moisture. Air-dried wood is at or below 20%, and decay already in the wood stops if it's kept dry (Wood Handbook, p. 314; 🖼️ rot fungi). What rots houses and draws termites (USDA FB 1993, p. 7): wet, unventilated crawl spaces; scrap wood left on the soil; wood touching soil (especially dirt-filled porches); wood buried in masonry near the ground; no gutters or roof overhang; roof and plumbing leaks. The fixes (FB 1993, p. 3): no wood touching soil, an 18-in crawl space, vents on opposite sides (or roll roofing laid over the soil), and an inspection every winter or early spring. Termites build earthen tubes up foundations (🖼️ photo): break them, and block the route with mortar or pitch. Carpenter ants (USFS R10-TP-128, pp. 4, 7; 🖼️ winged ants): - More than 20 ants indoors, especially in winter, means a nest inside the house. - Their frass looks like sawdust mixed with insect parts (🖼️ photo). - They don't eat wood — they hollow out wet, softening wood. Fix the moisture, find and remove the nest wood, keep firewood and debris away from the house, and store food sealed. Which woods last (heartwood only; Wood Handbook, Table 14-1, p. 316): | Decay resistance | Western species |

keep firewood and debris away from the house, and store food sealed. Which woods last (heartwood only; Wood Handbook, Table 14-1, p. 316): | Decay resistance | Western species | | Very resistant | Pacific yew | | Resistant | Port-Orford-cedar, incense-cedar, western redcedar, junipers, white oaks, old-growth redwood | | Moderately resistant | Douglas-fir, western larch | | Slightly or not resistant | True firs, hemlocks, red alder, maples, tanoak, cottonwood, most pines | Locally, Port-Orford-cedar and incense-cedar grow in the valley and the Siskiyous. Use their heartwood for sills, posts, shakes and anything touching the ground. Port-Orford-cedar killed by root disease still has sound, durable heartwood (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1993 Decay and Termite Damage in Houses — spotting decay and termite tubes (ignore its poisons); Wood Handbook ch. 14 — decay, insects and durable species; USFS Carpenter Ants — finding the nest. Pictures: Carpenter ant, Termite, Wood-decay fungus, 🖼️ termite or winged ant? FB 1993 p. 5.

🪚 Hand-tool carpentry and drying lumber Square a corner with 6-8-10 (FM 5-426, p. 48; 🖼️ the same idea with 3-4-5): 1. Measure 6 ft along one line and 8 ft along the other. 2. Move the lines until the diagonal between those two marks is exactly 10 ft. Never use less than 6 ft. 3. When the whole rectangle is laid out, check that both diagonals are equal (🖼️ drawing). Batter boards hold the lines (p. 46; 🖼️ batter boards). Handsaw basics (Disston, p. 10): start on the waste side of the line with your thumb against the blade, and draw back a few times to make a groove. Crosscut at about 45° to the board with full-length strokes. Support the waste piece so it doesn't splinter off. Hewing a log flat (An Ax to Grind, p. 52): hew green, freshly cut logs — dry logs hew badly. Set the log on V-notched yokes about knee high. Snap a chalk line, score down to it with a single-bit axe, then flatten with a broadaxe (🖼️ step-by-step drawings). Roofs and joints: rafter lengths by the step-off method (FM 5-426, p. 108) or the steel square (Brace and Mayne, p. 199; 🖼️ rafter pitch); mortise-and-tenon joints (Griffith, p. 105; 🖼️ drawing). Air-drying lumber (OCHA/IFRC/CARE Timber, pp. 45, 68): - A 1-inch (2.5 cm) board takes about a year to air-dry, depending

🖼️ rafter pitch); mortise-and-tenon joints (Griffith, p. 105; 🖼️ drawing). Air-drying lumber (OCHA/IFRC/CARE Timber, pp. 45, 68): - A 1-inch (2.5 cm) board takes about a year to air-dry, depending on species. Thicker takes longer. - Stack it off the ground on bearers, with stickers (spacer sticks) between every layer (🖼️ stacking drawing). - Seal or paint the ends — they dry fastest and crack. - Cover the top loosely so air still moves through. Wood shrinks most along the growth rings, about half as much across them, and hardly at all along its length (Wood Handbook, p. 84). Green wood opens gaps as it dries. 📚 Go deeper: FM 5-426 Carpentry — layout, framing, rafters and roofing; USFS Handtools for Trail Work, p. 46 — adzes and broadaxes; Timber in Humanitarian Operations — felling, drying and joining timber. Pictures: Broadaxe, Hewing, Adze, Wood drying, 🖼️ air-drying yard, Wood Handbook p. 317.

🪵 Splitting and laying your own shingles and shakes Splitting (NPS Brief 19, p. 2): 1. Cut the log into bolts as long as the shingle, then quarter them. 2. Rive off thin boards along the grain with a froe and mallet (or an axe) (🖼️ froe drawing; 🖼️ photos). 3. For a taper, flip the bolt end-for-end after each split. 4. Use heartwood only. Sapwood rots fast. 5. Old shingles were 3/8–3/4 in thick, 3–8 in wide and 14–36 in long, smoothed with a drawknife so rain doesn't sit in the grain. If a split runs off to one side, start again from the other end of the billet and split back to meet it (Beard, p. 115). Laying wood shingles (USDA FB 1751, pp. 6–7) on a roof of 1/4 pitch or steeper (flatter roofs are hard to keep tight): | Shingle length | Show to the weather | | 16 in | 5 in | | 18 in | 5 1/2 in | | 24 in | 7 1/2 in | - Gaps of 1/4 in between dry shingles, 1/8 in between green ones. - Two rust-resistant nails per shingle, no more than 3/4 in from the edges and 1–2 in above the next butt line. - Break joints by at least 1 1/2 in from the course below. - Double the first course at the eaves

edges and 1–2 in above the next butt line. - Break joints by at least 1 1/2 in from the course below. - Double the first course at the eaves and let it overhang about 1 in. For our wet winters, nail shingles to spaced 1×4 slats (spaced the same as the exposure) instead of solid boards. Air reaches the underside so they dry out, and it takes less lumber (FB 1751, p. 6). A cedar roof on raised, ventilated battens lasted over 60 years in a harsh, wet climate (NPS Brief 19, p. 4). 📚 Go deeper: NPS Preservation Brief 19 — hand-split shingles and why wood roofs fail; Beard Shelters, Shacks and Shanties — shakes and clapboards with only an axe. 🏕️ Log buildings Cutting the logs (USDA FB 1660, pp. 5–6): - If you will peel the logs, fell in winter. Spring-cut logs stain and decay. - Logs over 20 ft are heavy and seldom needed. - Season them stacked in the shade with air around them. Peel them — bark has no practical advantage and invites beetles (🖼️ peeling with a drawknife or bark spud). Foundations: - Wicks sets cedar posts in holes at least 3 ft deep, or uses stone piers — large flat stones or cobbles bedded firmly and chinked with small stones. Hew the sill logs flat on top (Wicks, pp. 15–17). - Keep the bottom logs high and dry. Wicks cuts posts off 10 in above ground; later Forest Products Lab guidance is 12–18 in, with eaves of about 24 in on a one-story cabin (that bulletin is not on the drive). A sill log touching soil is already rotting or soon will be (NPS Brief 26, p. 8). Notching: the common corner notches — saddle, V, dovetail, square — are drawn in NPS Brief 26, p. 5 and FB 1660, p. 12. Notches that cup upward hold rain and rot first (Brief 26, p. 9), so cut the notch in the underside of the upper log (rule of thumb). Chinking and daubing (NPS Brief 26, pp. 6, 12–13; 🖼️ methods drawn) — three layers:

9), so cut the notch in the underside of the upper log (rule of thumb). Chinking and daubing (NPS Brief 26, pp. 6, 12–13; 🖼️ methods drawn) — three layers: 1. Blocking: wood slabs or stones wedged into the gap. 2. Soft packing: moss, oakum or clay. 3. Daub: clay mixed with lime, troweled on wet. Wet the joint first; mix only what you can use in about 30 minutes; don't daub in full sun, heat or frost (p. 13). Daubing is the least durable part of a log building. Patching it is a seasonal chore (p. 12). Delay chinking as long as you can so the logs dry first (FB 1660, p. 12), and fit doors and windows only after the logs have shrunk (Wood Handbook, p. 84). 📚 Go deeper: Wicks Log Cabins and Cottages — a cabin step by step; USDA FB 1660 Logs and Poles — notching, chinking and pole buildings; NPS Brief 26 — repairing rotted logs and daubing mixes. Pictures: Log cabin, Chinking, Log building, 🖼️ log-hewing tools, NPS Brief 26 p. 5.

🧱 Earth building — with the Cascadia caution ⚠️ Heavy, unreinforced earth walls can collapse in a big quake. The Peace Corps handbook calls for steel reinforcement in footings and walls in earthquake areas (Building Homes of Earth, pp. 70–75). In southern Oregon, keep earth walls low, light and single-story, or use earth only as infill or inside walls within a braced wood frame (rule of thumb). Ribbon test for building soil (Building Homes of Earth, pp. 24–25; 🖼️ drawing): roll damp soil into a cigar shape and squeeze it out between thumb and finger into a ribbon. | Ribbon length | What it means | | 8–10 in | Lots of clay — walls last only if you stabilize or temper it | | 2–4 in | Medium clay — often good | | No ribbon | Too little clay | | Springs back like a sponge | Organic topsoil — unusable | Adobe bricks (USDA FB 1720, pp. 9–10): 1. Puddle clayey loam with water. Mix in no more than 1 part loose straw to 5 parts mud. Too much straw, or manure, weakens the brick. 2. Mould the bricks (🖼️ forms; 🖼️ step by step). After a few days, stand them on edge. 3. Dry them 2–3 weeks under cover from rain. Never let uncured brick freeze. 4. Lay them in mud mortar with 1/2–1 in joints.

few days, stand them on edge. 3. Dry them 2–3 weeks under cover from rain. Never let uncured brick freeze. 4. Lay them in mud mortar with 1/2–1 in joints. Adobe works in wet climates only if the walls are kept dry and the site never floods (p. 3) — so give it wide eaves and a raised foundation. Rammed earth (USDA FB 1500, pp. 9, 11–12): - Right moisture is about 12% water: a squeezed handful should break apart when dropped. - Ram it in 4–5 in layers between forms (🖼️ rammers; 🖼️ forms). - The foundation is masonry as thick as the wall (generally 18 in), at least 12 in above ground so rain can't splash the earth, with a damp-proof course on top. Cob, straw bale, light straw-clay, hempcrete, earth and lime plasters: see the Natural Building guide. 📚 Go deeper: Peace Corps Handbook for Building Homes of Earth — soil tests, blocks, footings and roofs; USDA FB 1720 Adobe — mixing, curing and plasters; USDA FB 1500 Rammed Earth — forms and rammers. Pictures: Adobe, Rammed earth, 🖼️ adobe footings, FB 1720 p. 13, 🖼️ rammed-earth forms, Peace Corps p. 120.

🧯 Chimneys and stovepipe Building or checking a masonry chimney (USDA FB 1889; 🖼️ whole-chimney diagram): - It should rise at least 3 ft above a flat roof and 2 ft above any ridge within 10 ft (p. 4). - It needs a fire-clay flue lining and a footing on solid ground below the frost line (p. 6). - Keep 2 in of air between the chimney masonry and any wood framing (p. 8). - Smoke test before use: build a smoky fire at the base, cover the top tightly with a wet blanket, and look for smoke leaking through the walls. Fix every leak first (p. 10). - Stovepipe must never pass through floors, closets or hidden spaces, or enter the chimney in the attic (p. 10). Single-wall stovepipe needs 18 in from anything that burns; only proper shielding allows less (CMHC, p. 36). Repointing loose chimney mortar: rake it out and refill with 1 part portland cement, 1 part lime and 6 parts sand (FB 1751, p. 24). When cement runs out, use lime and sand, about 1:3 — and keep hard cement off soft old brick (rule of thumb). Cleaning and chimney fires: see the Firewood guide. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1889 Fireplaces and Chimneys — flues, footings, clearances and cleanouts; CMHC Guide to Residential Wood Heating — current clearances. 🌎 Earthquake and wildfire hardening Earthquake (FEMA 232): - Masonry chimneys are heavy, rigid and often brittle. They have been damaged in most moderate to severe U.S. earthquakes, and a damaged chimney becomes a falling hazard. Light flues do better (pp. 144–145). Don't put beds beside a brick chimney (rule of thumb). - The best-value retrofits: bolt the sill plate to the foundation, and sheathe crawl-space cripple walls (the short stud walls between foundation and floor) with plywood. Replace decayed sill wood while you're there (pp. 168–170; 🖼️ sill bolts; 🖼️ cripple-wall bracing). - Check your house: look under it for bolts in the sill — no more than 6 ft apart on a one-story house, 4 ft on a two-story (Living on Shaky Ground, p. 15). Wildfire — embers cause up to 90% of house ignitions and can fly miles ahead of a fire (OSFM, p. 5). They blow into vents and light the debris in gutters (FEMA P-737, p. 13): - Vents: cover with 1/8-in metal mesh, or fit ember-rated vents (OSFM, p. 8). 1/16-in mesh stops more embers but clogs; replace or cover any 1/4-in mesh (Oregon BCD, p. 5). - Gutters: metal gutters with noncombustible leaf guards. Mesh guards still let pine needles build up, so check and clear them (FEMA P-737, pp. 45–46). - Woodpiles at least 30 ft from the house, on bare or

guards. Mesh guards still let pine needles build up, so check and clear them (FEMA P-737, pp. 45–46). - Woodpiles at least 30 ft from the house, on bare or gravelled ground (P-737, p. 23). Never store firewood or fuel under a house on an open foundation (p. 58), and keep the space under decks clear (p. 59). 📚 Go deeper: FEMA 232 ch. 9 — retrofitting existing houses; Living on Shaky Ground — Oregon's checklist; FEMA P-737 — vents, roofs, decks, windows and siding; Oregon Home Hardening Guide. ⛺ Emergency tarp and plastic shelters Fixing plastic so it doesn't tear (IFRC/Oxfam Plastic Sheeting, p. 26): - Spread the load. Plain nails pull straight through. Nail through wooden battens, or use washers or bottle caps (sharp side away from the plastic), or fold the plastic over a rope. - Fold the sheet over on itself wherever you fasten it (🖼️ good and bad fixings). Keep it tight and sloped (p. 29): a loose sheet flaps in the wind and holds puddles, and both tear it. Keep nail heads flush, smooth anything that touches the plastic, and keep branches and hot metal (stovepipes) away. Tarping a damaged roof (rule of thumb): run the tarp over the ridge so rain can't get under its top edge, and hold it down with battens nailed through it, not with nails alone. Out in the open: a poncho lean-to needs only a poncho, 2–3 m of cord, three stakes and two trees (FM 21-76, p. 49; 🖼️ drawing). For fallout shelters, see the Nuclear Fallout guide. 📚 Go deeper: IFRC/Oxfam Plastic Sheeting — fixing, repairs and warm rooms; Beard — bark and brush lean-tos up to pole houses; Kearny Expedient Shelter Handbook — quickly built earth-covered shelters.

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - Poisons for termites and rot: DDT, sodium arsenite, pentachlorophenol and trichlorobenzene (USDA FB 1993, pp. 26–27; p. 20). All are banned or highly toxic. Use none. Control moisture, keep wood off the soil, and break termite tubes instead. - Coal-tar creosote painted on logs, cut ends and posts (FB 1660, p. 5; FB 1500, p. 13; Beard, p. 188). It is toxic and causes cancer; never use it in living space. Use durable heartwood and keep it dry. - Asbestos shingles, siding and heat shields (FB 1751, p. 9; AH 73, p. 92; NPS Brief 9, p. 5). Don't cut, break, sand or burn it. For a heat shield use aluminum foil on gypsum board, which the same page offers. - Lead paint — white-lead and red-lead paints for roofs, flashing and primer (FB 1751, p. 21; AH 73, p. 194), and heat on old paint (NPS Brief 9, p. 3). Don't make or use lead paint; scrape old paint wet, never heat it. - Stovepipe 9 in from woodwork (FB 1889, p. 10). Use 18 in for single-wall pipe. The same bulletin lets framing sit 1/2 in from 8-in masonry (p. 11) — keep 2 in. - 1/4-in vent mesh (FEMA P-737, p. 40). Oregon now says 1/8 in. - Cabin posts 10 in above ground (Wicks, p. 15). Go

(p. 11) — keep 2 in. - 1/4-in vent mesh (FEMA P-737, p. 40). Oregon now says 1/8 in. - Cabin posts 10 in above ground (Wicks, p. 15). Go 12–18 in. - FEMA 232's code numbers (2003 IRC, e.g. p. 144) are out of date; its bolting, cripple-wall and chimney advice still holds. 📚 Go deeper: Wood Handbook ch. 14 — durable species instead of poisons; Oregon Home Hardening Guide — current vent rules.

🧱 Natural Building: Cob, Straw, Clay, Hemp & Lime Building walls, plasters and floors from local earth, straw, hemp and lime that stand up to Cascadia shaking, wet winters and fire season — plus burning your own lime and thatching sheds. The books are in Natural-Building\ (Cob-Earth, Straw-Bale-Light-Clay, Hemp-Lime, Plasters-Lime-Floors, Roofs-Thatch, Quake-Moisture). The soil ribbon test, adobe, rammed earth, log chinking and quake retrofits are in the Shelter guide; cordwood and earthbag how-tos are only in the Appropedia archive in Manuals\DIY-Appropedia. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Never build earth or straw walls where floods reach. Cob walls collapsed outright when floodwater rose up them (DSIR 1922, p. 19). Our river soils flood (Soil Survey, p. 17). - Keep the roof light and off the earth walls. The deadliest quake failure is walls falling out and the roof falling in (Minke, p. 13). One storey. - Quicklime burns eyes and skin, and damp quicklime can start a fire. Goggles and gloves; store it airtight (NBS Circular 30, p. 10). - No cement or plastic over earth or straw. They trap water and rot the wall from inside (NPS Brief 5, p. 5; BSD-112, p. 12). - Loose straw is tinder. In fire season plaster bales promptly, sweep up straw daily, and never thatch a house with a stove (rule of thumb). - Serpentine rock can carry natural

straw is tinder. In fire season plaster bales promptly, sweep up straw daily, and never thatch a house with a stove (rule of thumb). - Serpentine rock can carry natural asbestos. Never crush or sieve it dry (rule of thumb).

🧭 Choosing a system for our conditions The key advice: in Cascadia country, build a braced timber frame that carries a light roof, and use earth or straw only as infill or a skin. Keep it one storey. Never build on floodplain soils. Shaking forces grow with weight, and mud-walled houses have caused the most quake deaths (PA EQ Housing, p. 2). The safest layout puts the roof on its own posts (Minke, p. 38): if the walls fall, the roof stays up. 🌎 Quake rules for earth walls Minke's 10 mistakes that collapse earth houses (p. 12): (1) no ring beam; (2) lintels too short; (3) too little wall between a door and a window; (4) openings too close to corners; (5) no plinth; (6) windows too wide for their height; (7) walls too thin for their height; (8) poor mortar — part-filled joints, or joints over 15 mm (⅝ in); (9) too heavy a roof; (10) a roof not fixed to the walls. Shape and size: square beats rectangle, circle beats square; split an L-shape into separate blocks (Minke, p. 9). Walls no taller than 11.5 ft, no unsupported wall longer than 23 ft, no gables, wall tops tied together (PA, p. 3). Doors and windows (Minke, p. 41; PA, p. 3): - Windows no wider than 4 ft, nor more than ⅓ of the wall's length. - Openings at least 2 ft from corners; wall between openings at least 3¼ ft and ⅓ of its height. - Lintels bear 40 cm (Minke) or 50 cm (PA) into the wall each side — use 20 in, or make the lintel part of the ring beam. - Doors open outward, with a big window or second door opposite as an emergency exit. Ring beam: a closed timber ring with stiff corners, tied down by vertical wooden rods from the foundation up to

big window or second door opposite as an emergency exit. Ring beam: a closed timber ring with stiff corners, tied down by vertical wooden rods from the foundation up to a double timber ring beam (Minke, p. 35; 🖼️ PA timber bond-beam drawings). Block walls also need vertical bars at corners, openings and every 5 ft (CSEB manual, p. 12). Siting: don't cut into a slope, build on one, or sit below a steep one; level a platform well back (Minke, p. 8). Avoid fill, river banks, landslide ground and slopes over 20° (CSEB, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: Minke — plinths, ring beams and separate roofs, drawn; CSEB manual — bands and reinforcement step by step. Pictures: 🖼️ the ten mistakes drawn, Minke p. 12, 🖼️ good and bad openings, p. 41, 🖼️ where not to build, p. 8.

🎩 "A good hat and good boots": keeping walls dry "Giv'un a gude hat and pair of butes an' 'er'l last for ever" — cob asks only for dry foundations and a good roof (Williams-Ellis, p. 46). Boots — raise the wall off the ground: | Wall | Stone or masonry base above ground | | Cob | About 2 ft (Williams-Ellis, p. 56) | | Earth walls in quake country | At least 12 in, on a footing 8 in wider than the wall and 16 in deep (Minke, p. 34) | | Plastered straw bales | At least 6 in; 8–12 in better (BSD-112, p. 6) | Don't lay a smooth damp-proof layer on the plinth — in a quake the wall slides off. Key it with vertical wooden rods every 12–20 in and a rough plinth top (Minke, p. 34). Hat: an overhang, a pitched roof and nearby shelter can cut the rain on a wall tenfold (BSD-112, p. 5; 🖼️ how walls get wet). Minimum overhangs: 16 in on one storey, 24 in on two, with gutters (p. 11); here, go wider (rule of thumb). Hip the roof rather than build tall earth gables (Williams-Ellis, p. 57). Grade the ground away, dig a gravel drain trench, keep shrubs off (p. 5). Let the wall breathe: - Cement doesn't bond to earth. It hangs on nails that rust, cracks, lets water in and stops the wall drying (NPS Brief 5, pp. 3, 5). A New Mexico church plastered in cement in 1967 had to be stripped 11 years later (Minke, p. 49). - No building paper or plastic behind plaster on straw — it stops the wall drying (BSD-112, p. 12; 🖼️ how walls dry). 📚 Go deeper: NPS Preservation Brief 5 — how water destroys earth walls; BSD-112 — rain control for straw walls. ⛏️ Local materials: clay, sand, straw and stone Clay — the Pollard soils. Under the loam topsoil is red subsoil about 50% clay; the typical profile is half a mile south of Kerby (Soil Survey, p. 157). They cover high terraces and hillsides in the Illinois River and Deer Creek valleys (p. 18) and are rated "too clayey," with moderate shrink-swell (p. 223): a fat clay that needs lots of sand. Use the ribbon test in the Shelter guide and a shrink box — pack damp soil in a 2-ft box; more than ¼ in of shrinkage means it will crack (PA Mud Plasters, p. 4). Be wary of serpentine clay. Brockman soils, on alluvial fans in the valley (🖼️ photo), formed from serpentinite and are "very sticky and very plastic" (Soil Survey, p. 141). Expect bad cracking; make test bricks first, and keep it damp (rule of thumb). Sand and gravel: the Takilma and Kerby low terraces are cobbly loam over extremely gravelly sand (p. 18). Screen out stones over ¼ in (5–6 mm) for blocks and plaster (PA Soil Blocks, p. 10). Straw, never hay. Building straw is the dead stalks of wheat, barley or oats (BSD-112, p. 3). Hay molds (rule of thumb), and leftover grain draws mice and birds that tunnel in (Beard, p. 80). Grain straw comes from the Klamath Basin and Willamette Valley; buy

3). Hay molds (rule of thumb), and leftover grain draws mice and birds that tunnel in (Beard, p. 80). Grain straw comes from the Klamath Basin and Willamette Valley; buy tight, dry, bright bales and store them off the ground under cover (rule of thumb). Limestone and marble: see the deposit table under Making lime. 📚 Go deeper: Josephine County Soil Survey — maps of clay and gravel; PA Soil Blocks — shrink and drop tests. 🏺 Cob, step by step Cob is mostly aggregate held by about one-fifth clay: old Devon cob tested at 24% stones, 52% sand, 21% clay, about 1% straw (DSIR, p. 16). Here, use it for infill between frame posts, garden walls and small sheds — not tall load-bearing walls. Cob); 🖼️ old Devon cob cottages. Season: Devon built March to September (Williams-Ellis, p. 56). Here, build May–September and get the roof on before the October rains (rule of thumb). 1. Plinth: stone, about 2 ft high, keyed with wooden rods (see above; 🖼️ drawing). 2. Mix: heap the earth beside the wall and pick out big stones. Four people turn the heap with forks, treading all the while; one sprinkles water, another straw. Turn it twice (p. 53). 3. Lay: tread it onto the wall in diagonal layers, working the heels, overhanging the base about an inch for paring (pp. 54–55). 4. Lifts: about 2 ft; each takes 2–3 weeks to dry, so work several walls in turn. Pare each lift plumb when firm (p. 55). 5. Thickness: 18 in minimum, one storey only (p. 57). 6. Openings: wooden lintels well tailed in (20 in each side); frames fixed to wooden blocks built into the cob (p. 61). 7. Corners crack, so round them (DSIR, p. 16). 8. Top: a closed timber ring beam (🖼️ drawing), then a light hipped

wooden blocks built into the cob (p. 61). 7. Corners crack, so round them (DSIR, p. 16). 8. Top: a closed timber ring beam (🖼️ drawing), then a light hipped roof with good eaves. 9. Dry: don't render the outside for one to two years; protect it from frost and rain meanwhile (Williams-Ellis, p. 56). Labor: eight mostly green men took three months to raise one cottage's walls (p. 49). 📚 Go deeper: Williams-Ellis Cottage Building in Cob — mixing, lifts, finishing; DSIR Building in Cob and Pisé — regional methods and why cob fails. Pictures: 🖼️ cob walls ready for mud render, PA Mud Plasters p. 1, 🖼️ clay-lump and mud-wall houses, DSIR p. 31.

🌾 Straw bale Bales (BSD-112, p. 3): two-string 18 × 14 in; three-string 24 × 16–18 in; 32–40 in long; at least 7 lb per cubic foot. Straw is fine up to about 20% moisture; rot begins at 25–30% (CMHC 00-103, p. 2). Straw-bale construction. How it works: plaster skins (lime or cement 1–1½ in, earth 2–3 in) carry 95–99% of the load; the bales insulate (BSD-112, p. 4). Here, use bales as infill in a timber frame (rule of thumb). Building it: toe-up 6 in or more, with a capillary break between foundation and plaster (CMHC, p. 3); wide overhangs and gutters; careful flashing at window and door sills and heads, where rain gets in (BSD-112, p. 11); earth or lime plaster straight onto the straw. The wet-coast warning (CMHC 00-103, pp. 2–3): the walls that rotted had two or more of these: minimal overhangs; no capillary break; heavy indoor wetting; bales below grade; poor splash protection; a north-facing wall. Straw in floors rotted to "nothing but a pile of black compost." On the rainy coast a north wall stayed damp from humid air alone; CMHC urges "extreme caution" with north walls in high-rain climates. Never put straw under a floor. Fire: a wall of 7.5 lb/ft³ wheat bales with 1 in of earth plaster each side passed a 1-hour fire test and the hose stream. The plaster: 3

a floor. Fire: a wall of 7.5 lb/ft³ wheat bales with 1 in of earth plaster each side passed a 1-hour fire test and the hose stream. The plaster: 3 parts clay, 2 chopped straw, 6 sand, in two ½-in coats (Intertek, pp. 13, 16). Fire-season site rules (rule of thumb): plaster within days; rake up loose straw every evening; keep water and a hose on site; no grinding or welding near straw; store spare bales well away from buildings — FEMA puts sheds holding combustibles 50 ft or more from a house (FEMA P-737, p. 23). 📚 Go deeper: BSD-112 Building Science for Strawbale — moisture, overhangs, plaster; Intertek fire test — photos and plaster mix. 🪵 Lighter systems: straw-clay, hempcrete, wattle, bags, blocks, cordwood Light straw-clay (slip-straw) (CMHC 05-109, pp. 2–3; Light clay): clay-coated straw packed into forms around a timber frame. It carries no load, dries fast (no vapour retarder over it), and insulates R-0.8 to 2.1 per inch. It settles about 7% as it dries, so top it up. Four hours of propane torch burned only 2 in in, and it is ductile — it soaks up quake energy. Method (general practice): dip straw in thick clay slip, tamp it into 12-in forms on the frame, and let it dry through a summer before plastering. Hempcrete (Hempitecture, pp. 6, 9, 11; Hempcrete): binder (lime plus pozzolan) to hemp hurd 1.5 to 1 by weight — 50 lb of binder, 33 lb of hurd, about 6 gallons of water. A squeezed ball should hold when tossed 2–3 ft. Use within 30 minutes, out of the sun; place 2 in at a time, tamping hardest along the forms. Walls are 8–12 in, R-2.2 to 2.5 per inch, and need diagonal bracing since they can't be sheathed in plywood. Gloves and eye protection (p. 3). Reality (general practice): hurd means retting and breaking stalks by hand, and the binder needs lime. Wattle and daub (quincha): poles and woven sticks packed with earth — the most flexible earth system; one survived a heavy Guatemala quake (Minke, pp.

and the binder needs lime. Wattle and daub (quincha): poles and woven sticks packed with earth — the most flexible earth system; one survived a heavy Guatemala quake (Minke, pp. 13, 28; 🖼️ a wattle-and-daub store). It cracks as the wood moves and holes harbor insects, so patch it yearly. Keep poles out of the soil, where they rot (PA, p. 3). Earthbags: test houses used jute or cotton tubes of earth, given 4 coats of lime against rot, with a ring beam and the roof on separate posts (Minke, p. 30). Plastic bags rot in sunlight within months — plaster them soon (general practice). Earthbag construction. Pressed blocks (Compressed earth block): the mix is right when a ball dropped from shoulder height breaks into a few pieces (PA Soil Blocks, p. 10; 🖼️ pressing a block). A 50%-clay soil like Pollard subsoil needs lime: try blocks at 5, 7 and 9% lime by weight (p. 8). Keep lime blocks damp a week and don't use them for 37 days (p. 12). Cordwood: seasoned log rounds laid crosswise in mortar — heavy, unreinforced, so for sheds, not houses (general practice). Cordwood construction. 📚 Go deeper: Hempitecture manual — forms and packing; Minke — wattle and daub, earth-filled bags. Pictures: 🖼️ earth-filled cloth hoses, Minke p. 30, 🖼️ CINVA-Ram block press, Peace Corps p. 99, Rammed earth.

🎨 Earth plasters, lime plaster, limewash and floors Earth plaster (PA Mud Plasters, pp. 3–5; Earthen plaster): 1. Aim for 10–15% clay — at least 3 parts sand to 1 clay — plus straw chopped to 1–2 in, about 85 lb per cubic yard. Try test patches. 2. Brush off dust and wet the wall. Throw on a clay-rich first coat up to ¾ in thick; scratch it. 3. When dry, dampen it and add a thinner, sandier finish coat (🖼️ photo). Shade the work; skip hot, windy days. 4. Limewash it. Lime-soil plaster is 1 hydrated lime : 2 clayey soil : 3–6 sand (p. 4). - Fill holes with dry earth bricks in slurry, not wet mud, which shrinks (Irish Thatch guide, p. 50). Lime plaster and stucco: - Mortar: 1 lime putty : 3 sand (NPS Brief 2, p. 2; 🖼️ mixing it, photos). - Stucco: base coats 1 lime : 3 sand with 6 lb of goat or cattle hair (½–2 in) per cubic yard; finish 1:3 without hair (NPS Brief 22, p. 15; 🖼️ stucco layers drawn). Best is ⅜-in scratch and brown coats, then a ⅛-in finish (NPS Brief 21, p. 3; 🖼️ plastering tools). - Cure slowly: mist and cover with burlap for 3 days; plastic only if tented off the wall (NPS Brief 2, p. 11). Limewash yearly to fill hairline cracks

tools). - Cure slowly: mist and cover with burlap for 3 days; plastic only if tented off the wall (NPS Brief 2, p. 11). Limewash yearly to fill hairline cracks before they let water in (NPS Brief 22, p. 7); one coat lasts about a year (Irish guide, p. 50). Make the first coat watery so it soaks 2–3 mm in (Minke, p. 49). Tint with ochre or umber (rule of thumb). Earthen floors (Peace Corps, pp. 139–141): 1. Dig out topsoil to 6–7 in below the finished floor and tamp — but don't ram swelling clay. 2. Lay 4 in of tamped sandy gravel (6 in over swelling soil) against rising damp. 3. Ram two 1½-in layers of stabilised earth; the top one with enough lime that a nail barely scratches it. 4. Cure it damp several days. Seal with oil, hot beeswax or tallow. Old floors were painted with ox blood (DSIR, p. 17). Farm-made stabilisers (PA Additives to Clay, pp. 3–4; 🖼️ a bark-stabilised render): dung (up to a third, fermented several days); horse urine; fresh blood with lime; casein from soured milk; glue from boiled skins and bones; linseed oil; oak bark tannin (here, oak or tanoak (rule of thumb)). Use animal products only from healthy animals — anthrax. Often none is needed. 📚 Go deeper: PA Mud Plasters and Renders — mixes and two-coat work;

🔥 Making lime ### ⚠️ Lime burns - Quicklime is hazardous (PA Lime, p. 1) and "highly caustic" (Irish guide, p. 50). Alkali burns, as from plaster and cement, are worse than acid burns (ATP 4-02.11, p. 118). - Lime in an eye: flood it with clean water at once and keep rinsing at least 20 minutes (p. 118). Plain water only. - Goggles, gloves, long sleeves. Slake in an open tub, never a closed one; keep children away (rule of thumb). - Damp quicklime heats up and can start a fire. Store it airtight (NBS Circular 30, p. 10). - Burn lime only in the wet season, never in fire season (rule of thumb). Stone: at least 95% calcium carbonate; marble and shells work too (PA Lime, p. 1). Known deposits (DOGAMI Ore Bin 1958, p. 5): | Deposit | Where | Notes | | Lime Rock (Holton Creek) | ~2 mi southeast of Kerby | Marble, over 98% | | Elder Creek | Near Takilma | Burned for the old Takilma smelter | | Jones Marble Quarry | ~4 mi west of Williams | Over 99% | | Turvey | ~4 mi west of Williams | 95% | | Grizzly Gulch | 2 mi south of Oregon Caves | Small; may now be inside the park, which was enlarged in 2014 — check before digging (rule of thumb)

| Grizzly Gulch | 2 mi south of Oregon Caves | Small; may now be inside the park, which was enlarged in 2014 — check before digging (rule of thumb) | | Oregon Caves | National monument and preserve | "Not available" — never quarry there | Get the landowner's or agency's permission (rule of thumb). Burning (PA Lime, pp. 1–2; Lime kiln): break stone to 4–6 in and hold it at about 1,830°F (1,000°C) for several hours. The simplest burn — a ring of logs with limestone heaped on top — gives under 1,100 lb of lime (🖼️ loading a kiln). A shaft kiln must be at least 6 times as tall as it is wide (PA Kiln, p. 1; 🖼️ building drawings); stone and fuel go in the top, lime comes out the bottom. A wood-fired kiln used about ½ cord per ton of lime (NBS Circular 337, p. 117; 🖼️ old shaft kilns). Underburn rather than overburn: overburned lime is yellow, heavy and won't slake; underburned stone can go back in (p. 13). Slaking (NBS Circular 337, p. 119): 1. Test: barely cover two or three fist-sized lumps with water. Crumbling in under 5 minutes = quick-slaking; 5–30 = medium; over 30 = slow. 2. Quick: add lime to plenty of water, never water to lime, and hoe hard at the first steam. Medium: water to half-cover.

5–30 = medium; over 30 = slow. 2. Quick: add lime to plenty of water, never water to lime, and hoe hard at the first steam. Medium: water to half-cover. Slow: moisten, wait, add water a little at a time. Too hot and it "burns"; too much water "drowns" it (NBS 30, p. 11). 3. Sieve the putty and keep it under water at least two weeks before plastering (p. 119). Pit-slake dolomitic) lime much longer, or it swells in the wall (PA Lime, p. 3). 4. Always add sand — putty alone cracks to pieces (NBS 30, p. 11). 📚 Go deeper: PA Small Vertical Shaft Lime Kiln — drawings and a day-by-day build; PA Testing Lime — field tests for homemade lime. 🏚️ Thatch — for sheds only - Pitch 45° or steeper (Irish guide, p. 18). - Material: any stiff, hollow-stemmed grass or reed at least 3 ft long (p. 19). Thresh grain straw clean or mice dig in; lay it 10–12 in thick (Beard, p. 80). - Life: reed wears about ¼ in a year, so 6 in of cover lasts about 24 years (Irish guide, p. 31). A re-thatch can weigh 3 tonnes — check the timbers (p. 41). Fire: most thatch fires start at the chimney — cracked flues, sparks, stovepipes through the thatch (pp. 61–62). Oregon calls even untreated shakes "not desirable" (Oregon BCD, p. 3). Thatch only sheds 50 ft or more from the house (FEMA P-737, p. 23), never a dwelling with a stove. Thatching. 📚 Go deeper: Irish Thatch guide — materials, fixing, repair, fire prevention; Beard — a simple thatched roof. Pictures: 🖼️ fixing a course with scollops, Irish guide p. 31.

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - Hot pitch or tar "skirting" on cob bases (Williams-Ellis, p. 61). Coal tar causes cancer; use a high stone plinth and limewash. - Cement-lime render as "probably the best" for cob (same page). Use lime or earth (NPS Brief 5, p. 5). - Powdered glass in the wall base against rats (p. 62). Use render over wire mesh (same page). - "Salamanders" (open coke braziers) to speed lime setting indoors (NBS Circular 30, p. 11). Carbon monoxide kills. - Hot bitumen cut with kerosene in plaster (PA Mud Plasters, p. 4). Fire and fume hazard; not needed. - Copper sulphate ("bluestone") on thatch (Irish guide, p. 41). It irritates eyes and skin and poisons streams. - Whitewash called "fireproof," tinted with chrome yellow (Household Discoveries, p. 270). It isn't fireproof, and chrome yellow is a lead pigment. Use ochre and umber. - Tall unreinforced cob — "no apparent limit" to height (Williams-Ellis, p. 57). Both old cob books pre-date quake design; follow the quake rules above. 📚 Go deeper: Minke — plasters and paints that work on earth; NPS Brief 5 — why cement fails on earth walls.

🪵 Firewood: Cutting, Splitting, Seasoning & Burning How to keep a household warm and cooking with wood: which local trees give the most heat, how much you'll need, felling and bucking safely, splitting, drying wood in our wet winters, burning it cleanly, keeping the chimney from catching fire, handling ashes in fire country, and growing your own firewood from oak, madrone and tanoak stumps. The manuals are in Firewood\ (Cutting-Felling, Splitting-Seasoning, Burning-Stoves-Chimneys, Woodlot); saws, axes and sharpening are in Engines-Motors\Chainsaws-and-Saws and the Blacksmithing guide. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst injuries and fires - Felling kills more woodcutters than anything else. Leave snags and dead trees to someone experienced, never cut alone, and keep everyone two tree-lengths away (WorkSafeBC Part 1, p. 13). - Plan your escape before you cut, about 45° back and away from where the tree will fall (🖼️ drawing). - Never use an axe as a wedge or to drive one; wear eye protection when striking steel wedges (U. of Minnesota, p. 12). - Ashes start wildfires. Lidded metal can, on bare ground, well away from the house, for days. - Carbon monoxide and chimney fires — a CO alarm near the bedrooms, and a clean chimney.

🔥 Which wood, and how much All dry wood gives about the same heat per pound (~9,000 BTU) — so heavier (denser) wood gives more heat per cord (PNW-GTR-810, p. 9). | Local tree | Heat per cord (million BTU, dry) | How it burns | | Oregon white oak | ~30 | Hard to light, long-lasting coals — best overnight wood | | Pacific madrone | ~30 | Same; dries slowly and checks | | Tanoak | ~24–27 (estimated from density) | Excellent coals | | California black oak | ~22–24 (estimated) | Good coals | | Douglas-fir | ~21–24 | Easy to light, hot, some sparks | | Bigleaf maple | ~20–24 (estimated) | Good all-round | | Red alder | ~17–18 | Fast, clean; spring and fall fires | | Ponderosa pine / sugar pine | ~15–22 | Lights easily, burns fast, poor coals | | Incense cedar | ~15–17 (estimated) | Kindling — lights instantly, sparks a lot | (Oak, madrone, fir, alder and pine from OSU EC1628, p. 4 and PNW-GTR-810; burn traits from U. of Minnesota, p. 14.) Use the right wood for the job: cedar and pine for kindling and quick spring or fall fires; oak, madrone and tanoak for cold nights and overnight burns (rule of thumb). Creosote comes mostly from wet wood and smoldering fires, not from the kind of tree

How much: - A cord) is a stack 4 ft × 4 ft × 8 ft (128 cubic ft) (🖼️ drawing). A face cord is 4 ft high by 8 ft long with shorter pieces — three face cords of 16-inch wood make one full cord (CMHC, pp. 62, 64). A cord of green wood weighs roughly 5,000 lb (Cornell). - A whole house heated only by wood: 2–4 cords a winter; a stove that helps out: 1–2 cords (CMHC, p. 64). Add a cord or two if you also cook with wood, and keep a year ahead so next winter's wood is drying now (rule of thumb). - Trees per cord (trunk width at chest height): 10-inch ≈ 0.15 cord; 14-inch ≈ ⅓ cord; 22-inch ≈ 1 cord (Cornell, p. 1). 📚 Go deeper: PNW-GTR-810 Fuelwood Characteristics — tables for every Northwest tree; CMHC Guide to Residential Wood Heating; OSU EC1628. Pictures: Firewood, Pacific madrone, Oregon white oak.

🌲 Felling trees safely (OSU EC 1124 Safe and Effective Use of Chain Saws, written for Oregon woodland owners; USFS sawyer course) 1. Size it up. Don't fell in gusty wind, fog, snow or ice. Check the lean from two sides (a weight on a string works), look up for dead limbs ("widow-makers") and vines tying it to other trees, and bore in once to check for rot (🖼️ drawing). Alder and maple often have rotten hearts (EC 1124, pp. 3–4). 2. Dead trees and snags) are a different job. They can fail across a circle 1–1½ times their height, farther downhill (USFS FS-1273, p. 36). Tanoak killed by Sudden Oak Death rots fast and can snap before it's fully dead — treat it as very high risk, and don't move infected tanoak wood to new areas (FS-1273, p. 181). 3. Clear an escape path about 45° back and away from the fall direction, and clear brush around the trunk (EC 1124, p. 5). 4. Notch (undercut) on the side it will fall, about one-third of the way through the trunk. The two cuts must meet exactly — if they don't, the trunk can split up and kick back ("barber chair"). An open-face notch (about 90°) is the most controlled (EC 1124, pp. 6–7; 🖼️ the three notches). 5. Back cut from the other side, level and about 1 inch

chair"). An open-face notch (about 90°) is the most controlled (EC 1124, pp. 6–7; 🖼️ the three notches). 5. Back cut from the other side, level and about 1 inch higher than the floor of the notch. Stop to leave a hinge of uncut wood 1–1½ in thick — the hinge steers the tree. Wedge the back cut early. When it goes, set the saw down and walk out your escape path (EC 1124, pp. 7–8; 🖼️ back cut and hinge). 6. Hung up in another tree? Don't cut the tree it's leaning on and don't work under it — see the professional fallers' methods for hang-ups and leaners (WorkSafeBC Part 2). With hand tools: a sharp crosscut saw and axe still fell and buck trees when fuel runs out — the USFS Crosscut Saw Manual, Saws That Sing (🖼️ how the teeth cut) and An Ax to Grind (🖼️ felling with an axe) cover it, and the Engines guide covers chainsaw care. 📚 Go deeper: OSU EC 1124 — the whole felling sequence with drawings; WorkSafeBC Faller Standard Part 1; USFS hazard-tree guide — reading snags and rot. Pictures: 🖼️ how far a snag can reach, FS-1273 p. 36, 🖼️ felling factors, U. of Minnesota p. 9, Tree felling.

🪚 Bucking and limbing - Stand uphill of the log. Cut the side that's being squeezed (compression) first with a shallow cut, then finish from the side that's being stretched (tension) — this keeps the saw from pinching (EC 1124, pp. 8–9; 🖼️ uphill stance). - Log supported at both ends (it sags in the middle): cut down from the top first, then up from below. Supported at one end: cut up from below first (U. of Minnesota, p. 11). - Bent-over saplings ("springpoles") whip when cut. Stand to the side and shave the inside of the bend with shallow cuts (EC 1124, p. 10). - Cut length to fit your stove — usually 16 in, a little shorter than the firebox. - Fire season: saws start fires. Cut early in the morning, keep the spark arrester in place, carry a shovel and extinguisher, and stay a while after you stop (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: WorkSafeBC Part 2 — binds and safe bucking; U. of Minnesota — bucking without pinching, p. 11. Pictures: 🖼️ chainsaw kickback, EC 1124 p. 11, 🖼️ limbing with an axe, An Ax to Grind p. 48, 🖼️ bucking with an axe, p. 50, Chainsaw.

🪓 Splitting (UW-Extension Harvesting Firewood, pp. 15–16; U. of Minnesota, pp. 11–12) - Tools: a 6–8 lb splitting maul handles nearly everything; two steel wedges and a sledge for tough rounds. Keep wedge heads ground smooth — mushroomed steel throws chips. - Set up: a big round as a chopping block, at a height where the maul handle is level when it hits. An old tire bolted on top holds pieces upright. - Technique: swing with your legs and body, all the way through — half swings stick the maul. Aim for existing cracks, put knots at the bottom, and work slabs off the edges of big rounds before trying the middle (🖼️ safe and unsafe splitting). - Size: split everything to 6 inches or less so it dries — rounds of 6–10 in at least in half, 10–14 in at least in quarters. - Safety: goggles, boots and shin protection; bystanders 20 ft away. - Easiest when: green wood splits easier than dry for most species; frozen wood splits easier still (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: UW-Extension Harvesting Firewood from Your Woods; An Ax to Grind — axes and mauls. Pictures: 🖼️ twist the axe as it bites, An Ax to Grind p. 52, Axe, Wedge.

☀️ Seasoning: drying wood in a wet climate Wet wood wastes heat — a ton of wood at 60% moisture gives about 5.6 million BTU; dried to 20% it gives about 10.7 million (U. of Minnesota, p. 14). It also makes creosote and smoke. - How long: softwoods about 6 months, hardwoods about 12 (EPA Wet Wood is a Waste, p. 2); big oak and madrone pieces up to 2 years (CMHC, p. 61). In western Oregon: cut and split by spring, stack through a dry summer, cover before the rains — two summers is better (OSU EC1628, p. 2). - Cut early. Wood split in August is only half dry by November, and wood that isn't dry by November won't dry outdoors over the winter — move it under cover (USFS 1943 test). - Stacking: single rows, off the ground on rails or pallets (4–6 in), bark side up, in sun and wind (🖼️ stacked piles). Cover only the top — side tarps trap moisture. Wood dried inside a closed shed takes nearly twice as long as wood in sun and wind (UW-Extension, pp. 16–18; EPA, p. 2). - Keep the woodpile at least 30 ft from the house so it can't carry a wildfire to the walls (UW-Extension, p. 17). - Is it dry? Cracks in the ends, faded gray color, a hollow knock when two pieces are

so it can't carry a wildfire to the walls (UW-Extension, p. 17). - Is it dry? Cracks in the ends, faded gray color, a hollow knock when two pieces are struck together, lighter weight, no hissing in the fire — or a moisture meter reading 20% or less on a freshly split face (CMHC, p. 61; EPA, p. 2). - Woodsheds and racks: plans for a 1-cord shed and cheap pallet or block racks (EPA shed plans; EPA 4 simple racks; 🖼️ rack drawings; 🖼️ shed drawing). 📚 Go deeper: EPA Wet Wood is a Waste; UW-Extension — stacking and drying; CMHC — drying tests, p. 61. Pictures: Wood drying.

🏠 Burning safely: stoves, chimneys, ashes Burn hot and dry. Smoldering fires and wet wood coat the chimney with creosote, which condenses below about 250 °F and turns to sticky tar below 150 °F (E-1388, p. 2). Flaky, dry creosote means you're burning well; black, shiny tar means you're not (CMHC, p. 46). Chimney cleaning: at least once a year; some say every 3 cords. After cleaning, check after 2 weeks, 1 month and 2 months to learn how fast yours builds up, and check the stovepipe every 2–3 months (E-1388, pp. 3, 5). A stiff brush on rods or a rope (🖼️ chimney brushes), from the top down, with the stove sealed below (rule of thumb). Chimney fire — roaring sound, shaking pipes, sparks out the top (E-1388, p. 3): 1. Close every air inlet and the damper to starve it. 2. Get everyone out; have someone watch the roof for sparks and check the attic. 3. A dry-chemical (ABC) extinguisher or baking soda thrown into the firebox can knock it down. 4. Chimney fires reach 2,000–3,000 °F — inspect the chimney before using it again; metal chimneys can be ruined after 2–3 fires. Clearances: follow the stove's label. For an unlabeled stove: 36–48 in from anything that burns, 18 in for stovepipe, and a non-combustible floor pad reaching 18 in in front (CMHC, p. 31; U. of Minnesota,

For an unlabeled stove: 36–48 in from anything that burns, 18 in for stovepipe, and a non-combustible floor pad reaching 18 in in front (CMHC, p. 31; U. of Minnesota, p. 24; 🖼️ clearances and a wall shield). Keep wood, furniture and drying clothes 3 ft away (USFA card). Ashes in fire country (Crystal Lakes fire district; USFA): - Leave ashes in the stove 4+ days if you can; then into a metal can with a tight metal lid, set on dirt or concrete at least 10 ft from anything that burns, for at least a week — or soak and stir them with water. - Never a plastic bucket, cardboard box, or the garden in fire season. Buried "dead" coals have started wildfires. - Cold, wet wood ash is useful: lye for soap, nixtamal for corn, and potash for the garden. Carbon monoxide: smoke and CO alarms near bedrooms; both wear out after about 10 years (Crystal Lakes, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: E-1388 The Creosote Problem; CMHC — stoves, chimneys and clearances; Aprovecho Capturing Heat — homemade stoves; Arkansas Basics of Heating with Firewood. Pictures: 🖼️ chimney height above the roof, U. of Minnesota p. 25, Wood-burning stove, Chimney sweep.

🌳 Growing your own: thinning and coppicing Our hardwoods regrow from the stump — cut once, harvest again and again ("coppicing") (USFS PSW-GTR-185): - Black oak, tanoak and madrone all resprout from the root crown (🖼️ tanoak sprouts), and it's almost impossible to stop them. - Cut stumps low — under 8 inches. Sprouts from tall stumps attach weakly and rot early (p. 35). - Cut in winter or spring: black oaks cut December–May sprouted 92% of the time; cut June–November, only 45% (p. 36). - In full sun, black oak and tanoak sprout clumps reached about 20 ft tall in 10 years (p. 36). Thin clumps to 3–4 of the best stems after a few years. - Bigleaf maple resprouts strongly; red alder only from young stumps (rule of thumb). Thin for firewood and fire safety at the same time: remove small, crowded trees and lower limbs ("ladder fuels", 🖼️ drawing) and space out the crowns — the cut becomes firewood, and the woods burn less hot in a wildfire (OSU EC 1573, p. 3; EC 1574). In oak woodland, removing the Douglas-fir crowding the oaks gives both firewood and healthier oaks (KBO/Lomakatsi oak guide). 📚 Go deeper: PSW-GTR-185 — sprouting of black oak, tanoak and madrone; OSU EC 1573 — thinning; Restoring Oak Habitats in Southern Oregon; Wikipedia: coppicing. The books are in Off-Grid-Power\ (Solar-PV, Batteries, Electrical-Basics, Micro-Hydro), with homemade generators in Engines-Motors\Motors-as-Generators, solar well pumps in Water-Wells-Pumps\Pumps-No-Grid, and Practical Action's battery and lighting briefs in Homestead-Skills\Household-Make-Do. The short version is in Illinois Valley — Start Here. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Batteries give off hydrogen, which explodes at just 4% in air (DOE-HDBK-1084, p. 22). Vent the top of the room, and never mount a controller, switch or relay in or above a battery box (IEA, p. 53). - A shorted battery can explode. One golf-cart battery can push about 8,000 amps (Sandia, p. 15). Fuse at the + terminal, connect the battery last, and if a tool shorts it, don't grab it: get away (IEA, p. 22). - Never plug a generator into a wall outlet. Backfeeding can kill line workers and neighbors. Generators run outdoors only (CPSC, p. 1). - Panels are live whenever light hits them. Cover them with an opaque tarp before touching wiring (fire FAQ, p. 3). - Lithium: never charge below 32 °F,

p. 1). - Panels are live whenever light hits them. Cover them with an opaque tarp before touching wiring (fire FAQ, p. 3). - Lithium: never charge below 32 °F, never "equalize" it, and never cover or pick up a burning pack; soak it with water from a distance (FAA SAFO 09013). - Battery acid blinds. Goggles and rubber gloves; flush skin or eyes with water at least 15 minutes (NEETS 1, p. 96).

📋 Start with a load list For each thing you'll run, multiply watts × hours a day = watt-hours (Wh) a day, and add them up (Sandia, p. 16). Take watts from the nameplate or a plug-in watt meter. An example (use your own numbers): | Item | Watts | Hours a day | Wh a day | | 4 LED bulbs | 40 | 5 | 200 | | Laptop | 50 | 4 | 200 | | Radio and phone charging | 20 | 5 | 100 | | Fridge or freezer (watt-meter reading) | — | — | 450 | | Inverter idling | 10 | 5 | 50 | | Total | | | 1,000 Wh = 1 kWh | - Kill hidden loads. Standby "phantom" loads can add up to 100 W around the clock (NRCan, p. 14): 2.4 kWh a day. An idling inverter uses 10–50 W; switch it off (rule of thumb). - Skip the inverter for 12 V lights, fans, pumps and USB chargers (Arizona, p. 5; 🖼️ 12 V loads pictured). - Motors need about 6 times their running current to start: a 1 hp motor may need 6 kW for a moment (DOE Microhydro, p. 67). - Store water, not electricity. A solar pump run from its panels through its own controller, filling a raised tank, needs no battery: the

a moment (DOE Microhydro, p. 67). - Store water, not electricity. A solar pump run from its panels through its own controller, filling a raised tank, needs no battery: the tank is the storage (NRCS, pp. 9, 27; 🖼️ a solar pump layout). Keep 3–5 days of water in the tank (Practical Action, p. 2). ☀️ Our sun, month by month Average "peak sun hours" a day at Medford, the nearest station, for a panel facing south tilted at our latitude, 42° (NREL Redbook, p. 181): | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec | Year | | 2.3 | 3.5 | 4.6 | 5.6 | 6.2 | 6.5 | 7.1 | 6.9 | 6.4 | 4.8 | 2.4 | 1.9 | 4.9 | - A panel makes 3½–4 times more in July than in December. The worst December on record averaged only 1.2. - The county has "persistent cloudiness in winter" (Soil Survey, p. 5). Plan on Medford's numbers or a little less at Cave Junction, and expect wildfire smoke to cut output in August and September (rule of thumb). - Tilt steeply for winter (🖼️ the sun's path through the year). At latitude + 15° (about 57°) a panel gets 2.0 in December; laid flat, only 1.2 (Redbook, p. 181). If your mount adjusts, go steeper in winter and flatter in summer, and never below 10°, so rain washes the glass (Practical Action, p. 3). - Snow: Cave Junction averages 24 in a season (Soil Survey, p. 5). 🧮 A worked example Panels: panel kW = (kWh a day ÷ sun hours) × 1.2 for losses (Sandia, p. 20). For the 1 kWh load above: - December: 1 ÷ 1.9 × 1.2 ≈ 630 W of panels. - July: 1 ÷ 7.1 × 1.2 ≈ 170 W. Check: each rated panel watt gives about 0.85 Wh per sun hour (Practical Action, p. 4), and 630 × 0.85 × 1.9 ≈ 1,020 Wh. Batteries: only 40% of a lead-acid label is usable (IEA, p. 17), so label Wh needed = daily Wh × days of backup ÷ 0.4. Above 40° latitude the IEA suggests 7–9 days of backup for solar alone (same page): 17,500–22,500 Wh of label for 1 kWh a day. Four 6 V, 220 Ah golf-cart batteries in series (🖼️ drawing) make 24 V × 220 Ah = 5,280 Wh, about 2 days at 40% (arithmetic). The cheaper fix: use less in winter, add panels (salvaged ones are plentiful), and fill the gap with creek hydro or a generator. When either more panels or more batteries would do, add panels; don't put a new battery into an aged bank (IEA, p. 38). Controller: at 24 V with an MPPT controller, 630 W ÷ 24 V × 1.25 ≈ 33 A, so a 40 A controller (Arizona, p. 4). 📚 Go deeper: Sandia, p. 20 — a full

an MPPT controller, 630 W ÷ 24 V × 1.25 ≈ 33 A, so a 40 A controller (Arizona, p. 4). 📚 Go deeper: Sandia, p. 20 — a full worked example; IEA Lead-Acid Battery Guide, p. 17 — battery sizing. Pictures: 🖼️ 2 V cells wired into a 24 V bank, Arizona p. 5.

🔍 Salvaging and testing panels Count the cells: 36 cells is a "12 V" panel; 60 cells give about 30 V, and 72 cells about 36 V (Arizona, p. 2; 🖼️ reading a panel's label). House-roof panels are 60- or 72-cell; they charge a 12 or 24 V bank well only through an MPPT controller (rule of thumb). Rooftop grid-tie systems go dead when the grid does. A grid-tied inverter "cannot operate disconnected from the grid" (Navy NWC TP 6563, p. 23; 🖼️ grid-tied system); modern string and micro-inverters shut down the same way, by design (rule of thumb). The panels are fine: rewire them through a charge controller to batteries. Testing a used panel (Navy, pp. 26, 50–51): 1. Look for cracked glass and peeling layers (delamination). 2. In clear sun, face the panel squarely at the sun. 3. Open-circuit voltage (nothing connected): within 10% of the label, allowing for heat (hot panels read lower) (🖼️ drawing). 4. Short-circuit current (🖼️ drawing): meter on its 10 A range across the leads, one panel at a time (rule of thumb): within 20% of the label. A 20-year-old panel usually still makes 80–90% of its label (rule of thumb). Wash panels with plain water early in the morning, so cold water can't crack hot glass (p. 26). Bypass diodes let current flow around a dead module; a blocking diode stops the

with plain water early in the morning, so cold water can't crack hot glass (p. 26). Bypass diodes let current flow around a dead module; a blocking diode stops the battery draining back through the panels at night (p. 19). 📚 Go deeper: Navy Maintenance of Photovoltaic Power Systems — testing and troubleshooting with only a voltmeter. Pictures: 🖼️ a stand-alone system, Navy p. 11, Solar cell.

🎛️ Charge controllers and inverters | | PWM | MPPT | | Panels | Must match the battery (36-cell for 12 V) | Any higher-voltage string, including 60/72-cell house panels | | Wire | Heavier | Thinner, at higher voltage | | Size it at | Panel short-circuit amps × parallel strings × 1.25 | Array watts ÷ battery volts × 1.25 | (Arizona, pp. 3–4; 🖼️ PWM controllers; 🖼️ MPPT controllers.) The IEA uses × 1.3, because sun off cloud edges can reach 1,300 W/m² (IEA, p. 41). A good controller has (IEA, p. 21): - an equalize mode and a charge display; - battery temperature compensation, about −5 mV per °C per cell (IEA, p. 26); - a low-voltage load disconnect, typically off at 12.0 V and back on at 13.2 V for a 12 V battery (p. 36); - a fuse and lightning protection. Inverters: use pure sine-wave for electronics and radios (Arizona, p. 7), and size for the motor-start surge. Keep a spare controller and inverter in a Faraday can (EMP guide). 📚 Go deeper: IEA Recommended Practices for Charge Controllers — set points and features; Arizona, p. 7 — inverter types. Pictures: 🖼️ how controllers switch the charge, IEA p. 15, 🖼️ AC and DC loads with an inverter, Arizona p. 6.

🔋 Choosing batteries and reading their charge Best to worst for solar: solar batteries; then leisure, golf-cart and traction batteries; then truck starting batteries. Avoid car batteries (IEA, p. 13). A car battery survives about 20 deep discharges. A deep-cycle battery emptied 80% each time lasts about 800 cycles; emptied 20%, about 6,000 (Practical Action Batteries, p. 5). Count on 40% of the label: a battery is worn out at 80% of new capacity, and should give at most half of that a day: 0.8 × 0.5 = 0.4 (IEA, p. 17). Series adds volts; parallel adds amp-hours (🖼️ drawing). No more than 3–4 strings in parallel, all the same age and size, with equal cables (p. 18). How full is it? - Voltage at rest: a 12 V lead–acid battery reads 12.0 V empty to 12.9 V full (IEA, p. 26). Half-full is about 12.4 V (rule of thumb). - Under load, never below about 10.8 V (p. 15). - Hydrometer (🖼️ how to read one): full is about 1.280; recharge below 1.250 (Navy CE, p. 68). In cycled solar batteries it reads true only after an equalizing charge (IEA, p. 26). Heat and cold: at 14 °F a battery gives only 60% of its capacity, and every 18 °F above 68 °F doubles plate corrosion (IEA, pp. 18–19). A discharged battery can freeze and crack; protect it below

battery gives only 60% of its capacity, and every 18 °F above 68 °F doubles plate corrosion (IEA, pp. 18–19). A discharged battery can freeze and crack; protect it below about 19 °F (IEA controllers, p. 31). Here: shade batteries from 100 °F summer heat and insulate them for January cold snaps (the record low is −6 °F) (rule of thumb). Storage: recharge stored lead-acid batteries every 3–6 months (IEA, p. 23), sealed ones every 3 (Practical Action, p. 6). 📚 Go deeper: IEA Lead-Acid Battery Guide for Stand-Alone PV — choosing, sizing and care; Practical Action Batteries — plain-language basics.
