💧 Keeping lead-acid alive Watering: use distilled water, added after charging, up to the fill line. In freezing weather add water only if a charge follows, or it may freeze before it mixes (DOE-HDBK-1084, p. 44). If the plates show, top up at once; clean rainwater will do now and then (IEA, p. 25). Adding acid doesn't recharge a battery (NEETS 1, p. 97). Equalizing is a deliberate overcharge that brings every cell up and stirs the acid (IEA, p. 27; 🖼️ gassing vs. voltage chart): - Flooded: hold about 2.45–2.50 V per cell (14.7–15.0 V on 12 V) for about 5 hours. - AGM: only about 2.35 V per cell (14.1 V) for about 8 hours (p. 46). Gel or AGM higher only if the maker allows (p. 21). - Remove catalytic recombiner caps first (p. 27). - With a hydrometer: charge at about 5 A until specific gravity stays steady for 4 hours, easing off if the acid reaches 110 °F (Navy CE, p. 67). - How often: monthly, or when cells drift apart (rule of thumb). Never equalize lithium. "Desulfators": plate sulfate from sitting deeply discharged "can never be recovered" (IEA, p. 23); equalizing restores cells that were only undercharged (p. 20). Treat pulse gadgets as unproven: equalize, then time the battery under a known load before trusting it (rule of thumb). Cleaning: neutralize spilled acid with

were only undercharged (p. 20). Treat pulse gadgets as unproven: equalize, then time the battery under a known load before trusting it (rule of thumb). Cleaning: neutralize spilled acid with about 1 kg baking soda in 4 L water (2 lb per gallon), then rinse (DOE-HDBK-1084, pp. 44–45). Grease the terminals (IEA, p. 25). 📚 Go deeper: DOE Primer on Lead-Acid Storage Batteries — watering, charging and care; IEA controllers, p. 46 — charge set points. Pictures: 🖼️ voltage and specific gravity through a charge, DOE-HDBK-1084 p. 29.

💥 Battery safety Hydrogen (DOE-HDBK-1084, pp. 22, 46): - Overcharging makes about 0.42 L of hydrogen per amp-hour, and 4% in air can explode. - Many explosions follow long, unregulated charging of a battery out of its vehicle: moving it vents gas, and a spark sets it off. - Vent from the highest point of the room; hydrogen collects under the ceiling (IEA, p. 24). Put conduit openings below the battery tops (Sandia, p. 51). - Check water with a flashlight, never a flame (Practical Action, p. 6). Shorts: put the main fuse right at the battery's + terminal (🖼️ fuse and disconnect), and connect the battery last, after all wiring is checked (IEA, p. 28). Take off rings and watches, and tape wrench handles (rule of thumb). Acid and gases: goggles and rubber gloves; flush for 15 minutes. Overcharged batteries can also give off toxic arsine and stibine; the venting that keeps hydrogen low keeps them low too (DOE-HDBK-1084, p. 46). Where batteries go: out of living areas and not under electrical panels. A lockable polyethylene tool box holds four L-16 batteries (Sandia, p. 52). Up to about 20 six-volt batteries in a large, drafty room may not need forced venting (p. 51). 📚 Go deeper: DOE-HDBK-1084 — hydrogen, acid and toxic gases; Sandia, p. 51 — battery rooms and boxes. Pictures: 🖼️ a stationary battery bank, DOE-HDBK-1084 p.
forced venting (p. 51). 📚 Go deeper: DOE-HDBK-1084 — hydrogen, acid and toxic gases; Sandia, p. 51 — battery rooms and boxes. Pictures: 🖼️ a stationary battery bank, DOE-HDBK-1084 p. 36, Goggles.

🔥 Lithium, LiFePO4 and salvaged packs Types (Lighting Global, pp. 3, 10; 🖼️ cylindrical, prismatic and pouch cells): - LiFePO4 (LFP), 3.2 V per cell: the safest and longest-lived (1,000+ full cycles), but bulkier. - Phone, laptop, tool and e-bike cells pack more energy but are less stable. - Every pack needs a battery management system (BMS). Charging rules (Lighting Global, pp. 6–8): - Overcharge tolerance can be 50 mV or less per cell, and cells in series must be balanced. - Never charge below 32 °F (0 °C) or above about 113 °F: cold charging grows metal "dendrites" that short the cell and start fires. NFPA says 32–105 °F (NFPA, p. 1). - Draining a cell below 2.5–3 V can ruin it. Store at 20–40% charge near room temperature. - A 12.8 V LiFePO4 bank charges at about 14.2–14.6 V and needs no equalizing; follow the maker's datasheet (rule of thumb). In our winters, keep it where it stays above freezing, or use a BMS with a cold-charge cutoff (rule of thumb). Salvaged e-bike and tool packs: stop using one that smells, changes color, heats, swells, leaks or makes odd noises. Charge it with its own charger, never on a bed or couch, and not after it's full (NFPA, p. 1). Discard swollen, dented or long-dead packs; never build packs from mixed salvaged cells without a balancing BMS; in

a bed or couch, and not after it's full (NFPA, p. 1). Discard swollen, dented or long-dead packs; never build packs from mixed salvaged cells without a balancing BMS; in fire season, charge in a detached shed, on stone (rule of thumb). If one burns (FAA SAFO 09013): one cell's thermal runaway sets off the next, and the fire flares again and again. 1. Put out the flames with water or any extinguisher. 2. Soak the pack with water to cool it. Don't cover it, use ice, or pick it up. 3. Get out of a room with a burning battery bank: the gas is toxic and flammable, and a pack can reignite hours or days later (fire FAQ, pp. 2–3). 📚 Go deeper: Lighting Global Lithium-ion Batteries — types, charging and storage; Home Lithium-Ion Battery Fire Safety FAQ — fire behavior. Pictures: 🖼️ lithium batteries for solar, Arizona p. 5, Lithium-ion battery.

🔌 Wiring, fuses and grounding Voltage drop: volts lost = 2 × one-way feet × amps × (ohms per 1,000 ft) ÷ 1,000. Aim for 3–5% loss between array and battery (IEA, p. 53). Longest one-way run for a 3% drop at 10 amps (copper; halve it for 20 A, double it for 5 A), from NEETS 4, p. 20 (arithmetic): | Wire | Ohms per 1,000 ft | 12 V | 24 V | 48 V | | 10 AWG | 1.02 | 18 ft | 35 ft | 71 ft | | 8 AWG | 0.641 | 28 ft | 56 ft | 112 ft | | 6 AWG | 0.403 | 45 ft | 89 ft | 179 ft | | 4 AWG | 0.253 | 71 ft | 142 ft | 285 ft | | 2 AWG | 0.159 | 113 ft | 226 ft | 453 ft | - Example: 240 W at 12 V (20 A) over 50 ft of 10 AWG loses 2 V, about 17%. At 24 V it loses 1 V, about 4% (arithmetic). - Hot wire loses more: Sandia figures 11.2 V lost in 400 ft of 8 AWG at 36 A (p. 102). Round up a size. - Minimum: 14 AWG on a 10 A fuse, 12 AWG on a 20 A fuse (IEA, p. 33). Fuses) must be

36 A (p. 102). Round up a size. - Minimum: 14 AWG on a 10 A fuse, 12 AWG on a 20 A fuse (IEA, p. 33). Fuses) must be DC-rated. Car blade and glass fuses have no DC interrupting rating and a 32 V maximum; keep them off battery and array circuits (Sandia, p. 42). Protect the battery cable with a current-limiting DC fuse (class T or RK5) close to the battery (p. 45). Use time-delay fuses where motors start (NEETS 3, p. 94). Grounding): bond the DC negative to ground at one point only (Sandia, p. 31; 🖼️ example grounding system). Drive ground rods 8 ft deep with #6 copper (FM 5-424, p. 49), about 6 ft apart if you use several (p. 117). For lightning, use one ground electrode, bond all metal frames, and run + and − wires side by side so they don't form loops (IEA Lightning, pp. 7, 13; 🖼️ bad and good module wiring). 📚 Go deeper: Sandia PV Systems and the NEC — fuses, disconnects, grounding; Army FM 5-424 — ground rods. Pictures: 🖼️ crimpers and terminals, Sandia p. 21, 🖼️ wire on terminals, FM 5-424 p. 24, Crimp).

⛽ Generators, cars and backfeed - Never backfeed. A generator plugged into a wall outlet sends power out onto the lines and can electrocute line workers and neighbors on the same transformer (CPSC, p. 1). Use a transfer switch (🖼️ diagram), or plug appliances straight into the generator. Outdoors only: carbon monoxide. - Run a generator under full load: charge batteries while it does other work (IEA, p. 46; 🖼️ solar-plus-generator layout). Violent gassing means the charge rate is too high (Navy CE, p. 67). - A generator's small "12 V DC" outlet is a weak, unregulated charger; a proper multi-stage charger on its AC is better (rule of thumb). - From a car: connect + to +, − to − (Alternator and Regulator Servicing, p. 48). Disconnect a car's battery before putting a fast charger on it, or you can burn out the car's diodes (p. 47). A car alternator) rarely fills a deep-cycle bank, and idling for hours wastes fuel and makes CO (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: CPSC Portable Generator Hazards — CO and backfeed; Alternator and Regulator Servicing — charging and testing. Pictures: 🖼️ how an alternator works, p. 8, Engine-generator.

🌊 Creek hydro, and why not wind While Oregon's water laws are enforced, most Illinois Valley creeks are closed to hydro by state rule (see Start Here). Measure the drop (head) (🖼️ what head means): run a hose full of water downhill with a pressure gauge at the bottom; psi × 2.31 = feet of head (NCAT, p. 6). Measure the flow: time how long the creek takes to fill a container: a 55-gal drum in 40 seconds is 82.5 gallons a minute (gpm) (NCAT, p. 3). For a bigger creek: width × average depth (sq ft) × float speed (ft per second) × 0.25 for a shallow rocky bed, up to 0.75 for a smooth one, gives cubic feet per second (cfs); 1 cfs = 449 gpm (p. 4; 🖼️ measuring a stream's cross-section). Power ≈ gpm × feet of head ÷ 10 watts (NCAT, pp. 8–9). A real case: 100 gpm with 35 ft of head left at the turbine (15 psi) gives about 200 W around the clock, nearly 5 kWh a day, to a 24 V bank (NRCan, p. 29). The rule predicts 350 W: small systems often fall short. Pipe size matters. Head lost per 100 ft of PVC (NCAT, p. 7): | Flow | 2-in | 3-in | 4-in | | 25 gpm | 1.3 ft | 0.2 ft | 0.04 ft | |

100 ft of PVC (NCAT, p. 7): | Flow | 2-in | 3-in | 4-in | | 25 gpm | 1.3 ft | 0.2 ft | 0.04 ft | | 50 gpm | 4.7 ft | 0.7 ft | 0.2 ft | | 100 gpm | 16.8 ft | 2.3 ft | 0.6 ft | | 200 gpm | 60.6 ft | 8.4 ft | 2.0 ft | - Size for late-summer low flow (NCAT, p. 2; NRCan, p. 12). Only about 15% of the county's rain falls April–September (Soil Survey, p. 5), and small creeks shrink sharply or dry up. Measure yours in September and in winter (rule of thumb). - Hydro is strongest in winter, when solar is weakest. A 400 W turbine with batteries and an inverter can still supply 5 kW peaks (NRCan, p. 28). - Use a dump-load (diversion) controller, not a solar controller (NCAT, p. 18; 🖼️ how a load controller is wired). See micro hydro and the Pelton wheel (🖼️ a small Pelton runner). - Screen the intake (🖼️ a wooden intake screen): openings no larger than 3/32 in; passive screen area (sq ft) = flow (cfs) ÷ 0.2, (ODFW, p. 1). For 100 gpm, about 1.1 sq ft (arithmetic). Small wind is usually poor here. An off-grid wind system needs an average of at least 9 mph (DOE Small Wind, p. 20).

100 gpm, about 1.1 sq ft (arithmetic). Small wind is usually poor here. An off-grid wind system needs an average of at least 9 mph (DOE Small Wind, p. 20). Medford averages 4.7 mph, and 3.6 in December (Redbook, p. 181). Power rises with the cube of wind speed, so half the wind gives one-eighth the power (p. 11), and the rotor must sit 30 ft above anything within 300 ft (p. 7). Only exposed ridgetops are worth testing; put money into solar and hydro first (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: NCAT Micro-Hydro Power — measuring and sizing; NRCan Buyer's Guide — battery systems; DOE Small Wind. ⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - MPPT called "less important" and a risk to reliability (IEA, p. 21), worth only 5–10% (IEA controllers, p. 39). It is now standard and reliable, and essential for salvaged house panels on a 12 or 24 V bank. - Equalizing weekly at 2.5–2.6 V per cell (IEA, p. 20) or every 2 weeks (IEA controllers, p. 26). Modern makers say monthly, or when cells drift (rule of thumb); never past the limit on AGM or gel; never on lithium. - LEDs at 25–50 lumens per watt (Practical Action Rural Lighting, p. 3). Modern LEDs give about 80–150, so a 9–10 W LED replaces a 60 W bulb. - The 1983 appliance table of 300 W fridges and tube radios (DOE Microhydro, p. 66). Measure your own. - "Waking up" NiCd cells by fully discharging them (Practical Action Batteries, p. 4). Only for old sealed NiCd, never NiMH or lithium. (Its warning that a flat series pack can reverse-charge its weakest cell still holds.) - Car batteries for lighting (Rural Lighting, p. 5). About 20 deep cycles: a stopgap only. - Sandia's NEC section numbers (Sandia) are from the 1999 code; the principles still hold. - 1930s–70s wind and generator books (Homemade Six-Volt Wind-Electric Plants, Wind Power for Farms) predate modern charge control. principles still hold. - 1930s–70s wind and generator books (Homemade Six-Volt Wind-Electric Plants, Wind Power for Farms) predate modern charge control. ⛽ Fuel Guide How long gasoline, diesel, kerosene and propane keep, how to tell when fuel has gone bad, what can be rescued, how to store fuel for the long haul — and how to get fuel out of gas-station underground tanks, drums and vehicles when there's no grid power. Wood gas, biodiesel and alcohol fuel are in Homestead-Skills\Fuels. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent fires and deaths - Gasoline vapor explodes. No flames, smoking or sparks within 50 feet of open fuel. Use only pumps made for gasoline — ordinary electric motors spark. (FM 10-67-1, p. 21) - Static sparks ignite fuel. Touch bare metal with your bare hand before opening any cap. Keep the nozzle touching the can or tank the whole time you pour. Fill portable cans on the ground, never in a truck bed or on carpet (rule of thumb). (FM 10-67-1, pp. 21–23) - Never climb into a tank sump, manway or tank. Fuel vapor pushes out oxygen and can kill without any smell or warning; the lids are heavy. Work from ground level. (EPA Sumps and Spill Buckets, p. 5; DoD UFM 3-460-03, p. 24) - Never put gasoline in a kerosene heater or lamp, and never store fuel inside the house. - Propane sinks into basements and ditches. Smell gas: put out flames, get out,

Never put gasoline in a kerosene heater or lamp, and never store fuel inside the house. - Propane sinks into basements and ditches. 🔍 Is this fuel still good? - Jar test: pour a sample from the bottom of the can or tank into a clean clear jar. Good fuel is clear and bright. Let it stand 15 minutes. Haze, droplets or a second layer at the bottom = water. Water fully settles out in about a day. (FM 10-67-2, p. 36; p. 97; 🖼️ Army samplers that reach the bottom) - Bad signs: darker color, a sour or varnish smell, or a drop on glass that leaves a sticky film when it dries (gum). Gum sticks valves and clogs carburetors. - E10 with a bottom layer has phase-separated (E10 blends): the bottom is ethanol plus water, not just water. E10 at 60 °F holds only about 4 teaspoons of water per gallon (3.8, to be exact) before this happens — less in the cold. Humid air rarely causes it; rain and water sitting in tanks do. (EPA phase-separation memo, p. 2; pp. 4–5) What the jar tells you: | You see | It means | Do this | | Clear and bright | Good fuel | Use it | | Haze or tiny droplets | Water mixed in | Let it settle a day, take fuel off the top, filter | | A separate bottom layer | Free water — or, in E10, ethanol + water | Drain the bottom off; see

a day, take fuel off the top, filter | | A separate bottom layer | Free water — or, in E10, ethanol + water | Drain the bottom off; see "Rescuing" below | | Grit, rust or black specks | Dirt, rust or microbe slime | Settle, then filter through a fine filter | | Dark, sour, sticky | Old, gummy fuel | Blend small amounts with fresh, or don't use | The Army's field kit for these checks is pictured in 🖼️ FM 10-67-2, p. 47. 📚 Go deeper: FM 10-67-2 Petroleum Testing — Army fuel tests and what the results mean; EPA Water Phase Separation — how much water E10 can hold.

🔧 Rescuing old fuel (FM 10-67-2 Petroleum Testing, p. 97) - Water and dirt can be fixed: let the fuel settle a few hours to a day, then pour or siphon off the top (Siphon), leaving the bottom inch behind, and filter it. The Army lets gasoline and diesel settle at least 2 hours after a tank is filled; water drops out in about 24 hours. - Phase-separated E10: the layers won't remix. Drain off and discard the bottom layer. The top is weaker (lower-octane) gasoline — fine for lawn, farm and older carbureted engines. - Stale but clean gasoline: blend it with fresh. The Army mixes a small test batch ("pilot blend") first and tests it. In its worked example, gummy old gasoline needed about 6 parts fresh to 1 part old to come back within limits. (FM 10-67-2, p. 98; 🖼️ blending-ratio graph) Rule of thumb: 1 part old to 4 or more parts fresh for mildly stale gas, and use it in simple engines (generators, mowers, older trucks) — not modern high-compression or turbo engines. The staler it is, the more fresh fuel it needs. Blending can't save fuel that's bad in many ways at once. (FM 10-67-2, p. 97) - Can't be fixed: heavy gum and varnish, and gasoline mixed into diesel. Diesel normally won't catch fire at storage temperatures, but a little gasoline in it

10-67-2, p. 97) - Can't be fixed: heavy gum and varnish, and gasoline mixed into diesel. Diesel normally won't catch fire at storage temperatures, but a little gasoline in it changes that — and gasoline in diesel can badly damage a diesel engine. (FM 10-67-1, p. 17; Alberta, p. 12) Diesel mixed into gasoline is usually less serious for a gas engine. (Alberta, p. 12) - Starting on old gas: a little fresh gas or starting fluid in the carburetor helps it catch; stale gas has lost the light parts that make it start. (Rule of thumb) - First tank of ethanol gas in an old engine: it may loosen old deposits and start running rough. Changing the in-line fuel filter often fixes it. (K-State, p. 2) 📚 Go deeper: FM 10-67-2 — reclaiming, blending and downgrading fuel; Oklahoma BAE-1746 — old fuel and small engines; Engines guide — cleaning a gummed-up carburetor.

🛢️ Diesel care - Water is the enemy. Drain water from the bottom of tanks and drums regularly, and check for it every time you gauge — the Army checks with water-finding paste every time and drains water the day after new fuel comes in, before it rises high enough to be drawn into the outlet. Keep drum bungs tight and covered so rain can't seep in. (FM 10-67-1, p. 141; 🖼️ gauging the water in a tank) - "Diesel bug": yeast, fungus and bacteria grow where fuel meets water — brown, black or gray slime that clogs filters and eats tanks. A puddle of water in the tank bottom is enough to feed big colonies, and it's worst in hot, humid weather. Prevent with zero water and a biocide; badly slimed tanks must be drained and scrubbed. Tanks left unused for a long time collect water at low points. (DoD UFM 3-460-03, pp. 29–30) - Expect old station diesel tanks to be corroded inside. EPA found moderate or severe corrosion in 83% of the diesel tanks it inspected, and ethanol had crept into 90% of the diesel samples. (EPA Corrosion in USTs with Diesel, p. 8; p. 10; 🖼️ photos of badly corroded tank parts) Filter station diesel well. - Keep it moving. Diesel kept for a generator lasts better if the same tank also feeds something used every

photos of badly corroded tank parts) Filter station diesel well. - Keep it moving. Diesel kept for a generator lasts better if the same tank also feeds something used every day (a heater or tractor) so the fuel turns over. Keep spare filters. (FEMA P-1019, p. 91) - Cold gelling: thin diesel with No. 1 diesel or kerosene (the Army blends kerosene in for winter — FM 10-67-2, p. 98) or add a cold-flow additive — before it gets cold; additives won't un-gel it. Additives don't change the temperature at which wax first clouds the fuel; they only help it keep flowing through filters a few degrees colder. (NREL Biodiesel Handling Guide, p. 29) "Summer" diesel bought in July can gel on a frosty valley morning — buy diesel in the season you'll burn it. (Alberta, p. 12) - Substitutes: diesel engines can run on No. 2 heating oil, which is nearly the same fuel (FEMA P-1019, pp. 91, 106). Kerosene and Jet A are close to No. 1 diesel. Kerosene is "dry" (low lubricity) and harder on modern injection pumps; older mechanical-pump diesels tolerate substitutes best. (Rule of thumb) Pictures: Diesel fuel, Heating oil, Cloud point (the temperature where wax first clouds the fuel), Jet fuel. 📚 Go deeper: DoD UFM 3-460-03 Petroleum Fuel Systems Maintenance — water, microbes and tank cleaning; EPA Corrosion in Diesel USTs — what's

🏪 Getting fuel out of gas-station tanks Why this matters here: a 2016 emergency exercise in Portland on a Cascadia earthquake found it would have catastrophic impacts on Oregon's petroleum infrastructure and make resupply very hard. Once delivery trucks stop, the fuel already in local station tanks may be all there is. (NASEO Petroleum Shortage Planning, pp. 7–8) What's under the concrete (EPA Sumps and Spill Buckets; North Dakota training; cutaway drawings: 🖼️ station tank, pump and piping, 🖼️ diesel tank equipment): - Each tank is usually 8,000–20,000 gallons, about 8–10 ft across, with its bottom roughly 10–14 ft below the pavement. (Rule of thumb) - Fill pipes sit inside small round spill buckets (5–25 gallons, lids 1–2 ft) (EPA Sumps and Spill Buckets, p. 7; 🖼️ photo of the lids; 🖼️ spill-bucket photo). The cap colors usually tell you the fuel: white = regular, blue = mid-grade, red = premium, yellow = diesel; orange marks vapor-recovery pipes, not fuel. (Rule of thumb — check by gauging.) - A large manhole (3–4 ft lid) right over each tank covers the turbine-pump sump — the pump, piping and leak sensor (🖼️ sump photos). Other small risers are the tank gauge, spare ports and vents. - Lifting lids: big steel lids are heavy — get help. Square or oval lids can fall through the hole and smash the pump or piping below.

ports and vents. - Lifting lids: big steel lids are heavy — get help. Square or oval lids can fall through the hole and smash the pump or piping below. Expect fuel vapor when you open them. (EPA, pp. 5, 8) - Bail out the spill bucket first. Rain and snowmelt fill them; if you open the fill cap under water, the water runs into the fuel. (Vermont Simple Suction manual, p. 4) Step 1 — measure what's there (EPA Doing Inventory Control Right): - Use a long wooden stick (won't spark), marked in inches (the EPA uses ⅛-inch marks), with zero at the very end. Varnish keeps fuel from creeping up the wood. (EPA, p. 6; 🖼️ Army gauge-stick drawing; Dipstick) - Lower it slowly down the fill pipe or gauge port, let it touch bottom gently, then bring it up quickly, and read the wet line. Wipe it and do it twice. (EPA, p. 8) - Water-finding paste on the tip changes color where there's water in the bottom; fuel-finding paste smeared where you expect the fuel line makes the reading sharper. A tank chart (if you can find one in the station office) converts inches to gallons. (EPA, pp. 6–7) Step 2 — the easy way: power the station. - At "suction" stations the pump is inside the dispenser — power the dispenser and it pumps. A

(EPA, pp. 6–7) Step 2 — the easy way: power the station. - At "suction" stations the pump is inside the dispenser — power the dispenser and it pumps. A check valve just under that pump keeps the line full ("primed") between uses. (Vermont, p. 3; 🖼️ suction-system diagram) - At most modern stations the pump is the submersible turbine in the sump, usually 240-volt, ¾–2 hp (rule of thumb), plus the dispenser's electronics. That takes a stout generator. Connect only through the station's transfer switch — never by backfeeding. (🖼️ transfer-switch diagram; Transfer switch) Several states have paid to prewire stations with generator hookups or "quick connects" (Florida required some by law in 2006). (NASEO, pp. 71–73; Florida SB 528 analysis) If the owner is around, work with them: they know their tanks and may already have a generator hookup. Step 3 — no power: pump it up by hand. - A siphon won't work — the fuel is below you, and a siphon only flows downhill. - Hose down the fill pipe: there's a drop tube inside with a flapper valve (it slams shut when the tank is about 95% full). The drop tube ends close to the tank bottom — within 6 inches in Vermont's manual, within 1 foot in EPA's. A smooth hose usually slides past when the tank isn't full, but it can snag; the

tank bottom — within 6 inches in Vermont's manual, within 1 foot in EPA's. A smooth hose usually slides past when the tank isn't full, but it can snag; the separate gauge port is another way in. (Vermont, p. 5; EPA Inventory Control, p. 7; 🖼️ drop-tube valve photos) - Suction lift is the limit. Air pressure can push water up at most about 33 feet in a perfect vacuum at sea level, and real pumps do far worse; gasoline's own vapor pressure cuts the lift further, especially when it's hot. (FM 10-67-1, pp. 485, 487) Hand and 12-volt suction pumps typically lift gasoline 10 feet or less (less in hot weather — gasoline boils in the hose). They work while the tank is fairly full and fail as it drops. (Rule of thumb, from the physics in FM 10-67-1) - For a deep or low tank, use a pump that goes down into the tank — a 12-volt submersible fuel-transfer pump rated for gasoline on a long hose — or a hand pump on a long rigid pipe. (Submersible pump, Hand pump) - Keep the hose end a few inches off the bottom to avoid water and sludge, pump into metal cans on the ground, keep everything bonded (metal-to-metal contact or a ground wire), and filter through a water-separating funnel. Bonding and grounding, the Army way (FM 10-67-1, pp.

into metal cans on the ground, keep everything bonded (metal-to-metal contact or a ground wire), and filter through a water-separating funnel. Bonding and grounding, the Army way (FM 10-67-1, pp. 21–22; drawings: 🖼️ bond wire and ground wire, 🖼️ grounding a tank truck, 🖼️ bonding a farm tank; Static electricity, Ground)): - Bond = connect the two metal things (nozzle to can, pump to tank) so no spark can jump between them. Make the bond before you open the cap and keep it until the cap is back on. - Ground = a wire from the equipment to a metal rod driven down to permanently damp soil, clamped to clean, bare, unpainted metal. Rod depth by soil: clean sand or gravel 6 ft, clay 4 ft, silt, silty sand, peat or muck 3 ft. - In dry or rocky ground, dig a hole about 1 ft deep and 3 ft across, pour in 5 lb of salt dissolved in 5 gallons of water, drive the rod there and keep it damp. If hand pumping goes wrong (rule of thumb, except where a page is given): | Problem | Likely cause | Try this | | Pump sucks air, never primes | Fuel level too far down; air leak at a hose joint | Tighten joints; switch to a pump that goes down into the tank | | Flow sputters and

| Fuel level too far down; air leak at a hose joint | Tighten joints; switch to a pump that goes down into the tank | | Flow sputters and foams on a hot afternoon | Gasoline boiling in the suction hose | Work in the cool early morning; shorten the lift (FM 10-67-1, p. 487) | | Hose stops partway down the fill pipe | Hitting the drop-tube flapper | Turn and wiggle gently, or use the gauge port | | Water or sludge in the can | Hose end too low | Lift it a few inches; settle and filter (see above) | Underground storage tank, Gas pump. 📚 Go deeper: Vermont Simple Suction UST Training Manual — how suction stations, spill buckets and flappers work; EPA Doing Inventory Control Right — sticking a tank and reading a tank chart; EPA Sumps and Spill Buckets — what's under each lid; FM 10-67-1 — Army fuel safety, bonding and pumping.

🚗 Drums and vehicles - Drums: a rotary or lever drum hand pump threads into the 2-inch bung; the Army's have a bonding wire and a strainer. Keep the drum grounded, and cover the pump's suction pipe when it's not in use. (FM 10-67-1, p. 353; 🖼️ drum pumps in a 55-gallon drum) - Open bungs slowly on a drum that's sat in the sun or been bumped around — pressure can spray out fuel and vapor. (FM 10-67-1, p. 14; 🖼️ drum bungs and chimes) - Cars and trucks: most modern fillers have an anti-siphon screen or rollover valve, so a hose won't reach the fuel. It's usually easier to disconnect the fuel line at the engine and let the car's own fuel pump push fuel into a can (key on, or power the pump relay) — or drain from the fuel-filter or tank fittings underneath. Older vehicles and many diesel trucks have no screen. (Rule of thumb) - Gas in old vehicles goes stale too — jar-test it before trusting it. Drum pump. More pictures: Fuel pump (what the car's own pump looks like). 📚 Go deeper: FM 10-67-1 — drum pumps and handling; TM 9-8000 Principles of Automotive Vehicles — how vehicle fuel systems are laid out.

🔥 Kerosene and propane Kerosene heaters (CPSC Kerosene Heater Safety, pp. 1–2): - Only water-clear 1-K kerosene (Kerosene), never gasoline (even a little is dangerous). Store it in blue cans that have never held gasoline, away from other fuel cans. - Refuel outdoors with the heater off and cool, and don't fill above the "full" mark — that space lets the fuel expand. - Keep it at least 3 feet from furniture and clothes. - Unvented heaters make carbon monoxide: run it with the room's door open to the rest of the house, and crack a window about an inch if the door must be closed or the house is tight. - Keep the wick clean and set at the right height. - If it flares up, don't carry it and don't throw water on it. Use its shut-off switch; if that fails, get everyone out. Propane (Texas RRC Propane Safety Tips; Propane, Gas cylinder): - Store cylinders outdoors and upright, never in a closed building; vapor is heavier than air and pools low. (p. 4) - Never put your head over a tank's valves — the relief valve can pop. Liquid propane causes frostbite on skin and eyes. (p. 4) - Keep big tanks painted white or silver; a dark, rusty tank heats up and can vent through its relief valve. Cap every line not connected to an appliance.

4) - Keep big tanks painted white or silver; a dark, rusty tank heats up and can vent through its relief valve. Cap every line not connected to an appliance. (p. 5) - Reading the tank gauge: the 5–95 dial is percent full, not gallons. A 500-gallon tank at 40% holds about 200 gallons. (p. 6) - How much is in a grill cylinder: run a wet finger down the side — the streak dries faster over the empty part. Don't use a dented, bulged, burned or badly rusted cylinder. (p. 8) - Before a flood or storm: close the tank valve and turn off pilots. After a flood, have tanks and lines checked before use — a regulator or appliance control that's been under water must be replaced. (p. 10) - If you smell gas: put out flames, don't flip any switches or use phones inside, get everyone out, close the tank valve, and don't turn it back on until the leak is fixed. (p. 11) Kerosene heater. 🌲 When the stored fuel runs out These are big projects — read the books before you build anything. - Wood gas: in World War II, cars, trucks and stationary engines in Europe ran on gas made by burning wood in a sealed canister. FEMA's plans fit 4-stroke gasoline engines of 10–150 hp; a diesel can run mostly on wood gas with a little diesel to light it. (FEMA Simplified Wood Gas Generator, p. 19; drawings: 🖼️ WWII Imbert gasifier, 🖼️ FEMA's simple gasifier, 🖼️ exploded view of the parts, 🖼️ photo on a tractor) Wood gas is about 20% carbon monoxide (Carbon monoxide poisoning). Many people died of "generator gas poisoning" in WWII. The danger is greatest when refueling, idling, or after shutdown — the unit keeps making gas after the engine stops — so keep it away from closed or poorly aired spaces. (FEMA, pp. 8, 73–74) - Alcohol: a farm still makes about 190-proof ethanol — too wet to mix with gasoline, but it runs most spark-ignition engines after you advance the timing, enlarge the carburetor jets and add preheat for cold starts. A gallon replaces about ⅔ gallon of gasoline. It's a poor diesel fuel on its own. (USDA Small-Scale Fuel Alcohol Production, p. 23; 🖼️ how a still concentrates alcohol, 🖼️ column still diagram; Still, Ethanol fuel) - Biodiesel is made from vegetable oil with

its own. (USDA Small-Scale Fuel Alcohol Production, p. 23; 🖼️ how a still concentrates alcohol, 🖼️ column still diagram; Still, Ethanol fuel) - Biodiesel is made from vegetable oil with methanol and lye — methanol is poisonous (it can blind or kill) and highly flammable, and lye burns skin and lungs. Goggles, gloves and good ventilation every time. (Penn State Biodiesel Safety, pp. 5, 8; 🖼️ venting methanol vessels outdoors; 🖼️ a small village reactor; Biodiesel, Methanol, Lye) - Charcoal and firewood don't run engines but do cook and heat — see Homestead-Skills\Fuels (🖼️ pit and earth kilns, 🖼️ portable metal kiln, 🖼️ oil-drum kiln, 🖼️ photo of a portable metal kiln; Charcoal). (CPSC Portable Generator Hazards, p. 1) - Never refuel a hot or running engine. Keep the can touching the tank while pouring (stops static sparks). (TM 5-6115-271-14, p. 60) - Never plug a generator into a wall outlet ("backfeeding") — use a transfer switch or interlock. It can kill someone working on the lines. (🖼️ how a transfer switch is wired; Transfer switch) - Capacitors bite. Motor capacitors (and microwave ovens) can hold a deadly charge after unplugging. Discharge across the terminals with an insulated screwdriver or a resistor before touching. - Pull the spark plug wire before working on a mower blade, saw chain or anything the engine turns. - Keep away from diesel injection lines while the engine turns. Pull the spark plug wire before working on a mower blade, saw chain or anything the engine turns. - Keep away from diesel injection lines while the engine turns. The injection pump pushes fuel at 4,000–10,000 psi (Practical Action Diesel Engine Repair, p. 13). Never hold a hand or face near a cracked line or a nozzle that is spraying. ⛽ Small gas engines: why it won't start Every engine needs three things: compression, spark and fuel. Find which one is missing. (MAVCC Small Engine Repair, p. 590; how it works: 🖼️ the four strokes drawn, Four-stroke engine, Two-stroke engine) 1. Fuel: pull the plug, cover the hole with a finger and pull the starter 2–3 times. A wet finger means fuel is arriving. If dry, check: fuel in the tank, shutoff valve open, cap vent not blocked, carburetor bowl (drain it — water or gum?), fuel filter and line. (MAVCC, pp. 595–598; 🖼️ drawings) 2. Spark: put a spare plug on the plug wire, rest it against the metal head and crank. A bright blue spark is good. Yellow, weak or none = clean or replace the plug, check the kill-switch wire, then the coil/magneto. (MAVCC, pp. 599–600; 🖼️ spark-tester drawing) 3. Compression: spin the flywheel backward against compression — a sharp rebound is good. Weak = loose plug or head, stuck valve, worn rings. With a compression gauge, crank at least six times before you read it. (MAVCC, pp. 602–603; 🖼️ flywheel check and gauge drawings) Quick troubleshooting chart (MAVCC, p. 592): | What it does | Look at these first | | Won't start, plug dry | Empty tank, fuel valve shut, plugged tank vent, stuck or clogged float valve, blocked filter or line, choke not closing

at these first | | Won't start, plug dry | Empty tank, fuel valve shut, plugged tank vent, stuck or clogged float valve, blocked filter or line, choke not closing | | Won't start, plug wet | Choke stuck or overused, stale fuel, water in fuel, flooded (mixture too rich), too much oil in 2-stroke mix, fuel-soaked air filter | | Won't start, no spark | Kill button or wire grounded, bad plug, bad plug wire, dirty or wrongly gapped points (older engines), bad coil | | Won't start, weak compression | Loose plug or head bolts, blown head gasket, valve stuck open, worn rings or bore | | Starts but lacks power | Dirty air filter, carburetor out of adjustment, clogged muffler or exhaust port, low compression, governor fault | | Overheats | Cooling fins or blower blocked, engine overloaded, clogged muffler, late ignition timing | | Smokes or uses oil | Wrong oil, oil diluted by a rich mixture, worn rings, clogged crankcase breather, wrong 2-stroke mix | | Kicks back when you pull it | Ignition timing off, sheared flywheel key (🖼️ drawing), loose blade | Old fuel is the #1 problem. Gas goes stale in about 60 days without stabilizer (sooner with ethanol). For longer storage, drain the tank and run the carburetor dry, or add stabilizer and run it a few minutes so it reaches

60 days without stabilizer (sooner with ethanol). For longer storage, drain the tank and run the carburetor dry, or add stabilizer and run it a few minutes so it reaches the carburetor. Keep cans sealed — water in ethanol gas separates and ruins engines. (Oklahoma Extension BAE-1746, p. 2) - Ethanol is a solvent. In an old, neglected engine it can loosen years of deposits that then clog the filter and tiny carburetor passages — the main reason for "ethanol trouble." Older engines (before about 1995) may also have rubber or cork parts that suffer. (BAE-1746, pp. 1–2) Cleaning a carburetor (AAVIM Small Engines Vol 2; 🖼️ float-type carburetors, 🖼️ floats, needle valve and float settings): - Take a photo before you take it apart. Soak metal parts several hours in carb cleaner, then blow out every passage with air. (AAVIM, p. 97) - Plastic or nylon parts no more than 30 minutes; never soak cork or coated floats. (AAVIM, p. 95; p. 93) - Don't poke jets with wire — it enlarges them. Use a bristle, fishing line or air. - Always fit new gaskets. Float too high = floods; too low = starves. A metal float with gasoline sloshing inside, or a crushed one, must be replaced. (AAVIM, pp. 92–93; 🖼️ checking float height) Two-stroke fuel (chainsaws, trimmers): mix oil at the ratio printed on the engine or

sloshing inside, or a crushed one, must be replaced. (AAVIM, pp. 92–93; 🖼️ checking float height) Two-stroke fuel (chainsaws, trimmers): mix oil at the ratio printed on the engine or in its manual (MAVCC, p. 186). Never run straight gas — it seizes the engine in minutes. Rule of thumb: most modern saws are 50:1 (about 2.6 oz of 2-stroke oil per gallon); older gear is often 16:1–32:1. Don't mix mineral and synthetic 2-stroke oils. (Two-stroke oil) Routine care: check oil every use (4-strokes), clean the air filter often (a choked filter makes an engine run rich and weak), keep cooling fins clear, replace the plug yearly. (Air filter) Replacing a starter rope: for a wrap-around (non-recoil) starter, use 3/16-inch braided nylon rope, usually 4–5 feet long — enough to wrap the pulley 3–5 times plus about 6 inches. Singe the cut ends with a match so they don't fray, and tie a figure-eight or double overhand knot in each end. (AAVIM, pp. 14–15; knots drawn step by step: 🖼️ figure-eight, 🖼️ double overhand) Recoil starters take thinner rope — most often 5/32 inch — that fills the pulley groove without binding. 🚜 Diesel engines Diesels have no spark plugs — squeezing the air makes it hot enough to light the fuel. So a diesel needs compression and clean fuel with no air in the lines. (Practical Action Diesel Engine Repair, p. 5; 🖼️ gasoline and diesel strokes side by side; Diesel engine) Diesels usually need less maintenance than gasoline engines because they have no ignition system. (FM 5-424, p. 114) Won't start or keeps dying: suspect air in the fuel lines (an "air lock"), an empty tank or a clogged filter. (Practical Action, p. 12) Bleed the air out (p. 16): 1. Fill the tank with clean diesel and open the tank valve. 2. Loosen the bleed screw on the fuel filter (and on the injection pump) until fuel runs out in a steady stream with no bubbles. Tighten it. 3. Loosen the injection line nut at the injector and crank the engine until fuel comes out without foam. 4. Tighten the nut and check every joint for leaks. What the smoke and symptoms tell you (Practical Action, pp. 11–14): | Symptom | Common causes | | Lots of black smoke | Faulty injector (p. 14) | | Overheating | Low coolant, loose or torn fan belt, blocked water jacket, bad water pump, low oil, overload, long running at high speed | | Burns too much fuel | Leaks in tank

coolant, loose or torn fan belt, blocked water jacket, bad water pump, low oil, overload, long running at high speed | | Burns too much fuel | Leaks in tank or lines, clogged air cleaner, wrong valve timing, overload, lots of stopping and starting, idling when not needed | | Burns oil | Worn or wrongly fitted piston rings, worn cylinder, damaged seals or head gasket | | Knocking or noise | Poor-quality fuel, loose connecting rod, worn or badly adjusted parts | Cleaning an injector nozzle: soak the nozzle valve and body in clean diesel, scrub the soot off with a copper (not steel) wire brush, and check the needle slides freely. (Practical Action, p. 15; 🖼️ injector valve, taken apart; 🖼️ cleaning the spray holes; Fuel injection) Don't run a diesel generator lightly loaded for long. It runs too cool, soot builds up in the engine and exhaust ("wet stacking"), and over time this can permanently damage it. (FEMA P-1019, p. 150) Give it a real load when you run it. Diesel fuel catches fire less easily than gasoline, but once burning a diesel fire is fierce (Practical Action, p. 6). 🪚 Chainsaws, crosscut saws and axes - A sharp chain throws chips; a dull one makes dust — and dust clogs the filter and raises kickback risk. (USFS Chain Saw and Crosscut Saw Training Course, p. 25) - The four chain rules: sharp, depth gauges set right, correctly tensioned (more bar and chain trouble comes from wrong tension than anything else), and well oiled. The chain should not hang below the bar but should still turn freely by hand. (USFS, p. 31; 🖼️ parts of the chain; 🖼️ right and wrong tension; Saw chain) - Filing: use the file size for your chain, with a guide. Hold the file level with about one-fifth of it above the cutter's top plate, guide mark parallel to the chain. File from the inside of each cutter outward, all of one side, then turn the saw around. Keep all cutters the same length. If the chrome is chipped, file until the chip is gone. (USFS, pp. 33–34; 🖼️ filing angles; 🖼️ file height and direction) - Depth gauges (the little humps in front of each cutter): check with a gauge tool every few sharpenings, file down only to the tool, and round off the front. Never file one lower than the tool. (USFS, p. 34; 🖼️ what the depth gauge does; 🖼️ gauge tool and rounding off) - After several hand filings, the angles

front. Never file one lower than the tool. (USFS, p. 34; 🖼️ what the depth gauge does; 🖼️ gauge tool and rounding off) - After several hand filings, the angles drift. The Forest Service then grinds the chain on a chain grinder to restore them — if you have none, file slowly and check angles against a new chain. (USFS, p. 32) Cleaning a saw (USFS, p. 31): - Take off the bar and chain. Clean the bar groove from the tip toward the base, clear the oil holes, check the rails for wear or flared edges (🖼️ rail wear drawn), grease the nose sprocket, and turn the bar over when you refit it so it wears evenly. - Air filter: tap it gently clean. Never blow it out with an air hose and never wash it in saw fuel — a damaged filter lets grit into the engine. - Spark plug: the tip should be tan (beige), not black, and dry. (🖼️ pictures of fouled and overheated plugs) - Spark arrester screen in the muffler: replace it if it has any holes. Illinois Valley summers are fire season — a saw spitting sparks into dry grass can start a wildfire. - Check the chain brake, loose bolts, and the rubber anti-vibration mounts. Things that make kickback more likely (USFS, p. 32; 🖼️ the kickback zone on the bar nose):

Things that make kickback more likely (USFS, p. 32; 🖼️ the kickback zone on the bar nose): a loose or dull chain, wrong filing angles, depth gauges filed too low or left square, loose rivets or cracked links, and anti-kickback parts removed. Running out of fuel isn't the end of cutting. A sharp crosscut saw and ax still fell and buck trees. Raker depth for a crosscut: 0.008 in for hard, dry wood up to 0.030 in for soft, springy wood; start at about 0.012 in. 🔋 Generators Where to put it (CPSC, p. 1): - Outdoors, far from doors, windows and vents, exhaust pointed away from buildings. Put a battery-powered CO alarm in the house. (Engine-generator, Carbon monoxide poisoning) - In rain, run it under an open, canopy-like roof on dry ground where water can't puddle under it. Dry your hands before touching it. - Use heavy outdoor extension cords rated for more than the total watts on them, with all three prongs and no cuts. Don't pinch them in doors or windows. - Turn it off and let it cool before refueling. Keep its fuel outside living areas. - Set it nearly level — the Army 3 kW set allows no more than 15° of tilt — on planks or timbers if the ground is soft. (TM 5-6115-271-14, p. 60) Maintenance (rule of thumb — the generator's own manual comes first): oil change every 50–100 hours (sooner when new), clean air filter, fresh or stabilized fuel, run it under load for 20–30 minutes once a month. Machines that sit idle for long periods should be "exercised" on a schedule to keep oil moving and moisture out. (TM 5-683, p. 41) Load: add up the running watts of what you'll plug in, plus the start surge of motors (fridges, pumps, power tools can need 2–3× their running watts for a second — rule of thumb).

running watts of what you'll plug in, plus the start surge of motors (fridges, pumps, power tools can need 2–3× their running watts for a second — rule of thumb). Keep steady load under about 80% of the generator's rating. - Motors need extra generator size. When a big motor starts, voltage dips and other motors can stall. Unplug the other loads, start the big motor, then plug the small loads back in. (FM 5-424, p. 113) - A generator feeding only heaters, cookers or light bulbs (a "resistive" load) can carry only about 80% of its kVA rating — e.g. a 6.25 kVA Army set carries 5 kW. (FM 5-424, p. 115) Grounding: follow the generator's own manual. The Army 3 kW set procedure (TM 5-6115-271-14, pp. 60–61; drawings of 🖼️ rod, plate and pipe grounds, 🖼️ ways to ground a generator and 🖼️ driving a ground rod; Ground)): - Drive a ground rod — or a ¾-inch copper or steel pipe — at least 8 ft into the ground. - In rock or hard ground, a buried metal plate can stand in (the manual gives sizes). - Soak the ground around the rod with water to help it conduct. - Run copper wire from the rod to the generator's ground stud — braided cable is best, No. 6 or heavier solid wire will do — and tighten it

conduct. - Run copper wire from the rod to the generator's ground stud — braided cable is best, No. 6 or heavier solid wire will do — and tighten it securely. No output but the engine runs? Check the breaker on the generator, then the brushes and voltage regulator (most small generators). A generator that sat unused can lose its residual magnetism — see "flashing the field" below. 📚 Go deeper: CPSC Portable Generator Hazards — CO, shock and fire rules on one page; TM 5-6115-271-14 3 kW generator — grounding, troubleshooting tables and field flashing; FM 5-424 Electrical Systems — picking and loading a generator, wiring and grounding; FEMA P-1019 — generator sizing and fuel planning.

⚙️ Electric motors: testing and repair When a motor won't run, check the simple things first, in this order (Illinois Electric Motors for Farm Use, pp. 24–25; know the parts first: 🖼️ cutaway of an induction motor, 🖼️ main parts laid out, Induction motor): 1. Power: is the right voltage reaching the motor terminals? Check fuses, breakers and the switch. 2. Load: take the belt off. If the motor now runs, the machine it drives is stuck. 3. Bearings: power off, turn the shaft by hand. If it won't turn freely, a bearing is dry, worn or stuck. 4. Thermal protector: many motors have a red reset button; others reset themselves once cool. A tripped protector means something else is wrong — find it. 5. Starting switch: a motor that hums but won't start, yet runs if you spin the shaft by hand, has a fault in its starting circuit (see below). 6. Windings: a burned winding has a strong burned smell, and you may see charred insulation. Single-phase motor hums but won't start (pumps, compressors, shop tools): suspect the start capacitor or the centrifugal start switch, which should click open at about ¾ speed (Illinois, p. 28; 🖼️ capacitor-start motor; 🖼️ the two parts of a centrifugal switch; Motor capacitor). Discharge the capacitor and check it; if it's open or shorted, replace it (TM 5-683, p. 56). A bulged

motor; 🖼️ the two parts of a centrifugal switch; Motor capacitor). Discharge the capacitor and check it; if it's open or shorted, replace it (TM 5-683, p. 56). A bulged or leaking one is dead; a meter with a capacitance setting tells for sure. Replace with the same microfarads and same or higher voltage (rule of thumb). Switch contacts can be dirty, burned or pitted, or a wire can burn in two. (Illinois, p. 24) Basic winding checks with a meter (Navy Electrician's Mate): - Windings must have no opens (infinite ohms through a winding), no shorts (much lower reading than its twin), and no grounds (any reading from a winding to the frame). - The three windings of a 3-phase motor should read nearly the same resistance; a high reading between any two leads means an open winding. (Navy Electrician's Mate, p. 237) - Insulation test (megger): right after shutdown while warm and dry, with capacitors disconnected. At least 0.5 megohm for motors 250 V and under, 1 megohm up to 1000 V. Write readings down — a steady fall over months warns of trouble even above the minimum. (TM 5-683, p. 54) - Armatures (brushed motors): test bar-to-bar on the commutator with a low-ohm meter; a "growler" finds shorted coils (a hacksaw blade buzzes over the bad coil). (Navy EM, pp. 238–239; 🖼️ armature test drawings; 🖼️ how

on the commutator with a low-ohm meter; a "growler" finds shorted coils (a hacksaw blade buzzes over the bad coil). (Navy EM, pp. 238–239; 🖼️ armature test drawings; 🖼️ how a growler is built; Armature)) Bearings: a rumbling or hot bearing is the most common motor failure. Replace with the same number stamped on it. Fit new bearings by heating them to no more than about 200 °F (oil bath or oven, not a flame). (Navy EM, p. 225, with 🖼️ bearing-puller drawings) Never wash sealed bearings in solvent — factory-sealed bearings shouldn't be disturbed. Open bearings get repacked half to two-thirds full of motor bearing grease; too much grease makes heat. (Illinois, p. 23; TM 5-683, p. 58; 🖼️ greasing a bearing step by step; Ball bearing) Brushes and commutators (drills, saws, mixers, car starters, DC motors): replace brushes that stick, are chipped, or are worn to about half their original length (or to within ⅛ inch of a riveted clip). (Navy EM, p. 228; 🖼️ brush holder and brush; Brush)) Seat new brushes by pulling fine sandpaper (grit toward the brush) under them in the direction the motor turns, lifting the brushes on the return stroke, then blow out the carbon dust. (Navy EM, p. 229; 🖼️ sanding a brush to fit) A blackened, grooved commutator can be cleaned with a commutator stone or fine sandpaper — never

out the carbon dust. (Navy EM, p. 229; 🖼️ sanding a brush to fit) A blackened, grooved commutator can be cleaned with a commutator stone or fine sandpaper — never emery cloth; emery dust conducts electricity and causes shorts (Illinois, p. 24; 🖼️ commutator stone) — or turned lightly on a lathe (no more than 0.010 in per cut). (Navy EM, p. 233; 🖼️ turning a commutator) Keeping spare motors (salvage is your parts store): wipe them clean, lubricate the bearings, grease the bare shaft against rust, wrap them in heavy paper, and store them dry. (Illinois, pp. 23–24) Rewinding a burned motor (Braymer & Roe Rewinding Small Motors; DOE Repair Specifications): - Before stripping, record everything: turns per coil, wire size, coil span (slots), how coils connect, and lead markings. (DOE Repair Specifications, p. 8) - Rewind with the same total copper area per turn and same turns (two thinner wires in parallel can replace one thick one). Varnish and bake below about 195 °F to dry. (DOE, p. 9; p. 11) - Small burned motors are often easier to replace from salvage than to rewind

🔁 Motors as generators What works best, easiest first: 1. Permanent-magnet DC motors (treadmill motors, wheelchair, scooter, some cordless tool motors): spin them and they make DC directly. Output voltage rises with speed, so choose one that makes at least 14–15 V at the speed you can actually turn it to charge a 12 V battery. Add a blocking diode so the battery can't run it as a motor. (Rule of thumb) (Brushed DC motor, Diode) 2. Car alternators: built-in rectifier and regulator, but they need high speed (rule of thumb: about 1,500+ rpm — step-up pulleys or belts for wind, water or pedals) and a battery connected to power their field — they are not self-starting. The field draws about 3 A, which wastes a lot at low power. (Alternator and Regulator Servicing, p. 11; 🖼️ how an alternator makes current; 🖼️ testing the rotor) 3. Induction motors (ordinary AC motors) as generators: drive it about 1–5% faster than its synchronous speed — e.g. a motor rated 1725 rpm (1800 synchronous) is driven at about 1820–1890 rpm. Output rises with the extra speed. (DOE Microhydropower Handbook Vol 1 Pt 2, p. 54) On its own (not tied to the grid) it needs capacitors across the windings to excite it. Sources disagree here: the DOE handbook (same page) and the European hydro guide say an induction generator can't run cut

Sources disagree here: the DOE handbook (same page) and the European hydro guide say an induction generator can't run cut off from the grid (ESHA Layman's Guidebook Pt 2, p. 30), while village hydro schemes run them off-grid with a capacitor bank and controller (Practical Action Micro-Hydro O&M, p. 23). Expect some trial and error. - Rule of thumb: start with run capacitors whose current at rated voltage roughly matches the motor's no-load current, then trim until voltage and frequency are right. Use AC motor-run (film) capacitors, never electrolytic start capacitors. - Expect about 70–80% of the motor's rating as output (rule of thumb). Needs a ballast (dump) load or controller so voltage doesn't swing as loads switch. Aging capacitors make frequency creep up; a capacitor running hotter than the others is failing — feel them once a month. Too many capacitors overheat the generator. (Practical Action, pp. 23–26) 4. Build a permanent-magnet alternator from magnets and magnet wire for a wind turbine or slow water wheel — full plans in Hugh Piggott's Axial Flux Alternator and PMG Construction Manual. 🧰 Make-Do Household Guide How to make or replace everyday necessities when the store is gone — from basic supplies, things you can scavenge, and what grows around the Illinois Valley. Each section points to the detailed manuals in Homestead-Skills\ (especially Household-Make-Do\, Soap-Candles\ and Sanitation-Water\) and Electronics-Repair\. The links open each book on the drive at the right page. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst accidents - Never mix cleaning chemicals. Bleach + ammonia (or urine) makes toxic chloramine gas; bleach + vinegar or any acid makes chlorine gas. Use one product, rinse, then the next. - Lye (from ashes or the store) burns skin and blinds. Gloves and eye protection; flush any splash with plenty of water for 15 minutes. Never use aluminum pots with lye. - Label every container. Never store chemicals or fuel in food or drink bottles, and never reuse a container that held chemicals or fuel for food or water. - Never put gasoline in a lamp, stove or heater, and never burn charcoal, a camp stove or a generator indoors (carbon monoxide). - Never throw water on burning wax or fat — it spreads the fire. Cut the heat and smother it with a metal lid or damp cloth.

🧽 Cleaning and disinfecting - Most cleaning is just soap, hot water and scrubbing — it removes most germs along with the dirt. Homemade lye soap works fine (see the soap section below). - Scouring powder: baking soda, fine wood ash, or fine sand on a damp rag. - Glass and hard-water film: white vinegar mixed half and half with water (not on marble or stone, and never together with bleach). - Disinfecting with bleach (for kitchen surfaces, sickrooms, after flooding): plain unscented household bleach, 5 tablespoons (⅓ cup) per gallon of water, or 4 teaspoons per quart. Clean first, leave it wet for at least a minute, and mix it fresh every day — diluted bleach loses strength. Drinking water needs a much weaker dose — use the table in Water\EPA - Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water (p. 2). - No bleach? Boiling water, scrubbing with soap, and drying things in full sun all kill germs. - Wash hands with soap (🖼️ how-to drawing; Hand washing) before handling food or eating, after the toilet, after cleaning up a child or caring for a sick person, and after touching animals or garbage. Hand sanitizer (at least 60% alcohol) only works on hands that aren't visibly dirty. (OSU Twin-Bucket Toilet, p. 4) 📚 Go deeper: WHO/WEDC Technical Notes on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in Emergencies — chlorine, latrines and hygiene after

🧼 Soap from fat and ashes 1. Make lye from ashes. Use hardwood ashes (they make the best lye); ashes of paper, cloth or garbage won't work (VITA, p. 342). Fill a bucket with ashes (🖼️ VITA's leaching drawing; Lye), pour on boiling water and stir, top up with ashes and water, then let it stand 12–24 hours and carefully pour off the clear liquid (Practical Action Soapmaking, p. 2). 2. Check the strength. Lye that floats a fresh egg or a potato is right. Too weak? Run it through fresh ashes again, or boil it down. (VITA, p. 343) 3. Make soft soap. Boil ½ cup of ash lye for every cup of clean fat until it is thick, rubbery and foamy. Age the brown jelly at least a month before use. (VITA, p. 344) Ash lye is potash, which only makes soft soap; hard bars need store lye (caustic soda), or boiled soap "salted out" with salt water (USDA 1940, p. 3; Practical Action, p. 4). Hard soap with store lye (USDA): weigh 2½ lb clean fat, melt it and let it cool to lukewarm. Dissolve 5½ oz lye in 11 oz cold water (lye into water, never water onto lye), pour it into the fat and stir, heat and stir until smooth, stir in another 5½ oz water, and pour into a box. Cut into cakes after

water onto lye), pour it into the fat and stir, heat and stir until smooth, stir in another 5½ oz water, and pour into a box. Cut into cakes after 24 hours; let them harden a week or more out of the sun. (USDA 1940, p. 3) - Clean kitchen grease first: melt it with about an equal amount of hot water, stir, let it cool, and lift the clean fat off the top (USDA 1940, p. 3). - Is it done? Cool a drop on a plate. Clear = ready. Weak and grey = needs more lye. A grey skin that slides on the plate = too much lye — add more fat (Practical Action, p. 3). - New ("green") soap is still caustic. Wear gloves to handle it and let bars cure at least 3 weeks (Practical Action, p. 4). - Keep children away and don't breathe the fumes. Splashes: water, lots of it (some old books say vinegar — use water). | Soap problem | Likely cause (Practical Action, p. 4) | | Won't thicken | Not enough lye, too much water, too cool, not stirred enough, or too much liquid oil | | Oily layer on top as it cools | Too much fat or not enough lye | | Hard and brittle | Too much lye | 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Soapmaking — lye

top as it cools | Too much fat or not enough lye | | Hard and brittle | Too much lye | 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Soapmaking — lye from ashes, soft and hard soap, recipes; VITA Village Technology Handbook, p. 342 — leaching lye and soft soap with drawings; CAWST Soap Making Fact Sheet — modern measured recipes; MSU Making Soap at Home — store-lye bars.

👕 Laundry - Laundry soap: grate one bar of soap and mix with 1 cup washing soda (add 1 cup borax if you have it). Use 1–2 tablespoons per load, dissolved in hot water first. - Make washing soda from baking soda: spread baking soda in a pan and bake at 400 °F (200 °C) for about an hour, stirring now and then, until it turns dull and grainy. It's stronger than baking soda — wear gloves. - Ash water (old-time "lye wash"): soak hardwood ashes in water, let it settle, and use only the clear liquid for greasy or very dirty clothes. It's caustic — gloves, and never on wool or silk. - Washing by hand: soak overnight, agitate with a clean plunger in a bucket (or a washboard)), rinse twice, wring hard, and dry in the sun — sunlight helps disinfect. Stains (USDA Stain Removal from Fabrics): - Treat it while fresh, and try cold water first — hot water and soap set many stains. Test any remover on a hidden seam. (pp. 4, 6) - Blood: soak in cold water until the stain turns light brown, then wash in warm soapy water. Strong salt water (about 2 cups salt per gallon) loosens old stains. Never hot water. (p. 15) - Grease: rub in cornstarch, chalk or talc, let it soak up the grease, brush off (p. 8).
