(p. 15) - Grease: rub in cornstarch, chalk or talc, let it soak up the grease, brush off (p. 8). - Chlorine bleach destroys wool and silk, and rots cotton if left on more than a minute or two (p. 5). Skip the bulletin's gasoline and carbon tetrachloride — fire and poison hazards. 📚 Go deeper: USDA Stain Removal from Fabrics, p. 4 — an A-to-Z of stains; Household Discoveries (1909) — washing, soap and laundry methods.

🪥 Personal care - Teeth: how you brush matters more than the paste. Brush twice a day with water, a little baking soda, or salt (or a 50-50 mix of the two). No brush? Chew the end of a fresh green twig until it frays into bristles (chew stick), or wrap rough towel around a finger. Use thread as floss. (Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 17, p. 2; Medical\Manuals-PDF\Where There Is No Dentist, p. 63) - Deodorant: wash daily; dust on baking soda or cornstarch (baking soda can irritate some skin). - Salve: melt 1 part beeswax with 4 parts oil or clean tallow (by weight) over low heat and pour into small tins. Lip balm is firmer: about 1 part wax to 2 parts oil. - Hair: wash with soap, then rinse with a cup of water with a spoonful of vinegar in it to remove soap film. 📚 Go deeper: Where There Is No Dentist, p. 63 — gum care and keeping teeth without a dentist; Where There Is No Doctor, ch. 17 — teeth, gums and mouth.

🩲 Menstrual pads and diapers - Reusable pads (photos): several layers of absorbent cotton (old flannel or towel) sewn or folded into a pad, held in underwear. Rinse in cold water first, wash with soap, and dry in the sun. See Where Women Have No Doctor (Medical\). Change pads several times a day; a homemade tampon must be changed at least 3 times a day or it can cause a serious infection (Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 5, p. 4). - A pad that buttons on: a sleeve of heavy cotton about 4½ × 9½ inches with two button wings, plus removable folded towel liners about 6 × 8 inches. Wash and add bleach if you have it; dry in the sun, never under the bed — damp pads mold and cause itching. (WASHplus pattern — 🖼️ step-by-step drawings) - Cloth diapers: absorbent cotton folded in layers, with a wool or plastic cover. Rinse, soak in a lidded bucket, wash hot with soap, dry in the sun. 📚 Go deeper: WASHplus Making Reusable Menstrual Pads — sewing pattern with drawings; Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 5 — periods and staying clean.

🧻 Toilet paper alternatives - Water: a squeeze bottle of water, then wash your hands with soap — the cleanest option. - "Family cloth": cotton squares, used once, kept in a lidded bucket and washed hot, separately from other laundry. - Leaves: big soft thimbleberry leaves (common along roads and forest edges here in summer) or first-year mullein leaves. - ⚠️ Learn poison oak first — it's everywhere in the Illinois Valley. Leaves in threes, lobed like small oak leaves, shiny or dull, red in fall. The bare stems in winter still cause the rash. (🖼️ drawing) It grows as a shrub or a climbing vine, and the roots and stems carry the oil too (OSU EM 9184, p. 24). Also avoid stinging nettle. 📚 Go deeper: OSU EM 9184, p. 24 — poison oak photos and control; FM 3-05.70 Survival, p. 514 — poison oak and other plants to avoid.

🚽 Toilets when the water is off - Don't flush if the sewer lines might be broken, even if your pipes look fine. A septic system can keep working if nothing leaks or backs up. (OSU Twin-Bucket Toilet, pp. 4–5) - Twin-bucket toilet (Bucket toilet): two 5-gallon buckets marked "pee" and "poo". The poo bucket is lined with a heavy (3 mil or thicker) black bag; after each use, cover it with about ½ cup of sawdust, wood shavings, shredded paper or peat. Keeping urine out of the poo bucket is what stops the smell. (OSU, pp. 2–3) - Emptying: dilute urine with wash water and pour it on the ground, a different spot each time. Fill the poo bucket no more than half, then double-bag it with gloves on and store it sealed, away from food and water. In the country you can bury it — never within 100 feet of a well, spring or creek. (OSU, p. 3) - Hand-washing station: a jug of clean water with a spigot, a catch bucket, and soap in the toe of a sock tied to the jug — one by the toilet, one by the kitchen (OSU, p. 3). - Trench latrine (🖼️ drawing; Pit latrine) for longer outages: about 1 foot wide, 5 feet deep and 13 feet long, well away from and downhill of any well or creek. Cover

latrine (🖼️ drawing; Pit latrine) for longer outages: about 1 foot wide, 5 feet deep and 13 feet long, well away from and downhill of any well or creek. Cover each use with soil; fill it in when the contents are 1 foot from the top (WHO/WEDC, p. 56). Hot ashes tipped into a pit cut smell and flies (Practical Action VIP Latrine, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: OSU Survival Basics: Sanitation — twin-bucket setup and supply list; WHO/WEDC Technical Notes, p. 55 — trench, family and borehole latrines; Practical Action Compost Toilets — longer-term options; EPA Composting Toilets — how they work.

🔥 Fire and light without stores - Fire starters: cotton balls rubbed with petroleum jelly; fatwood (resin-soaked heartwood from old pine or fir stumps — smells like turpentine and lights even when damp); dry bark and pine pitch. - Char cloth (catches a spark): put squares of 100% cotton cloth in a metal tin with a small nail hole in the lid, set it in a fire until smoke stops coming out, then let it cool before opening. - No matches: a ferro rod or flint-and-steel onto char cloth (🖼️ drawing) (steel struck on flint, quartz or pyrite throws sparks); a magnifying glass in sun (🖼️ drawing); touching a 9-volt battery (or two AAs) to fine steel wool (🖼️ drawing); or a bow drill (🖼️ drawing) — drill about ⅝ in thick and a foot long, of dry cedar, fir, cottonwood or basswood, on a board of the same wood with a notch cut to the center of the pit; tinder of dry grass with shredded cedar bark (Seton's Book of Woodcraft, pp. 192–194, and the Army survival manuals — FM 21-76, ch. 7). - Oil lamp: a glass jar or tin, a wick of twisted cotton string or a cotton strip held up by a bent wire or a tin-lid holder, and any vegetable oil or melted fat. Keep the flame small. Never gasoline. Tallow candles: Soap-Candles\. - Dipped

cotton strip held up by a bent wire or a tin-lid holder, and any vegetable oil or melted fat. Keep the flame small. Never gasoline. Tallow candles: Soap-Candles\. - Dipped candles: dip wicks in melted tallow, cool, dip again until thick enough (🖼️ hand-dipping drawing) (Household Discoveries, p. 98). 2 parts beeswax to 1 part tallow is firmer than plain tallow (p. 99). Melt wax in a pot set in hot water, not over the flame (Practical Action Candlemaking, p. 3). - Rushlights: peel rushes and dip the pith in tallow like a candle (Household Discoveries, p. 99). How much light you get (lumens, roughly — Practical Action Rural Lighting, p. 3): candle 1 · wick oil lamp 1–10 · hurricane lantern 10–100 · mantle lamp ~1,000 · a 1-watt white LED 25–50. 📚 Go deeper: FM 21-76 Army Survival Manual, ch. 7 — tinder, fire lays and fire without matches; Seton Book of Woodcraft, p. 192 — the classic bow-drill method; Practical Action Candlemaking — dipping, pouring and molding; Practical Action Rural Lighting — lamps, LEDs and batteries compared.

🪵 Glue, patching and waterproofing - Pine pitch glue: gently melt pine resin (🖼️ pine drawing) (it's flammable — heat beside the fire, not in it), stir in powdered charcoal (about 1 part to 3–4 parts resin) plus a pinch of fine plant fiber, and use while warm. Sets hard — for hafting tools, patching containers and seams. Plain heated resin works as glue too (FM 3-05.70, p. 455). - Flour paste: cook flour and water to a thick paste — for paper and labels. - Casein (milk) glue — skim-milk curd mixed with slaked lime and two other chemicals — makes wood joints as strong as the wood — water-resistant but not waterproof. Full recipe: VITA, p. 313. - Waterproof cloth or leather: rub in beeswax, tallow or a beeswax–oil mix, then warm it so it soaks in. - Waterproof boots (USDA): melt together 1 lb petroleum jelly + 2 oz beeswax, or 12 oz tallow + 4 oz cod oil. Apply warm (never hotter than your hand can bear), working it into the welt and sole edge, where shoes leak most. (USDA Care of Leather, pp. 12–13) 📚 Go deeper: Henley's Twentieth Century Formulas (1916) — hundreds of glues, pastes and cements; VITA Village Technology Handbook, p. 313 — casein glue; USDA Care of Leather, p. 10 — oiling and waterproofing shoes and harness.

👟 Clothing and footwear - Mending: running stitch for seams (🖼️ drawing), backstitch where it must be strong (🖼️ drawing), whipstitch for edges (🖼️ drawing), and darning for holes (weave thread back and forth across the hole, then across the other way — 🖼️ drawing). Patch from the inside for strength. Needles from stiff wire; thread from unraveled fabric, dental floss or fishing line. - Mend early — a few stitches on a weak seam or loose button save a big patch later. Shrink new patch cloth first and cut it on the straight of the weave. Darn with yarn raveled from a seam allowance, and don't pull it tight (it puckers). (USDA ABCs of Mending, pp. 4–8) - Sandals from old tires: trace your foot on tire tread, cut with a very sharp knife wetted with soapy water (steel belts make it slow — choose worn tread with no wire showing), sand the edges, and tie on with straps cut from an inner tube or with cord through slots. - Shoe care: work grease in well where the sole meets the upper, and let shoes dry somewhere warm, not hot. Re-sole before the welt and insole wear through — after that they're rarely worth fixing. (USDA Care of Leather, pp. 10–11) - Stay warm: wool keeps you warm even when wet; wet cotton pulls heat away — avoid it

after that they're rarely worth fixing. (USDA Care of Leather, pp. 10–11) - Stay warm: wool keeps you warm even when wet; wet cotton pulls heat away — avoid it in cold rain. 📚 Go deeper: USDA ABCs of Mending — patches, darns and tears for every fabric; Bower Practical Shoe Repairing — soles, heels and stitching; Leland Manual of Mending and Repairing — fixing almost anything in the house; USDA Knitwear Make-Overs — reusing worn sweaters.

🔧 Simple plumbing - Dripping faucet): shut the water off first, then replace the washer (🖼️ cut-away drawing). A temporary washer can be cut from leather (cold taps) or rubber (hot taps). If the washer screw is stuck, put on a drop of kerosene and tap it; if the head splits, deepen the slot with a hacksaw. (USDA Simple Plumbing Repairs, pp. 4–5) - Toilet tank keeps running: usually a leaky, waterlogged float or a worn flapper/ball (🖼️ ball cock drawing; Ballcock). A tank should empty in about 10 seconds. (pp. 9–11) - Clogged drain: put a little water in the sink and plunge hard; if that fails, open the trap) under the sink (🖼️ drawing) and dig out the grease and hair with a bent wire (p. 12). - When you shut off the water for repairs, open the highest faucet so a vacuum can't suck dirty water back into the pipes from a tub or toilet (p. 12). - Frozen pipe: open the faucet and thaw from the faucet end back toward the supply — never from the middle, where trapped water can burst the pipe (🖼️ drawing). Thaw drains from the low end upward. (USDA Simple Plumbing Repairs, p. 14.) 📚 Go deeper: USDA Simple Plumbing Repairs in the Home — faucets, valves, tanks, clogs and thawing, with drawings; Oregon DEQ Reusing Graywater — using wash water
Repairs, p. 14.) 📚 Go deeper: USDA Simple Plumbing Repairs in the Home — faucets, valves, tanks, clogs and thawing, with drawings; Oregon DEQ Reusing Graywater — using wash water on the garden.

🔌 Electronics: repair and salvage Manuals are in Electronics-Repair\ (and device-by-device guides in the iFixit archive in Kiwix). Start with the Navy safety manual and the Kuphaldt multimeter and soldering guides. To protect spare radios and parts from an EMP or solar storm, see the EMP Guide. Which book for what | You want to… | Read | | Learn electricity from zero | NEETS 1 Matter, Energy and DC, then Kuphaldt Lessons in Electric Circuits vol. 1 | | Stay alive around it | Navy Electronics Technician vol. 1 Safety, p. 31 | | Fix power supplies, diodes, transistors | NEETS 7 Solid-State Devices and Power Supplies | | Use a meter | Kuphaldt Multimeters, NEETS 16 Test Equipment | | Find a fault logically | Kuphaldt Troubleshooting Strategy, p. 26, NEETS 21 Test Methods | | Solder | Kuphaldt Soldering and Desoldering, p. 24, NASA Hand Soldering Workbook | | Antennas and radio repair | Army FM 24-18, p. 55, NEETS 10 Antennas | Safety first - Unplugged isn't safe. Capacitors hold a charge after unplugging. Discharge them with an insulated tool or shorting probe (🖼️ drawing) across the terminals and to the metal chassis, and recheck. (NEETS 16, p. 31; NEETS 21, p. 33) - Microwave ovens can kill: the capacitor holds about 2,000 volts. Short it out before touching anything inside, never run the oven with

16, p. 31; NEETS 21, p. 33) - Microwave ovens can kill: the capacitor holds about 2,000 volts. Short it out before touching anything inside, never run the oven with the cover off, and don't break the magnetron's ceramic parts (toxic). Old tube TVs and monitors (CRTs) hold high voltage and can implode — leave them alone unless you know how. - Household 120 V can kill — especially with wet hands. Work with one hand when anything might be live. With a typical body resistance of about 1,500 ohms, 120 V pushes about 80 milliamps through the body — more than enough to stop a heart; wet skin lets far more through. Take off rings and watches first. (Navy ET Safety, pp. 32–34) - If someone is being shocked, don't touch them. Cut the power, or push them free with a dry rope, belt or wooden stick, then start CPR if needed (p. 33). - Lithium batteries (laptops, phones, tools): throw out any that are swollen, dented, hot, or below about 2.5 volts. Charge only with a proper lithium charger, on a non-flammable surface, never unattended. Heat, overcharging and age can set off a fire that spreads fast with toxic fumes — get out (Lithium battery FAQ, pp. 2–3). Finding the fault — check the simple things first: power cord and plug, fuse, switch, batteries and their contacts, loose

toxic fumes — get out (Lithium battery FAQ, pp. 2–3). Finding the fault — check the simple things first: power cord and plug, fuse, switch, batteries and their contacts, loose wires. Then measure voltages, then test parts. Test a part in the circuit before you desolder it. Bulging or leaking capacitors (photos) are the most common failure in power supplies and chargers. - Look before you plug in — about 2 minutes finds most visible faults: loose or corroded connections, stray solder or wire bits (shake it and listen), charred resistors, and a white crust at an electrolytic capacitor's seal (🖼️ how one is built). A discolored or leaking transformer means a short somewhere. If anything smokes or sizzles when powered, pull the plug at once. (NEETS 6, pp. 210–211) - The simplest explanation that fits all the symptoms is usually right (Kuphaldt, p. 37). Multimeter quick tests (touch the probes together first — the meter should read near zero ohms — Kuphaldt Multimeters, p. 30) - Continuity (beep): fuses, switches, cords, broken wires. - Diode (🖼️ test drawing): conducts one way only — about 0.5–0.7 V on the diode setting forward, nothing backward. Both ways = shorted; neither = open. On an ohmmeter, a power rectifier should read at least 10 times higher backward than forward (NEETS 7, pp. 56–57). - Transistor (🖼️ ohmmeter test): test it like two

open. On an ohmmeter, a power rectifier should read at least 10 times higher backward than forward (NEETS 7, pp. 56–57). - Transistor (🖼️ ohmmeter test): test it like two diodes back to back (base-emitter, base-collector), and check collector-emitter reads high both ways. Avoid the lowest ohms range (R×1), which can damage small transistors. (NEETS 7, p. 111) - Capacitor (discharged first): on the ohms setting a good one shows a brief "kick" then rising resistance; no kick = open, steady low reading = shorted. (NEETS 6, p. 171) Resistor color code (🖼️ chart): black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9. Bands 1–2 are digits, band 3 is the number of zeros, the last band is tolerance (gold 5%, silver 10%). Example: yellow–violet–orange–gold = 47,000 Ω ±5%. (Kuphaldt vol. 5, pp. 26–27) Soldering: use rosin-core solder (never acid-core plumbing solder); a 25-watt iron for circuit boards. Make the wires hold mechanically first, heat the joint, not the solder, and don't move it while it cools (🖼️ a good joint; 🖼️ a joint moved while cooling). Remove old solder with copper wick or a solder sucker. - Put the iron's tip on the bigger piece of metal (the pad or lug), not the thin wire; a little fresh solder on the tip helps the heat flow. (Kuphaldt Soldering,

the iron's tip on the bigger piece of metal (the pad or lug), not the thin wire; a little fresh solder on the tip helps the heat flow. (Kuphaldt Soldering, pp. 24–26) - 63/37 tin-lead solder is best for electronics; zinc-chloride (acid) fluxes corrode circuit boards (NEETS 14, p. 80; Navy 2M, p. 195). Batteries (Practical Action Batteries): - Run dry cells in a radio until it quits, then finish them in a flashlight. Don't mix old and new cells (pp. 3–4). - A car battery is ruined after only about 20 deep discharges. Any lead-acid battery lasts far longer if you only use about half its charge before recharging. (p. 5; Rural Lighting, p. 5) - Top up vented lead-acid batteries with distilled water or clean rainwater — never acid (Rural Lighting, p. 5). What to salvage before throwing anything out: - Radios and clock radios: power transformers, cords, switches, knobs, speakers. - Computer power supplies: 12 V and 5 V power, fans, heat sinks, wire, connectors. - Printers and scanners: small motors, gears, rods, belts, switches. - Microwaves (after discharging!): fan and turntable motors, door switches, fuses, magnets. - Cars: batteries, alternators (12 V charging), lights, wire, fuses, relays — see Army TM 9-8000 in Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals (charging systems, p. 304). - Also: LEDs, magnet wire from motors and transformers, fuses, batteries, cords. - Motor run capacitors can be

relays — see Army TM 9-8000 in Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals (charging systems, p. 304). - Also: LEDs, magnet wire from motors and transformers, fuses, batteries, cords. - Motor run capacitors can be reused; motor start capacitors can burst if used continuously. - Insulators for antennas: plastic or glass is best (spoons, buttons, bottle necks), then dry wood, then rope. A broken wire antenna: clean, twist and solder the ends. (FM 24-18, p. 55) Crystal radio — no batteries needed (NBS Circular 120, 1922): a long wire antenna (about 75 ft, on insulators), a ground wire to a water pipe (never gas) or a rod in damp soil, a tuning coil wound on an oatmeal box, a crystal detector (the 1922 plans use a galena crystal; a germanium diode salvaged from an old radio does the same job and is easier (rule of thumb)), and a high-impedance earphone. It picks up AM stations with no power at all (🖼️ wiring diagram). The 1922 plans put the antenna at least 30 feet up with a lightning switch to ground it when not in use, and drive the ground rod 3–6 feet into moist soil. (NBS 120, pp. 5–11) 📚 Go deeper: Navy Electronics Technician vol. 1 Safety, p. 31 — shock, measuring live circuits, shorting probes; NEETS 7, p. 203 — how power supplies work and fail; Kuphaldt Troubleshooting Strategy, p. 26 — a

🍲 Hay-box cooking (saves fuel) Bring the pot to a full boil, then nest it tightly in hay, wool, newspaper or blankets in a box with a padded lid; it keeps cooking for hours on its own heat. Bring food back to a boil before eating if it has cooled below hot (food is safest kept above 140 °F). - Building one (Haybox; 🖼️ cut-away drawing): a wooden box, old trunk or bucket with at least 4 inches of packing all round the pot, below it and in a thick cushion on top. Crumpled newspaper, packed hard, is the best cheap packing. Use a pot with straight sides and a tight lid, sized to the food — a big half-empty pot cools fast. (USDA FB 771, pp. 6–9) (The 1919 bulletin suggests asbestos — never use it.) - Times: boil beans or meat 20–25 minutes first, then 2–2½ hours in the box; soft foods need only a few minutes' boil and about 25 minutes in the box. It cuts fuel use by about 40%. (Practical Action Fireless Cookers, pp. 2, 5) - Meat and beans are the riskiest — don't leave them in the box too long, and reboil before eating (p. 5). - A hot stone or brick under the pot cooks hotter, but then the nest must be metal-lined so it can't scorch the packing (FB 771, p.

eating (p. 5). - A hot stone or brick under the pot cooks hotter, but then the nest must be metal-lined so it can't scorch the packing (FB 771, p. 6). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 771 Homemade Fireless Cookers — building plans and recipes; Practical Action Fireless Cookers — a basket cooker from scraps; Aprovecho Capturing Heat — haybox, rocket stove and solar cooker plans.

🫙 Containers and storage - Food-grade buckets (recycling number 1 or 2 on the bottom, from bakeries and restaurants), glass jars and metal cans with lids. Wash with soap, then rinse with the bleach solution above. Never store food in trash bags, paint cans or chemical drums. Containers of 20–30 lb are easy to lift and get used up before bugs move in. (USU Food Storage in the Home, pp. 11–12) - Keep mice out: metal cans or glass; hang sacks from wire. Set snap traps along walls. Seal cracks, keep food off the floor, and keep the store room between freezing and 70 °F — cooler keeps longer (USU, p. 9). - Clay-pot cooler (zeer): a small clay pot inside a bigger one with wet coarse sand between, and a wet cloth on top (🖼️ how it works). Evaporation keeps vegetables cool — it works best in hot, dry weather, which suits our summers. Keep it in shade with a breeze and wet the sand three times a day. (Practical Action Clay Pot Cooler, pp. 1, 6) 📚 Go deeper: USU Food Storage in the Home — containers, storage rooms and shelf life; Practical Action Clay Pot Cooler — making and using a zeer pot; WSU Root Cellars — storing vegetables and fruit without power.

💧 Clean water from plastic bottles (SODIS) Fill clear plastic (PET) bottles of 2 liters or less with clear water, lay them on a roof or shiny surface in full sun for 6 hours (🖼️ drawing; SODIS) (two full days if it's more than half cloudy). Doesn't work with cloudy water — let it settle or filter it first. Details: Sanitation-Water\ and Water\. - Clear enough? Stand the full, open bottle on a page of large print (letters about ½ inch high) and look down through it. If you can read it, the water is clear enough. - Fill ¾, shake 20 seconds, then top up — the air helps kill germs. Lay bottles flat, on metal roofing if you have it. Drink straight from the bottle so it isn't re-contaminated. - Not green or brown bottles; replace scratched, cloudy ones (about yearly). SODIS does nothing for chemical pollution. (Eawag SODIS Manual, pp. 26, 86–87) - In long rainy spells, boil or use stored or rainwater instead (p. 27). 📚 Go deeper: Eawag SODIS Manual, p. 26 — step by step, with a question-and-answer section from p. 85; OSU Survival Basics: Water, p. 3 — boiling and bleach; CAWST Biosand Filter Manual — build a filter for cloudy water.

🐜 Pests - Roaches and ants (🖼️ common roaches; German cockroach): powdered borax mixed with sugar or flour, dusted into cracks (roaches), or a sponge soaked in borax-and-sugar syrup in their trail (ants). Keep borax away from children and pets. - Mosquitoes: screens, netting over beds (🖼️ drawing), and smoke; homemade repellents are weak. Cover water barrels and screen their vents so they don't breed there (Practical Action Household Water Treatment, p. 2). - Lice (🖼️ drawing; head louse, body louse): comb wet hair with a fine-tooth (nit) comb (🖼️ drawing) every day for two weeks; wash bedding hot. Body lice live in clothing seams — wash clothes and bedding at least weekly (FM 21-10, p. 96). - Ticks (🖼️ western blacklegged tick photo; Ixodes pacificus): check every evening, especially after brush; pull straight out with tweezers. ⚒️ Blacksmithing and Hand Tools How to set up a simple forge, pick the right scrap steel, forge and heat-treat it, and make or repair basic hand tools — chisels, punches, tongs, knives, axes — plus how to sharpen and re-handle the tools you already have. The full books are in Blacksmithing-Tools\ (Blacksmithing, Heat-Treating-Steel, Hand-Tools); axe and crosscut-saw manuals are in Engines-Motors\Chainsaws-and-Saws. Farm blacksmithing (plow shares) and a short Practical Action brief are in Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst injuries - Hot steel looks exactly like cold steel. Assume everything near the forge is hot; pick things up with tongs, and set hot pieces down where no one will grab them. - Eye protection at the anvil, grinder and when quenching. Never use a cracked grinding wheel, never wear gloves at the wheel, stand aside when you switch it on. (Navy Steelworker, p. 22) - Never heat galvanized (zinc-coated) metal indoors — the fumes cause "metal fume fever." Strip the zinc first (rule of thumb: soak overnight in vinegar) and work outdoors. Drinking milk does not help, despite old advice (TM 10-440, p. 60 still recommends it — ignore that). - Quench oil can catch fire. Use a metal container with a close-fitting metal lid next to it, enough oil to fully cover the piece, and plunge it in quickly and completely. Never put water on an

a metal container with a close-fitting metal lid next to it, enough oil to fully cover the piece, and plunge it in quickly and completely. Never put water on an oil fire — smother it with the lid. (Rule of thumb) Oil fires usually start when there's too little oil for the piece. (Practical Action Blacksmithing, p. 3) - A coal or charcoal forge makes carbon monoxide — work outdoors or under an open-sided roof. - Fire season: Illinois Valley summers are dry. Keep a full water bucket or trough by the forge for embers as well as quenching (Practical Action, pp. 1–2), clear dry grass and leaves well back from the forge, and never leave a fire unattended. (Rule of thumb) - Oily rags can catch fire by themselves. Throw them out or keep them in a bucket of water. (USFS An Ax to Grind, p. 34)

🔥 A simple forge and anvil Rule-of-thumb setups; the books have full plans. - Forge: anything that holds a fist-sized pile of burning fuel with air blown up into the middle — a brake drum or steel tub lined with clay, or a brick or stone hearth with a pipe coming in at the bottom (the "tuyere"). The ICS Shop Equipment book and the Peace Corps manual show how to build forges and bellows. (ICS, p. 21; drawings: 🖼️ brick forge, 🖼️ tuyere, 🖼️ village forges, 🖼️ how a bellows works; Forge) - Air: a hand-crank blower, homemade bellows, a hair dryer or a small fan with a valve or gate to control it. Too much air wastes fuel and burns steel. (🖼️ hand-built fan and pump designs; 🖼️ a blower) - Fuel: charcoal (easy to make — see Homestead-Skills\Fuels), or coal turned to coke in the fire. Keep the fire clean: rake out clinker (glassy lumps), and work in the hot center. Screen coke to get rid of dust before you use it. (Practical Action, p. 2; Charcoal, Coke), Clinker)) - Anvil: a real anvil is best, but a chunk of railroad rail, a big block of steel, or a sledgehammer head set in a stump works. Set the face at about knuckle height when you stand with your arm hanging. Practical Action also shows a stone with an

a sledgehammer head set in a stump works. Set the face at about knuckle height when you stand with your arm hanging. Practical Action also shows a stone with an iron insert and an old casting used as anvils. (Practical Action, p. 3; 🖼️ improvised anvils; 🖼️ parts of an anvil) - First tools: a 2–3 lb cross-peen hammer, a pair of tongs (or make them — they're a classic first project), a bucket of water, a file, and a magnet. (🖼️ hammer types; 🖼️ common tongs; 🖼️ holding work in tongs; Tongs) - Water trough: big enough to sink the whole piece — at least about 5 gallons. (Practical Action, p. 2) Running the fire (TM 10-440, pp. 26–27; cross-sections of 🖼️ open and side-banked fires and 🖼️ a hollow fire; 🖼️ building the fire): - The hottest spot is about 5–7 inches above the tuyere. Keep the fire just big enough to surround the piece with glowing coals. - A thin fire lets unburned air reach the steel and covers it in scale (an "oxidizing" fire). A deep fire uses up the air first — slower, but it doesn't scale the steel. - Pack wet, unburned fuel around the edges to keep the fire from spreading; it cokes there and feeds the center as you need it. | Fire problem | Likely cause | Fix | | Steel

🌡️ Heat colors (in shade, not sunlight) | Color | About °F | What it's for | | Dull red | 1,050–1,175 | Stop hammering — steel worked colder than this cracks. | | Cherry red | 1,250–1,375 | Hardening temperature for most carbon steel; bending. | | Orange to yellow | 1,725–1,975 | Normal forging heat — hammer here. | | Bright yellow-white, "flowing" surface | about 2,000 | Forge welding (mild steel and wrought iron, about 2,000 °F). | | White with sparks shooting off | 2,200 and up | Burned. The steel is ruined — cut that part off. | (°F from TM 10-440's color table, p. 25; colors look different in different light and to different eyes, so learn them on your own forge.) High-carbon steel burns at a lower heat than mild steel, so forge tool steel no hotter than orange-yellow. Burned steel can't be fixed by any later heat treatment. Keep hammering until the steel cools to a low red — forging refines the grain and makes it tougher. (TM 10-440, p. 24) Basic moves: drawing out (hammering thinner and longer), upsetting (hammering the hot end to make it thicker), bending over the anvil horn or edge, punching holes hot, cutting on a hardy (a chisel set in the anvil), twisting, and forge welding. Ilgen's Forge Work and the Selvidge Shop Manual walk through

horn or edge, punching holes hot, cutting on a hardy (a chisel set in the anvil), twisting, and forge welding. Ilgen's Forge Work and the Selvidge Shop Manual walk through each one step by step. Drawings: 🖼️ drawing out, 🖼️ upsetting, 🖼️ bending, 🖼️ hardy and chisels, 🖼️ top and bottom fullers; Blacksmith. Punching a hole (TM 10-440, p. 33; 🖼️ drawing): center-punch the spot, heat to a good working heat, drive the punch two-thirds of the way through, flip the piece, and punch out from the other side over the anvil's round (pritchel) hole. Cool the punch often so it doesn't soften, and drop a little dry coal in a deep hole to stop the punch sticking. Forge welding, step by step (Selvidge, pp. 45–47; TM 10-440, pp. 30–31): 1. Prepare: upset each end to about 1½ times its thickness, then hammer a scarf (a bevel) on each, slightly rounded, not hollow, so scale squeezes out from the middle. (🖼️ good and bad scarfs; 🖼️ shaping the scarf) 2. Clean fire, clean anvil: rake out clinker, have plenty of coke ready, brush scale off the anvil face, and set your hammer where you can grab it. 3. Heat slowly under a covering of live coals, turning the pieces so both heat evenly. (🖼️ both pieces in the fire, scarf up) 4. At bright red, sprinkle flux — borax or

under a covering of live coals, turning the pieces so both heat evenly. (🖼️ both pieces in the fire, scarf up) 4. At bright red, sprinkle flux — borax or clean sand — on the scarfs; it keeps air off and melts the scale so it can squeeze out. 5. Keep heating until the surface looks wet and flowing. Pull both pieces, knock off loose scale, lap the scarfs and strike light blows first, then heavier. (🖼️ laying the pieces together; 🖼️ lap-weld drawings) 6. Don't keep hammering once it drops below welding heat. If it doesn't stick, cut off the tips, re-scarf and try again. Use as few heats as possible. | Forging problem | Likely cause | Fix | | Cracks while hammering | Worked below dull red | Reheat sooner; stop at dull red | | Sparks and a crumbly end | Burned | Cut back to sound metal | | Weld won't stick | Not hot enough, dirty fire, no flux, scale between faces | Clean fire, flux at bright red, reach full welding heat | | Weld lets go later | Hammered after it cooled; hollow scarfs trapped scale | Round the scarfs; weld in fewer, hotter heats | | Thin tip burns before the thick part is hot | Fast heating | Heat slowly and keep the thin end back from the hot spot

🔩 Which scrap steel to use (Peace Corps Basic Techniques of Blacksmithing, p. 31) | Steel | Found in | Good for | | Low carbon — won't harden | Car body panels, most rebar (Rebar), nails, bolts, rail spikes (Railroad spike), pipe, drums | Hooks, hinges, brackets, tongs, anything that bends instead of cuts. Forge-welds easily. | | Medium carbon — hardens | Leaf and coil springs (Coil spring), axles, torsion bars, shock-absorber rods | Chisels, punches, hammers, axes, hoes, pry bars, springs. The best all-round tool stock. | | High carbon — hardens hard | Old files, saw blades, drill bits, dies, bulldozer blades | Knives, scrapers, wood chisels, plane irons — tools that must hold a keen edge. | Sources disagree on springs. The Peace Corps puts car springs, axles and torsion bars in the medium-carbon group; Practical Action calls coil springs, leaf springs and torsion bars high carbon. Test each piece and treat springs as hardening steel either way. Practical Action also warns that rebar often has a bit more carbon than true mild steel. (Practical Action, p. 5) - Quick test: heat the tip to light cherry red and quench it in water. If a file skates over it like glass, it will harden. If the file bites, it's low-carbon. (Peace Corps, p. 32) - Spark test on a grinder: low-carbon steel throws long streams

file skates over it like glass, it will harden. If the file bites, it's low-carbon. (Peace Corps, p. 32) - Spark test on a grinder: low-carbon steel throws long streams with few forks; high-carbon throws shorter, bushier streams full of bright bursts; cast iron throws short dull red sparks. Practice on known pieces first. In the Navy Steelworker's pictures the low-carbon stream runs about 70 inches, high-carbon about 55 inches with more volume, and gray cast iron only about 25 inches, red near the wheel and straw-colored at the end. Watch a spot about a third of the way back from the tip of the stream. (Steelworker, pp. 22–24; 🖼️ the parts of a spark stream; 🖼️ spark patterns of common metals) - Other clues (Peace Corps, p. 32): drop it on concrete and compare the ring with known pieces; see whether a cold chisel nicks it easily; and think about its old job — anything that had to be springy, tough or wear-resistant is probably medium or high carbon. Spark testing, Leaf spring. More pictures: Carbon steel. 📚 Go deeper: Peace Corps manual, scrap identification — what's in scrap and how to test it; Navy Steelworker Vol 1 — spark and chip tests with pictures; Practical Action Blacksmithing brief — mild, medium and high carbon steel from old vehicles.

🧪 Hardening and tempering 1. Anneal (soften) old steel before reshaping it cold or filing it: heat slowly to red, then bury it in dry wood ashes, lime or powdered charcoal and leave it until cold. (Selvidge, p. 56; Annealing)) 2. Harden: heat evenly to cherry red — rule of thumb: just past the point where a magnet stops sticking to it — and quench. - Plain carbon steel (springs, files, most scrap): water or brine (about ¾ lb salt per gallon) cools fastest and most evenly. Thin or very high-carbon pieces (files, knives) can crack in water — warm oil (80–150 °F; vegetable oil works) is gentler. (Steelworker, pp. 35–36) - Alloy steels: oil only. - Keep the piece moving in the quench. Steam and gas bubbles otherwise cling to it and leave soft spots, which can later crack or warp. (Selvidge, p. 57; Steelworker, p. 35; 🖼️ a quench tank; Quenching) - The steel is now glass-hard and brittle — temper it right away, before it's fully cold. The Navy Steelworker manual takes parts out of the quench at about 200 °F — still too hot to touch — rather than letting them cool through the "cracking range" below that. (Steelworker, p. 31) 3. Temper: polish a spot bright with sandpaper or a stone, then reheat gently (over the fire, on a hot plate, or in an oven)

below that. (Steelworker, p. 31) 3. Temper: polish a spot bright with sandpaper or a stone, then reheat gently (over the fire, on a hot plate, or in an oven) and watch the colors run. Quench when the edge reaches the color you want: | Color | About | Use | | Pale yellow | 430 °F | Engraving and lathe tools, scrapers | | Straw | 460 °F | Taps, punches, dies, knives for a very hard edge | | Brown-yellow (deep straw) | 500 °F | Wood chisels, drills, plane irons, hammer faces | | Purple | 530–540 °F | Light cold chisels, shears, axes | | Blue tinged with purple | 550 °F | Ordinary cold chisels | | Blue | 570–600 °F | Springs, picks | The further toward blue, the softer and tougher. Books disagree a little — one old table puts most chisels and knives at light blue — so test your tool and adjust. (Bacon, p. 263; Selvidge, p. 59; TM 10-440, p. 26) One-heat method for chisels and punches: heat the working end to cherry red, quench only the tip inch or so (bob it up and down), pull it out, quickly polish the tip, and watch the heat from the shank run colors toward the edge. When the right color reaches the edge, quench the whole tool. (Steelworker, p. 34; Selvidge,

polish the tip, and watch the heat from the shank run colors toward the edge. When the right color reaches the edge, quench the whole tool. (Steelworker, p. 34; Selvidge, p. 58) Many pieces at once: temper them in a pot of oil over the fire with a thermometer instead of by color — steadier and more even. 🛠️ Making basic tools - Cold chisel (first real project): a 6–8 inch piece of coil spring or axle. Straighten it, draw one end to a wedge, grind or file the edge to about 60°, harden and temper to purple at the edge (one-heat method). Leave the striking end soft. (TM 10-440, pp. 33–34; 🖼️ forging a chisel; Chisel) - Hot chisel vs cold chisel: a hot chisel is left soft and used only on hot steel; a cold chisel is hardened and tempered and used only on cold steel. Don't swap them. (Practical Action, p. 4; 🖼️ hot and cold chisels side by side; 🖼️ hot and cold cutters) - Center punch / drift: same steel, drawn to a round taper; temper the point straw to brown. - Tongs: two matching pieces of mild steel, forged with jaws and a boss, punched and riveted together. Richardson Vol 2 and Selvidge have patterns. (Step drawings: 🖼️ Drew, 🖼️ ICS) - Knife: from an old file or saw blade. Anneal first, forge or grind to shape (on a grinder, dip often — blue on the edge means you've ruined the temper), harden in oil, temper straw to brown. - Axe, hoe, hammer: the Peace Corps manual covers forging each from scrap, including punching the eye with a drift. (🖼️ axe step by step; 🖼️ field hoe; 🖼️ cross-peen hammer) - Fullers

hammer: the Peace Corps manual covers forging each from scrap, including punching the eye with a drift. (🖼️ axe step by step; 🖼️ field hoe; 🖼️ cross-peen hammer) - Fullers (grooving tools) and other top and bottom tools can be made of plain mild steel. (Practical Action, p. 4; 🖼️ the tools a smith needs; 🖼️ top fuller, 🖼️ bottom fuller) - Repairing tools ("dressing"): reforge mushroomed chisel heads, re-point picks, and redraw worn hoes and drill bits — ICS Shop Equipment, Hand Forging and Tool Dressing. Sharpening a plow share — gardens and fields here depend on it (Drew Farm Blacksmithing, pp. 62–64; 🖼️ drawing out a share's edge; Ploughshare): 1. Use a round-faced 2½–3 lb hammer. Draw the edge out by hammering the top side while the bottom lies flat on the anvil. 2. Don't burn the edge while heating — it's thin and heats fast. 3. If the point bends over, rest the edge on a hardwood block, not the anvil, while you drive it back. 4. Harden a good-steel share at full red, plunging it thick side first into water or brine. For stony ground, leave it less hard so it doesn't chip. 5. A worn-out point can be replaced by welding on a piece of old plow steel (not a rasp — too high in carbon to weld easily), using borax as flux. Practice on

point can be replaced by welding on a piece of old plow steel (not a rasp — too high in carbon to weld easily), using borax as flux. Practice on scrap first. 🪓 Keeping hand tools working Hanging an axe handle (USFS An Ax to Grind): - First check whether you need a new handle at all — often just a new wedge will do. (An Ax to Grind, p. 28) - Line the edge up with the center of the handle. Laid flat, the blade should touch the table one third of the way from the heel. (p. 24; 🖼️ a correctly hung ax) - Saw the wedge slot about two-thirds of the depth of the eye. Drive the head on by striking the end of the handle on a block, not the head. (pp. 30–31, photographed step by step: 🖼️ p. 30, 🖼️ p. 31) - Drive a hardwood wedge in until it stops, leaving ¼–½ inch, then trim. No metal wedges, screws or epoxy. Soaking a loose head in water only works for a day. (pp. 32–33; 🖼️ wedging, pictured) Soaking the head in linseed oil is a better temporary fix. (p. 33) - Good handle woods: straight-grained ash (Oregon ash grows here), hickory, oak. (Rule of thumb) The grain should run straight along the handle and in line with the wedge slot. (p. 26; 🖼️ good and bad grain; Oregon ash, Hickory) Sharpening: - Never sharpen an axe on a fast dry bench grinder — it draws the temper (the edge turns blue). Use a file (cuts on

grain; Oregon ash, Hickory) Sharpening: - Never sharpen an axe on a fast dry bench grinder — it draws the temper (the edge turns blue). Use a file (cuts on the push stroke only; lift on the return, wear gloves and use a knuckle guard), a slow wet grindstone, then a whetstone. File until a burr forms, then switch sides. Aim for about 25°, slightly convex. (An Ax to Grind, pp. 34–36; Handtools for Trail Work, p. 22; 🖼️ filing with a guard; 🖼️ edge-shape gauge to copy; 🖼️ field sharpening) - If you do blue an edge, the temper is gone for at least 3/16 inch back — grind or file past it. On a pedal grindstone, keep it wet and turn it toward you, into the edge. File in a fan shape 2–3 inches back from the middle of the edge, and hone every morning you use the axe. (An Ax to Grind, pp. 34–36) - Chisels and plane irons: grind at about 25°, then hone on an oilstone or water stone until a fine burr forms, flip and flatten the back, and strop. The grindstone shapes; only the stone sharpens — hone at a hair steeper angle than you ground. (Griffith Essentials of Woodworking, pp. 68–69; 🖼️ holding the chisel on the stone) - Hand saws (Disston): clamp with the gullets just above the jaws. Joint the

than you ground. (Griffith Essentials of Woodworking, pp. 68–69; 🖼️ holding the chisel on the stone) - Hand saws (Disston): clamp with the gullets just above the jaws. Joint the teeth level with a flat file, set them (never deeper than half the tooth), then file. Crosscut: every other tooth with the file angled about 45° toward the handle, then turn the saw around for the rest. Rip: straight across at 90°. 🧵 Clothing, Textiles, Leather & Shoes How to keep a household clothed and shod for years with no stores: dressing for our cold-wet winters, heavy mending, sewing machines, wool from sheep to yarn, linen, natural dyes, weaving, knitting, tanning, and boots and moccasins. Simple stitches, darning, tire sandals and boot-grease recipes are in the Make-Do Household guide; this guide goes further. The books are in Clothing-Leather\ (Sewing-Mending, Knitting-Hats-Gloves, Spinning-Weaving-Dyeing, Tanning-Hides, Shoes-Boots, Cold-Weather-Clothing), Homestead-Skills\Household-Make-Do, Homestead-Skills\Food-Crafts-Tools and Trapping\Hides-Tanning. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Wet, not cold, is what kills here. Wear wool under a waterproof shell, no cotton in the winter rain, and change to dry socks at least twice a day (TC 21-3, p. 12). - Fleece and nylon melt onto skin. Wear wool or cotton at the stove, at the forge and near any fire (rule of thumb). - Never use the old poisons in tanning, fur and dye recipes: arsenic, mercury chloride, chrome, sulfuric or oxalic acid, gasoline, burning sulfur. Brains, bark, salt, alum, soap and smoke are enough. - Wear gloves with brains (deer and elk can carry chronic wasting disease) and lime (rule of thumb), and never put cut or cracked hands in alum liquor (USDA FB1334, p. 22). - Dye pots, tanning barrels and mordants never go back to food use, and stay away from children (rule of thumb). - Wet leather

alum liquor (USDA FB1334, p. 22). - Dye pots, tanning barrels and mordants never go back to food use, and stay away from children (rule of thumb). - Wet leather burns easily. Dry boots slowly; leather hotter than your hand can bear is almost sure to burn (USDA FB1183, p. 9).

🌧️ Dressing for our cold-wet winters Our winters are "cold-wet" — near freezing, freeze-thaw, rain, wet snow, slush and mud — the hardest weather to dress for. You need a waterproof or water-repellent, windproof outer layer over insulation, and waterproof footwear. "Cold-dry" weather (below 14 °F) is colder but easier (TC 21-3, p. 6; 🖼️ cold-wet vs cold-dry). On the valley floor most winter nights are in the 20s–30s °F, with weeks of rain from November to March (rule of thumb). The COLD rule (TC 21-3, p. 10; 🖼️ drawing; FM 21-76, p. 176): | | Rule | Why | | C | Keep clothes clean | Dirt and grease clog the air spaces | | O | Avoid overheating | Better a little cool than sweaty; shed a layer before you work | | L | Wear it loose and in layers | Trapped air insulates; a tight outer layer crushes it (🖼️ drawing) | | D | Keep it dry | Wet clothing carries heat away far faster than dry | Wool, not cotton. Cotton underwear, T-shirts, jeans and flannel lose what little warmth they have when wet and pull heat from the body. Wool keeps you warm when wet (hunter manual, p. 77). The Army's fallback is all-wool clothing, except perhaps a windbreaker (FM 21-76, p. 176). Cover the head and neck too — their blood vessels

when wet (hunter manual, p. 77). The Army's fallback is all-wool clothing, except perhaps a windbreaker (FM 21-76, p. 176). Cover the head and neck too — their blood vessels don't narrow in the cold the way the hands' do (rule of thumb). Feet (TC 21-3, pp. 12, 41–42): trench foot (🖼️ photo) comes from days of cold, wet feet, not from freezing; in bad cases the skin dies and amputation follows. 1. Change to dry socks at least twice a day. 2. Dry and massage your feet. 3. Dry leather boots whenever you can. 4. Wear socks that aren't tight, and only one pair of cushion socks at a time. Drying clothes (TC 21-3, p. 14; FM 21-76, p. 177): - Hang items separately, high in the shelter, away from the stove and steaming pots. Nylon melts if dried too close. - Pin damp socks inside your outer layer as you walk. Never put damp clothes in a sleeping bag. - Dry leather slowly; boots can dry between the sleeping-bag shell and liner. Bedding: wet down loses much of its warmth. No bag? Sew two layers of cloth and stuff them with dry leaves, pine needles or moss (FM 21-76, p. 177). Wool blankets beat heavy cotton quilts (Household Discoveries, p. 53). 📚 Go deeper: TC 21-3 Cold-Weather Soldier's Handbook — layers, feet, drying clothes, cold injuries; FM 21-76

🪡 Mending and hand sewing Hand-sewing basics (TM 4-42.21, pp. 17–22): - Cut thread about 36 inches, never more than a yard (it tangles). Cut it; never bite or break it. - Basting (🖼️ drawing) holds work in place for a while. Backstitch (🖼️ drawing) is the strong seam. Catch (cross) stitch (🖼️ drawing) holds hems invisibly. Whipstitch (🖼️ drawing) binds raw edges. - Darns are for holes under 1 inch; patches for bigger ones (pp. 39, 43; 🖼️ four darns; 🖼️ top patch). Cut a top patch 2½ inches bigger than the hole all round, with ½ inch turned under, its grain matching the garment's. Mend early (ABCs of Mending, pp. 5–6): overcast fraying seams, tape-stay pocket corners, rework raveled buttonholes with buttonhole stitch (🖼️ drawing), and sew buttons on with a thread "shank" so the cloth isn't strained. Canvas, packs, tarps and leather (TM 4-42.21, pp. 71–74): - Use a triangular sailmaker's needle (🖼️ drawing), pushed with a sewing palm (a leather strap with a metal pad — 🖼️ putting one on). - Pull the thread across a cake of beeswax, and rewax it as you go (🖼️ drawing). - Cut 2-strand thread 6 times the seam length, 4-strand 12 times. The lockstitch with a saddler's sewing awl — the same stitch a machine makes (TM 4-42.21, p. 79; 🖼️ threading the awl; 🖼️ the finished stitch; Lockstitch):

4-strand 12 times. The lockstitch with a saddler's sewing awl — the same stitch a machine makes (TM 4-42.21, p. 79; 🖼️ threading the awl; 🖼️ the finished stitch; Lockstitch): 1. Thread the awl, leaving ½ inch out of the needle. Pull out enough thread to reach the end of the seam. 2. Push the needle through; pull all that slack through to the underside; hold it and withdraw the needle. 3. Push the needle in a stitch-length away and pull it halfway back, forming a loop underneath. 4. Pass the slack thread through the loop. Pull the needle out, then pull handle and thread equally hard to lock the stitch in the middle of the cloth. Repeat. Waxed thread for leather (The Saddler, p. 15; Hasluck, p. 36): twist 3–6 strands of flax (linen) thread. Taper each end first by untwisting it on your thigh and pulling it apart. Saddler's wax works best near 75 °F; cold wax is brittle. For shoes use waxed flax, never cotton — it is stronger, and the wax seals the stitch holes (FB1183, p. 9). 📚 Go deeper: TM 4-42.21 General Fabric Repair — every hand stitch, four darns, patches, canvas and webbing; USDA ABCs of Mending — darns and patches for every fabric. Pictures: Backstitch.

✂️ Fibers, first garments and sewing machines Tell the fiber before you trust a salvaged garment (Turner, p. 95): | Burn a few threads | Fiber | | Burns fast, little ash, no smell | Cotton | | Burns slowly, black ball of ash, smells like burning feathers | Wool | | Melts and drips into a hard bead | Synthetic — keep it away from fire (rule of thumb) | Boiling a sample in weak lye (in an enamel pot) destroys wool but leaves cotton — so never wash wool with lye or chlorine bleach (rule of thumb). A first garment with no pattern (Turner, pp. 122–123): a kimono nightgown takes cloth twice the shoulder-to-floor length, plus a hem. Fold it crosswise, lay the drafted pattern on the fold, and cut the neck with the garment on the wearer. Its long straight seams (French or felled) are good machine practice. To remake old clothes, rip, wash and press first, and check the cloth is worth the work (Make-overs from Coats and Suits, p. 4). Lice live in seams: hang infested clothes in the cold, then beat and brush them. This does not kill the eggs (FM 21-76, p. 177). Rescuing a gummed-up treadle or electric machine (USDA FB1944, pp. 4–12; 🖼️ two views of the machine; Sewing machine): 1. Pick out the oil holes. Run the machine while squirting

Rescuing a gummed-up treadle or electric machine (USDA FB1944, pp. 4–12; 🖼️ two views of the machine; Sewing machine): 1. Pick out the oil holes. Run the machine while squirting kerosene or cleaning fluid into every hole and bearing, then oil each one freely. Never oil the tension discs. Never use gasoline indoors. 2. A stuck screw: soak it with cleaning fluid. "Left is loose, right is tight" (p. 5). 3. Replace a dirty wool wad in a long-bobbin oil well with raw wool (p. 8). 4. Then one drop per hole after each day's work, and now and then when idle (p. 10). 5. Skipped stitches: usually a needle of the wrong length or set wrong — the short groove faces the shuttle point. Sharpen a dull needle on a fine emery stone; scratch marks on the machine to record the needle length (pp. 11–12). Many electric heads from about 1900–1960 fit a treadle cabinet, run by a 3/16-inch leather round belt if the hand wheel has a belt groove. Stock spare needles, bobbins and belts now (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Turner Sewing and Textiles — seams, measuring and simple garments; USDA FB1944 — cleaning and adjusting machines.

🐑 Wool: from sheep to yarn Shearing (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 81–82; 🖼️ handling the fleece; Sheep shearing): once a year when spring warms. If cold, wet weather follows, house the sheep 10–14 days or leave some wool on. Shear white sheep first, keep colored wool apart, and never throw hay over sheep's backs — it ruins the fleece. Here, shear in late April–May as the rains ease (rule of thumb). Washing without felting: - Raw fleece: soak a few ounces at a time in warm water with mild soap for about 30 minutes. Don't stir it or it felts. Rinse in water of the same temperature (CSU 4-H Spinning, p. 17). - Finished woolens: lukewarm suds (about 95 °F), rinses the same temperature. Never boil, rub, wring or twist; squeeze, pull to shape and dry away from the fire (USDA, p. 9; Household Discoveries, p. 206). - Local soap: the bulb of soaproot lathers "like ordinary soap" and has no alkali, which suits wool better than lye soap (Chesnut, p. 332). It grows on dry, rocky slopes here (rule of thumb). Carding and combing (CSU, p. 17; Hooper, p. 43): carding (🖼️ hand cards) gives soft, fuzzy yarn; combing gives smooth yarn. Spread wool on one hand card, draw the other across it a few times, and roll the fibers off into a soft roll. No cards? A metal

gives smooth yarn. Spread wool on one hand card, draw the other across it a few times, and roll the fibers off into a soft roll. No cards? A metal dog comb, or your fingers. Make a drop spindle) (CSU, p. 16; 🖼️ spinning with distaff and spindle): 1. Sand a 12-inch, ½-inch dowel to a point at one end. Cut a ⅛-inch notch 1 inch from the blunt end as a hook. 2. Glue a 2–3-inch wooden disk (the whorl) 1½ inches from the point. Spin it like a top; if it wobbles, re-center the whorl. Spin and finish (CSU, pp. 18–19): 1. Tie on an 18-inch leader of yarn. Twist the spindle and draw the fibers out as the twist runs up. Too much twist makes drafting hard; too little and the yarn falls apart. 2. Wind a skein around a chair back and tie it in 4 places. Soak it 20 minutes and hang it to dry with a weight. A balanced skein hangs straight. Angora rabbits give wool from a hutch: shear every 10–12 weeks, leave ½ inch of wool in winter, and keep newly shorn rabbits warm (USDA Handbook 309, p. 61). 📚 Go deeper: CSU 4-H Spinning — spindle, washing, carding, skeins; Hooper Hand-loom Weaving — carding, distaff and spindle.

🌾 Linen, nettle and native fibers Fiber flax (USDA FB669; 🖼️ the plant): 1. Climate: moderately cool, damp weather while growing and a dry spell at harvest. Heat and drought make it ripen early and short (p. 7). Here, sow very early on moisture-holding soil, or irrigate (rule of thumb). 2. Sow thickly — about 6 pecks an acre — so stalks grow tall and unbranched (p. 11). 3. Pull, don't cut, when the stalks yellow and the lower leaves drop (p. 12). 4. Ret to rot the gum that holds fiber to stalk: spread it on grass 2–8 weeks, turning once (dew retting), or weight bundles under soft water 6–15 days and watch closely — "a few hours' delay often causes loss" (pp. 16–17). 5. Dry the straw, break it (🖼️ a flax brake), then scutch (beat) out the woody bits (Hooper, p. 37). Native fibers: - Douglas iris: the leaf edges are "as fine and strong as silk" and made the strongest nets and snare rope (🖼️ twisting fiber into cord) — about six weeks' work for a 12-foot rope (Chesnut, p. 343). - Hemp dogbane: good fiber, but poisonous to livestock (AIB 415, p. 50). - Stinging nettle: gather with long rubber gloves and sleeves (OSU EM 9373, p. 2). Cut tall creek-side stalks after they brown in late summer or fall, then ret, break and scutch

nettle: gather with long rubber gloves and sleeves (OSU EM 9373, p. 2). Cut tall creek-side stalks after they brown in late summer or fall, then ret, break and scutch like flax (rule of thumb; no book here covers nettle fiber). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB669 Fiber Flax — growing, retting, breaking and scutching; Chesnut (1902) — native fiber and soap plants of our region.

🎨 Natural dyes with safe mordants Mordant with alum (USDA, p. 10): for each pound of dry wool, dissolve 4 oz alum and 1 oz cream of tartar in 4–4½ gallons of soft water. Bring it slowly to the boil, simmer 1 hour, and leave it overnight. The Navajo used raw alum, or water from burned green juniper needles (Navajo Native Dyes, p. 19). Skip the "chrome" mordant on the same USDA page — it causes cancer (see the last section). | Color | Plant | How | | Dull greenish yellow | Oregon grape roots, stems and leaves | With raw alum (Navajo, p. 39; USDA, p. 24) | | Soft brown | Alder bark peeled in fall | No mordant needed (Navajo, p. 23; Worst, p. 207) | | Black | Tannin (oak or tanoak bark, sumac) plus "iron liquor" | Steep iron filings in vinegar for days; mop it onto tanned leather (FB1334, pp. 19–20) | - Use enamel pots — tin or aluminum changes the color (Navajo, p. 12). - Test fastness: sun a sample half-covered with cardboard (USDA, p. 6). - Dye pots are never used for food again (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Navajo Native Dyes — plant dyes with only alum or juniper ash; USDA Home Dyeing with Natural Dyes — mordanting and dye recipes. Pictures: Mordant; Natural dye.

🧶 Weaving and knitting The simplest loom (Hooper, pp. 60–61): the one part every loom needs is the cross in the warp (🖼️ securing the crosses) — alternate threads cross between two rods so they can't tangle. A board with the warp wound around it and two rods holding the cross is a working loom. For 10-yard warps, build a warping board (🖼️ drawing) at least 6 ft × 1 ft with smooth hardwood pegs 1 inch thick, and tie cords through both crosses before taking the warp off, or it "will be irretrievably spoiled" (pp. 64–68). The next step up is the foot-power loom (Worst, p. 11; 🖼️ parts named). Picture: Warp and weft. Knitting habits from the WWI sock drives (Nicoll, pp. 25–26): - Join yarn without a knot: ravel both ends 3 inches, remove half the strands of each, overlap them and rub between damp palms. - Cast on (🖼️ drawing) and off loosely. Press with a damp cloth and a cool iron — wool scorches. - Tie a few needlefuls of the same yarn to each article for darning later (🖼️ repairing knitting). Socks, hats and mittens (Nicoll): - Socks: measure your own rounds per inch and adjust the pattern (p. 133). Graft) the toe closed so no seam blisters the foot (🖼️ heel, sole and toe) (p. 139); knit extra into the heel (p. 143).

and adjust the pattern (p. 133). Graft) the toe closed so no seam blisters the foot (🖼️ heel, sole and toe) (p. 139); knit extra into the heel (p. 143). - Helmet: 100 stitches in knit 2, purl 2 ribbing, with a face opening (p. 28); balaclava) (p. 31); mittens (p. 71). - Fur caps: rip apart an old cloth cap for the pattern and line it with wool. Muskrat is "as warm as any fur" (Farnham, p. 246). - Leather or fur mittens: woodsmen make them unlined and wear a knit liner they can pull out and dry. Trace the hand, add ¼–½ inch for seams, test the pattern in old cloth, and leave a long cuff (Farnham, pp. 248–249). 📚 Go deeper: Nicoll Knitting and Sewing — seventy patterns for socks, caps and mittens; Dillmont Encyclopedia of Needlework — stocking proportions and every stitch.

🦌 Tanning hides Hold a hide until you can work it (USDA FB1334, p. 8): salt it with 1 lb of salt per lb of hide; it keeps 3–5 months. Never let it freeze or heat. Work in wooden barrels, never iron (🖼️ tools). Lime takes off the hair in 6–16 days (🖼️ unhairing); a gallon of vinegar removes the lime (pp. 10–14). Bark tanning) — sole and harness leather (pp. 14–16): 1. Per hide, steep 30–40 lb of oak or hemlock bark, ground no coarser than corn, in 20 gallons of boiling water. Use rain water, and keep it away from iron. 2. Strengthen the liquor every 5 days; then bury the hide in wet bark for 6 weeks, and again for about 2 months. 3. It is done when a cut edge shows no white streak. Sole leather needs 2 months more. 4. Finish with dubbin (equal parts tallow and neatsfoot or cod oil), slicking (🖼️ drawing) and staking (🖼️ drawing). Local bark: tanoak bark "has high tannin content" and was once used widely to cure leather (USDA NRCS, p. 2); Oregon white and black oak bark also work. Sudden oak death kills tanoak and is under quarantine in Curry County, next door: don't haul tanoak bark, wood or leaves out of infested areas (rule of thumb). Brain-tanned buckskin) (Farnham, pp. 73–74, 142–147; Brain tanning)): 1. Soak the

in Curry County, next door: don't haul tanoak bark, wood or leaves out of infested areas (rule of thumb). Brain-tanned buckskin) (Farnham, pp. 73–74, 142–147; Brain tanning)): 1. Soak the skin in water, or water with wood ashes, until the hair and the grain (outer skin) slip. 2. Flesh it on a beam (🖼️ a fleshed hide), then scrape off hair and grain. 3. Boil the brains about an hour in a gallon of water; cool until you can hold your hand in it. Work the skin in it and wring it out. 4. Pull and stretch it without stopping until it is dry. Repeat if it is still stiff. 5. Smoke it over a cool smudge of punky hardwood inside a little tepee of sticks. Unsmoked buckskin dries hard every time it gets wet. Soap or lard can replace brains. Wear gloves with brains — the prions of chronic wasting disease concentrate in brain and spinal cord; use soap or egg yolk if in doubt (rule of thumb). Furs: salt-alum (FB1334, p. 27): 1. Dissolve 1 lb alum in 1 gallon of water. Dissolve 4 oz washing soda and 8 oz salt in ½ gallon of water, and pour it in very slowly. 2. Thicken with flour to a paste; spread 2–3 coats on the flesh side, a day apart. 3. Rinse, oil, and work the skin over a

it in very slowly. 2. Thicken with flour to a paste; spread 2–3 coats on the flesh side, a day apart. 3. Rinse, oil, and work the skin over a stake as it dries. If it dries stiff, dampen it and work it again. Rawhide (AFH 10-644, p. 257): flesh the hide, cover the hair side with wet hardwood ashes, roll it up for several days, and scrape off the hair. Wash it, stretch it in a frame and dry it slowly in the shade. Soak to soften. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB1334 Home Tanning — bark, alum and fur tanning (skip its chrome and acid recipes); Farnham Furs and Skins — buckskin, robes, caps and mittens (skip its poisons).

👢 Boots, shoes and moccasins Boot care (USDA FB1183, pp. 9–12): - Wet boots: wash off mud, grease work boots while damp, stuff with paper, dry slowly. - Harder grease in summer, more grease in winter (p. 12); recipes are in the Make-Do guide. - Soles: stand them 15 minutes in warm grease, no hotter than your hand can bear (FB1334, p. 16). A home repair kit (FB1183, p. 9): last holder, 3–4 iron lasts, hammer, pincers, knives, rasp, awls, sole and heel nails, flax thread, bristles and wax. Half-soling sewn shoes (Leno, p. 131; Bower, p. 29): 1. Wet the new leather. 2. Take off the old sole without cutting the welt. 3. Carry the new sole well back into the waist (the narrow middle). 4. Cut a channel deep enough to bury the stitches, and sew with stout, well-waxed thread. Pegged soles: one well-driven row of pegs usually holds; two rows make a stiff, tiring sole (Leno, p. 109). Fit: measure the foot's length seated, then trace it on paper standing — it lengthens under load, and the difference sets the allowance (p. 45; 🖼️ measuring diagram). Leno also covers pumps (turnshoes) and leggings. Moccasins in a wet climate (Farnham, pp. 260–266): frontier moccasins were one piece of buckskin stuffed with deer hair or dry leaves. In wet weather wearing them was "a decent way of going barefooted,"

climate (Farnham, pp. 260–266): frontier moccasins were one piece of buckskin stuffed with deer hair or dry leaves. In wet weather wearing them was "a decent way of going barefooted," because the leather is spongy. Improve them: - Add a rawhide sole, or sew on a thick "tap" that runs up the sides (p. 266). - Shape them by wetting and wearing them until dry (p. 264). - For uppers, 10–12 oz cotton duck rubbed with paraffin and ironed is waterproof and wears well. A child's moccasins can be cut from an old leather handbag (MP614, p. 9). Here, keep moccasins for indoors and the dry season, and save real boots for winter mud (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Leno Boot and Shoemaking — lasts, uppers, welted and pegged boots, mending; Bower Practical Shoe Repairing — soles and heels; USDA FB1183 — care of shoes and harness.

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - Arsenic sprinkled on stored furs (Farnham, p. 64), as a hair remover (p. 120) and to "poison" fur robes (p. 224); arsenical soap and corrosive sublimate (mercury chloride) in Lee's, p. 225. Deadly; old mounts and furs may still carry it (ATSDR Arsenic). Instead: salt, dry, cold storage. - Chrome tanning — FB1334, p. 17; the bulletin itself says the spent liquor "probably would be fatal to farm animals" (p. 19). Also the chrome (dichromate) dye mordant — USDA dyes, p. 10. Chromium(VI) causes cancer (ATSDR Chromium). Instead: bark or alum. - Sulfuric acid "salt-acid" pickle — FB1334, pp. 27–28; Farnham, p. 113. Burns and fumes. Instead: salt-alum. - Oxalic acid tan liquors — Farnham, p. 116; Household Discoveries, p. 409. Poisonous. Instead: brains, bark or alum. - Gasoline baths for furs — FB1334, pp. 25–26; Farnham, p. 150. Fire and fumes. Instead: lukewarm soapy water (rule of thumb). - Burning sulfur to bleach sheepskins — Farnham, p. 151. Toxic fumes. Instead: keep the natural color. - Formaldehyde and borax-heavy "pickles" in old taxidermy recipes (rule of thumb). Instead: salt and alum. - "40 to 45 percent of body heat" lost from the head — FM 21-76, p. 176. The real figure is about 10%, in proportion to skin area (rule of thumb) — but still cover head and neck. -

🚲 Bicycles, Carts & Hauling Without Fuel When the gas runs out, everything you move goes on your back, on wheels you push, or on a bicycle. This guide covers how much one person can move and how fast, travel times from Cave Junction, loading a bike, building a trailer (welded steel or no-weld pallets), hitches and trailer brakes, wheelbarrows and handcarts, hills, keeping a bike running with few tools, spares to stock, and local hazards. The books are in Bicycles-Carts\ (Bicycle-Repair and Trailers-Carts). Pack animals, wagons and harness are in Horses-Draft-Animals\ and the Horse guide; brazing and forge work are in Blacksmithing-Tools\ and the Blacksmithing guide. Know the limits of the books. The repair manuals date from 1896 to 1978. Their methods for tubes, tyres, spokes, cup-and-cone hubs, chains and steel frames still work. But the library has little on modern parts: hydraulic disc brakes, tubeless tyres, indexed ("click") shifting, suspension and e-bikes. Stock their spares (pads, bleed kit and fluid, sealant, cables) now. A plain steel bike with rim brakes is the easiest to keep running (rule of thumb). ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - A loaded bike takes longer to stop (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 97), and wet rim brakes stop much worse. Start every descent slowly, test the brakes at the top, and remember that a trailer with no brake shoves the bike

p. 97), and wet rim brakes stop much worse. Start every descent slowly, test the brakes at the top, and remember that a trailer with no brake shoves the bike downhill (rule of thumb). - Don't wreck your body. A normal day load on your back is 10–20 kg (22–44 lb); 50 kg (110 lb) only for short distances (World Bank, p. 65). Put heavy loads on wheels. - Never ride a kinked frame tube or fork. A buckled tube is weakened and must be replaced (Burr, p. 73). Keep at least 2 in of seat post inside the frame (Henry, p. 54). - Never clean parts in gasoline. Use kerosene, diesel or degreaser, outdoors, away from flames. - Fire season (June–October): don't drag metal. A chain or trailer part scraping on rock can start a wildfire. Haul in the cool early morning and carry water (rule of thumb). - Braze outdoors, and only steel frames. Brass gives off zinc fumes. Aluminium and carbon frames cannot be brazed.

🏋️ How much one person can move The biggest lesson in these books: get the load off your back and onto wheels. The World Bank's planning table — rough, order-of-magnitude numbers only (World Bank, p. 66): | How you move it | Load | Speed | Typical trip | | Carried (back or head) | 20 kg (44 lb) | 5 km/h (3 mph) | up to 10 km (6 mi) | | Sledge (dragged) (Sled) | 100 kg (220 lb) | 4 km/h (2.5 mph) | short | | Wheelbarrow | 100 kg (220 lb) | 4 km/h (2.5 mph) | about 1 km | | Handcart | 150 kg (330 lb) | 4 km/h (2.5 mph) | about 5 km (3 mi) | | Bicycle | 60 kg (130 lb) | 10 km/h (6 mph) | about 20 km (12 mi) | | Cycle rickshaw or tricycle | 150 kg (330 lb) | 8 km/h (5 mph) | — | On your back: - A wheelbarrow or handcart lets the same person move 50–100 kg (110–220 lb) comfortably, against a normal 10–20 kg carried (World Bank, p. 65). - Weight costs distance. In a 6-hour march you cover about 2 km less for every 10 lb carried over 40 lb (FM 21-18, p. 65). Porters can carry 120 lb for several days at 12 mi a day; 150

about 2 km less for every 10 lb carried over 40 lb (FM 21-18, p. 65). Porters can carry 120 lb for several days at 12 mi a day; 150 lb brings exhaustion and injury (p. 71). - A packboard (pack frame) makes 50 lb an easy load; most people can manage 100 lb. Pack it compact and high, heaviest items on the upper half, lashed tight. To lift it, sit against the upright board, put on the straps, roll onto hands and knees and stand. For very big loads the bike is pushed, not ridden. Bikes work best on flat, hard surfaces (World Bank, p. 65). 🗺️ Travel times from Cave Junction Walking pace with a load (FM 21-18, p. 89): on roads 4.0 km/h (2.5 mph) by day, 3.2 km/h at night; cross-country 2.4 km/h by day, 1.6 km/h at night. A normal day is 20–32 km (12–20 mi), or 5–8 hours on the move. - Rest 15 minutes after the first 45 minutes, then 10 minutes in every hour (FM 21-18, p. 48). - At halts, lie down with your feet up. Carry spare socks; tape known hot spots before they blister (FM 21-18, p. 101; 🖼️ photo of friction blisters; Blister). In hills, plan by time, not miles. Add one-third to the map distance, then 1 hour for every 1,000 ft (300 m) of climb, or every 2,000 ft (600 m) of descent (FM 3-97.6, p. 72). Bike times use the World Bank's loaded-bicycle speed of 10 km/h (p. 66) and are moving time only. Add the climbing allowance, rests, flats and pushing up steep grades (rule of thumb). 🎒 Loading a bicycle How to load it (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 97): - Touring cyclists usually carry 30–50 lb, on the bike — a backpack makes balance harder. (Bicycle touring) - Put heavy items low in the panniers and split the load front and rear. Too much weight in front spoils the steering. - A loaded bike needs lower gears, sways more and takes longer to stop. Practise with the load before a real trip. Making a bike carry more (Practical Action, Bicycles): - Panniers can be sacks or baskets hung from wood across the carrier, or a light steel frame. Keep the sides balanced, and strengthen the carrier (p. 2; 🖼️ pannier frame drawing; Pannier). - The load is limited by the rear wheel and tyre; a stronger rear wheel helps (p. 3). - Longer carrier without cutting the frame: bolt on extra stays and move the rear wheel back about 250 mm (10 in). The chain and brake rods must be lengthened (p. 3; 🖼️ extension drawings). - A small 20-inch rear wheel is stronger, keeps the load low and makes pedalling easier, but handles potholes worse (p. 4; 🖼️ drawing). Pushing big loads: in Zambia, people pushed two 50 kg sacks of maize on one bicycle up to 30 km (19 mi) to town (Bicycle Trailers in Zambia, p. 1). Before a loaded trip (rule of

pushed two 50 kg sacks of maize on one bicycle up to 30 km (19 mi) to town (Bicycle Trailers in Zambia, p. 1). Before a loaded trip (rule of thumb): tyres firm, brakes grabbing hard, carrier bolts tight, nothing able to swing into the spokes, and patch kit, pump and water aboard. Learn the names of the parts from a 🖼️ labeled bicycle drawing (the key is on p. 31). 📚 Go deeper: Adult Cycling Manual — loaded touring and riding skills; Practical Action Bicycles — dimensioned pannier frames and carrier extensions. 🛒 Bicycle trailers: welded steel or no-weld pallets A trailer lets a rider move about three times the bike's own load, roughly 200 kg (450 lb) (Practical Action, Bicycle Trailers, p. 1). But not always. In northern Ghana, trailers promoted in the 1990s failed: heavy to pull loaded, poor on footpaths, and twice the cost of a bicycle. A plain bike with a strong carrier was more flexible (World Bank, p. 39). Welded steel trailer (Bicycle Trailers, pp. 3–4; frame drawings: 🖼️ p. 2, 🖼️ p. 3): - Frame: 19 mm (3/4 in) mild-steel square tube, or round tube at least 22 × 1.5 mm (25 × 1.5 mm is better). Reinforce each joint with a piece of tube or bar inside it. - Ordinary bike wheels are fine for light loads on good roads, but not for heavy loads on rough tracks. Use strengthened wheels (p. 4). - A local welder in Zambia built these from the drawings for about $100 each (Zambia report, p. 1). No-weld pallet trailer — about one day and about 20 euros (Low-tech Lab). You need 2 pallets, 2 bicycle wheels, wood screws and 1 old inner tube; a crowbar, hammer, saw and screwdriver. 1. Decide what it must carry. Keep it no wider than 1 m (39 in) (p. 3). 2. Take the pallets apart with the crowbar and hammer (p. 3). 3.

1. Decide what it must carry. Keep it no wider than 1 m (39 in) (p. 3). 2. Take the pallets apart with the crowbar and hammer (p. 3). 3. Build the frame from the centre outward. The side boards must be as thick as the wheel so they frame it (p. 4; 🖼️ the numbered boards; Pallet). 4. Fix the wheels before the outer boards go on (p. 5). 5. Hitch it to the bike's rear rack with the inner tube (p. 6). Hitches (Bicycle Trailers, p. 4; 🖼️ hitch design; 🖼️ Poston's scrap-steel hitch): - Hitch above the rear wheel, to the carrier or the frame under the seat. It is simpler than an axle-level hitch, works on earth roads, and lets the trailer double as a handcart. - The recommended joint is a rubber ball in a steel socket. - Any hitch must hold the load, let the bike lean, come off easily, and take braking and pulling forces from every direction (Low-tech Lab, p. 6). Trailer brakes and carrying the injured (Bicycle Ambulance, pp. 2–3; 🖼️ frame diagram): a stretcher trailer carries two people, with a shock absorber and a ball-joint hitch so the bike can turn. Its overrun brake works by itself: when the bike slows, the trailer pushes a rod into a sprung tube, which pulls a brake cable on the trailer wheel. No

turn. Its overrun brake works by itself: when the bike slows, the trailer pushes a rod into a sprung tube, which pulls a brake cable on the trailer wheel. No trailer brake? Slow down early, drag a foot, or walk it down steep hills (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: Practical Action Bicycle Trailers — parts list with tube sizes and frame drawings; Low-tech Lab pallet trailer — the no-weld build; Bicycle Ambulance — hitch and overrun-brake part sizes; Trailer Hitch (Poston) — a lathe-free hitch from scrap steel and rubber. 🛞 Wheelbarrows, handcarts, sledges and travois A better wheelbarrow (Wilson, The Wheelbarrow): - Use one large wheel with most of the load directly over it. Leave little weight on the handles, and take that with a shoulder strap. The traditional Chinese barrow built this way carried up to six people (p. 1). - A homemade barrow wheel can run on a standard bicycle axle and cone bearings, with a solid tyre of strips cut from old car tyres (p. 2; 🖼️ wheel drawing). - Choose air-filled tyres (adjust pressure for rough ground), keep the load low, and make several light trips rather than one heavy one (USFS Handtools for Trail Work, p. 42, with 🖼️ wheelbarrow drawings). Handcarts: - A balanced handcart, with most of the weight on the wheels, is easier than a one-wheel barrow (World Bank, p. 65). - A good load cart has a low centre of gravity, a wide wheelbase and big wheels. Pulled carts are easier to control on rough ground. A cart pulled from a hip belt finished a 3.2 km mixed course 54% faster than people carrying rucksacks. The carts were noisy in brush and rock, and gear caught in the wheels — so guard the wheels (Knapik, p. 37). - Cart bodies are often built on scrap car or pickup axles. Large wheels roll through ruts and holes better than small ones

so guard the wheels (Knapik, p. 37). - Cart bodies are often built on scrap car or pickup axles. Large wheels roll through ruts and holes better than small ones (Starkey, p. 85; 🖼️ big wheel vs small wheel in a rut; 🖼️ cart wheel, hub and bearing, labeled; Handcart). Sledges are cheap and narrow, and go where carts can't — too steep, muddy or narrow. But they pull harder, snag on stumps, and their ruts turn into gullies (Starkey, p. 83; 🖼️ simple wooden sledge; Sled). Travois (behind a horse or mule): two straight poles 14–20 ft long with a platform 2–3 ft wide behind the animal, and three people to handle it at ditches and streams (FM 25-7, p. 166; 🖼️ travois drawing). 📚 Go deeper: Wilson The Wheelbarrow — the big-wheel barrow and a homemade wheel; Wheelbarrow construction drawings — six dimensioned sheets for a steel barrow; Selvidge, p. 104 — replacing a wagon spoke, and p. 95 — shrinking on an iron tyre.
