⛰️ Hills and grades The extra push on a slope is roughly the total weight times the grade (rule of thumb, simple physics). A 10% grade rises 10 ft for every 100 ft along the road (Grade)). | Grade | Extra push for a 220 lb (100 kg) load | | 5% | about 11 lb | | 10% | about 22 lb | | 15% | about 33 lb | That is on top of the push needed on the flat. (Rules of thumb:) - Pushing much over 25–30 lb for long is very tiring. - On grades over about 10%, use two people (one pulling with a rope or hip belt), or split the load. - A loaded bike on a steep Forest Service road is often faster walked and pushed than ridden. - Going down: a trailer with no brake shoves the bike. Slow down at the top, not halfway. Drag a foot or add a brake. On a handcart, put someone behind holding back on a rope. 📚 Go deeper: Knapik Load Carriage — terrain factors and energy cost; FM 3-97.6 — moving in steep country.

🩹 Flat tyres: patching tubes and booting tyres Patching a tube (Henry, pp. 61–65): 1. Before you take the tyre off, mark where it sits against the valve, or count spokes from the valve, so you can find the thorn later (p. 63). 2. Lever one side of the tyre off and pull the tube out. Careless levering tears the tube (p. 64; Tire lever, Inner tube). 3. Find the leak: pump the tube up a little and listen or feel near your face, or dunk it in water and watch for bubbles (p. 64). 4. Find the cause: feel inside the tyre at the matching spot for the thorn (p. 64). 5. Roughen around the hole with sandpaper (p. 65). 6. Coat tube and patch with rubber cement. Wait about 10 minutes until it is tacky (p. 65). 7. Press the patch on hard, dust with talc ("French chalk") and refit the tube dry (p. 65). Tips: old inner tubes make good patch rubber (p. 61). A patch kit more than a year old may have gone bad (p. 62). If a tyre goes soft with no hole, check the valve first (p. 62). Tyres lose 10–20 psi within a week anyway, so check pressure often (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 72). Booting a cut or burst tyre: - Glue canvas inside the tyre over the damage, or a patch

a week anyway, so check pressure often (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 72). Booting a cut or burst tyre: - Glue canvas inside the tyre over the damage, or a patch cut from an old tyre (Henry, p. 70). - Fill small tread cuts with leather dust (rasped from scrap leather) mixed into rubber cement (Henry, p. 69). - A modern road kit: two denim boots about 1 × 2 in, 6 patches, 2 tyre levers, a spare tube, talc and a pressure gauge (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 34). 📚 Go deeper: Henry Cycle Building and Repairing — tyres, tubes, valves and repairs; Adult Cycling Manual — the tool and tyre kit. 🔩 Wheels, hub bearings and chains Truing a wobbly wheel (Henry, pp. 44–46; 🖼️ truing a wheel in its own fork with chalk; Wheelbuilding): 1. Spin the wheel in the frame and hold chalk beside the rim so it marks the spots that stick out. 2. A spoke pulls the rim toward its own side of the hub. At each chalk mark, tighten the spokes that run to the other side of the hub, a little at a time, with a spoke (nipple) key. 3. Fix out-of-round the same way: tighten spokes at the high spots, loosen them at the low spots. 4. File off spoke ends that poke through the nipples, or they will puncture the tube. 5. Replace broken spokes one at a time, so you keep the lacing pattern (🖼️ lacing drawing; Spoke). Hub bearings (Henry, pp. 46–47; 🖼️ hub parts named; 🖼️ cup, cone, balls and locknut, with how to hold the spanners): - A clicking wheel usually has a broken ball or worn cones. Open the hub; clean cups, cones and axle in kerosene. - Throw away chipped balls. Take a sample ball when you look for new ones. - Grease the cups, put the balls back, screw the cone up tight, then back it off about half a turn. Twisted by its spokes, the wheel should spin freely with almost no side play. Chains:

Chains: - Soak a filthy chain in kerosene for 2–3 days, hang it to drip, wipe it, then oil it (Henry, p. 52). - To shorten an old riveted chain, file off the burred pin heads and punch the pins out (Henry, p. 53; 🖼️ chain links drawn; 🖼️ putting a chain on). - Modern chains need a chain tool: push the pin almost out, leaving about 1/32 in in the side plate so it can go back in. A chain wears out in 1–2 years of average use, and a new chain may skip on a worn freewheel, so the two often need replacing together (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 104; Freewheel). 📚 Go deeper: Henry — lacing and truing wheels, hubs and chains; Adult Cycling Manual, p. 103 — chain cleaning, oiling and stiff links; Burr Bicycle Repairing — bearings, forks and shop-made tools. 🛑 Brakes, gears and field fixes Rim brakes (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 48; 🖼️ center-pull and side-pull brakes): released, the pads should sit about 1/16 in from the rim, and they should hit the rim before the lever reaches the handlebar. New cables stretch — tighten them again after about a week. Derailleur gears (p. 81; 🖼️ rear derailleur with its screws lettered): won't shift onto the largest cog? Back out its limit (stop) screw. Still short? Take up cable slack with the barrel adjuster. Shifts by itself? Tighten the thumbscrew holding the shift lever. Field fixes: - Bent crank: hold the bike steady and push the crank back with your foot — usually straight enough to finish the trip (Henry, p. 47). - Bent frame tube: a slight bend can be straightened, but a buckled (kinked) tube cannot. Replace it (Burr, p. 73; 🖼️ truing a frame; Bicycle frame). - Broken steel frame tube — braze it over a sleeve (Rowe, pp. 60–61; 🖼️ Burr's drawings of a tube mended over an inner sleeve; Lugged steel frame): 1. File the broken ends smooth and clean them bright, inside and out. 2. Fit a sleeve of light steel tube inside both ends; pin it if needed to hold the frame in line. 3. Coat the joint with borax mixed with water to a paste (the flux) (Borax). 4. Heat it

both ends; pin it if needed to hold the frame in line. 3. Coat the joint with borax mixed with water to a paste (the flux) (Borax). 4. Heat it in a charcoal fire or a blacksmith's forge. At a low red heat, lay on brass spelter and let it flow into the joint. Don't overheat. 5. Work outdoors (zinc fumes). 🌲 Illinois Valley hazards (Rules of thumb for our area.) - Goatheads (puncturevine) grow in dry, disturbed ground — road edges, driveways, bare lots. Carry extra patches or thorn-resistant tubes. Learn the plant and pull it before it seeds (weed photo list, p. 53; Puncturevine). - Rocky and serpentine Forest Service roads cause pinch flats under load. Run tyres firmer when loaded, and walk the worst rock. (Serpentinite) - Fire season (June–October): keep chains and metal parts from dragging and throwing sparks. Haul in the early morning with plenty of water. - Wet winters wash the oil off chains and rust them. Wipe and re-oil after every rain ride. - Rim brakes stop much worse when wet. Brake earlier; drag them lightly first to wipe the rims. 📚 Go deeper: Adult Cycling Manual, p. 97 — riding a loaded bike safely; Knapik, p. 37 — carts on rough ground.

⚠️ Old advice in the library to ignore - Homemade rubber cement from rubber dissolved in "benzine" (gasoline or naphtha) (Henry, p. 61). Very flammable, and benzene fumes are toxic. Use bought cement; if you must make it, mix it outdoors, far from any flame. - Boiling a chain in mutton tallow (Henry, p. 52). Hot fat is a fire hazard, and tallow holds grit. Soak in kerosene, wipe, and oil lightly. - Wrapping joints in asbestos cloth or wicking while brazing (Rowe, p. 61; p. 60). Asbestos causes cancer — use wet rags or a sheet-metal shield. Brass spelter gives off zinc fumes that cause "metal fume fever," so braze outdoors. - "Cleaning solvent from gasoline station" in the tool list (Adult Cycling Manual, p. 34). Never clean parts in gasoline. Use kerosene, diesel or degreaser, outdoors. - Obsolete parts: single-tube and beaded-edge tyres, cotter-pin cranks (Henry, p. 47) and 1890s frames. Skip those pages; the hub, wheel, patching, brazing and truing methods are still good. - Military load limits of 30–45% of body weight (Knapik, p. 20) are for fit young soldiers. Plan family loads on 10–20 kg. 📚 Go deeper: Henry, p. 46 — the sound old method: hubs cleaned in kerosene; Adult Cycling Manual, p. 103 — kerosene chain cleaning.

📐 Practical Math, Measuring & Geometry Homestead math with no stores: measuring with your body and a string, mixing by ratio, squaring a foundation, areas, tanks, woodpiles and loads, slopes and heights you can't reach, and the numbers behind water, power and medicine — each with a worked Illinois Valley example. The books are in Math-Measuring\Arithmetic-Geometry (Navy Mathematics courses), Math-Measuring\Measuring-Surveying (USDA surveying, quantities, timber measuring) and Math-Measuring\Units-Tables (NIST unit tables, Army Engineer Field Data); Ray's arithmetic is in Children-Learning\Arithmetic, and FM 5-426 Carpentry and FM 5-125 Rigging in Manuals\ArmyFieldManuals. The interactive 🔢 Unit converter & calculators page (Unit converter) does the arithmetic; this guide shows how to do it with a pencil. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst mistakes - Same units before you multiply. Turn everything into feet (or inches) first. Mixing inches and feet is the commonest error — off by 12, 144 or 1,728 times. - A British or Canadian "gallon" is about 20% bigger than a US gallon (NIST HB 44, p. 8). Check where a recipe or manual came from. - Medicine: only doses printed in the medical books, in mg and mL, never drops. A second person redoes the arithmetic before anyone swallows it. - Loads are heavier than they look. A cubic yard of damp packed earth weighs about 2,600 lb (FM 5-34, p. 292). Never stand under a lift. - Measure

📏 Measuring with no tools Your body is a ruler — measure yours once (rule of thumb): | Measure | What it is | Typical adult | | Thumb width | Across the knuckle | about 1 in | | Span | Thumb tip to little-finger tip, spread | 8–9 in | | Cubit | Elbow to fingertip | 17–19 in | | Arm spread | Fingertip to fingertip | about your height | | Pace | One step | 2–2½ ft | Pace count (NRCS Surveying, p. 33): walk a measured 500 ft until the count varies by no more than 2–3 paces. Pace factor = distance ÷ paces; pacing is good to about 2%. Example: 500 ft in 200 paces = 2.5 ft per pace, so 340 paces along a fence is 850 ft. The Army counts every step, the Forest Service every second step — pick one (FM 3-25.26, p. 52; Navigation guide). Hills and brush add steps; count with pace count beads. Known sizes (standard sizes): a dollar bill is 6.14 in long; a "2×4" is 1½ × 3½ in; letter paper 8½ × 11 in. A string knotted every foot is a tape. Level, plumb and straight: - Water level): clear tubing full of water; both ends settle at the same height however long the tube (rule of thumb: get every bubble out). With a

and straight: - Water level): clear tubing full of water; both ends settle at the same height however long the tube (rule of thumb: get every bubble out). With a measuring rod it also measures a creek's drop (NRCan, p. 42). - Plumb bob: any weight on a string — "use a rock, half-brick, or small piece of metal" (FM 5-426, p. 88). - Straight: a tight string or a snapped chalk line (FM 5-426, p. 44). Equal parts (🖼️ Navy Mathematics Vol. 1, p. 197): for 5 equal strips, slant a ruler so 0 and 10 in touch the board's edges and mark at 2, 4, 6 and 8. 📚 Go deeper: NRCS Surveying, pp. 32–34 — pacing and taping on slopes; Navy Vol. 1, ch. 6 — percentage and measurement; Tape measure.

➗ Fractions, percents, ratios and mixing Percent = part ÷ whole × 100: 15 sick hens of 60 is 25% (Navy Vol. 1, pp. 62–64). Scaling a recipe: factor = amount wanted ÷ amount the recipe makes. Bread for 6 loaves, wanted 10: 10 ÷ 6 = 1⅔, so 3 cups of water becomes 5. Scale every ingredient (ratio and proportion, p. 148). Mixing by parts — add the parts; each part is the batch ÷ that total. All by volume, same bucket: | Mix | Parts | Source | | 2-stroke fuel | Ratio on the engine; most modern saws 50:1 = 2.6 oz oil per gallon (40:1 = 3.2 oz; 32:1 = 4 oz) | MAVCC, p. 186; (rule of thumb) | | Concrete toilet slab | 1 cement : 2 gravel : 3 sand + water till it holds together | 🖼️ Hesperian ch. 7, p. 20 | | Chimney mortar | 1 portland cement : 1 lime : 6 sand | FB 1751, p. 24 | Example: 3 cu ft of that concrete is 6 parts: ½ cu ft cement, 1 gravel, 1½ sand. 📐 Right angles and layout The 3-4-5 triangle (Pythagorean theorem): from the corner, mark 3 ft along one string and 4 ft along the other; when the marks are exactly 5 ft apart, the corner is square (🖼️ Navy Vol. 1, p. 199). Multiples work — 6-8-10, 9-12-15, 12-16-20 — and bigger is more accurate: never start under 6 ft; use 12-16-20 for a 50 × 100 ft layout (FM 5-426, p. 48). Check the diagonals: a rectangle is square only when both diagonals are equal (same page). For a 20 × 30 ft shed, √(400 + 900) = 36.06 ft (36 ft ⅝ in) each. Hang the lines on batter boards set back from the corners so they survive digging (FM 5-426, p. 46). With a string and stakes (a rope compass): - Bisect a line: swing equal arcs from each end; the line through the crossings halves it at a right angle (🖼️ Navy Vol. 1, p. 198). Bisect an angle the same way from its arms (🖼️ p. 199). - Center of a round thing (tank, millstone): bisect two chords; the lines cross at the center (🖼️ p. 200). - Circle: string on a center stake; 10 ft of string gives 62.8 ft around (C = 2πr). - Oval (ellipse) bed or pond, 20 × 12 ft (geometry): two stakes 16 ft apart on the long center

ft of string gives 62.8 ft around (C = 2πr). - Oval (ellipse) bed or pond, 20 × 12 ft (geometry): two stakes 16 ft apart on the long center line (√(10² − 6²) = 8 ft each side of center), a loop of string 36 ft around (20 + 16) over both, pulled taut with a marking stick and walked around. A straightedge method is on 🖼️ p. 200. 📚 Go deeper: Navy Vol. 1, ch. 18 — constructions; FM 5-426, pp. 44–48 — layout tools, batter boards, squaring; Steel square.

Fences: posts on a straight run = length ÷ spacing + 1; on a closed loop = perimeter ÷ spacing. A 1-acre square is 835 ft around: posts every 10 ft = 84. Roofs: roof area = flat (plan) area × the slope factor (table in the slope section). Roofing is sold by the square = 100 sq ft (Ray's, p. 330). (🖼️ NRCan, p. 42). - Eye height and pace: sight level from the bottom to the spot at your eye height and pace to it: eye 5½ ft ÷ (10 paces × 2½ ft) = 22% (🖼️ FM 5-34, p. 148). - Hand level or Abney level: a hand level carries rough levels 400–500 ft with sights under 50 ft; an Abney reads percent (🖼️ NRCS Surveying, p. 47; 🖼️ p. 51). - Slope distance exceeds level distance: 175.6 ft taped on a 30% slope = 168.2 ft level (🖼️ p. 32). - A-frame level for contours (rule of thumb): two 6-ft poles in an "A" with a crossbar and a plumb line from the top. 🌲 Heights and distances you can't reach Shadows (similar triangles)): height = your height × tree's shadow ÷ your shadow, at the same moment (🖼️ Navy Vol. 1, p. 207). You: 6 ft, 4½-ft shadow; the fir's shadow 48 ft → 6 × 48 ÷ 4.5 = 64 ft. Stick (45°) method (similar triangles): hold a stick upright at arm's length with as much above your fist as from your eye to your fist. Back up until the fist lines up with the base and the stick top with the treetop: your distance from the trunk ≈ the height. A cruiser's stick does the same with printed marks (🖼️ FB 1210, p. 14; Biltmore stick). Abney or clinometer (percent): height = level distance × (top % − base %) ÷ 100, base negative if below your eye. At 66 ft, top +110%, base −8%: 66 × 1.18 = 78 ft. Felling: see the Firewood guide. Width of a river: - Compass: at A, opposite tree B, read B's bearing; walk along the bank until it has changed by 45°. The distance walked = the width (🖼️ FM 5-34, p. 162). - No compass (geometry): from A pace 50 steps along the bank and plant a stick (C), 50 more to D; from D walk straight away from the river until C lines up with B. Those paces = the width.

the bank and plant a stick (C), 50 more to D; from D walk straight away from the river until C lines up with B. Those paces = the width. Thumb jump (rule of thumb): thumb at arm's length, close one eye then the other; it "jumps" along the far hillside. Judge the jump from a known width (a 60-ft barn) and multiply by 10 — arm's length is about ten times the space between your eyes. Check yours on a paced distance. Maps: ground distance = map distance × the scale's bottom number (FM 3-25.26, p. 44): on a 1:24,000 map, 1 in = 2,000 ft. The contour interval is in the margin (p. 17): with a 40-ft interval, lines ¼ in apart = 40 ÷ 500 = 8% (p. 113). More in the Navigation guide. 📚 Go deeper: Navy Vol. 1, ch. 19 — right triangles, with sine and tangent tables at p. 220; Navy Vol. 2, ch. 5 — solving any triangle; FB 1210, pp. 8–14 — measuring standing trees.

🏋️ Levers, pulleys and loads Lever: push × your side of the pivot = load × load side. The mechanical advantage is how many times it multiplies your push — 10 lb lifting 100 lb is 10 (FM 5-125, p. 105). A 6-ft bar with the pivot 6 in from the load: 5½ ÷ ½ = 11, so a 100-lb push lifts about 1,100 lb. Block and tackle: count the rope lines holding the moving block — that's the advantage (FM 5-125, p. 110; 🖼️ p. 112). Each sheave adds friction of about 10% of the load (p. 114); pull = (load + friction) ÷ advantage (p. 115). A 600-lb engine on 4 lines over 4 sheaves: (600 + 240) ÷ 4 = 210 lb. A person pulls about 100 lb straight down, 60 lb along the ground (same page): put three on it. Ramps (physics; friction adds more): push ≈ weight × height ÷ ramp length: a 500-lb log up a 12-ft skid onto a 3-ft wagon bed takes 125 lb plus friction (Bicycles & Carts guide). Rope: safe load = breaking strength ÷ at least 4; knots, sharp bends and age cut strength up to 50%. Fiber rope rule: safe tons = diameter in inches squared — ½-in rope = ¼ ton (FM 5-125, p. 20). Weights for guessing loads (lb per cu ft, FM 5-34, pp. 291–292):

rule: safe tons = diameter in inches squared — ½-in rope = ¼ ton (FM 5-125, p. 20). ⚡ Electricity by the numbers - Watts = volts × amps (NEETS 1, p. 120): a 12-V pump drawing 5 A uses 60 W. - Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms — cover the one you want on the circle (🖼️ NEETS 1, p. 116). A 12-ohm heater on 120 V draws 10 A = 1,200 W. - Watt-hours = watts × hours; 1,000 Wh = 1 kWh (p. 126). The pump 2 hours a day = 120 Wh. - Battery energy = volts × amp-hours. A 12-V, 100-Ah battery is 1,200 Wh on the label, but size a lead-acid bank on only 40% of that (IEA, p. 17): 480 Wh → the pump for 4 days. - Long wires waste power: volts lost = 2 × one-way feet × amps × ohms per 1,000 ft ÷ 1,000. Use the Off-Grid guide's wire table (Voltage drop). - 1 horsepower = 746 W (NIST SP 811, p. 62). 📚 Go deeper: NEETS Module 1, ch. 3 — Ohm's law, power and energy with practice questions; Off-Grid Power guide — load lists and battery sizing.

💧 Water flow and pressure - Flow by bucket and stopwatch: a 5-gallon bucket in 20 seconds = 5 ÷ 20 × 60 = 15 gpm; a 55-gallon drum in 40 seconds = 82.5 gpm (NCAT, p. 3). - Pressure from height (head): each foot of water = 0.433 psi (DOE, p. 113); each psi = 2.31 ft (NRCan, p. 41). A tank 40 ft above the house gives 17 psi before pipe friction; 60 psi on a gauge at the bottom of a full hose = 139 ft of drop (🖼️ DOE, p. 114). - Suction lift has a hard limit: 21.2 ft at 1,000 ft elevation, 20.4 ft at 2,000 ft (USDA FB 1448, p. 28). At our ~1,300 ft keep a suction pump within about 20 ft of the water; deeper, the pump goes down the well. A siphon has the same limit. - Creek power: watts ≈ gpm × feet of head ÷ 10, about what NCAT's table of typical outputs shows (NCAT, p. 9): 30 gpm falling 50 ft ≈ 150 W, day and night. Pipes, summer flow, water law: Off-Grid guide. 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 1448, pp. 27–28 — pressure and suction tables; NRCan, pp. 41–44 — measuring head and flow; Micro hydro.

💊 Food, medicine and time math A year's food: people × calories a day × days, at 2,100 kcal per person a day and about 1,500 kcal per pound of dry grain (Food Security guide): 4 × 2,100 × 365 = 3,066,000 kcal ≈ 2,000 lb of grain-equivalent for a family of 4. Days of supply = stock ÷ daily use: 50 lb of flour at 1½ lb a day = 33 days. ### ⚠️ Medicine arithmetic — read this first - Use only doses printed in the medical books (Medical guide; WTND green pages). This is arithmetic only. - Write the unit on every number — mg, mL, kg. Mixing mg and mL, or lb and kg, kills. - A second person redoes it without seeing yours. If the answers differ, stop. - Never measure medicine in drops or with unchecked kitchen spoons. Dose by weight (mg/kg): kg = lb ÷ 2.2 (WTND ch. 8, p. 4); mg = mg per kg × kg. Made-up numbers, not a real dose for any medicine: 10 mg/kg for a 44-lb child: 44 ÷ 2.2 = 20 kg; 20 × 10 = 200 mg; from a liquid with 100 mg in 5 mL: 200 ÷ 100 × 5 = 10 mL. Dosing an overweight child by actual weight can give far too much (WHO Formulary, p. 15). Spoons: 1 tsp = 5

mL: 200 ÷ 100 × 5 = 10 mL. Dosing an overweight child by actual weight can give far too much (WHO Formulary, p. 15). Spoons: 1 tsp = 5 mL, 1 Tbsp = 15 mL. Household spoons vary — mark one at exactly 5 mL of water from a syringe (🖼️ WTND ch. 8, p. 3). Drops are unreliable: two books here put 64 (USU, p. 20) and 75 (Henley's, p. 706) drops in a teaspoon, before the dropper or liquid changes. Time: "every 8 hours" = 3 times a day; "every 6 hours" = 4. 📚 Go deeper: WTND ch. 8 — grams, milligrams, spoons, child doses; Food and Nutrition Needs in Emergencies — adjusting calories; Field Care guide.

Ham (Amateur), CB, Shortwave, GMRS/FRS & MURS — how they work and how to use them This guide explains, in plain language, how to communicate by radio when the internet and phones are down. It covers what each type of radio is, what it can do, which frequencies/channels matter in an emergency, and the basic procedures for calling for help. Legal note (normal times): Transmitting on ham (amateur) frequencies requires a license (easy to get — see below). GMRS requires a cheap license (no test). CB, FRS, MURS need no license. Shortwave listening needs no license (you're only receiving). In a genuine life-threatening emergency, FCC rules (47 CFR §97.405) let anyone use any means of radio to call for help. Listening is always legal. Learn and practice before you need it.

1. The quick version — what to grab and what to know | Need | Best tool | License | Range (typical) | | Talk to family nearby (same property / neighborhood) | FRS / GMRS walkie-talkie (FRS) | FRS none; GMRS cheap | 0.5–2 mi (up to 5+ with GMRS + height) | | Talk across town / coordinate a group | GMRS (with repeater) or Ham VHF/UHF (GMRS) | GMRS cheap; Ham test | 5–50 mi via repeater | | Talk regionally / long distance / into other states | Ham HF (Amateur radio) | Ham (General class) | 100s–1000s mi | | Hear news & official broadcasts from anywhere | Shortwave receiver (Shortwave radio) | none (listening) | Worldwide | | Road / vehicle convoy, truckers | CB (Citizens band radio) | none | 1–15 mi | Three things everyone should know: 1. Monitor, don't just transmit. A cheap receiver tells you what's happening. 2. Higher antenna = more range. Antenna height matters more than watts (🖼️ why: line-of-sight drawing). 3. Have a plan: agree on a channel/frequency and check-in times with your group in advance (write them down — see the card at the end). 📚 Go deeper: ARRL ARES Field Resources Manual, p. 6 — what to do first, checklists, message forms; NOAA Weather Radio brochure — how alerts work.

2. In the Illinois Valley 🏔️ The valley is ringed by mountains (Klamath Mountains): VHF/UHF needs a repeater on a peak (🖼️ why: radio waves travel in straight lines), and NOAA warns that mountain valleys may get little or no weather radio even inside the usual 40-mile range (NOAA brochure, p. 3). - Weather radio: try Medford 162.400, Mt. Ashland 162.475 and Brookings 162.550 MHz; SAME code 041033. - Ham: JCEC repeater 145.490 (−, tone 136.5), Eight Dollar Mtn; net Mondays 8:00 pm. - No license: Monday check-in on FRS channel 3 and MURS channel 3 after the 7:00 pm IVARC net. - HF: Oregon Emergency Net, nightly 6:00 pm, 3.980 MHz LSB. (Club websites, Nov 2026 — verify. Full lists: Illinois Valley guide.) 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 144 — radio in mountains; FM 24-18, p. 102 — picking a radio site; NOAA Weather Radio brochure, p. 3 — reception in valleys.

3. How radio actually works (the 60-second version) - A radio turns your voice into radio waves at a certain frequency (measured in kilohertz kHz or megahertz MHz). Another radio tuned to the same frequency turns the wave back into sound. - Both radios must be on the same frequency/channel AND the same mode (e.g. FM, AM, SSB) to hear each other. - Only one person talks at a time. You press PTT (push-to-talk) to transmit, release it to listen. You cannot hear others while you hold PTT. - Frequency bands behave very differently: - VHF/UHF (high frequency numbers, ~30 MHz–3 GHz): travel in roughly straight "line of sight." Great locally, blocked by hills/buildings. Used by FRS, GMRS, MURS, and ham 2m/70cm. Extended by repeaters (see below). - HF / shortwave (low numbers, ~3–30 MHz): can bounce off the ionosphere and travel hundreds or thousands of miles ("skip"). Used by ham HF, CB (27 MHz), and shortwave broadcasters. Range changes with time of day and the sun. (🖼️ ground waves and sky waves; 🖼️ layers of the ionosphere; Ionosphere, Skywave) - Skip zone: HF can leave a zone of silence — a nearby station unheard while a far one is loud (NEETS 10, p. 106; 🖼️ skip-zone drawing). - Match the antenna: vertical talks best to vertical, horizontal to horizontal (FM 24-18, p. 45; 🖼️ polarization drawing). Handhelds and car

loud (NEETS 10, p. 106; 🖼️ skip-zone drawing). - Match the antenna: vertical talks best to vertical, horizontal to horizontal (FM 24-18, p. 45; 🖼️ polarization drawing). Handhelds and car whips are vertical — hold the radio upright. 📚 Go deeper: NEETS Module 10, p. 100 — the ionosphere by day and night; NEETS Module 12 — AM, FM and SSB.

4. CB Radio (Citizens Band) — no license, simple, vehicle-friendly - What it is: 40 channels around 27 MHz (in the HF band). No license needed. Cheap, everywhere, popular with truckers and off-roaders. - Range: usually 1–15 miles (more in flat/open terrain; occasionally hundreds of miles when "skip" conditions bounce signals off the ionosphere). - Power limit: 4 watts AM / 12 watts SSB (SSB radios reach farther). - Key channels: - Channel 9 — traditional emergency / help channel. - Channel 19 — highway / trucker channel (road conditions, traffic, convoys). - Channel 1–40 — general use; pick an unused one for your group. - Modes: Most CB is AM. Higher-end radios add SSB (USB/LSB) for more range — but both radios must use the same mode (Single-sideband modulation). - Good for: vehicle-to-vehicle, convoys, short local coordination with zero setup (🖼️ common whip antennas; Whip antenna). 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 55 — repairing a broken whip antenna (🖼️ repair drawing); Citizens band radio — channels, history and photos.
5. FRS / GMRS / MURS — the walkie-talkie families These are the little handheld radios ("walkie-talkies"). Great for family/group.

FRS (Family Radio Service) — no license - The blister-pack walkie-talkies (Family Radio Service). 22 channels in UHF (462/467 MHz). - Low power (0.5–2 W), fixed antenna. Range ~0.5–2 miles. - No license, no setup. Good for keeping a family/group in touch on foot.

GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service) — cheap license, no test - Shares channels with FRS but allows higher power (up to 50 W), detachable antennas, and repeaters — so range can reach 5–50+ miles via a repeater. - One GMRS license (~$35, no exam) covers your entire family for 10 years. - Best all-round family emergency radio: cheap, legal, powerful, easy (General Mobile Radio Service).

MURS (Multi-Use Radio Service) — no license - 5 channels in VHF (151/154 MHz), up to 2 W. No license (Multi-Use Radio Service). - VHF often works better outdoors/rural than FRS/GMRS UHF. Good for property/farm. In hill country: use high ground, get clear of buildings and leafy trees (they soak up more signal than evergreens), and keep away from power lines (🖼️ good radio sites; 🖼️ poor radio sites). 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 102 — choosing a good radio spot; Walkie-talkie — photos of handheld radios.

6. Ham (Amateur) Radio — the serious emergency option Ham radio is the backbone of emergency communications. When everything else fails, hams relay health-and-welfare traffic, weather, and coordination across towns, states, and continents (Amateur radio; Amateur radio emergency communications).

Licensing (USA) — easier than you think Three license levels, each a multiple-choice test (questions are public — you can study the exact pool): 1. Technician — entry level. Grants VHF/UHF (local, repeaters) plus some HF. Enough for local/regional emergency comms. ~1 evening of study. 2. General — adds most HF privileges → long-distance / cross-country. 3. Amateur Extra — full privileges. Get at least a Technician license now while it's easy, and ideally General so you can use HF for long distance. In a true emergency you may legally transmit without a license to save life/property — but you'll be far more effective if you've practiced.

The main ham bands and what they do - 2 meters (144–148 MHz, VHF) and 70 cm (420–450 MHz, UHF): local simplex + repeaters. Your everyday "talk around town" bands. - HF bands (e.g. 80m, 40m, 20m): long distance. - 40m (7 MHz): reliable regional (100s of miles), day and night — great for a state/region emergency net. - 20m (14 MHz): long-distance (cross-country / international) in daytime. - 80m (3.5 MHz): regional at night.

Repeaters — how hams get range from a handheld A repeater is a radio on a tower/hilltop that receives your weak signal and re-transmits it with a big antenna and power, massively extending range. To use one you set your radio to the repeater's output frequency, an offset (so it transmits on the input), and sometimes a CTCSS "tone." Local repeater lists (and emergency nets) are worth printing out for your area (Repeater).

Simplex (radio-to-radio, no repeater) If repeaters are down, you talk simplex — directly, radio to radio, line of sight. The national 2m simplex calling frequency is 146.520 MHz. Wilderness protocol: back-country hams listen and call on 146.52 for 5 minutes at the top of the hour, every 3 hours from 7 AM to 7 PM, so someone beyond a repeater can be relayed (ARRL manual, p. 84).

HF from a valley: "NVIS" A wire dipole hung low — 1/10 to 1/4 of a wavelength up (roughly 25–60 ft on 80m, worked from the formula in section 8) sends its signal almost straight up; it comes back down like a fountain over a few hundred miles with no skip zone, and the hills matter much less (FM 24-18, p. 279; 🖼️ the "fountain" drawing; 🖼️ Army NVIS antennas; Near vertical incidence skywave).

Nets A net is a scheduled on-air meeting. In a directed net a net control station says who talks next. Listen first, check in when invited, keep a log, and tell net control if you leave (ARRL manual, p. 7, 18).

Ham digital & data (advanced, FYI) Hams can also send text/email/images with no internet via Winlink (email over radio), FT8 (weak-signal), and APRS (position/text). Useful but needs more gear and practice (Winlink, FT8, APRS). 📚 Go deeper: ARRL manual, p. 14 — ARES, traffic nets and RACES; FM 24-18, p. 278 — NVIS in full.

7. Shortwave (SWL) — hearing the outside world - What it is: Using a shortwave receiver to listen to broadcasts on the HF bands (roughly 1.8–30 MHz). No license needed to listen. - Why it matters: When local media and internet are down, shortwave lets you hear international news, government/emergency broadcasts, and ham traffic from far away — because HF signals bounce worldwide. - What to listen for: - International broadcasters (news from outside the affected area). - NOAA Weather Radio (VHF 162.400–162.550 MHz) — continuous US weather & emergency alerts. Every emergency kit should have a NOAA weather radio. - Ham bands (40m/20m) — to hear emergency nets and relays. - AM/FM broadcast and Emergency Alert System (EAS) on a normal radio. - Modes: Broadcasts are usually AM; ham/utility voice is often SSB (USB/LSB). A radio with SSB hears far more. - Tip: A simple long wire antenna dramatically improves shortwave reception (🖼️ long-wire antenna drawing). - NOAA Weather Radio: repeats every 4–6 minutes; a SAME radio set to your county code wakes up only for your county's alerts (NOAA brochure, p. 2; Specific Area Message Encoding). - No batteries at all: a crystal radio — wire, a homemade coil, a crystal detector and headphones — hears AM stations; in 1922 tests, high-power ones up to about 50 miles away (NBS Circular 120, p. 4; 🖼️ wiring diagram and

coil, a crystal detector and headphones — hears AM stations; in 1922 tests, high-power ones up to about 50 miles away (NBS Circular 120, p. 4; 🖼️ wiring diagram and parts). 📚 Go deeper: NBS Circular 120 — build a crystal set step by step; NBS Circular 121 — a sharper version.

8. Antennas, power & range (the practical stuff) - Antenna height beats power. Getting the antenna up high (roof, tree, mast) adds more range than buying a bigger amplifier. - Use the right antenna for the band. A proper resonant antenna (correct length for the frequency) works far better than a random wire. - Line of sight (VHF/UHF): range ≈ limited by the horizon and obstructions. Height = range. Repeaters overcome this. - HF skip: range changes with the time of day and solar conditions. Lower bands (80m) are better at night; higher bands (20m) are better in daytime. - Power: keep radios charged. Stock spare batteries, a 12V battery, a solar panel, and car-charging cables. A radio with a dead battery is a paperweight. - Grounding & safety: never put an antenna where it can touch power lines; ground equipment to reduce static/lightning risk. - EMP and solar storms: in government tests, most ham equipment wasn't damaged when its power cord was unplugged and the antenna coax disconnected (NCS TIB 85-10, p. 166) — more in the EMP Guide.

Build a wire antenna (half-wave dipole) Total length in feet = 468 ÷ MHz (3–50 MHz; FM 24-18, p. 47), cut in two equal halves with the coax at the center. 3.980 MHz (Oregon Emergency Net): 117.6 ft · 7.2 MHz: 65 ft · 14.3 MHz: 32.7 ft. Look first: 🖼️ center-fed wire antenna between two supports, 🖼️ improvised half-wave doublet, 🖼️ how a dipole radiates. 1. Any wire works in an emergency; copper or aluminum is best. 2. Insulators at the ends and center — plastic or glass (plastic spoons, bottle necks) beat wood or rope. The wire must touch nothing else (FM 24-18, p. 55; 🖼️ improvised insulators; Insulator)). 3. Tie one end through a spring or strip of inner tube so swaying trees don't snap it. 4. Adjust length and height for the strongest signal from a distant station. ⚠️ Transmitter off before touching the antenna — it can cause serious injury (p. 56). For 2m/70cm, a J-pole from TV twin-lead is cheap (ARRL manual, p. 12; 🖼️ what twin-lead looks like; Twin-lead). Rocky mountain ground is a poor ground, so use a dipole, or a vertical with a counterpoise — wires spread just above the ground (FM 24-18, p. 144; 🖼️ wire counterpoise; 🖼️ ground-plane antenna). Set up high on a slope, not in a ravine, and away from your own generator and battery charger —

(FM 24-18, p. 144; 🖼️ wire counterpoise; 🖼️ ground-plane antenna). Set up high on a slope, not in a ravine, and away from your own generator and battery charger — they add noise (p. 102–103). Batteries: a car battery survives only about 20 deep discharges; deep-cycle batteries take 1,000 or more, and shallow use lasts far longer (about 800 cycles at 80% discharge vs 6,000 at 20%). Recharge stored sealed batteries about every 3 months. Charging batteries give off hydrogen — no sparks or flames (Practical Action, p. 5–6). Lightning: a lightning switch grounds the antenna whenever you're not using it — No. 14 or heavier copper wire to a water pipe or ground rod, never a gas pipe (NBS Circular 120, p. 8; Lightning arrester). 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-18, p. 55 — field repair and expedient antennas; NEETS Module 10 — how antennas work.

9. How to call for help (procedure) 1. Listen first. Make sure you're not interrupting other emergency traffic. 2. Use the emergency call: - Voice distress: say "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY" (life-threatening) or "PAN-PAN" (urgent but not immediately life-threatening), then your info (Mayday, Pan-pan). - On CB, call on Channel 9. On ham, break into the local emergency net or call on a repeater / 146.520 simplex. 3. Give the essentials — slowly, clearly, repeat: - Who you are (name / call sign). - Where you are (address, cross-streets, GPS coords, landmarks). - What the emergency is (injury, fire, trapped, etc.). - What you need (medical, rescue, relay a message). 4. Spell hard words with the phonetic alphabet (below). 5. Stay on, don't wander off frequency. Keep the radio on so responders can call back. Repeat your message at intervals if no answer.

NATO phonetic alphabet Alpha Bravo Charlie Delta Echo Foxtrot Golf Hotel India Juliet Kilo Lima Mike November Oscar Papa Quebec Romeo Sierra Tango Uniform Victor Whiskey X-ray Yankee Zulu. Numbers: say digits individually ("one-two-zero"). (NATO phonetic alphabet)

Common "pro-words" - "Over" = I'm done talking, your turn. - "Out" = conversation finished (don't say "over and out"). - "Roger" / "Copy" = I received and understand. - "Say again" = repeat (don't say "repeat"). - "Affirmative / Negative" = yes / no. - "Break" = pause / someone with emergency traffic wants in. (Procedure word) 📚 Go deeper: ARRL manual, p. 58 — procedure words, phonetic alphabet, signal reports; Pub 102, pp. 148–149 — the international voice distress procedure, with worked Mayday examples.

10. Passing messages for others Much of radio's work after a disaster is carrying short messages for people with no radio. Send in this order (ARRL manual, p. 36): EMERGENCY (life and death — when in doubt, don't) → PRIORITY (important, time-limited) → WELFARE ("Is my family OK?" / "All well here") → ROUTINE (last). - Write the message down first and count the words, so the receiver can check it (🖼️ a filled-in radiogram, part by part). - Ready-made welfare texts include "Everyone safe here. Please don't worry." (🖼️ blank welfare message form) - Log the time, station, frequency and message. 📚 Go deeper: ARRL manual, p. 33–34 — welfare form, standard texts, how to write a radiogram; ICS 213 General Message form — the standard paper form emergency offices use.

11. When the radio can't reach: signals without one - Three of anything means distress: three fires in a triangle, three columns of smoke, three shots (FM 21-76, p. 238–243). In wildfire country keep signal fires small, cleared around and watched (rule of thumb). - A whistle carries up to about a mile; a mirror is the best signal on a sunny day (🖼️ aiming a signal mirror). SOS: three short, three long, three short (SOS). - Ground-to-air symbols in a clearing: V = need help · X = need medical help · N = no · Y = yes · arrow = going this way. Make them at least 6 m (20 ft) long (the two Army manuals differ on width) (FM 3-05.70, p. 329; 🖼️ the symbols drawn). 📚 Go deeper: FM 3-05.70, p. 318 — signaling devices and how to use them; Signals and Morse guide — mirrors, ground symbols, Morse by light and sound; AFH 10-644, p. 509 — the Air Force signaling chapter, with pictures.

📡 Signals, Morse Code & Messages How to get a message across with no phones and no working radio: learning Morse by ear, sending it by lamp, whistle, flag or smoke, calling for help from the ground to an aircraft, mirrors and signal fires (and their danger in fire season), semaphore, alarm codes, runners, message forms, a neighborhood OK/HELP card plan, and what to listen to. The books are in Comms-Signals\Morse-Code, Comms-Signals\Visual-Sound-Signals and Comms-Signals\Messaging-Plans. Radios: the Radio guide and the Radio-Weather folder. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Three of anything means "help" — three fires, three blasts, three shots. Use threes for nothing else (FM 3-05.70, p. 318). - No signal fires or "tree torches" in fire season (roughly June–October). In our dry summers they can start a wildfire that kills the people signaling. Use a mirror, cloth panels, ground symbols and sound instead. - Learn only today's 5-symbol ground code: V = need help, X = need medical help (Pub 102, p. 144; 🖼️ the five symbols drawn). An old Army code in the library uses X for "unable to proceed". - Never hold a mirror flash on a pilot's cockpit for more than a few seconds — it can blind them (FM 3-05.70, p. 324). - Learn Morse from the International table only. The 1911 Scout handbook prints old American Morse, different for many

few seconds — it can blind them (FM 3-05.70, p. 324). - Learn Morse from the International table only. The 1911 Scout handbook prints old American Morse, different for many letters. - Agree every alarm signal in advance, and use the alarm bell or horn for nothing else (FM 24-5, p. 129).

👂 Learning Morse by ear Morse is sounds, not dots on paper. Think of each letter as a sound ("di-dah" is A), never count dots and dashes, and practice by whistling or saying the sounds aloud (TM 11-459, pp. 3–5). Two proven methods (Pierpont, pp. 159–161; pp. 171–172): - Koch method: start with two letters sent fast (12 words per minute or more). Add one new letter at a time, and only when you copy 90% correctly. Don't look at a chart. - Farnsworth method: each letter is always sent at full speed (18–25 wpm), with wide gaps between letters that you close up as you improve. - Both avoid the "10 wpm plateau" of learning slowly (p. 161). - Short sessions work best: Koch recommended two half-hour sessions a day, spread apart; even 45 minutes gave less (p. 160). A 30-day plan (rule of thumb, built on Koch's rules). A partner sends from the table below by whistle or flashlight while you write what you hear. If you fall behind, stretch the plan — accuracy matters more than the calendar. | Days | What to do (two half-hour sessions a day) | | 1–2 | Two letters that sound very different, such as K and M, in random mixes, until you get 9 in 10. | | 3–20 | Add one letter each time you reach 90% on a

very different, such as K and M, in random mixes, until you get 9 in 10. | | 3–20 | Add one letter each time you reach 90% on a 5-minute mix. A common Koch order: K M R S U A P T L O W I N J E F Y V G Q Z H B C D X (general practice). | | 21–25 | Numbers, then period, comma, question mark and slash. Keep mixing in all the letters. | | 26–28 | Procedure signals (AR, K, SK, BT, AS) and the calling routine below. Short real messages. | | 29–30 | Whole messages with your partner, by lamp and by whistle, across a field. | - Send each letter at full speed, even as a beginner — slow down only by leaving longer gaps between letters (TM 11-459, p. 4). - Look-alikes (S/H, U/V, and mirror pairs like B/V, D/U) cause most errors — give the ones you miss extra practice (Pierpont, p. 159). - Copy behind: at higher speeds, let a letter or two go by before writing (TM 11-459, p. 5). - After day 30, ten minutes a day keeps the skill (rule of thumb). 🔦 Morse without a radio: light, sound, flags and smoke - Light: flashlight, lantern or car headlights, with a hat or board as a shutter. Short flash = dot, longer flash = dash (Bluejackets, p. 442). Best at dusk and night. See Signal lamp; aiming a lamp's beam at a far station: 🖼️ FM 24-5 drawing. - Sound: whistle, horn or bugle (Whistle, Bugle) — short blast = dot, long blast = dash. On a drum, one tap = dot, two quick taps = dash. Sound works in fog and at night (Signal Book 1916, p. 34) but is slow and easily confused — keep to short, pre-agreed messages (Pub 102, p. 17). - Flags or arms: call with "AA AA AA" and end with AR (Pub 102, pp. 19–20). The Army rule: flag swung to your left for a dash, to your right for a dot (FM 3-05.70, p. 328). - Smoke: spread a blanket over a smoky fire and lift it off to send short and long puffs (Seton, p. 270). Not in fire season — see the fire section below. See Smoke signal. - Knocking through a wall: Morse, or the 5×5-grid tap code (general practice). | If this goes wrong | Try this (rule of thumb) | | Dots and dashes blur together | Very short dots, long dashes, clear gaps | | They keep missing

If this goes wrong | Try this (rule of thumb) | | Dots and dashes blur together | Very short dots, long dashes, clear gaps | | They keep missing words | Lengthen the gaps, not the letters; send each word twice | | Lamp can't be seen by day | Use a mirror or a flag | 📚 Go deeper: Pub 102, pp. 17–20 — sound, flag and arm signaling; Signal Book 1916, p. 34 — whistle and drum codes.

🆘 Distress signals and talking to aircraft - Threes: three fires, three columns of smoke, three shots or three whistle blasts mean distress, because nature rarely makes things in threes (FM 3-05.70, p. 318; AFH 10-644, p. 509). - SOS by light, sound or flag: three short, three long, three short, sent as one sound and repeated (FM 3-05.70, p. 328). - A flag flown upside down signals distress (Signal Book 1916, p. 41). Body signals to aircraft — stand in the open, move slowly and repeat until understood (FM 21-60, p. 59; 🖼️ the signals drawn): | Signal | Means | | Both arms straight up | "Pick us up" | | One arm up | "All OK, do not wait" — easy to confuse with the one above, so be deliberate | | Lying on your back, arms stretched overhead | "Need medical assistance" | | Arms waving, crossed overhead | "Do not land here" | | Cloth waved up and down / side to side | Yes / No | | Arms out to the sides, slowly raised and lowered again and again | Official distress signal (Pub 102, p. 140) | How a plane says "understood" (Pub 102, p. 144; AFH 10-644, p. 518): it rocks its wings by day, or flashes its landing or navigation lights twice at night (or flashes Morse T or R).

(Pub 102, p. 144; AFH 10-644, p. 518): it rocks its wings by day, or flashes its landing or navigation lights twice at night (or flashes Morse T or R). Not understood: it flies straight and level without rocking, or flashes RPT (🖼️ aircraft replies drawn; Search and rescue). 📚 Go deeper: FM 21-60, p. 59 — body signals drawn; Pub 102, p. 140 — official distress signals; Distress signal.

🪞 Signal mirrors The best daytime signal. A mirror flash has been seen up to 100 miles away and it works even on hazy or overcast days (AFH 10-644, p. 509). See Signal mirror. Aiming without a sighting hole (AFH 10-644, pp. 510–511): 1. Hold one arm out and make a V with two fingers, with the plane or distant hill in the V (🖼️ drawing; 🖼️ FM 3-05.70 drawing). 2. Tilt the mirror so the bright spot of light lands on your fingers, then work it through the V onto the target. 3. Or line the target up with the top of a 4–5 ft stake, and sight along the mirror's top edge onto the stake top (🖼️ drawing). 4. Keep sweeping the horizon even when nothing is in sight — a pilot may see you first. - No mirror? A can lid, polished metal, foil or a shiny card will do (p. 510). The military mirror with a sighting hole, for comparison: 🖼️ the MK-3 signal mirror. - Don't flash rapidly, and don't hold the beam on the cockpit for more than a few seconds — it can blind the pilot (FM 3-05.70, p. 324). - Talking with mirrors: the old Army heliograph flashed Morse by mirror between hilltops; two people on sunny ridges can do the same (general practice). 📚 Go deeper: AFH 10-644, pp. 509–511 —

mirrors: the old Army heliograph flashed Morse by mirror between hilltops; two people on sunny ridges can do the same (general practice). 📚 Go deeper: AFH 10-644, pp. 509–511 — mirror aiming with pictures; Signal Book 1916 — the heliograph and lantern.

🔥 Signal fires and smoke — and the wildfire danger What the manuals teach (AFH 10-644, pp. 511–512): - Three fires in a triangle or a line. AFH 10-644 says about 100 ft apart; FM 3-05.70 says 25 m (83 ft) (p. 318). Bright flames at night, lots of smoke by day. - Smoke works best on calm, clear days and has been seen up to 50 miles away. - White smoke (green leaves, moss, wet plants) shows against dark forest. Black smoke (rubber, oily rags, plastic) shows against snow or sky — stay upwind of it (general practice). - Lay the fires before aircraft come, ready to light in seconds. ⚠️ Illinois Valley: June to October, do NOT build signal fires. - Only about 15% of our yearly rain falls April to September, and summer afternoon humidity runs 25–30% (NRCS soil survey, p. 5). A tree torch or a spark can start a wildfire that kills the people signaling (Wildfire). - Clearing to bare earth under a tree torch, as the manuals say, is not enough in our brush and grass (AFH 10-644, p. 513; FM 3-05.70, p. 319). - A gasoline smoke pot can explode when lit (AFH 10-644, p. 514). Pen flares and tracer rounds start fires too (FM 3-05.70, p. 321). - In fire season use: mirror, cloth panels and ground symbols, a banner on a

10-644, p. 514). Pen flares and tracer rounds start fires too (FM 3-05.70, p. 321). - In fire season use: mirror, cloth panels and ground symbols, a banner on a pole, whistles and horns. - If you must burn (wet season, or truly no choice): a small fire on a cleared, wetted patch, with water, a shovel and a person watching it, put dead out afterward (general practice). 📚 Go deeper: AFH 10-644, pp. 511–514 — fire and smoke signals; Firewood guide — ashes and fire-season burning rules.

🚩 Flags, semaphore and signal stations Simple flag colors (FM 21-60, p. 37; 🖼️ Army flag signals drawn): red = danger; green = all clear / understood; yellow = disregard. At night use colored flashlights. Good for a gate or a lookout. Semaphore spells words with two flags (or bare arms) held at clock positions — by day and in sight only. Pictures: Bluejackets Manual, pp. 444–447 and Flag semaphore; full charts: 🖼️ Bluejackets alphabet, 🖼️ Signal Book 1916 hand-flag chart, 🖼️ FM 24-5 semaphore code. - Letters A to G use one arm stepping around a circle (Scout Handbook 1911, p. 234). - After the numeral sign, A–I mean 1–9 and K means 0. - Always face the receiving station. The receiver stops the sender by holding both arms straight out sideways (Signal Book 1916, pp. 22–23). Siting a flag or lamp station (Signal Book 1916, pp. 43–44): - Stand where the background behind you, as the other station sees it, is one plain color. Use a white flag against green or dark hillsides. - Record the compass bearing to each partner station and drive two aiming stakes in line with it (Compass). - How far you can see to a ground-level object: eye 10 ft up, about 4 miles; 30 ft, about 7; 100 ft, about 13. Ridges around the valley make good relay points (Horizon). 📚 Go

to a ground-level object: eye 10 ft up, about 4 miles; 30 ft, about 7; 100 ft, about 13. Ridges around the valley make good relay points (Horizon). 📚 Go deeper: Bluejackets, p. 444 — semaphore drawn; Signal Book 1916 — semaphore and station siting; FM 21-60 — arm-and-hand signals.

📣 Whistles, bells and alarm codes - Range: most whistle or shout contacts happen within 200 yards, a few at about a mile. A pole banged on a hollow log also carries (AFH 10-644, p. 509). - Rapid strokes of a bell, horn or whistle = "general alarm — act now", no answer needed (Signal Book 1916, p. 38). - Every alarm must be agreed in advance, known to everyone, and used only with good cause (same page). A bell, siren or air horn kept for alarms is never used for anything else (FM 24-5, p. 129; Air horn, Siren)). Visual signals get misunderstood — standardize and practice them (FM 21-60, p. 5). - The 1911 Scout whistle code is a good start: one long blast = "attention, look out for my next signal"; two short = "all right"; a string of short, sharp blasts = "rally, danger, alarm" (Scout Handbook 1911, p. 236). 🏃 Runners, relays and written messages Briefing a runner (FM 24-5 (1939), pp. 68, 70) — tell them: - who the message is for and where to find them; - which route, and which danger spots to avoid; - how fast to go, and whether to wait for a reply; - where to report back, and what to do if it can't be delivered. Spoken messages must be short. The runner repeats it back to you and memorizes it (p. 70). Write it down whenever you can. Speeds and relays (FM 24-5, pp. 69, 71–72): a runner covers about 3 mph routine and 5 mph urgent; a rider 6 and 8 mph. On dangerous routes send two runners in sight of each other, each with a copy, or use two routes. Mark routes with arrows at forks. For long, frequent runs, set up relay posts — say, a house halfway to O'Brien (rule of thumb). Use a standard form. The ICS 213 has To, From, Subject, Date, Time (24-hour clock), Message, Approved by, Reply and Replied by. The sender keeps a copy; the reply comes back on the bottom (ICS Forms Booklet, pp. 65–66; 🖼️ the blank form; Incident Command System). Log every message and event with date and time on an ICS 214 activity log (p. 68). The ham "radiogram" works on paper too (ARRL manual, p. 34): number

System). Log every message and event with date and time on an ICS 214 activity log (p. 68). The ham "radiogram" works on paper too (ARRL manual, p. 34): number and precedence, address, text of 25 words or fewer (X for a period), and signature. The "check" is the word count, so the receiver knows nothing was lost (🖼️ a filled-in example, part by part). Precedence (ARRL, p. 36): EMERGENCY (life or death — when in doubt, don't) → PRIORITY → WELFARE → ROUTINE. Short codes save time: - "ARL ONE" = "Everyone safe here. Please don't worry." "ARL TWO" = "Coming home as soon as possible." (ARRL, p. 39). - One-letter signals you can flash or sound: V = I need assistance; W = I need medical assistance; K = I wish to communicate; N = no; C = yes (Pub 102, p. 26). Note: at sea W means medical help; on the ground the symbol is X. See International Code of Signals; the same letters as ship flags: International maritime signal flags. 📚 Go deeper: FM 24-5 (1939) — messengers, relay posts and a message center; ICS Forms Booklet — print blank 213 and 214 forms now; ARRL manual, pp. 33–39 — radiogram form and numbered texts.

🏘️ The neighborhood OK/HELP plan From the rural edition of Map Your Neighborhood (MYN Rural, pp. 1–2): 1. Pick a Neighborhood Communication Site everyone knows: a mailbox cluster, a crossroads, or a central home or barn. 2. After a disaster, each household takes its OK/HELP card there with name, date and time, plus the kind of help needed, and tapes it up. 3. Anyone who can help writes on the card what they'll do and when, then reports back. 4. Someone checks every home. Who to check first (MYN Discussion Guide, p. 8): HELP homes, then homes with no card — people there may be hurt. Then recheck the OK homes. Print the HELP/OK window card now (🖼️ what it looks like). Your household plan: a meeting place, a way to find each other if separated, and an out-of-area contact, posted at home (Oregon 2 Weeks Ready, p. 6; FEMA, p. 18). Add the neighborhood site, your signal card and a check-in time (rule of thumb). Locally: the county plan counts on door-to-door notice, broadcast stations and amateur radio, and the RVCOG Disaster Registry lists residents needing special help (County EOP, p. 71). Know who they are on your road. 📚 Go deeper: MYN Discussion Guide — the first meeting, 9 steps after a disaster, neighbor map; MYN Rural — rural sites, wells and propane.

📻 Listening when you can't transmit - NOAA Weather Radio repeats its message every 4–6 minutes; a SAME radio wakes up only for your county (NOAA brochure, p. 2; NOAA Weather Radio; Specific Area Message Encoding; Emergency Alert System). For Josephine County program SAME 041033 and try WXL85, 162.400 MHz (Medford). It officially covers eastern Josephine County, and mountain valleys may get poor reception — also try 162.475 and 162.550 and note which works at home (NOAA brochure, p. 3; Illinois Valley guide). - AM reaches farther at night: the layer of the sky that soaks up AM signals by day fades after dark (Navy Basic Electronics, p. 328; 🖼️ layers of the ionosphere; Skywave). Listen for outside news after sunset. - Keep every battery radio in the shelter. Small AM sets with built-in antennas are the most likely to survive an EMP (Nuclear War Survival Skills, p. 35). - Log what you hear (time, station, message) and post news at the Neighborhood Communication Site, so one radio serves the whole road (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: NOAA Weather Radio brochure — how SAME alerts work; Radio guide — shortwave, crystal sets and local frequencies.

🧭 Navigation & Weather Without GPS or Forecasts How to find your way in the hills around the Illinois Valley with a paper map and compass — or with neither — and how to read the weather coming when there is no forecast: map reading, declination, pace count, terrain association, finding yourself when lost, the sun and stars, clouds and wind, our local weather from valley fog to east-wind fire days, lightning, and a home weather log. The books are in Navigation-Weather\Land-Navigation and Navigation-Weather\Weather; the local topo maps are in Maps\Topo-USGS and Maps\Forest-Service (see the Maps section of the Illinois Valley guide). ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Set your compass to 14° East. Older maps print bigger numbers; always use the newest. Ignoring declination puts you about a quarter mile off for every mile you walk. - Leave a written trip plan with someone who stays home. With no search and rescue, nobody comes unless someone knows your route and your return time (NPS Trip Plan). - When you hear thunder, move: off peaks and ridges, away from taller trees, and out of rock overhangs and cave mouths. Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder (Backcountry Lightning, pp. 1–2). - Never cross fast water. Six inches can knock you off your feet; two feet carries away most vehicles (Spotter Guide, p. 12). - A dry east

Lightning, pp. 1–2). - Never cross fast water. Six inches can knock you off your feet; two feet carries away most vehicles (Spotter Guide, p. 12). - A dry east wind after a front in late summer or fall is extreme fire weather — the pattern behind the September 2020 fires. Be ready to leave. - Sun, watch, moon and moss methods are rough. Check any no-compass direction with a second method before you commit to a long walk.

🗺️ Reading a topo map Scale. The library's local quads (US Topo and FSTopo) are 1:24,000: 1 inch = 2,000 ft (🖼️ using the bar scale; Topographic map). On the 1:100,000 Forest Service sheet, 1 inch is about 1.6 miles. Map distance is "as the crow flies"; walking a steep slope is farther (USGS FS 035-01, p. 1; PMS 475, p. 133). Contour lines (FS 035-01, p. 1; PMS 475, pp. 41–42; Contour line; 🖼️ a contour map beside the land it shows; 🖼️ FM 3-25.26, p. 107): - Brown lines join points of equal height; the heavier, labeled ones are index contours. - Close together = steep. Far apart = gentle. Circles inside circles = a hilltop. - V-shaped bends point uphill and upstream — creeks and draws. - U-shaped bends point down a ridge — spurs and ridge ends. Name the land. Learn to spot these on the map and on the ground — it is the heart of navigating without GPS (FM 3-25.26, pp. 115–118): | Feature | On the map | On the ground | | Hill (🖼️ drawing) | Closed rings | Ground falls away on all sides | | Saddle) (🖼️ drawing) | Hourglass between two hills | Low dip between two high points | | Valley (🖼️ drawing) | V or U contours with a stream | Low ground between ridges | |

between two hills | Low dip between two high points | | Valley (🖼️ drawing) | V or U contours with a stream | Low ground between ridges | | Ridge (🖼️ drawing) | Long line of high ground | Ground falls away on three sides | | Depression (🖼️ drawing) | Ring with tick marks inside | A hollow | | Draw (🖼️ drawing) | Small V pointing uphill | Small gully | | Spur) (🖼️ drawing) | Small U pointing downhill | Finger of high ground off a ridge | | Cliff (🖼️ drawing) | Contours touching or merged | Near-vertical drop | Symbols: US Topo Map Symbols (2023) matches the library's GeoPDF maps; the older USGS symbol booklet matches older quads and FSTopo. Grid position. The valley is in UTM Zone 10 ("10T" on the quads). Grid lines are every 1,000 m. Read right first (easting), then up (northing) (USGS FS 077-01, pp. 1–2; 🖼️ grid lines; 🖼️ reading a UTM coordinate; UTM). 📚 Go deeper: FM 3-25.26 — the Army's full map-reading course; PMS 475 — firefighter workbook with exercises; FSTopo Cave Junction — practice on your home sheet.

🧭 Compass and declination Use 14° East for the Illinois Valley. NOAA's model gives 13.9° E for Cave Junction in November 2026, shrinking about 0.1° a year. The FSTopo Cave Junction sheet prints 14°8′ (2024) and the US Topo sheet 14°18′ (2023). Older maps print larger numbers — use the newest value. See Magnetic declination. Which way to correct (FS 035-01, p. 2; PMS 475, p. 86): - Here the magnetic north (MN) arrow sits to the right (east) of true north (🖼️ north arrow on a quad; 🖼️ declination diagrams). - Map → compass: subtract 14°. A map bearing of 90° becomes 76° on an unadjusted compass. - Compass → map: add 14°. - Memory aid: "declination east, compass least." - Easiest: set the compass's declination screw to 14° E once and forget it. Why it matters: 1° of error puts you about 920 ft off in 10 miles (PMS 475, p. 86). Ignoring all 14° puts you about 1,300 ft off for every mile (general practice: worked out from the angle). Grid north on the Cave Junction quad is only about half a degree from true north — ignore it on foot. That's why the margin shows three norths (FM 3-25.26, p. 62; 🖼️ three norths). The way back (back azimuth): add 180° if the bearing is 180° or less; subtract 180° if more. A slip here can

norths (FM 3-25.26, p. 62; 🖼️ three norths). The way back (back azimuth): add 180° if the bearing is 180° or less; subtract 180° if more. A slip here can be disastrous — check it twice (FM 3-25.26, p. 58; 🖼️ direct and back bearing). Compass habits (PMS 475, p. 84; FM 3-25.26, p. 97; 🖼️ parts of a compass): - Hold it level at waist height (🖼️ centerhold), take every bearing twice, and walk where the direction-of-travel arrow points, not where your hunch says (🖼️ following a bearing). - Keep away from metal: 55 m (180 ft) from high-voltage lines, 18 m (60 ft) from a truck, 10 m (33 ft) from barbed wire or phone lines, half a meter from a rifle. Belt buckles and clipboards throw it off too. 📚 Go deeper: USGS Finding Your Way — taking a bearing off a topo map; PMS 475, pp. 82–86 — parts of a compass and setting declination.

👣 Pace count: measuring distance on foot (FM 3-25.26, pp. 52–53; PMS 475, pp. 133–134) 1. Measure a 100 m (328 ft) course on ground like where you'll travel — a road shoulder with a tape or a measured fence line works (rule of thumb). 2. Walk it naturally and count your steps. The Army's example is about 120 steps per 100 m. Walk it several times and average. 3. Expect more steps (🖼️ why the ground is longer than the map) uphill, into a headwind, in mud, sand, snow or brush, in rain, and in fog or darkness. 4. Keep a separate, shorter night count (p. 141). 5. Don't try to remember the count. Move a pebble from one pocket to the other, or tie a knot, every 100 m (pace count beads). ⚠️ The Forest Service (NWCG) counts a "pace" as two steps — every time the same foot lands. The Army counts every step. Pick one and never mix them. 📚 Go deeper: PMS 475, p. 133 — pacing worksheet; FM 3-25.26, p. 52 — pace count and other ways to measure distance.

🏞️ Terrain association: handrails, catching features, aiming off Match the map to the ground as you go (🖼️ drawing). It is far more forgiving than walking a compass line, because you keep comparing what you expected to see with what you do see. Pure compass walking piles up errors with every detour (FM 3-25.26, pp. 131, 139). Keep the map turned so its north matches the land (p. 140; 🖼️ by the land; 🖼️ by compass). Plan a route this way (FM 3-25.26, p. 140): - Handrail: a line you follow without careful compass work — a road, stream, ridge or power line. Ours include Hwy 199, the Illinois River and its East and West Forks, the Caves Highway (OR 46), and numbered Forest Service roads on the FSTopo sheets (local: rule of thumb). - Catching feature: something across your path that tells you you've gone too far. - Attack point: a sure landmark no more than about 500 m from the goal. From there, walk an exact bearing and pace count. Aim off on purpose (FM 3-25.26, p. 100; 🖼️ deliberate offset). Heading for a spot on a road or creek, aim about 10° to one side. When you hit the road, you know which way to turn. Each degree moves you about 18 m sideways per 1,000 m walked, so 10° is about 180 m. 📚 Go deeper:

hit the road, you know which way to turn. Each degree moves you about 18 m sideways per 1,000 m walked, so 10° is about 180 m. 📚 Go deeper: FM 3-25.26, ch. 11 — terrain association in depth; MVUM Wild Rivers — which forest roads are real roads.

📍 Finding yourself on the map (resection) Resection (FM 3-25.26, p. 68; Position resection; 🖼️ drawing; 🖼️ PMS 475, p. 131): 1. Orient the map. 2. Take compass bearings to two or three landmarks you can name on the map. 3. Turn each into a map bearing (add 14°, unless your compass is already set), then into its back azimuth (±180°). 4. Draw each line back from its landmark. Where they cross is you. Three lines make a small triangle — you are inside it. Local candidates are peaks on the FSTopo sheets such as Grayback Mountain, Kerby Peak and Eight Dollar Mountain — check on the sheet which you can really see from where you stand (rule of thumb). Modified resection (p. 70; 🖼️ drawing): if you know you're on a road, river or ridgeline, one bearing to one landmark is enough. You are where that line crosses your road or ridge. 📚 Go deeper: FM 3-25.26, pp. 68–70 — intersection, resection and modified resection with drawings; PMS 475, p. 131 — finding your own position by triangulation; AFH 10-644, p. 406 — azimuth, biangulation and triangulation.

🆘 Getting un-lost STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan (Today's Hunter, p. 80): 1. Stop. Admit you're turned around. Sit down. 2. Think. Retrace your route in your head: the last place you were sure of, and what you've passed since. 3. Observe. Look for the five terrain features, a peak you can name, the sound of a road or the river. Try a resection. 4. Plan. Pick the nearest big handrail on the map (a road or river) and walk a bearing to it, aiming off so you know which way to turn when you reach it. - If you can't get back before dark, stop early and spend the effort on shelter, warmth and a signal (p. 80; Signals guide). - Staying put only works if someone will come. That page assumes searchers in "a few days." Now it works only if someone at home has your trip plan. - Never shelter under a rock overhang in a thunderstorm — lightning arcs across the gap. Trip plan before every trip into the hills (NPS Trip Plan, pp. 1–2): who is going, the route, start and return times, a backup plan, the vehicle and the gear. Leave it with someone who isn't going, check in when you're back, and agree that they act at the deadline. 📚 Go deeper: NPS Trip Plan form — print a stack; Today's Hunter, pp.

who isn't going, check in when you're back, and agree that they act at the deadline. 📚 Go deeper: NPS Trip Plan form — print a stack; Today's Hunter, pp. 80–84 — shelter, fire, signals, cold and heat.

☁️ Reading the sky: clouds, wind and barometer Clouds that warn (AH 360, pp. 163–164; Cloudwise poster; Sky Watcher chart; List of cloud types): | You see | It often means | | High, thin wisps (cirrus, 🖼️ photo) thickening to a milky veil (cirrostratus, 🖼️ photo) | A warm front and rain coming; from the southwest in spring/summer, often 24–48 hours ahead at Roseburg (Garriott, p. 137) | | Rows of small, high puffs (cirrocumulus, 🖼️ photo) from the south or southwest in fall/winter | Rain in 12–24 hours (same page) | | Turreted, castle-top clouds (castellanus) in the morning | Thunderstorms that afternoon | | Smooth, lens-shaped clouds over the ridges (lenticular, 🖼️ photo) | Strong winds aloft | | Towering cumulus growing into an anvil (cumulonimbus, 🖼️ photo) | Thunderstorm, lightning, a gusty "gust front" that can arrive before the rain (AC 00-6B, pp. 167–168) | | Low gray layer with steady rain (nimbostratus, 🖼️ photo) | Steady rain or snow | Rain falls mainly from cumulus, cumulonimbus and nimbostratus. A thunderstorm cell lives about 30 minutes (🖼️ life cycle), but its gust front can set off new ones (AC 00-6B, pp. 167–168). Wind signs: - Roseburg (nearest station in the 1903 Weather Bureau study): in spring and summer, rain follows southwest winds and a falling barometer by 12–24 hours; in winter, southerly winds by about 12

(nearest station in the 1903 Weather Bureau study): in spring and summer, rain follows southwest winds and a falling barometer by 12–24 hours; in winter, southerly winds by about 12 hours (Garriott, p. 137). - Portland, Oregon: wind turning from northwest through northeast to southeast means rain; a shift to northwest means clearing (p. 131). - Cold front (🖼️ cold and warm fronts): wind from the south or southwest before it, then an abrupt shift to west, northwest or north (AH 360, p. 101). - Back to the wind, low pressure is on your left and a little ahead (AH 360, p. 84). - ⚠️ Valley winds are bent by the hills. Judge by cloud movement or ridgetop wind. Barometer: watch the trend, not the number. A drop of more than about 0.06 inch in 3 hours means change is coming; about 0.18 inch or more in 3 hours means a strong storm (general practice). The old Roseburg rule "rain after the barometer falls to 29.90" uses sea-level readings; at our ~1,300 ft an unadjusted barometer reads about 1.3–1.4 inches lower (general practice). Sayings that hold up (somewhat): "Evening red and morning gray…" (Red sky at morning; 🖼️ photo) has a basis, because weather mostly moves west to east (Garriott, p. 18). Hard, greasy, ragged clouds mean wind (Shifts and Expedients, p. 183). Forecasts weeks ahead from the moon, almanacs

a basis, because weather mostly moves west to east (Garriott, p. 18). Hard, greasy, ragged clouds mean wind (Shifts and Expedients, p. 183). Forecasts weeks ahead from the moon, almanacs or animals "can not stand the test of verification" (Garriott, p. 35). 📚 Go deeper: Garriott 1903 — station-by-station signs for Roseburg, Portland and Eureka; Sky Watcher chart — photos of 27 cloud types; AH 360 — clouds, fronts and mountain winds.

🌦️ Illinois Valley weather through the year The baseline (NRCS soil survey, p. 5): winter averages 40°F at Cave Junction (record low −6°F, December 1972), with about 24 inches of snow a season; summer averages 67°F, and Grants Pass has hit 108°F. Only about 15% of the rain falls April to September, and summer afternoon humidity runs 25–30%. It cools 3–5°F for every 1,000 ft you climb, and above about 4,500 ft it can freeze in any month. Most winters bring one or two damaging windstorms; every few years a continental air mass from the east brings days well below freezing in winter, or a sweltering week in summer. Valley fog and inversions (AH 360, p. 35; AC 00-6B, p. 146; EPA Smoke Guide, p. 26; Inversion)): - On clear, calm nights cold air drains off the slopes (🖼️ drawing) and pools on the valley floor, deepening until about midnight. Fog forms if the air is moist (🖼️ radiation fog). - Fog is common the morning after rain then clearing, and usually burns off by noon unless cloud moves in above it. - In winter an inversion can trap fog and woodstove smoke for days (🖼️ smoke under an inversion). Burn hot and dry (Firewood guide). Frost (Garriott, p. 137; AH 360, p. 35): heavy frost follows a high or rising barometer, evening temperature at 40°F or below, clearing sky

Burn hot and dry (Firewood guide). Frost (Garriott, p. 137; AH 360, p. 35): heavy frost follows a high or rising barometer, evening temperature at 40°F or below, clearing sky and light wind. Frost hits low spots first. The mid-slope "thermal belt" stays warmest at night — the best spot for tender crops, and also where wildfires stay active all night. Winter storms off the Pacific (NRCS, p. 5; Spotter Guide, p. 12): warm storms carrying a long plume of subtropical moisture (an atmospheric river) bring several inches of rain a day, high snow levels and fast-rising rivers (general practice). Cave Junction got 8.12 inches in one day on 22 December 1964. Stay off low crossings and out of creeks when they rise. Summer thunderstorms are most frequent over the mountains (NRCS, p. 5). In fire season, watch the ridges for smoke for a day or two after lightning (rule of thumb). Heat: in a hot spell, take regular breaks in shade and drink often; do heavy work in the cool morning (rule of thumb). Heat exhaustion — heavy sweat, pale clammy skin, dizziness, nausea — means shade, rest, water and cool wet cloths. Confusion or collapse is heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency — cool them fast (ATP 4-02.11, pp. 188–189; Field care guide). East wind = fire weather (AH 360, p. 211; NWS Medford, pp. 14–15; Foehn wind): in

a life-threatening emergency — cool them fast (ATP 4-02.11, pp. 188–189; Field care guide). East wind = fire weather (AH 360, p. 211; NWS Medford, pp. 14–15; Foehn wind): in late summer and fall, after a cold front, high pressure inland can send strong, dry north-to-east winds downslope, warming and drying as they come. On 7–9 September 2020, Medford's humidity fell to about 7% and Slater Butte (4,600 ft, near where the Slater Fire started south of Takilma and O'Brien) recorded gusts of 55–60 mph. Warning signs: very clear air, warm dry nights, and east wind on the ridges after a front. Pack the car and watch for smoke. Another nearby east-wind fire: the Chetco Bar Fire. Smoke: inversions hold smoke in the valley at night. With no air-quality reports, judge smoke by how far you can see (EPA Smoke Guide, pp. 95–96) — in daylight, not at sunrise or sunset, only when humidity is under 65%, looking at dark landmarks at known distances: | Farthest dark landmark you can see | Healthy adults | Children, elders, pregnant, heart or lung disease | | More than 10 miles | Watch for changes | Watch; shorten activity if you feel it | | 5–10 miles | Shorten and ease outdoor work | Minimize or avoid outdoor activity | | Under 5 miles | Minimize or avoid outdoor activity | Stay indoors

⚡ Lightning safety (Backcountry Lightning, pp. 1–2; NWS Lightning brochure, p. 2; Spotter Guide, p. 13) - If you can hear thunder, lightning is within about 10 miles. Start moving to shelter then. - Flash to bang: count the seconds and divide by 5 for miles. Don't stake your life on it. - Stay sheltered 30 minutes after the last thunder. People are struck going out too soon. - Ground current is the big danger, not a direct strike: about half of casualties come from current spreading through the ground; direct strikes cause only 3–5% of deaths. - Caught outside: get off peaks and ridges, away from taller trees, out of overhangs and cave mouths (🖼️ safer and riskier terrain). Spread a group 20 ft apart, so one strike can't hurt everyone. Crouch with feet together (🖼️ the lightning position). - A struck person carries no charge. Start CPR or rescue breathing right away (Field care guide). - The US averages about 300 people struck and about 30 killed a year. - At home: unplug radios and ground antennas (Radio guide). 📚 Go deeper: Backcountry Lightning — picking terrain, group spacing, the lightning position; NWS brochure — family rules and first aid.

🤝 Community, Barter & Keeping Watch How neighbors look after each other when no government, police or stores are coming: forming a neighborhood group, running meetings and making fair decisions, knowing who has what skills and tools, sharing work, trading fairly and keeping records, keeping watch, calming angry people, settling disputes and theft without violence, and looking after people's minds through grief and long hard months. The books are in Southern-Oregon\Community-Barter\ (Organizing-Neighbors, Barter-Trade, Watch-Conflict, Wellbeing); the Map Your Neighborhood plan and its OK/HELP card are in Southern-Oregon\Comms-Signals\Messaging-Plans. ### ⚠️ Rules that keep a group safe, fair and together - Rescuer safety comes first, and nobody goes alone — always teams of at least two. In the 1985 Mexico City earthquake untrained volunteers saved 700 lives, but about 100 of them died (CERT manual, pp. 2, 58). - Watchers watch and report. They don't confront, chase or carry weapons on patrol (Neighborhood Watch Manual, p. 20). - No punishment by force. Physical force is "never recommended" except to stop an injury (De-escalation slides, p. 4). Beatings and armed posses are crimes and start feuds that outlast the emergency (rule of thumb). - Help is voluntary. Pool work by agreement — never force people to work (a 1918 booklet on the drive says otherwise; see Old advice at the end). - Never announce who is away or what the group has stored

force people to work (a 1918 booklet on the drive says otherwise; see Old advice at the end). - Never announce who is away or what the group has stored (Watch Manual, p. 21). - Write it down — trades, stores and incidents (Braun, p. 19; De-escalation, p. 23).

🏘️ Forming a neighborhood group Keep it small. Map Your Neighborhood (MYN) uses 15–25 homes, ideally ones within sight of each other — any more can't all be checked in the "golden 60 minutes" after a disaster. In the country, include as many homes as you can check in an hour or two (MYN, pp. 3, 19). Invite people in person (a flyer on the porch doesn't bring them out), ask one or two neighbors to help, and meet in someone's home — attendance drops at a school or church (p. 19). The 9 steps after a disaster (MYN, pp. 14–16; rural changes from MYN Rural, p. 3): | Step | At home first (1–6), then together (7–9) | | 1 | Care for your own family. | | 2 | Protect head, hands and feet: hard hat or bike helmet, sturdy shoes, leather gloves — kept under the bed (p. 6). | | 3 | Smell or hear gas? Shut off the propane (MYN, p. 22; Propane). Propane is heavier than air and settles in low spots. | | 4 | Shut the house water valve (🖼️ what it may look like).
