🗳️ Meetings and fair decisions Small group: "friendly, serious, courteous discussion is preferable to formal parliamentary procedure" (Braun 1933, p. 13). A bigger meeting (Robert's Rules, 1915, pp. 281–282, 291): - The organizers agree beforehand on the place, time, who calls the meeting to order and who will be nominated chair. - Elect the chair by majority voice vote, then a secretary to keep minutes. Simple rules of order (Robert's Rules, pp. 32, 286): 1. A member proposes something ("I move that…"). 2. Someone else seconds it — otherwise it isn't discussed. 3. The chair repeats it so everyone knows exactly what's being decided. 4. Discussion. One speaker at a time; everyone who wants to speak gets a turn before anyone speaks twice (rule of thumb). 5. The chair asks "Are you ready for the question?" and takes the vote. 6. The secretary writes down the decision. Before founding anything permanent, make sure a majority agrees with the plan — groups that skipped this "have found themselves in the minority" (p. 290). Choosing what to do first: list the problems and rank them, then rank again asking "Which can we do with our own resources?" and "Which will benefit the most people?" (Peace Corps PACA, p. 116). Robert's Rules of Order. 📚 Go deeper: Robert's Rules of Order (1915) — Part II: calling a mass meeting and founding a society;

🤲 Sharing the work - Give everyone a job. People are less frightened when they have responsible jobs. Set a daily routine, post the assignments, and rotate the unpleasant tasks (FEMA HS-4, p. 97). A useful job (sorting supplies) also calms a disruptive person (CERT, p. 152). - Pool teams and machines. Three small farms that work together can each finish haying in two or three days instead of the whole season, then help the big farm (USDA Circular 112, p. 7). Barn raising. - A labor committee lists everyone with farm (or other) experience who volunteers, and sends them where they're needed at rush times (p. 9). - People new to hard work should do light work, a few hours a day, for the first days (p. 10). - Credit the hours in the group's points ledger (next section), so work counts as much as goods. 📚 Go deeper: USDA The Farm Labor Problem (1918) — pooling crews for planting and haying (use its methods, not its 1918 coercion); FEMA HS-4 — daily routine and duty rosters in a shelter.

🔄 Barter and fair trade What trades well (Barter): a good that many people need, that lasts, is cheap to store, divides into small amounts and is easy to carry (Menger 1892, pp. 30–31). Such goods naturally become money (p. 36; Commodity money). Plain barter fails when A wants what B has, B wants what C has, and C wants what A has (p. 21). Coincidence of wants. - Likely trade goods here: salt, sugar, coffee, soap, matches and lighters, seeds, canning lids, batteries, fuel, firewood — and skills: sewing, repair, medical care (general practice). - Don't trade prescription drugs casually (general practice) — fakes and wrong doses kill (see the Medical guide). Setting up a barter group (Braun 1933, pp. 13–15): a few people first survey what the community needs and has to trade; present it at a meeting; elect a steering committee; choose a trading place; write a membership agreement. Start small, "with people you know." Members meet weekly on practical trading business only — don't leave everything to one manager. The trader should be trustworthy, "a natural trader but not a sharp, hard bargain driver," and should arrange three-way trades: A has potatoes and wants oranges, B has oranges and wants beans, C has beans and wants potatoes (p. 15). Fair exchange — the points ledger (p. 19): - 1 hour of work = 100 points; an

has oranges and wants beans, C has beans and wants potatoes (p. 15). Fair exchange — the points ledger (p. 19): - 1 hour of work = 100 points; an 8-hour day = 800. Value goods in work: a cord) of wood = one day's work = 800 points (🖼️ what a cord looks like). - Record every credit and debit in the member's passbook and in a central book, and balance them regularly like a bank account. Rules that kept barter groups healthy (pp. 17, 21): put off paper scrip as long as possible; refuse junk; admit new members fully only after they show they cooperate; and nobody can take more from the group than they put in. Shared credit and local notes (Cleveland Fed, pp. 1–3): Ithaca Hours were pegged to one hour of local labor. Avoiding disputes (rule of thumb): agree on amount (scales) and quality before anything changes hands; have a witness for big trades; enter it in both books the same day; bring complaints to the weekly meeting, not to the street. 📚 Go deeper: Braun Barter Associations in California (1933) — a whole Depression-era barter group in question-and-answer form; Cleveland Fed Private Money — labor-hour notes and LETS in four pages; Menger On the Origins of Money — why some goods become money.

👀 Keeping watch Structure (Watch Manual, pp. 10–11): - One block captain per 10–15 houses. - A phone tree: call the next person, skip down if they're out, and the last person calls the captain to confirm. With phones down it becomes a runner chain (general practice). Practice it, and use it to stop rumors you've checked. - Daily check-in: OK/HELP cards at the communication site (MYN Rural, p. 2), or the radio check-ins on the Illinois Valley page. Patrol rules (p. 20): watch members "do not possess police powers and they shall not carry weapons or pursue." They "should never confront suspicious persons." Carry flashlights and radios that report to a staffed base. Walk in pairs, observe, report — don't intervene (general practice). Describing what you saw (p. 24): note what can't be changed — height, build, skin and eye color, scars, tattoos. Clothes can change. Write it down at once, even on your hand. Never hesitate to say "I'm not sure." Night watch: keep watch-standers on a consistent schedule rather than switching shifts, and protect their daytime sleep — sentry duty is among the jobs most damaged by sleepiness (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 154). Use 2-hour shifts in pairs with a fixed handover, and in fire season watch for smoke and glow too (general practice). | Shift (example) | Post | Pair | Handover | | 8–10 pm

🗣️ Calming an angry person From the Kentucky de-escalation slides (pp. 15–24): - Distance: slightly more than a leg's length, at an angle and off to the side (p. 17) — far enough that you can't be hit or kicked. Hands visible. Never touch a hostile person (p. 15). No face-to-face, toe-to-toe or finger-pointing (p. 16). - Voice: slow and calm (p. 19). Listen — really listen (p. 21). - Move onlookers away — they become "cheerleaders" or victims. Send one for help. Two calm people with one angry person lowers the chance of violence (same page). - Never say "I know how you feel," get into power struggles, raise your voice, threaten, or give ultimatums (p. 24). - Afterwards, write down every threatening incident (p. 23). 📚 Go deeper: Using Verbal De-Escalation — 25 plain slides on stance, voice and what not to say; CERT, p. 152 — giving a disruptive person a useful job; Conflict Resolution Education Guide, p. 31 — rules for fighting fair.

⚖️ Settling disputes and dealing with theft Where conflict comes from: limited resources, unmet needs, or different values. Values don't have to change — first admit each side sees it differently (Conflict Resolution Guide, pp. 22–23). Giving in ("soft") or threats ("hard") don't last; only "principled" responses tend to make agreements that hold (pp. 23–24). Four principles: separate the people from the problem; focus on interests, not positions; invent options that help both; use fair, outside standards. Six steps: set the stage, hear each side, find the interests, list options, judge the options, agree (pp. 24, 26). Fight fair: attack the problem, not the person; no put-downs; don't drag up the past (p. 31). Mediation (FAO, p. 27): a mediator helps both sides design their own solution; an arbitrator decides for them. To find interests, keep asking "Why is this important for you?" (p. 128). Turn insults into problems: "You are selfish, the whole community suffers" becomes "consider a solution that meets your family's interests and the community's" (p. 129). Water, firewood and fence-line disputes fit this well (general practice). Mediation. Protecting shared stores (general practice): don't advertise what you have; keep common stores in locked, rodent-proof containers with a written in-and-out log; two people to open them; rotate who guards and who counts. When something goes missing — a fair process (rule of thumb): 1. Write down the facts

written in-and-out log; two people to open them; rotate who guards and who counts. When something goes missing — a fair process (rule of thumb): 1. Write down the facts — what, when, who saw what. Not guesses or rumors. 2. Two calm people talk to the person privately. Listen first. 3. If it's still disputed, use a mediator; if both sides agree to it, three neutral members decide (arbitration). 4. Repair the harm: return it, replace it, or work it off in ledger points. 5. Repeated or serious harm: the group can vote, under its written agreement, to remove someone from the barter group or shared stores. Report crimes to the sheriff while there is one. 6. Never beatings, public humiliation, locking people up, or taking a family's own food. Remember that hungry people steal — fair food sharing prevents a lot of theft (see the Food Security guide). 📚 Go deeper: Conflict Resolution Education Guide — principled negotiation and mediation in plain English; FAO Negotiation and Mediation Techniques — disputes over land, water and wood.

💛 Grief, stress and psychological first aid Look, listen, link (WHO Psychological First Aid, p. 25): look for safety, urgent needs and people in severe distress; listen and help them feel calm; link them to practical help, information and loved ones. - Don't pressure anyone to tell their story. Sit quietly, offer water, allow silence (p. 21). - Don't say "You should feel lucky you survived," don't make false promises, and don't take away their sense of being able to care for themselves (p. 22). - Someone who seems unreal or far away: feet on the floor, tap their hands on their lap, have them name what they see and hear, breathe slowly (p. 30). - Most people recover once basic needs are met and others support them. Don't leave a severely distressed person alone (p. 27). - Don't label normal reactions as disorders (PFA Field Guide, p. 12). Accept emotional injury as being as real as a sprained ankle (FM 4-25.11, p. 174). To the grieving, never say "It could be worse," "Everything happens for the best," or to a child, "You're the man of the house now" (PFA Field Guide, p. 41). Look after the helpers (🖼️ self-care toolkit): work in pairs (WHO, p. 50); watch for helpers taking on survivors' feelings and burning out — time away helps (CERT, p. 144); sleep, exercise, eat, and balance work,

toolkit): work in pairs (WHO, p. 50); watch for helpers taking on survivors' feelings and burning out — time away helps (CERT, p. 144); sleep, exercise, eat, and balance work, play and rest (p. 146). Over months: expect a "disillusionment" low in the second half of the first year and again around the anniversary (CERT, p. 151). Counter it with scheduled good activities, problem-solving and helpful thinking (Skills for Psychological Recovery, p. 49), deliberately rebuilding friendships (p. 65), and regular support-group meetings (Where Women Have No Doctor, p. 14). Psychological first aid. 📚 Go deeper: WHO Psychological First Aid — a short field guide; PFA Field Operations Guide — children, grief and handouts; Skills for Psychological Recovery — worksheets for the months after.

👵 Children, elders and neighbors who need help - About 1 in 6 people has a disability that affects daily life (Where Women Have No Doctor, ch. 9). - Name one person to check on each older or disabled neighbor; keep wheelchairs and walkers in one fixed place; and ask neighbors now whether they're willing to help (Red Cross Seniors, pp. 8, 10, 15). - Older adults: speak clearly in a low pitch, and don't assume confusion is permanent (PFA Field Guide, p. 13). - Children: crouch to eye level and use simple feeling words — mad, sad, scared, not "terrified" (same page). Children cope the way their parents cope (FEMA Are You Ready?, p. 188). Schooling with no school: older children tutor younger ones (peer tutoring) (Peer Tutoring, pp. 17–21). Structured tutoring beats casual help; short focused stretches (up to 4 weeks) work best; math, then reading, show the biggest gains. Train tutors to be kind — untrained tutors drift into threats and put-downs (p. 21). The tutors gain skill and confidence too. For family talk and journaling, use the day-by-day prompts in the Oregon toolkit. One-room school. 📚 Go deeper: Red Cross Disaster Preparedness for Seniors by Seniors — written by elders after a two-week outage; NWREL Peer Tutoring — teaching mixed ages with few adults.

📍 Illinois Valley notes - Take a CERT class now. The Illinois Valley Fire District has run free CERT Basic classes in Cave Junction (local listings 2025–2026, not from a file — verify). - We're used to waiting. Sheriff patrols were cut back after public-safety levies failed from 2012 on (general knowledge) — one more reason to organize before anything happens. - Wells and propane: most Valley homes have both, so use the rural MYN steps (MYN Rural, p. 3). - Mailbox clusters on the side roads make natural communication sites (general practice). - Radios: cheap FRS/GMRS handhelds reach about 1–2 miles in our hills (general practice). Listen to the local nets now — see the Illinois Valley page and Signals guide. - Fire season (July–October): the night watch doubles as a fire lookout. 📚 Go deeper: MYN Rural Settings — the rural plan; Red Cross Seniors — building a support network before you need it.

🛡️ Home & Property Protection (Defensive Only) How to keep your family, home, food, tools and animals from being easy targets when no deputy is coming: looking like a poor choice to thieves, hearing trouble early, slowing people down, getting everyone to safety, calling the neighbors, and staying within Oregon law. This guide is strictly defensive. On purpose, it has nothing on fighting, patrolling or building traps. The books are in Southern-Oregon\Home-Security\ (Home-Hardening, Safe-Room, Neighborhood-Watch, Rural-Property, Law), with the watch and de-escalation books in Southern-Oregon\Community-Barter\ and guardian-dog books in Southern-Oregon\Animals\Planning-Predators-Toxic-Plants. ### ⚠️ Rules that prevent the worst outcomes - Never booby-trap anything: no spring guns, tripwires, spikes or rigged doors. Traps can't tell a thief from a child, a firefighter or a neighbor coming to help. In 2018 a man in Williams (here in Josephine County) rigged a house with shotgun traps. One went off into an FBI bomb technician's leg, and in 2023 he got 150 months in federal prison (U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Oregon, 2023). See the law. - Don't shoot at property, or at anyone who is not an immediate deadly threat to a person. Oregon never allows deadly force to stop theft or damage to property (ORS 161.229). - Know who is on your land before you do anything. At night the "intruder" may be a neighbor, a lost child, a confused elder or someone

property (ORS 161.229). - Know who is on your land before you do anything. At night the "intruder" may be a neighbor, a lost child, a confused elder or someone running from a fire. - Keep firearms locked away from children and thieves. It's Oregon law (ORS 166.395). - A person's life is worth more than any property. Let things go. Physical force is "never recommended" except to stop an injury (De-escalation, p. 4). - Avoid confrontation and call the neighbors. Watchers "should never confront suspicious persons" (Watch Manual, p. 20).

🧅 Layers: deter, detect, delay, respond Think of protection as layers. Each one makes a thief more likely to give up or be seen, and buys your family time. The Watch Manual compares it to sports: "the more defenses a team has... the less likely the opponent will be to score" (Watch Manual, p. 32). | Layer | What it means | On a Valley lot (examples) | | Deter | Make your place look like a poor choice | Someone home, a dog, no supplies on show, a locked gate | | Detect | Know early that someone is coming | Dog, geese, gate bell, gravel, motion light, radio check-ins | | Delay | Slow them down | Strong doors and strike plates, locked outbuildings, pinned windows | | Respond | Protect people, not things | Safe room or escape, whistle alarm, neighbors on the radio | Why layers matter more out here: - Secluded houses are attractive targets: set back on large lots, they "reduce the chance that neighbors or passersby will see or hear a burglar" (COPS Burglary, p. 22; 🖼️ photo). - Devices work best together. Burglars get in less often when a house has two or more (window locks, deadbolts, lights, alarms), and the devices "slow them down, making them more vulnerable to being seen" (p. 25). - Help is far away. Each layer must

or more (window locks, deadbolts, lights, alarms), and the devices "slow them down, making them more vulnerable to being seen" (p. 25). - Help is far away. Each layer must buy time for the family to reach safety (rule of thumb). "Respond" in this guide never means going out to fight. It means getting people safe and getting help. 📚 Go deeper: COPS Burglary of Single-Family Houses, pp. 20–25 — what the research says about which houses get picked; Neighborhood Watch Manual, ch. 9 — basic home "target hardening".

🤫 Don't be a target Look lived-in. "Most burglars do not target occupied houses, taking great care to avoid them"; some ring the doorbell first to check (COPS Burglary, p. 20). So: - Someone home most of the time, no set times when everyone leaves, and be seen around the property often (WSDA Farm Security, p. 1). - Never announce who is away (Watch Manual, p. 21). - No spare key under the mat or in the car. Leave one with a trusted neighbor (Seattle Police, Outside the Home, p. 2). Don't advertise supplies. Burglars read a house's contents from what they can see outside (COPS Burglary, p. 25). After a collapse the "signs of wealth" change (rule of thumb): | Gives you away | Quieter way (rule of thumb) | | Bright windows when every other house is dark | Curtains or blankets over lit rooms (cover windows people can see into: Seattle Police) | | A generator roaring every evening | Run it in daylight, only as needed, outdoors and away from windows (carbon monoxide). See the Off-Grid Power guide | | Cooking smoke and smells at all hours | Cook at the same times as the neighbors | | Empty food boxes and fuel cans by the road | Burn, compost or bury packaging well back from the road | | Talking about your stores at trades

| | Empty food boxes and fuel cans by the road | Burn, compost or bury packaging well back from the road | | Talking about your stores at trades | Keep amounts private. Share through the group, not at the roadside | Quiet sharing. Hungry people steal, so fair sharing prevents theft (Community guide). Give through the group or a welcome point (below), so no one house becomes "the place with food" (rule of thumb). What to say to strangers (rule of thumb): friendly and short. "We're getting by like everyone. The table at the crossroads has water and news." Don't say how many live here, who is away, what you have, or that you're armed. 📚 Go deeper: COPS Burglary, p. 20 — occupancy and how burglars check; Seattle Police, Deterring Burglary From Outside the Home — looking at your home "through the eyes of a burglar".

🚪 Doors, frames, locks and windows Doors get kicked, not picked. "The most common way used to force entry through a door with a wooden jamb is to kick it open." The weak point is "almost always the strike plate," which is held only by short screws into thin trim (Seattle Police, Door Security; 🖼️ how a strike plate sits in the jamb). The cheapest big fix (Seattle, Door Security): 1. Take out the short screws in every exterior door's strike plates and hinges. 2. Put in 3- to 4-inch wood screws that bite into the wall stud. "This one step alone will deter or prevent most through-the-door forced entries." 3. Better still, fit a four-screw heavy-duty strike plate, plus at least one long screw in each hinge. 4. Against pry bars, add a latch guard over the gap where the bolt meets the frame (🖼️ photo). Doors and locks (Watch Manual, pp. 32–33): - Exterior doors metal or solid wood. Hollow-core or poorly fitting doors "can mean trouble" (🖼️ door types; 🖼️ door and frame cross-section). - A deadbolt with a bolt that sticks out at least 1 inch, on every outside door and the door from the garage into the house. - Hinges on the inside, or pins that can't be pulled. Exterior doors carry 3 hinges (USDA AH 73, p. 146; 🖼️ hinge drawing). - Change the

into the house. - Hinges on the inside, or pins that can't be pulled. Exterior doors carry 3 hinges (USDA AH 73, p. 146; 🖼️ hinge drawing). - Change the locks when a place changes hands. - Double-cylinder deadbolts (key both sides) only where a thief could break glass and reach the thumb-turn, and keep the key in the inside lock while anyone is home so you can get out in a fire (Seattle, Door Security). - A door viewer (peephole) lets you see and talk without opening (general practice). Windows have latches, not locks (Seattle, Window Security): - Double-hung windows (🖼️ drawing; sash window): drill a hole down through the inner sash into the outer one and drop in a sash pin, a long nail or an Allen wrench (🖼️ photos). A second hole 5 inches up lets you pin it open for air. - Sliding glass doors and sliding windows: a snug dowel or a hinged "Charlie bar" in the inside track, plus screws half-way into the top track so the panel can't be lifted out (🖼️ p. 2). - Security window film makes glass shatterproof (p. 2). - Bars on bedroom windows must open from the inside. Every sleeping room needs a way out in a fire (p. 2). Nails in windows are a fire hazard (Watch Manual, p. 33). Garages and outbuildings: - About a third

Every sleeping room needs a way out in a fire (p. 2). Nails in windows are a fire hazard (Watch Manual, p. 33). Garages and outbuildings: - About a third of burglars force nothing. They walk in through unlocked doors and windows, especially garage and basement ones (COPS Burglary, p. 26). Lock the door between the garage and the house (Watch Manual, p. 33), and keep the garage shut (🖼️ why). - Lock sheds with a hasp and padlock, and lock up ladders and tools (Seattle, Outside the Home, p. 2). 📚 Go deeper: Seattle Police Door Security — strike plates, screws, deadbolts on one page; Seattle Police Window Security — every window type; USDA Wood-Frame House Construction, pp. 141–147 — how doors, frames and hardware go together.

🌳 Fences, gates, lighting and sightlines The three CPTED ideas (Crime prevention through environmental design; COPS CPTED, pp. 15, 17–19): 1. Control access. "Fences, tree lines, hedges, or berms define the boundaries"; drives and paths guide people; "gates and doors limit points of entry." 2. See and be seen. Lighting, windows that look out on the approaches, and plants chosen and trimmed so views are kept open (p. 18). 3. Show ownership. Gardens and upkeep "show that someone cares and is paying attention" (p. 19). Sightlines and brush, with fire safety first. Dense shrubs and privacy fences near doors and windows give a burglar cover (COPS Burglary, p. 21). Seattle Police use a 3/6 rule: shrubs under 3 ft, tree limbs above 6 ft (Outside the Home, p. 1; 🖼️ pictures). Here the stricter fire rules win: - Limbs on mature trees at least 10 ft up, none over the roof (OSU EM 9184, p. 8). - Nothing that burns within 5 ft of the house (Ready Set Go, p. 4; 🖼️ the zones). Seattle suggests thorny Oregon grape under windows; here, plant only beyond 5 ft, and pick fire-resistant shrubs (OSU PNW 590). - Clear brush that hides the driveway approach: 10 ft side clearance, 13.5 ft overhead, so a fire engine fits (OSU EM 9184, p. 8; wildfire section). Fences and gates: - The boundary "is the property

driveway approach: 10 ft side clearance, 13.5 ft overhead, so a fire engine fits (OSU EM 9184, p. 8; wildfire section). Fences and gates: - The boundary "is the property owner's primary line of defense." Make gates strong, mounted securely, and locked with heavy chain and padlock; use ditches, large rocks or locking posts to close side gaps (WSDA Farm Security, p. 1). - A solid privacy fence hides a burglar. See-through fencing such as chain-link keeps the view open (Seattle, Outside the Home, p. 2). - Make sure helpers can get in. Neighbors and the fire crew must be able to open or cut the gate fast (rule of thumb). Skip razor wire or spikes where children or firefighters might climb. Lighting (security lighting): enough to see about 100 ft at the entry, with motion lights on side and back yards (Seattle, p. 1). On a secluded lot a motion-activated light works as an alert, while steady light only helps if someone is there to see (COPS Burglary, p. 22). With no grid, aim solar lights along the approaches (Off-Grid Power guide). Signs and address: "No Trespassing" signs define the boundary (WSDA, p. 1), but signs "are only good if you can back them up" (Seattle, p. 2). Keep a reflective address sign visible from both directions, day and night, so neighbors and responders find you (OSU EM 9184,

if you can back them up" (Seattle, p. 2). Keep a reflective address sign visible from both directions, day and night, so neighbors and responders find you (OSU EM 9184, p. 8). 📚 Go deeper: COPS Using CPTED in Problem Solving — the three CPTED ideas with checklists; OSU EM 9184 — seasonal checklists for brush, driveways and address signs; WSDA General Farm Security — boundaries, gates and outlying fields.

🔔 Early warning with no grid Dogs. "A dog's presence is a close substitute for human occupancy, and most burglars avoid houses with dogs." Small dogs bark and draw attention (COPS Burglary, pp. 20–21). "A good watch dog in the house and yard area is one of the best security measures" (WSDA, p. 1; Guard dog). Livestock guardian dogs guard stock, not people. Common breeds are the Great Pyrenees, Anatolian Shepherd, Maremma and Akbash (Texas A&M, p. 5; Livestock guardian dog; Great Pyrenees; Anatolian Shepherd; Maremma; 🖼️ photo). Socialize them with people: unsocialized dogs may "harm employees" (same page). Known problems include dogs "overly aggressive to people" and dogs that roam onto neighbors' land (USDA AIB 588, p. 28). See the predator sections of the Rabbits & Chickens and Goats, Dairy & Bees guides. Other alarm animals. "Donkeys, llamas and cattle will sometimes protect sheep that graze with them" (Raising Healthy Sheep, p. 133; 🖼️ guard llama). Geese honk loudly at strangers and are an old farm alarm (general practice). Simple noise alarms (rule of thumb): - A bell on every gate and door that rings when it opens. - Cans with pebbles tied to fence wire, where people don't walk. - Gravel on paths and under windows crunches underfoot. - Never string a line across a path, driveway or doorway. It trips children, elders and firefighters in the dark,

walk. - Gravel on paths and under windows crunches underfoot. - Never string a line across a path, driveway or doorway. It trips children, elders and firefighters in the dark, and it's one step from a trap. Lights and radios: - Battery or solar motion lights on the approaches (above). - Radio check-ins: a set time each evening on FRS or GMRS. The local Channel 3 Project uses FRS channel 3 (Illinois Valley — Start Here; Radio guide; FRS). - An alarm code everyone knows: a string of short, sharp blasts on a whistle or air horn = "general alarm, act on the plan," and the horn is never used for anything else (Signals guide). 📚 Go deeper: USDA Livestock Guarding Dogs (AIB 588) — choosing, raising and the problems to expect; Texas A&M LGD Overview — breeds and socializing; COPS Burglary, p. 21 — dogs and alarms as substitutes for someone being home.

🏠 A safe room and a household plan A safe room is a place to wait behind a strong door while help comes. It is not a place to fight from. FEMA's full version. Taking Shelter from the Storm (FEMA P-320) has plans for reinforced tornado rooms, which also make a strong hardened room: - Where: a basement, a bathroom, closet or laundry room, or a separate room within 150 ft (p. 41; 🖼️ floor plans). - Size: at least 3 sq ft per person for a short stay, 7 for a long one, 10 for a wheelchair user (p. 37). - Door: ordinary steel house doors fail FEMA's tests; a real safe room needs a tested, labeled door (p. 53; 🖼️ label). - Cost: about $9,400–$25,500 new, plus the door, and more in an existing house (p. 56; 🖼️ construction drawings). The everyday version (rule of thumb, built from the door advice above): - An inside room with a solid-wood or metal door, a deadbolt, and the strike plate and hinges screwed into the studs with 3-inch screws. - A second way out (a window that opens from inside), a smoke alarm and a fire extinguisher (🖼️ how to use one). A locked room in a burning house is a death trap. If there is smoke, get out. - Kept stocked (P-320, p. 69): 1 gallon of water per

use one). A locked room in a burning house is a death trap. If there is smoke, get out. - Kept stocked (P-320, p. 69): 1 gallon of water per person per day, food, first-aid kit and medicines, a flashlight for every 4 people, a battery radio, a portable toilet, a crowbar to open a jammed door, plus a whistle or air horn and an FRS radio. The household plan (rule of thumb; fill it in on the Oregon My Pocket Plan): | Decide now | Example | | Who goes where | Kids and grandma to the back bedroom; one adult with the radio | | Who calls for help, and how | Air horn, then FRS channel 3 to the neighbors | | Two ways out | Front door; back bedroom window | | Outside meeting spot | The neighbor's barn | | Code words | "Safe room now," "all clear," and one that secretly means "I'm being forced, stay hidden" | Practice it, once at night too, until the children know it (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: FEMA P-320 — sizing, locations and full building plans; FEMA Are You Ready?, p. 62 — preparing a safe room.

🥫 Protecting food, water, fuel, tools and livestock Food and water: - Shared stores go in locked, rodent-proof containers with a written in-and-out log, and it takes two people to open them (Community guide). - Don't keep everything in one place. Split stores between the house, the cellar and an outbuilding, so a thief or a fire takes only part (rule of thumb). - A hidden cache (rule of thumb): sealed, rodent-proof containers of foods that keep (Food Security guide). Tell one other adult where. - Lock the pump house (rule of thumb; Wells guide). Fuel (WSDA, pp. 1–2): - Lockable caps on fuel outlets; fuel tanks, pumps and electric-fence units secured and locked. - Place fuel tanks where they can be seen from the house. Keep stored fuel, chemicals and fertilizer "to a minimum" and locked up. Storage and safety: Fuel guide. Tools, machinery and valuables: - Mark everything in at least two places, one easy to see and one hidden (WSDA, p. 2). - Operation ID (Watch Manual, p. 34): engrave your Oregon driver's license number starting with "OR" and ending with "DL". Never your Social Security number. Marked items are hard to sell, so burglars avoid them. - Keep a property list with serial numbers and marks, plus photos, stored away from the things themselves (p. 34). - Machinery: take the keys out; remove the distributor cap,

- Keep a property list with serial numbers and marks, plus photos, stored away from the things themselves (p. 34). - Machinery: take the keys out; remove the distributor cap, rotor or battery; chain it up; park it where a neighbor can see it (WSDA, p. 1). - Firearms are a top target. Burglars steal "cash and goods they can easily carry and sell," weapons included (COPS Burglary, p. 25). Lock them up (the law). Livestock: - Mark every animal with ear tags, ear notches or tattoos (🖼️ marking goats' ears), or branding. Keep records and photos of each one, with births, deaths, buys and sales (WSDA, p. 1). - Check stock daily, at different times. Keep loading ramps away from the road, and lock gates and ramps (same page). - At night, bring flocks into a predator-proof area near the home (Raising Healthy Sheep, pp. 132–133). The same book notes that "theft from human predators is a problem in some places." 📚 Go deeper: WSDA General Farm Security — fuel, machinery, livestock and records on two pages; Neighborhood Watch Manual, p. 34 — Operation ID and property lists.

👥 Neighborhood watch after the collapse How to set up a watch, block captains, the phone or runner tree, describing people and the night shift table are all in the Community guide: Keeping watch. The key rules: - Watchers watch and report. They "shall not carry weapons or pursue" and "should never confront suspicious persons" (Watch Manual, p. 20; Neighborhood watch). - What counts as suspicious (p. 24): someone peering into cars or windows, people at homes at unusual hours, tampering with gas, power or water, signs of forced entry, and "anything that feels uncomfortable or looks out of place." A roster that doesn't wear people out (rule of thumb, from the Community guide): - 2-hour shifts in pairs, the same nights each week, with a written handover. Protect watchers' daytime sleep (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 154). - Nobody stands watch two nights running. Spread it across every capable adult; give elders, parents of babies and the sick lighter daytime jobs. - In fire season the watch is also the fire lookout. Daily check-in: post OK/HELP cards at the communication site (MYN Rural, p. 2), or follow the Signals guide's OK/HELP plan. Checkpoints: a welcome point, not a roadblock (rule of thumb): - Never block a public road. Obstructing "vehicular or pedestrian traffic on a public way" is disorderly conduct under Oregon law (ORS 166.025). Gates on your own driveway

of thumb): - Never block a public road. Obstructing "vehicular or pedestrian traffic on a public way" is disorderly conduct under Oregon law (ORS 166.025). Gates on your own driveway are fine. - Put a table at a crossroads turnout, on private land with permission, with two calm, unarmed neighbors, a radio, water and a news board. - Everyone may pass. Nobody is stopped or searched. The table offers news and help, and quietly notes descriptions and vehicles (Watch Manual, p. 24). Helping people on the move (rule of thumb): meet them at the welcome point, not your house, and give through the group. Use look, listen, link: check urgent needs, listen, connect them to help (WHO Psychological First Aid, p. 25). Newcomers who stay join the group's work and barter rules (Community guide). 📚 Go deeper: Neighborhood Watch Manual, pp. 20–24 — patrol rules and what is suspicious; MYN Rural Settings — the rural check-in plan; COPS CPTED, p. 19 — showing a neighborhood is cared for.

🚧 Someone at the gate, strangers, or a break-in Before you open anything: 1. Find out who it is: through the viewer, a window, or by calling out. 2. Talk through the closed door or gate. Don't open it. Let them know someone is home; most burglars avoid occupied houses (COPS Burglary, p. 20). 3. Point them to help that isn't your house, such as the welcome point (rule of thumb). If they're upset, use the Community guide's Calming an angry person: a slow, calm voice, hands visible, never threats or ultimatums (De-escalation, pp. 15–24; De-escalation). If someone is trying to get in, or is already inside (rule of thumb): 1. Sound the alarm: air horn or whistle, a string of short blasts. 2. Everyone goes to the safe room, or out the escape route to the meeting spot. Take the kids and elders first. 3. Call the neighbors on the radio: who you are, where, what's happening. 4. Stay put. Don't go looking for the intruder. Let them take things. Property can be replaced. People can't. Remember what you saw (Watch Manual, p. 24): what can't be changed (height, build, skin and eye color, scars, tattoos) and the vehicle's make, type and plate. Write it down at once. "Never hesitate to say, 'I'm not sure.'" Afterwards (WSDA, p. 2): - Check everyone first, then give first aid (Injuries guide).

make, type and plate. Write it down at once. "Never hesitate to say, 'I'm not sure.'" Afterwards (WSDA, p. 2): - Check everyone first, then give first aid (Injuries guide). - Don't disturb the point of entry. Write down the facts and times, and list what's gone with serial numbers. - Report it when you can: to the group now, to the sheriff when there is one. - A stolen firearm must be reported within 72 hours, or within 24 hours of a way to report becoming available (ORS 166.397). - Write down every threatening incident (De-escalation, p. 23). Fix the weak point the intruder used. 📚 Go deeper: Using Verbal De-Escalation — stance, voice and what never to say; Neighborhood Watch Manual, p. 24 — describing people and vehicles.

⚖️ Oregon law on force in defense of people and property This is not legal advice. It quotes the Oregon Revised Statutes (2025 edition, from oregonlegislature.gov) in plain words. Laws change, and courts decide each case on its facts. The key test in every section is what you "reasonably believe," and other people judge that afterwards. | Situation | What the law says | In plain words | | Defending yourself or another person (ORS 161.209) | You may use physical force against "what the person reasonably believes to be the use or imminent use of unlawful physical force," and only "a degree of force which the person reasonably believes to be necessary" | Only against a real, present attack, and only as much force as needed | | If you started it (ORS 161.215) | No justification if you provoked it or were "the initial aggressor," unless you withdraw and make that clear | Starting a fight takes away your defense | | Deadly force (ORS 161.219) | Only if you reasonably believe the other person is committing or attempting a felony that uses or threatens force against a person, or a burglary in a dwelling, or is using or about to use unlawful deadly force against a person | Reserved for a threat to people's lives and bodies | | Your land and buildings (ORS 161.225) | Physical

or about to use unlawful deadly force against a person | Reserved for a threat to people's lives and bodies | | Your land and buildings (ORS 161.225) | Physical force to stop a criminal trespass when you reasonably believe it necessary. Deadly force only to defend a person (as above), or to prevent arson or "a felony by force and violence by the trespasser" | Trespassing alone never justifies deadly force | | Your things (ORS 161.229) | "Physical force, other than deadly physical force," to stop theft or criminal mischief | Never deadly force over property | | Pointing a gun (ORS 166.190) | Purposely pointing a loaded or empty firearm at someone "except in self-defense" is a crime | Don't wave guns at people at the gate | | Threatening (ORS 163.190) | Menacing: trying "to place another person in fear of imminent serious physical injury" by word or conduct | Threats are a crime too | "Deadly physical force" means force that "is readily capable of causing death or serious physical injury" (ORS 161.015). Booby traps and spring guns. No Oregon law allows them. A trap can't "reasonably believe" anything; it hits whoever comes: a child, a firefighter, a neighbor coming to help. Setting one creates "a substantial risk of serious physical injury to another person," which is recklessly endangering (ORS 163.195), and if someone is

a firefighter, a neighbor coming to help. Setting one creates "a substantial risk of serious physical injury to another person," which is recklessly endangering (ORS 163.195), and if someone is hurt or killed the charges grow. Courts have long made trap-setters pay even when the person hurt was a trespasser (Katko v. Briney; Spring-gun; Booby trap). Then there's the Williams case in the warning box at the top. Firearm storage: the Cindy Yuille and Steve Forsyth Act (SB 554 as passed): - Whenever a firearm is not carried by or under the control of its owner or an authorized person, it must be secured with an engaged trigger or cable lock, in a locked container, or in a locked gun room (ORS 166.395; trigger locks, gun safe). - It is not secured if the key or combination is "readily available" to someone not authorized. - The fine is higher if a minor gets an unsecured gun. If an unsecured gun is used to hurt someone within two years, the owner is treated as negligent in a lawsuit (with narrow exceptions). - Report loss or theft within 72 hours (ORS 166.397). Directly supervise any minor you hand a firearm to, with some hunting and target-range exceptions (ORS 166.403). Training: if you keep firearms, get real training from a qualified instructor. 🔥 Fire as a threat to your home A fire, whether set on purpose or blown in from the hills, can take everything at once. The defenses are those in the Illinois Valley wildfire section: - First 5 ft: nothing that burns. Firewood and lumber 30 ft away (OSFM, p. 13; Defensible space)). - Within 100 ft: grass short, trees spaced, and no ladder fuels (🖼️ drawing). - Vents covered with 1/8-inch metal mesh (🖼️ how embers get in). Water and tools ready (rule of thumb): full buckets or barrels, a charged hose if you have pressure, shovels and rakes by the door, and a fire extinguisher you know how to use (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep: 🖼️ CERT, pp. 171–172). At night: the watch looks for smoke and glow as well as people (Community guide). If the house is on fire, everyone gets out. Never stay in a safe room in a burning building. 📚 Go deeper: OSFM Defensible Space Homeowner Guide — the zones, step by step; FEMA P-737 — hardening the house itself; OSU EM 9184 — year-round checklists.

😴 Stress, fatigue and judgment The worst outcomes come from tired, frightened people deciding fast in the dark (rule of thumb). - Sleep is protection. Keep watch-standers on a consistent schedule (Ship's Medicine Chest, p. 154). - Check rumors before acting. Use the phone or runner tree to confirm facts (Community guide). - Don't escalate. Two calm people with one angry person is safer than one (De-escalation, p. 21). Swap out anyone losing their temper (rule of thumb). - Look after the helpers. Watchers and helpers burn out; time away helps (CERT, pp. 144–146). - After a scare, use psychological first aid: look, listen, link (Community guide; Psychological first aid). - Despair and guns don't mix. Oregon's legislature found that "a proven barrier to the impulse to commit suicide is securing firearms with a lock or storing firearms in locked containers" (SB 554, p. 1). In hard months, let a trusted person hold the key for anyone who is struggling (rule of thumb). 📚 Go deeper: WHO Psychological First Aid — a short field guide; CERT, p. 144 — stress in helpers.

⏳ What to Expect: Disaster Scenarios & Timelines What really happens, hour by hour and month by month, in the disasters most likely to hit the Illinois Valley, and what to do at each stage. The timelines come from official plans and after-action reports: the Oregon Resilience Plan, the Josephine County hazard plan, the state's review of the 2020 Labor Day fires, federal and state power-outage and fuel plans, and fifty years of disaster research. The books are in Disaster-Scenarios\ (Cascadia-Earthquake, Local-Hazards, Fire-Heat-Drought, Grid-Supply-Pandemic, How-People-Respond), with more in Wildfire\, Earthquake-Tsunami\, Nuclear-Radiation\ and EMP-Solar-Storms\. ### ⚠️ Five rules that hold in every scenario 1. Plan to be on your own for at least two weeks. The state's own Cascadia exercise said so (Cascadia Rising, p. 12). At the end of one highway, plan longer. 2. Leave early. Alerts fail when cell towers burn or lose power (2020 fire review, p. 9). A Level 3 notice may be the last one. 3. Check on people who live alone. Most who died in the 2021 heat dome lived alone (heat report, p. 10). 4. Generators, grills and camp stoves stay outdoors. Carbon monoxide kills in every outage (CPSC). 5. Expect neighbors to help, and be one. Panic and looting are rare; survivors do most of the rescuing (Quarantelli, p. 16).

🔥 1. Wildfire and smoke What it is and how likely here. Fires start here every summer: 1,175 in 2010–2019, about 80% started by people (county plan, pp. 72–73). Burn probability is "considerably higher along highway 199 between Grants Pass and Cave Junction," so a fire could cut the valley off (p. 71). In September 2020 the Slater Fire burned over 166,000 acres and closed highways around the county (p. 73), while east winds spread fires statewide: over 500,000 Oregonians were under some level of evacuation notice (state review, p. 20). ❄️ 2. Winter storm, ice, flood and landslides What it is and how likely here. The county rates winter storms #2 of all hazards: high probability, high vulnerability. Recent ones: in February 2019 fallen trees closed US-199 at the California line and 2,500 customers lost power around Grants Pass, Cave Junction and O'Brien; in January 2021 snow left 45,000 customers in the area without power (county plan, p. 64). The valley is "one way in, one way out": a storm on US-199 can strand Cave Junction and cut the whole valley's power "for an extended period" (p. 140). Floods are rated high probability, moderate damage. The benchmark is the Christmas flood of 1964: 10 inches of rain in six days, the Rogue and Illinois Valleys cut off and I-5 closed (p. 45). In 2015, water covered US-199 near Selma and closed roads near O'Brien (p. 46). 🌡️ 3. Extreme heat and drought What it is and how likely here. The county rates heat waves high probability, moderate damage. Days with a heat index over 90 °F are expected to rise from about 13 a year to about 40 by the 2050s (county plan, p. 57). In the June 2021 heat dome Josephine County saw 92–108 °F, with two more heat waves later that summer (p. 58). In Portland it killed 72 people; in a normal year, none. Most were 60 or older and lived alone, and half had only a fan (heat report, pp. 2, 8–12). Drought is also rated high probability: extreme drought years 1924, 1977 and 2001, severe ones as recently as 2014 and 2020 (p. 33). 🔌 4. Long power outage, including fire-season shutoffs What it is and how likely here. Storms knock out power almost every winter (scenario 2). Pacific Power has mapped areas near Cave Junction where it may cut power on purpose in dangerous fire weather, called a public safety power shutoff (county plan, p. 140; state fire review, p. 10). 🦠 5. Pandemic What it is and how likely here. A new germ spreads around the world, usually "within several weeks or months." The last century had flu pandemics in 1918, 1957, 1968 and 2009 (WHO, pp. 51–52), and then COVID-19 — so expect one or two in a lifetime (estimate). A pandemic comes in waves of several weeks to a few months, and a later wave can be worse: the mild spring wave of 1918 came before the deadly autumn one (p. 52; Spanish flu). ⛽ 6. Economic crisis, fuel and supply-chain breakdown What it is and how likely here. Oregon has no refineries; more than 90% of its fuel comes from four refineries near Seattle, mostly through one pipeline to the Portland fuel hub (fuel plan, p. 9). Gas stations hold about two to three days of fuel (p. 11). Groceries hold more shelf-stable food than most people think; the real problem in a catastrophe is delivery, not supply (CNA, p. 9). In the 1970s oil shortages states used odd-even days to cut gas lines (NASEO, p. 45; 1973 oil crisis). In the Great Depression people formed barter associations to trade work and goods (Braun 1933, p. 5). 🌎 7. Cascadia M9 earthquake (and the coast tsunami) What it is and how likely here. The Cascadia subduction zone last broke on January 26, 1700 (1700 Cascadia earthquake). About half of past quakes were centered off the southern Oregon coast; the odds of one hitting southern Oregon in the next 50 years are about 37% (Resilience Plan, p. 31). The county puts it at 37–43% for any Cascadia quake and 7–12% for the full M9, and rates our vulnerability high (county plan, p. 39). Studies estimate 650–5,000 deaths from the quake and another 600–5,000 from the tsunami (Resilience Plan, p. 40). Warning you'll get: none. The shaking is the warning. 🚨 8. Riots and law and order breaking down What it is and how likely here. Fifty years of disaster research found panic flight so rare that fire researchers stopped using the idea, and looting "unusual in the typical natural and technological disasters" of countries like ours (Quarantelli, pp. 6–7, 11–12). Mass looting did happen after Hurricane Hugo on St. Croix and after Hurricane Katrina, where three things came together: many poor people living beside obvious wealth, organized youth gangs, and a police force that was ineffective or corrupt (pp. 13–14). Even there, help between people "swamped" the theft, and after the first emergency days reported crime usually drops (p. 14). The EMP Commission warns that disorder becomes more likely when shortages cause conflict and police are absent for a long time (EMP Commission 2008, p. 167). ☀️ 9. Solar storm or EMP What it is and how likely here. A severe geomagnetic storm or a nuclear burst high above the country (EMP) mainly threatens the power grid. 🌋 11. Volcanic ash What it is and how likely here. The nearest potentially active volcanoes are Crater Lake, Medicine Lake, Mount Shasta, Newberry and the Three Sisters. The chance of 0.4 inch or more of ash here is about 1 in 10,000 a year; the risks are ashfall, bad air and disruption (county plan, p. 68). Winds usually carry ash east of the Cascades, away from us (p. 68). 🤝 What every scenario has in common The first 72 hours. No outside help, so neighbors are the first responders. In the first half hour after a disaster, about a third of survivors search for missing people and about one in ten actively rescue them (Quarantelli, p. 16). Your jobs: injuries, fires, water, a toilet, warmth or cooling, and checking the people next door. The 2-week mark. Oregon tells everyone to be ready for at least two weeks (Be 2 Weeks Ready, p. 2). The old 2004 FEMA book's "at least three days" (p. 33) is too short for here. Two weeks is also about when most big storm outages have ended, and the longest disruption most businesses can stand (Resilience Plan, p. 22). When things usually improve. Most storm, fire and heat emergencies ease within days to weeks. A Cascadia quake, EMP or national crisis takes months to years (see the tables). Plan for the long tail, not just the first days. Why most neighbors help. After disasters, help and sharing far outweigh theft, even in the worst cases (Quarantelli, p. 14); citizen groups spring up to clear debris, move supplies and pass messages (EMP Commission 2008, p. 167). Plan on cooperating, and organize early. Rumor control. Rumors make things worse. Pick one trusted source (a radio station, the ham net, a neighborhood runner) and write down news with

Plan on cooperating, and organize early. Rumor control. Rumors make things worse. Pick one trusted source (a radio station, the ham net, a neighborhood runner) and write down news with the time and who said it (rule of thumb); help correct misinformation (Psychological First Aid, p. 35). Mental health. Feeling overwhelmed, confused, afraid or numb is a normal reaction (WHO Psychological First Aid, p. 9). Keep routines, give everyone a job, keep children close and talking, and watch for anyone who stops eating or caring for themselves (rule of thumb). How-to: Community & barter and Psychological first aid. 📚 Go deeper: Quarantelli — how people really behave; Skills for Psychological Recovery — the weeks after; CERT manual — neighborhood search, first aid and organizing.

☢️ Nuclear Fallout Guide What to do if there is a nuclear detonation or a radiation release: how to shelter, how long, how to protect food, water and animals, how to clean up, and when potassium iodide (KI) helps. The full manuals — shelter plans, the homemade KFM fallout meter, farm and livestock guides — are in Nuclear-Radiation\. ### The three rules 1. Get inside. Stay inside. Stay tuned. Most deaths from fallout are avoidable just by being behind enough mass in the first day or two. 2. Fallout is dust. It hurts you from what lands on and near you, so put mass and distance between you and the roof, walls and ground outside. 3. Time is on your side. Radiation from fallout drops fast — 90% in the first 7 hours, 99% in 2 days.

⚡ The first minutes - If you see a flash: drop behind anything solid, face down, cover your head, and don't look at it — the flash can blind you even when you are too far away for the blast to hurt you (FEMA H-20, p. 14). The blast wave can arrive many seconds later — stay down until it passes. Being outdoors in the first minute can mean burns, cuts from flying glass and broken bones (FEMA Planning Guidance, p. 76). What happens in those seconds: 🖼️ flash, heat and blast drawing; Effects of nuclear explosions, Flash blindness. - Fallout near a blast can start arriving in 15–30 minutes; 100–200 miles downwind, often 5–10 hours or more. Use the time before it arrives to put out small fires, bring people, pets and water inside, and move to the best shelter you can reach. (FEMA Protection in the Nuclear Age, H-20, p. 7; 🖼️ how fallout comes down; Nuclear fallout) - Officials will tell everyone within about 50 miles to shelter until they know where the fallout is going. (FEMA Planning Guidance, 3rd ed., p. 54) - Know the sirens. A 3–5 minute steady blast means "turn on the radio." A 3–5 minute wavering tone (or short blasts repeated) is the attack warning — go to shelter now. (FEMA H-20, p. 12; what they look like: Civil defense siren) First-hour

A 3–5 minute wavering tone (or short blasts repeated) is the attack warning — go to shelter now. (FEMA H-20, p. 12; what they look like: Civil defense siren) First-hour checklist: get people and pets inside; close doors, windows and blinds; take a few minutes to check the house for fires — stamp out smoldering drapes, throw burning furniture outside (FEMA H-20, p. 26); fill containers and tubs while the taps run (rule of thumb); carry food, water, radio, medicines and the toilet bucket to the shelter spot. 📚 Go deeper: FEMA H-20 Protection in the Nuclear Age — warning signals, the flash, fallout timing, fires; FEMA Planning Guidance, 3rd ed. — today's official "Get Inside, Stay Inside, Stay Tuned" advice.

🏠 Where to shelter Best to worst: a basement (especially a corner below ground level) → the middle floors and center of a large concrete or brick building → a crawl space or interior room of a house → a vehicle (poor). See the 🖼️ FEMA drawing of protection inside different buildings and Fallout shelter. Most homes in the Illinois Valley are one-story wood frame with no basement. FEMA says these, and vehicles, are not adequate shelter on their own (Planning Guidance, p. 76). Plan now: a nearby building with a basement or thick masonry, a crawl-space shelter you can shield, or an outdoor trench shelter (plans in MP-79, In Time of Emergency, and Nuclear War Survival Skills Appendix A — see the 🖼️ Door-Covered Trench Shelter and 🖼️ Pole-Covered Trench Shelter drawings). Permanent backyard plans: 🖼️ FEMA H-12-1 outside concrete shelter, 🖼️ FEMA H-12-2 aboveground shelter. - Inside any building: get as far from the roof and outside walls as you can, away from windows and doors. Close and lock windows, turn off fans, A/C and forced-air heat, close fireplace dampers. (CDC Where to Go; 🖼️ CDC picture: best places inside a building) - No need to tape windows or hang plastic sheeting — fallout shelters don't have to be airtight. A building with minor damage still works if it is structurally sound. (EPA Protective Action Q&A, p. 31;

or hang plastic sheeting — fallout shelters don't have to be airtight. A building with minor damage still works if it is structurally sound. (EPA Protective Action Q&A, p. 31; Planning Guidance, p. 76) - Stuck in a poor shelter? If a good one is under 15 minutes away, move within about 30 minutes of the blast, before heavy fallout arrives. If you're already in a moderate shelter, stay 1–2 hours, then move. (FEMA Planning Guidance, p. 77) "Adequate" means it cuts your dose 10× or more. Concrete, brick, stone and earth stop a lot; wood, drywall and sheet metal stop little (Planning Guidance, p. 76; 🖼️ EPA dose-reduction diagram by building type). Adding shielding — each of these stops about as much as 4 inches of concrete (FEMA H-20, p. 22): | Material | Thickness | | Brick | 5–6 in | | Sand or gravel | 6 in | | Packed earth | 7 in | | Hollow concrete block (sand-filled) | 8 in (6 in) | | Water | 10 in | | Books or magazines | 14 in | | Wood (firewood stack) | 18 in | Pile it on the floor above you and around the walls of your shelter spot: earth-filled drawers and boxes, water jugs, firewood, books, heavy furniture. Every extra ~4 inches of packed earth roughly halves what gets through — about

the walls of your shelter spot: earth-filled drawers and boxes, water jugs, firewood, books, heavy furniture. Every extra ~4 inches of packed earth roughly halves what gets through — about 3 feet of earth cuts it around 1,000× (Nuclear War Survival Skills, 1979, p. 23: one "halving thickness" of packed earth is 3.6 in; 🖼️ halving-thickness drawing; Radiation protection). Crawl space: shelter under the center of the house, ring yourself with blocks or earth-filled containers, and pile mass on the floor above. Quick shelters, step by step (FEMA H-20, pp. 23–25; HS-4, p. 67): 1. Table shelter: a sturdy table or workbench in the most-underground basement corner, loaded on top and walled around with shielding. Crawl in and block the opening. (🖼️ drawing of a basement table shelter) 2. Door-roof shelter: walls of dressers or appliances, a roof of heavy doors propped and piled with shielding. Fill drawers and boxes with earth after they're in place — full ones are too heavy to carry. 3. Crawl-space shelter: cut an access now. Under the middle of the house, wall a spot with blocks or earth-filled containers up to the joists and pile mass on the floor above. Make sure no heavy appliance sits right above you. Dig down so you can sit up. 4. Last resort: dig a trench beside a slab house and tunnel no more than 4 feet under

appliance sits right above you. Dig down so you can sit up. 4. Last resort: dig a trench beside a slab house and tunnel no more than 4 feet under the slab; shore it and pile shielding on the slab inside. Ventilation: a crowded, sealed shelter gets dangerously hot in warm weather. Kearny's homemade air pump (KAP) — plans in Nuclear War Survival Skills and the ORNL Expedient Shelter Handbook — moves air without bringing in fallout dust (🖼️ KAP swinging in a doorway; 🖼️ photos of homemade KAPs). In a heat wave, plan on about 4 quarts of water and 10 grams of salt per person a day and as few clothes as practical (NWSS 1979, p. 62). 📚 Go deeper: FEMA H-20 — shielding table and home expedient shelters; FEMA HS-4 Citizen's Guide — rating and upgrading your house; Expedient Shelter Handbook ORNL-4941 — trench and log shelters, plus full Kearny Air Pump plans; MP-79 — construction drawings for homes without basements.

🧰 Stocking the shelter FEMA says to have at least two weeks of water, food and supplies ready to carry to the shelter (H-20, p. 13; 🖼️ illustrated 1961 supply chart). | Item | How much / what kind (FEMA H-20, pp. 29–31) | | Water | At least 1 quart per person per day, more is better. Kearny says store 15 gallons per person for two weeks (NWSS 1979, p. 71; 🖼️ storing water in lined bags and pits). | | Food | Canned or sealed, no cooking needed. ⏳ How long to stay in The 7-10 rule: every 7× increase in time after the blast cuts the radiation 10× (once the fallout has finished falling). (FEMA H-20, p. 8; see the 🖼️ seven-ten rule chart and the 🖼️ decay curve for the first two days) | Time after blast | Radiation level (example) | | 1 hour | 1,000 R/hr | | 7 hours | 100 R/hr | | 2 days | 10 R/hr | | 2 weeks | 1 R/hr | - Stay sheltered at least 12–24 hours unless officials say otherwise or fire, collapse or a medical emergency forces you out (FEMA Planning Guidance, pp. 53, 76). In heavy fallout areas it can be several days to two weeks, with only short trips out once levels drop (H-20, p. 9). USDA adds that where fallout is light or moderate you might be able to come out for part of each day after 2–3 days (PA-515, p. 6). - Late fallout decays more slowly where you are — if it arrives 8 hours after the blast, it takes about two days to fall to one-tenth (KFM report ORNL-5040, p. 69). - Gritty dust on ledges, cars or walks after an attack = assume fallout (H-20, p. 33). - Without a meter, listen for official word. With a meter, you can make your own decisions — see below.

walks after an attack = assume fallout (H-20, p. 33). - Without a meter, listen for official word. With a meter, you can make your own decisions — see below. Dose yardsticks — what a short-term whole-body dose does to a group of people (DCPA home-study course, p. 49; Acute radiation syndrome): | Dose received over a short time | What to expect | | 50 R | No visible effects | | 75–100 R | Brief nausea the same day in about 1 in 10 people | | 200 R | Up to half get some radiation sickness; 5–10% need care; deaths not expected | | 450 R | Serious sickness in most; about half die within 2–4 weeks | | 600 R | Serious sickness in all; nearly all die within 1–3 weeks | Sources set the line differently: the old civil-defense course says keep short-term doses under 100 R (DCPA, p. 50); today's EPA guideline for emergency workers is 5 rem, up to 25 rem only to save lives (EPA PAG Manual, p. 46). Treat 1 R of fallout as about 1 rem (rule of thumb). Lower is always better — the dose adds up. 📚 Go deeper: FEMA H-20 — the 7-10 rule and radiation sickness by dose; DCPA Introduction to Radiological Monitoring — dose effects and how to predict decay; EPA PAG Manual — official

🧼 Cleaning yourself up (decontamination) (CDC Decontamination; EPA Protective Action Q&A, p. 32; pictures: 🖼️ CDC step-by-step sheet, 🖼️ FEMA self-decontamination steps, Radioactive contamination) - Taking off your outer layer of clothes removes up to 90% of the fallout on you. Do it before you enter the shelter if you can, and do it gently so dust doesn't shake loose. Bag the clothes and put them away from people and pets. - Shower with soap and shampoo — no conditioner (it glues particles to hair). Don't scrub hard or scratch the skin; keep cuts covered. Keep suds out of your mouth and don't swallow the water. - No shower? Wipe exposed skin, blow your nose, wipe eyelids, ears and face with a damp cloth. - Clothes from closed drawers and closets are fine to wear. No clean clothes? Take off the outer layer, shake or brush it off, put it back on, then rewash your hands and face. - A cut or wound with fallout in it: flush with plenty of clean water or saline, or keep it covered (EPA Q&A, p. 33). - Visitors: have them strip the outer layer, bag it, and wash before coming in — then they're no danger to you (EPA Q&A, p. 33). Radiation sickness is not contagious (H-20, p. 9). - Pets: bring them in. Wash with soap or shampoo and water, wearing

they're no danger to you (EPA Q&A, p. 33). Radiation sickness is not contagious (H-20, p. 9). - Pets: bring them in. Wash with soap or shampoo and water, wearing gloves and a dust mask, keep your cuts (and theirs) covered, rinse completely, then wash yourself (EPA Q&A, p. 44). - Fallout looks like sand, ash or grit (🖼️ photos of real fallout particles). Brush or hose it off roofs and away from the house after levels drop; wear a dust mask, gloves and a hat, and wash afterward. If you must be out while dust is in the air, cover nose and mouth with a cloth (EPA Q&A, p. 30). 📚 Go deeper: CDC Decontamination for Yourself and Others — the one-page picture guide; EPA Protective Action Q&A — self-decontamination, visitors, wounds, pets and service animals.

💊 Potassium iodide (KI) - KI only protects the thyroid, and only from radioactive iodine. It does nothing against other fallout. Take it only when health officials say to — or, with no officials, when you have reason to believe fresh fallout or a reactor plume is arriving. Table salt and iodine tincture are not substitutes (tincture is poisonous to swallow). Iodine dietary supplements aren't either — use only FDA-approved KI. (CDC How KI Works; FDA, p. 12; 🖼️ CDC picture sheet: how KI fills the thyroid; where the gland is: Thyroid) - One dose protects about 24 hours. It works best just before or as the plume arrives and still helps 3–4 hours after. Avoid repeat doses for newborns and pregnant or breastfeeding women. (FDA, pp. 9–11) FDA dose by age (one dose per day) (FDA 2001, p. 9): | Who | Dose | 130 mg tablets | 65 mg tablets | | Adults over 18 (including pregnant or breastfeeding) | 130 mg | 1 | 2 | | Ages 12–18 (130 mg if 154 lb or more) | 65 mg | ½ | 1 | | Ages 3–12 | 65 mg | ½ | 1 | | 1 month – 3 years | 32 mg | ¼ | ½ | | Birth – 1 month | 16 mg | ⅛ | ¼ | Adults over 40 need it

month – 3 years | 32 mg | ¼ | ½ | | Birth – 1 month | 16 mg | ⅛ | ¼ | Adults over 40 need it only for a very large expected exposure. To make liquid doses for small children from tablets, use the two FDA sheets in Nuclear-Radiation\Government-Guidance. Making liquid KI for children — the two FDA sheets give the same recipe for one 130 mg tablet or two 65 mg tablets (FDA, one 130 mg tablet; FDA, two 65 mg tablets): 1. Put the tablet(s) in a small bowl with 4 teaspoons of water. Soak 1 minute. 2. Crush with the back of a spoon until there are no large pieces. 3. Stir in 4 teaspoons of milk, chocolate milk, orange juice, cola, formula, raspberry syrup or water. You now have 8 teaspoons of KI liquid. 4. Give once a day: 19 and older — 8 tsp; 13–18 years and 150 lb or more — 8 tsp; 13–18 under 150 lb — 4 tsp; 4–12 years — 4 tsp; over 1 month to 3 years — 2 tsp; birth to 1 month — 1 tsp. 5. Keep leftover liquid in the refrigerator; throw it out after 7 days. (The liquid sheet uses 150 lb for teens; the 2001 FDA guidance says 70 kg, about 154 lb. Either way a near-adult-size teen gets the adult

out after 7 days. (The liquid sheet uses 150 lb for teens; the 2001 FDA guidance says 70 kg, about 154 lb. Either way a near-adult-size teen gets the adult dose.) - A nursing mother's KI does not protect her baby — the baby needs its own dose, and newborns given KI should see a doctor afterward if one can be found (FDA, pp. 9–10; EPA Q&A, p. 38). - Repeat daily only while the risk of breathing or eating radioactive iodine continues (FDA, p. 9). Once the cloud has passed, FDA says the protection is controlling the food — especially fresh milk — not more KI. Stored grain and canned milk or vegetables kept weeks to months carry no radioiodine risk (FDA, p. 11). - Too much is dangerous too — don't double up "to be safe" (CDC). 📚 Go deeper: FDA KI dosing guidance — the official dose table and timing; FDA liquid KI sheet — step by step for children; CDC How KI Works — what it does and doesn't do. 🥫 Food and water (EPA Protective Action Q&A, p. 29; FDA; Nuclear War Survival Skills Ch. 8) - Food that was indoors is fine. Sealed cans, jars and bags that were outside are fine after wiping the outside — bag the wiping cloths. Stored grain and canned food have no radioactive-iodine risk. - Don't eat garden produce or anything left uncovered outdoors until levels have dropped and it's declared clear — then wash and peel it. Leafy vegetables: strip the outer leaves of cabbage and lettuce and wash the rest thoroughly. Roots and tubers: normal washing and peeling is enough. Fruit: wash before eating. (FB 2107, p. 14; PA-515, p. 7) - Don't drink fresh milk from animals grazing fallout-covered pasture for the first weeks (radioactive iodine concentrates in milk). Milk made into cheese and aged two months or more is fine — the radioactive iodine (Iodine-131) decays away (it loses half its strength every 8 days — USDA Ag Handbook 234, p. 9; USDA puts the wait at 30–60 days — PA-515, p. 8). If you have a baby, keep canned or dry milk in a protected place. - Water: bottled and sealed water is certain. Covered wells, tanks and cisterns are the best sources; deep wells are well protected. Tap water is fine for washing. - Boiling does not remove radioactivity. To clean doubtful water: stir in clay

and cisterns are the best sources; deep wells are well protected. Tap water is fine for washing. - Boiling does not remove radioactivity. To clean doubtful water: stir in clay soil, let it settle several hours, and pour off the clear water — or filter it through a bucket of packed earth. Both remove most fallout particles. Then disinfect as usual. - Cover rain barrels, tanks and well heads ahead of time. (Rain barrel) Water sources, safest first (NWSS 1979, pp. 76–77): deep wells and covered tanks → covered shallow wells → deep lakes → shallow ponds → streams (worst after the first heavy rains) → roof runoff → melted snow. With the power off, a well can still be used with a homemade bail-can on a rope (🖼️ bail-can drawing; Well). Settling method (NWSS 1979, pp. 78–79): 1. Fill a bucket three-quarters full of the doubtful water. 2. Dig clay or clayey soil from at least 4 inches below the surface (fallout stays near the top). 3. Stir in about 1 inch of dry clay for every 4 inches of water until it's all suspended. 4. Let it settle at least 6 hours. The clay carries the fallout down. 5. Dip or siphon off the clear water, then disinfect it. (USDA says settle a day, then strain through cloth; for stock, stir up a pond's mud bottom and let

5. Dip or siphon off the clear water, then disinfect it. (USDA says settle a day, then strain through cloth; for stock, stir up a pond's mud bottom and let it settle — PA-515, p. 8.) Earth filter (NWSS 1979, pp. 77–78; 🖼️ cut-away drawing of the filter can): 1. Punch about a dozen nail holes, from the bottom upward, within 2 inches of the center of the bottom of a 5-gallon can or bucket. 2. Put in 1½ inches of washed pebbles, then one layer of towel or burlap cut a bit bigger than the can. 3. Add 6–7 inches of crumbled soil with some clay in it, dug from 4+ inches deep, pressed down in layers. Not pure clay (too tight) or sand (too loose). 4. Cover with one layer of towel held by a few stones. Set the can on sticks over a pan. 5. Pour in (settled) water. Expect about 6 quarts an hour at first, 2 quarts an hour later. If it runs faster than a quart in 10 minutes, repack the soil. Replace the soil after about 50 quarts. Disinfect the filtered water. Disinfecting afterward: boil, or use plain unscented bleach — 8 drops of 6% bleach or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach per gallon, double if cloudy or very cold, wait 30 minutes (EPA Emergency Disinfection, pp. 1–2). 📚 Go deeper: Nuclear War

🐄 Livestock and gardens (USDA FB 2107, pp. 8–14, PA-516; Oregon ODOE, p. 2) - Shelter animals if you can (a barn helps), and take them off pasture. Feed protected feed — hay from inside the stack, covered silage, grain from closed bins (🖼️ USDA plan: dairy barn with a built-in family fallout shelter; Silage). - Water from a covered well, tank or flowing spring is best; open pond water clears more slowly but improves quickly. - Hold off on slaughter, fresh milk and eggs until levels drop. - Gardens: stop harvesting; after levels drop, wash and peel produce. Fallout on soil decays and is diluted by digging it in. More from USDA FB 2107 (pp. 8–14): - Animals are as sensitive to radiation as people. Crowd them into the barn — they shield each other; ventilation, not floor space, is the limit. Dairy animals first (Dairy cattle) — milk them before fallout arrives if you can, and turn calves in with the cows (pp. 9–11). - Feed: fallout only coats the outside of a haystack or stack of feed bags. Peel off the outer layer and feed the inside; a tarp over a field stack ahead of time is enough (p. 10). - Tanks and ponds: use what's already in a covered tank first. Pond water usually clears in a few days — keep stock off it a few

enough (p. 10). - Tanks and ponds: use what's already in a covered tank first. Pond water usually clears in a few days — keep stock off it a few days longer if it rains (pp. 9–10). - Poultry stand about twice the radiation cattle do; eggs clear soon after hens get clean feed (PA-515, p. 8). - Meat: an animal exposed only to outside radiation can be eaten if slaughtered before it shows sickness; keep hide and gut contents off the meat. Wash fallout off animals with any water, wearing coveralls, gloves and boots (p. 12). - Pasture: lightly contaminated pasture can be grazed again after one to a few weeks (p. 13). Bees: don't move or harvest hives until checked (ODOE, p. 2). Long-term garden choices: radioactive strontium (Strontium-90) acts like calcium. Liming acid soil cuts how much plants take up. Alfalfa, clover, soybeans and leafy greens take up more than grains, grasses, corn, potatoes and fruit — favor the latter on contaminated ground (FB 2107, p. 13). 📚 Go deeper: USDA FB 2107 Defense Against Radioactive Fallout on the Farm — livestock, feed, water, milk and crops; USDA Ag Handbook 234 — the science of fallout on soil, crops and animals; USDA Radiological Monitoring Handbook — checking pasture, water and livestock with a meter.

📟 Measuring radiation - A meter turns guessing into decisions — when to leave the shelter, which room is safest, whether the water is clear. - KFM (Kearny Fallout Meter): a homemade meter from a can, foil and paper. Build it before you need it. The patterns must print exactly to scale — check against a ruler; OISM warns online copies of the templates aren't fully reliable and recommends the printed book. Full patterns and tables: ORNL-5040 and Nuclear War Survival Skills Appendix C. See it first: 🖼️ photos of a finished KFM, 🖼️ full-scale cut-away drawing. It is a kind of electroscope. - Old civil-defense meters turn up at sales: the yellow CD V-715 reads high levels (fallout); the CD V-700 is a low-range Geiger counter for checking food, water and people (Geiger counter). Manuals and a home-study course are in Nuclear-Radiation\Measuring-Radiation. What a KFM is made of (ORNL-5040, pp. 33, 39): an 8-ounce can (or a cut-down soup can), 2 square feet of aluminum foil, clean thread, clear plastic, doorbell wire. A drying agent goes in the bottom — gypsum from heated drywall, or silica gel, not calcium chloride or salt. Charge it by rubbing a plastic ruler on dry paper (🖼️ the other way: charging with unrolled tape). Using it (ORNL-5040, pp. 69–73): 1. Charge it and read the gap between the two foil leaves on the

on dry paper (🖼️ the other way: charging with unrolled tape). Using it (ORNL-5040, pp. 69–73): 1. Charge it and read the gap between the two foil leaves on the paper scale. 2. Hold it on a stick about 3 feet above the ground for a set time — 1 minute if you have no idea of the level — then read again. The table on the meter turns the drop into a dose rate. 3. Dose = dose rate × time. At 1,200 R/hr, a 30-second dash outside is 10 R. 4. Keep a daily dose record for every person, and use the meter indoors to find the lowest-dose spot in your shelter, then add shielding there. 📍 Our area - The region's only operating nuclear power plant is the Columbia Generating Station at Hanford, Washington — roughly 350 miles from the Illinois Valley, far outside its planning zones. (Oregon ODOE, p. 1; Columbia Generating Station, Hanford Site) Its zones are a 10-mile plume zone (Oregon is not in it) and a 50-mile ingestion zone that reaches parts of northern Oregon (ODOE, p. 2). - The more realistic threats here are fallout drifting from detonations elsewhere and fallout carried across the Pacific on west winds. After Chernobyl (Chernobyl disaster), radioactive iodine showed up in milk in northwest Oregon. (Nuclear War Survival Skills, 1987) Even in the 1960s, Chinese test fallout put measurable radioactive iodine in American milk (NWSS 1979, pp. 117–118). Winds across the U.S. run mostly west to east, but change day to day (FEMA H-20, p. 7). - OISM, publisher of Nuclear War Survival Skills, is in Cave Junction — the printed edition (with accurate KFM patterns) may be easy to get locally (Nuclear War Survival Skills). - Stay tuned locally: NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts on seven frequencies, 162.400–162.550 MHz (FEMA Planning Guidance, p. 167; NOAA Weather Radio). ⚡ EMP, Solar Storms & Faraday Cages What a nuclear electromagnetic pulse (EMP) or a severe solar storm would really do, how to protect radios, solar gear and this library, how to build and test a Faraday container, what to do when a solar-storm warning comes, and how to check and repair equipment afterward. It's based on what government tests actually measured, not internet stories. The reports are in EMP-Solar-Storms\ (Effects-and-Threat, Protection-Shielding, Grounding-Surge, Recovery). ### The short version - The danger comes in through long wires — power lines, antennas, long cables. Small gear that isn't plugged into anything mostly survives. - Unplugged, switched-off cars and trucks were not affected in tests; a few running ones stalled and restarted. - A solar storm threatens the power grid, not your phone. You'd get 1–3 days' warning. - The real long-term problem is the grid going down for months. Plan for that (see the off-grid power section of the Illinois Valley guide). - Keep spares and a second copy of this library in a metal container, sealed at the seams.

⚡ Two different threats | | Nuclear EMP (a bomb exploded high above the U.S.) | Solar storm (geomagnetic storm, like 1859, 1921, 1989, May 2024) | | Warning | None | 18–72 hours after the Sun erupts; 20–45 min final warning (CISA, p. 21) | | Parts | E1: a pulse rising in billionths of a second — hits electronics through wires and antennas. E2: like lightning over a huge area. E3: slow, seconds to minutes — like a solar storm (EMP Commission 2004, p. 13; 🖼️ the three parts drawn) | Like a weak, hours-long E3 only — no fast pulse (Geomagnetically induced current) | | What it hits | Electronics connected to wires/antennas; computers and control systems; the power grid | Very long conductors: power lines, big transformers, pipelines, long phone cables. Also GPS and HF radio | | What it doesn't | People (a high-altitude burst puts no radiation on the ground) | Unplugged phones, laptops, radios, cars, solar panels | Why only long wires matter in a solar storm: the storm induces a few volts per kilometer — measured worst cases are about 7–20 V/km, and under 1.1 V/km in Colorado during the May 2024 storm (Meta-R-319; LANL 2024 storm study). A 6-ft cord sees hundredths of a volt; a 100-mile power line sees hundreds to thousands (rule of thumb arithmetic). In 1989 that was
