In 1989 that was enough to collapse Quebec's grid in 90 seconds and destroy a large transformer in New Jersey — and big transformers take about a year to replace (Meta-R-319, p. 149; 🖼️ photo of transformer damage from the 1989 storm; 🖼️ map of how far the 1989 storm reached; March 1989 geomagnetic storm, Transformer). E1 isn't the same strength everywhere: it's strongest south of the point under the burst, and averages only about a tenth of the peak over the affected area (Meta-R-320, p. 38; 🖼️ the "smile" map of E1 strength; 🖼️ how one high burst covers a continent). The 1962 test that showed it: 🖼️ Starfish photo, Starfish Prime. 📚 Go deeper: EMP Commission Executive Report — the plain overview; NOAA A Profile of Space Weather; Wikipedia: nuclear EMP · geomagnetic storm · Carrington Event.

🔬 What the tests actually found | Claim | What testing showed | | "Every car will die." | 37 cars and 18 trucks were tested up to about 50 kV/m. Vehicles that were off: no effects. Of running cars, 3 stalled (at 30 kV/m or more) and needed a restart; one had dashboard electronics damaged; most just had blinking lights. Of running trucks, 3 stalled — 2 restarted at once, 1 needed towing (EMP Commission 2008, p. 131). | | "All electronics fry." | Handheld and vehicle radios — stored, idle or operating — had no damage up to 50 kV/m; some locked up and worked after switching off and on (EMP Commission 2008, p. 169). Plugged-in household gear: at 6.7 kV/m 20% were upset (fixed by power-cycling); at 16.6 kV/m about 6% were damaged — mostly items on antenna cables (Harry Diamond Labs, p. 44). | | "Pocket radios are useless after." | Small battery radios weren't damaged unless near cables carrying huge currents (DCPA 1975). | | "Solar panels get destroyed." | Panels hit with up to 100 kV/m showed only very minor change (Sandia, p. 39; 🖼️ panels in the test chamber); rooftop microinverters survived 20–60 kV pulses (Sandia microinverter tests). The surge travels down the panel wires toward the charge controller/inverter — that's the part to keep a spare of. | | "A surge strip

The surge travels down the panel wires toward the charge controller/inverter — that's the part to keep a spare of. | | "A surge strip or the breaker protects me." | Lightning-rated surge suppressors don't stop E1 (Sandia TVSS tests; 🖼️ the suppressor tested); circuit breakers survive but give no real protection — some pulse passes even when they're off (Sandia, p. 6; 🖼️ the breakers tested). | | "Ham radios are toast." | 15 ham stations survived repeated simulated pulses when the power cord was unplugged and the coax disconnected; with protectors on both lines they were also fine (NCS TIB 85-10; 🖼️ the power and antenna protectors). | | "Networked computers will be fine." | They're the weak point — dispatch computers began failing at 3–6 kV/m, and every industrial control system tested failed (EMP Commission 2008). | How the tests were done: 🖼️ the outdoor pulse simulator used on household gear; 🖼️ an EMP simulator with test buildings. 📚 Go deeper: EMP Commission Critical Infrastructures Report — vehicles, p. 131; Consumer Electronics Testing.

🔌 Rule one: unplug and disconnect Wires are the antennas. Even a few feet of cable can pick up thousands of volts from E1; long power and antenna lines pick up far more (Low Cost EMP Protection (Navy 1982)). (CISA guidelines, p. 44; 🖼️ drawing: E1 reaches a radio the way a broadcast or lightning does) - Unplug at the device — power, data and antenna cables — not just at the wall. Coil any cable you can't remove. - Pull battery packs from small electronics in storage; turn phones and radios off and take them off chargers. - Disconnect outdoor antennas and coax (Coaxial cable) from radios when not in use. - Unplug everything or nothing: pulling only a TV's power cord while it stays on cable or phone lines removes its ground path (NIST Surges Happen, p. 11; 🖼️ NIST drawing of a surge crossing between two connections). - Backup generators: don't leave one connected to the grid through an automatic transfer switch without strong surge protection — the utility line can carry the pulse in (CISA, p. 45; Transfer switch). A generator stored disconnected is far better off. - Surge protectors still help with lightning and the surge when power comes back — just don't count on them for E1. Keep spare protectors and fuses (Surge protector). 📚 Go deeper: CISA EMP Protection and Resilience Guidelines —

surge when power comes back — just don't count on them for E1. Keep spare protectors and fuses (Surge protector). 📚 Go deeper: CISA EMP Protection and Resilience Guidelines — Level 1 steps, p. 44; NIST Surges Happen; MIL-HDBK-419A Vol 2 — grounding and surge arresters.

🗑️ Faraday containers: building one that works How it works: a closed metal shell keeps the pulse on the outside. It only works if the shell is continuous — the leaks are at seams, lid edges and holes, and a long narrow slot leaks far more than a round hole. Seams must be bare metal touching bare metal (no paint) (MIL-HDBK-419A Vol 1, p. 275; 🖼️ how fields leak through an opening; 🖼️ a badly joined seam, warped between rivets; Electromagnetic shielding). A plain metal box is not automatically a Faraday cage — ordinary cabinets gave little protection until their seams were taped and gasketed (Navy 1982). Options, best to simplest (CISA, pp. 45, 86): 1. Metal can with a tight metal lid (galvanized trash can, paint can, cookie tin, steel ammo can — Waste container, Ammunition box): - Wrap each item in a plastic or paper bag or cardboard so it doesn't touch the metal. - Seal the lid seam with conductive tape (aluminum or copper foil tape — the kind with conductive glue) all the way around. Trash cans leak at the lid, handles and base unless sealed. - Ammo cans: the rubber gasket breaks metal contact — scrape a strip of bare metal at the rim and add conductive tape over the closed lid seam (rule of thumb). - No wires passing through. Don't drill holes (🖼️

scrape a strip of bare metal at the rim and add conductive tape over the closed lid seam (rule of thumb). - No wires passing through. Don't drill holes (🖼️ right and wrong ways through a shield). 2. Foil wrap: item in a plastic bag, then 2 or more layers of heavy-duty foil, every seam folded and overlapped, any cables inside the wrap (Aluminium foil; folded-over joint: 🖼️ overlap seam). 3. Nesting adds protection: a foil-wrapped item inside a sealed metal can is better than either alone. 4. Microwave oven (unplugged, never switched on; Microwave oven): an expedient shield for small items — test it first. Weak or useless: Mylar food bags (little protection); refrigerators (plastic liner and rubber gasket); many cheap "Faraday bags" (the closure leaks). Does it need a ground wire? No — a closed storage container doesn't need to be grounded (rule of thumb). How good is good enough? For stored spare electronics, CISA considers 20 dB of shielding adequate (CISA appendix, p. 126); critical military gear uses 80 dB (DHS 2022). See the difference: 🖼️ modeled damage with 0, 10, 20 and 30 dB of protection; what "dB" means: Decibel. Testing yours (and what it doesn't prove): - Put a phone inside and call it, and a battery AM/FM radio tuned to a station. If the call won't ring and the radio goes silent, the shell

If the call won't ring and the radio goes silent, the shell has no big leaks at those frequencies. - This is a rough check, not a measurement — silence just means the signal dropped below what the radio can hear. The AM test matters most (low frequencies are hardest to block). Close the lid the same way every time (CISA, p. 45). 📚 Go deeper: CISA guidelines — foil and container methods, pp. 45 & 86; MIL-HDBK-419A Vol 1 — seams and slots, p. 275; Wikipedia: Faraday cage.

📦 What to keep in it From CISA's list plus practical extras (rule of thumb where not cited): - A second copy of this library on a USB drive or small SSD — and a cheap laptop or tablet with its charger to read it. - Battery AM/FM/NOAA weather radio, and a handheld ham or GMRS radio with a spare antenna (CISA, p. 44). - Spare solar charge controller and a small inverter — the parts of a solar system most at risk (Charge controller, Power inverter). - Multimeter (Multimeter), LED flashlights/headlamps, rechargeable batteries and a small USB solar charger. - Spare fuses (vehicle, equipment, solar), spare surge protectors and MOVs (Fuse), Varistor). - Small spare electronics you depend on (a phone, a radio's spare power supply). - For older vehicles, a spare ignition module or electronic part if you can get one. Handheld gear with no long wires attached is fairly tough anyway; the container is cheap insurance (CISA, p. 45). 📚 Go deeper: ORNL — radio communications and spare-equipment procedures; CISA — Level 1 steps for small equipment, p. 44; Radio guide.

☀️ When a solar-storm warning comes Pictures of where a storm starts: 🖼️ the May 2024 sunspot group; 🖼️ computer model of its eruptions heading for Earth; Coronal mass ejection, Sunspot. NOAA rates geomagnetic storms G1 to G5 (NOAA Space Weather Scales): | Level | How often (per 11-year cycle) | What happens | | G3 strong | ~200 | Grid voltage corrections; GPS and HF radio come and go; auroras as far south as Oregon (Aurora) | | G4 severe | ~100 | Widespread grid voltage problems; some protection systems trip; GPS degraded for hours | | G5 extreme | ~4 | Grid collapse and transformer damage possible; HF radio out 1–2 days; GPS degraded for days | For a G4–G5 warning (rule of thumb): 1. Charge batteries, power banks, radios and laptops; fill water containers; get fuel. 2. Unplug sensitive electronics from the wall — the risk is outages and surges when power returns. 3. Disconnect long outdoor antennas and feedlines. 4. Expect GPS and HF radio to be unreliable; have paper maps (Maps\) and use VHF/UHF locally. 5. Solar panels don't need protecting from a solar storm — their wiring is far too short. (S5 "solar panel damage" on NOAA's scale means satellites.) 6. Have the generator ready, connected only through a transfer switch or interlock — never backfeed. 📚 Go deeper: NOAA scales, p. 1; LANL

🔧 After an event: check and repair 1. Power-cycle anything that's locked up — in tests most "upsets" cleared this way (Harry Diamond Labs, p. 44). 2. Vehicles: restart. If one won't run, disconnect the battery for several minutes to reset the electronics, then check fuses (EMP Commission 2008, p. 131). 3. Fuses and breakers (Circuit breaker): a surge protector firing can blow the equipment's fuse — check and replace. Breakers are likely fine; reset them (ORNL radio study; Sandia breakers). 4. Surge protectors fail one of two ways: no power, or power with no protection left. Replace any that took a hit (NIST Surges Happen, p. 7). 5. Look and sniff: burnt smell, scorch marks, swollen or leaking capacitors. Discharge big capacitors before touching (inverters, microwaves, power supplies). What to look for: 🖼️ scorch marks where a capacitor blew off a board; 🖼️ a resistor exploding under a test pulse; swollen capacitors: Capacitor plague. 6. Radios: if dead, suspect the antenna input stage and power supply first — those took the damage in tests (ORNL radio study). 7. Solar: panels are probably fine; test the charge controller and inverter; swap in shielded spares. 8. Generators: check the output breaker, brushes and voltage regulator — see the Engines guide. 9. Expect the grid to stay down a long time — the EMP Commission expected months to years for recovery (Executive

Repair skills — finding and replacing burned parts, using a multimeter, soldering, salvaging parts — are in the electronics section of the Make-Do Household Guide and the Navy NEETS modules in Off-Grid-Power\Electrical-Basics. 📚 Go deeper: ORNL HEMP Emergency Planning for Electric Power Systems — why grid recovery is slow; EMP Commission 2008.

Mathematics Vol 1 - Arithmetic to Geometry and Trigonometry (US Navy NavPers 10069-C 1966). Navy self-study math course from the ground up: fractions, decimals, percent and measurement, square roots, ratio and proportion, formulas, plane figures (areas), geometric constructions with compass and straightedge, solids (volumes), right-triangle trigonometry. Tables of squares, roots, sines and tangents, weights and measures. In Southern-Oregon / Math-Measuring / Arithmetic-Geometry.

Mathematics Vol 2 - Trigonometry Vectors and Forces (US Navy NavPers 10071-B 1968). Second Navy math course: trigonometric measurement, solving any triangle (oblique triangles, law of sines and cosines) for land and distance problems, vectors and forces in balance (loads on ropes and frames), straight lines and slopes, then calculus and probability for those who want more. In Southern-Oregon / Math-Measuring / Arithmetic-Geometry.

Measuring and Marketing Farm Timber - Farmers Bulletin 1210 (USDA Forest Service 1955). Forest Service bulletin for woodlot owners: board feet and log rules, scaling logs, the cord and other stacked measures, measuring tree diameter and height with a cruiser stick or homemade calipers, estimating standing timber (old prices, but the measuring methods still apply). In Southern-Oregon / Math-Measuring / Measuring-Surveying.

NRCS Construction Surveying and Quantity Computations - NEH Part 645 Ch 5 (USDA NRCS 2012). Short USDA chapter on figuring quantities: lengths, areas of rectangles, circles, triangles and irregular plots, volumes of prisms, cylinders and cones, earth cut and fill by average end areas, and weights. In Southern-Oregon / Math-Measuring / Measuring-Surveying.

NRCS Engineering Field Handbook Ch 1 - Surveying (USDA NRCS 2022). USDA field surveying manual: pacing and taping distances, slope versus horizontal distance, hand level, Abney level and clinometer, leveling and rod reading, angles and bearings, right-triangle math, traverses, field notes, hand signals. In Southern-Oregon / Math-Measuring / Measuring-Surveying.

FM 5-34 Engineer Field Data (US Army 1987). Army engineers pocket data book: weights of materials, rope and wire rope strength and safety factors, concrete, timber and nail sizes, road slopes and drainage, trig tables, geometric figures and formulas, conversion factors and English-metric tables (combat chapters can be skipped). In Southern-Oregon / Math-Measuring / Units-Tables.

NIST Handbook 44 Appendix C - General Tables of Units of Measurement (NIST 2024). FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL CHAPTER 1 - INTRODUCTION This manual is based entirely on the keyword SURVIVAL. The letters in this word can help guide you in your actions in any survival situation. Whenever faced with a survival situation, remember the word SURVIVAL. SURVIVAL ACTIONS The following paragraphs expand on the meaning of each letter of the word survival. Study and remember what each letter signifies because you may some day have to make it work for you. S -Size Up the Situation If you are in a combat situation, find a place where you can conceal yourself from the enemy. Remember, security takes priority. Use your senses of hearing, smell, and sight to get a feel for the battlefield. What is the enemy doing? Advancing? Holding in place? Retreating? You will have to consider what is developing on the battlefield when you make your survival plan. Size Up Your Surroundings Determine the pattern of the area. Get a feel for what is going on around you. Every environment, whether forest, jungle, or desert, has a rhythm or pattern. This rhythm or pattern includes animal and bird noises and movements and insect sounds. It may also include enemy

a feel for what is going on around you. Every environment, whether forest, jungle, or desert, has a rhythm or pattern. This rhythm or pattern includes animal and bird noises and movements and insect sounds. It may also include enemy traffic and civilian movements. A cut artery issues bright red blood from the wound in distinct spurts or pulses that correspond to the rhythm of the heartbeat. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL CHAPTER 7 - FIRECRAFT In many survival situations, the ability to start a fire can make the difference between living and dying. Fire can fulfill many needs. It can provide warmth and comfort. It not only cooks and preserves food, it also provides warmth in the form of heated food that saves calories our body normally uses to produce body heat. You can use fire to purify water, sterilize bandages, signal for rescue, and provide protection from animals. It can be a psychological boost by providing peace of mind and companionship. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL CHAPTER 12 - FIELD-EXPEDIENT WEAPONS, TOOLS, AND EQUIPMENT As a soldier you know the importance of proper care and use of your weapons, tools, and equipment. This is especially true of your knife. You must always keep it sharp and ready to use. A knife is your most valuable tool in a survival situation. Imagine being in a survival situation without any weapons, tools, or equipment except your knife. It could happen! You might even be without a knife. You would probably feel helpless, but with the proper knowledge and skills, you can easily improvise needed items. In survival situations, you may have to fashion any number and type of fieldexpedient tools and equipment to survive. Examples of tools and equipment that could make your life much easier are ropes, rucksacks, clothes, nets, and so on. Weapons serve a dual purpose. You use them to obtain and prepare food and to provide self-defense. A weapon can also give you a feeling of security and provide you with the ability to hunt on the move. The weight may be a natural weight, such as a knot on the wood, or something added, such as a stone lashed to the club. Remember, cold weather is an adversary that can be as dangerous as an enemy soldier. Every time you venture into the cold, you are pitting yourself against the elements. With a little knowledge of the environment, proper plans, and appropriate equipment, you can overcome the elements. As you remove one or more of these factors, survival becomes increasingly difficult. Remember, winter weather is highly variable. Prepare yourself to adapt to blizzard conditions even during sunny and clear weather. Cold is a far greater threat to survival than it appears. It decreases your ability to think and weakens your will to do anything except to get warm. Cold is an insidious enemy; as it numbs the mind and body, it subdues the will to survive. Cold makes it very easy to forget your ultimate goal--to survive. COLD REGIONS AND LOCATIONS Cold regions include arctic and subarctic areas and areas immediately adjoining them. Most insect activity increases before a storm, but bee activity increases before fair weather. Low-Pressure Front Slow-moving or imperceptible winds and heavy, humid air often indicate a low-pressure front. Such a front promises bad weather that will probably linger for several days. You can "smell" and "hear" this front. The sluggish, humid air makes wilderness odors more pronounced than during high-pressure conditions. In addition, sounds are sharper and carry farther in low-pressure than high-pressure conditions. Page 192 of 277 Free Electricity and Water Solutions

FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL CHAPTER 16 - SEA SURVIVAL Perhaps the most difficult survival situation to be in is sea survival. Short-or long-term survival depends upon rations and equipment available and your ingenuity. You must be resourceful to survive. Water covers about 75 percent of the earth's surface, with about 70 percent being oceans and seas. You can assume that you will sometime cross vast expanses of water. There is always the chance that the plane or ship you are on will become crippled by such hazards as storms, collision, fire, or war. THE OPEN SEA As a survivor on the open sea, you will face waves and wind. You may also face extreme heat or cold. To keep these environmental hazards from becoming serious problems, take precautionary measures as soon as possible. Use the available resources to protect yourself from the elements and from heat or extreme cold and humidity. Protecting yourself from the elements meets only one of your basic needs. You must also be able to obtain water and food. Satisfying these three basic needs will help prevent serious physical and psychological problems. Precautionary Measures Your survival at sea depends upon-• Your knowledge of and ability to use the available survival equipment. • Your special skills and ability to apply them to cope with the hazards you face. • Your will to live. When you board a ship or aircraft, find out what survival equipment is on board, where it is stowed, and what it contains. For instance, how many life preservers and lifeboats or rafts are on board? Where are they located? What type of survival equipment do they have? How much food, water, and medicine do they contain? How many people are they designed to support? Down at Sea If you are in an aircraft that goes down at sea, take the following actions once you clear the aircraft. Whether you are in the water or in a raft -• Get clear and upwind of the aircraft as soon as possible, but stay in the vicinity until the aircraft sinks. • Get clear of fuel-covered water in case the fuel ignites. • Try to find other survivors. A search for survivors usually takes place around the entire area of and near the crash site. Missing personnel may be unconscious and floating low in the water. FM 21-76 US ARMY SURVIVAL MANUAL The best technique for rescuing personnel from the water is to throw them a life preserver attached to a line. Another is to send a swimmer (rescuer) from the raft with a line attached to a flotation device that will support the rescuer's weight. This device will help conserve a rescuer's energy while recovering the survivor. The least acceptable technique is to send an attached swimmer without flotation devices to retrieve a survivor. In all cases, the rescuer wears a life preserver. A rescuer should not underestimate the strength of a panic-stricken person in the water. A careful approach can prevent injury to the rescuer. When the rescuer approaches a survivor in trouble from behind, there is little danger the survivor will kick, scratch, or grab him. The rescuer swims to a point directly behind the survivor and grasps the life preserver's backstrap. The rescuer uses the sidestroke to drag the survivor to the raft.
